lens.name: silent-failures
lens.focus: Error handling and fallbacks. List every catch, .catch, default-on-error, optional chaining or ?? fallback, retry, timeout and early return that the change adds or touches. For each, ask: which unexpected errors could it hide; did the request or spec ask for this fallback; should the failure propagate or fail closed instead; is a retry limited to transient failures, bounded by one deadline, and does it keep the original failure and its classification; does every pending or in-flight state end on every path. A failed security, isolation or inspection check that ends in silent success or an unchecked path is a blocker.

lens.name: test-gaps
lens.focus: Tests. For each new or changed behaviour, find the test that would fail if that behaviour regressed, and say so when none exists. Flag tests that assert the defect they should catch, compare the code with itself, mock away the logic under test, pass for the wrong reason (invalid fixture, swallowed error, early return, wrong file), or were weakened, skipped or special-cased to pass. Name the missing or broken test case precisely. A test gap that hides a real defect in the change is at least major; report the underlying defect itself as its own finding.

lens.name: trust-boundaries
lens.focus: Secrets, untrusted input and isolation. Trace every credential, token, private value and untrusted input (issue or PR text, gate or test output, model output, configuration or scripts from the change) from its source to every sink: logs, events, errors, PR comments, commit metadata, branch names, model prompts, files and network. Check that redaction happens after decoding and before truncation, on error and retry paths as well as the normal one. Check sandbox profiles, deny lists and allowlists for path aliases, symlinks, files versus directories, environment variables and child processes. Anything that steers the factory must come from the base commit, never the change. When isolation or a check cannot be confirmed, the code must refuse with a clear reason, never fall back silently.

Verifier: 16 candidates, 16 checked, 2 refuted.

findings.title: A stale poller snapshot can permanently discard a land conflict
findings.detail: A land trigger is immediately evaluated against any saved poller snapshot, even if that snapshot predates the approved head. `startConflictTrigger` marks the trigger skipped when the saved head differs, and a later poll cannot reconsider it. The queue has already blocked the entry, so the requested conflict round never starts.
findings.suggestion: Refresh the PR observation before rejecting a land trigger for a stale head, or retain the trigger pending until a current observation can decide it.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller last observed head A; a review round pushes head B and B is approved before the next poll. Landing B conflicts with the base, but the saved snapshot still says A, so the B trigger is permanently skipped as `PR head moved`.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:16–21 reads the saved snapshot and calls `if (snapshot) store.startConflictTrigger(trigger.id, snapshot, now())`, bypassing a fresh lookup. src/db/store.ts:1126–1127 rejects `seen.headRefOid !== trigger.head` as `"PR head moved"`; lines 1137–1140 persist `state = 'skipped'`.
verification.trigger: Saved snapshot A plus a land trigger for approved head B permanently skips that land trigger. A later poller event may independently start a round.

findings.title: A conflict observed during another round is lost permanently
findings.detail: An active review or conflict round causes the trigger to be marked skipped. The poller emits `pr.conflicting` only on entry into the conflicting state, so if the active round fails or ends without changing the head, subsequent polls do not create another trigger. The unresolved conflict therefore never gets its own round.
findings.suggestion: Keep the trigger pending while another round is active and reconsider it when that round terminates, subject to a fresh PR observation and the daily cap.
findings.failure_scenario: A review round is in flight when the poller first observes the PR as CONFLICTING. The trigger is skipped; the review round later fails without pushing, and every subsequent poll still sees CONFLICTING, so no conflict round starts.

verification.evidence: src/db/store.ts:1130–1140 rejects any nonterminal round with `? "round in flight"` and permanently consumes the trigger via `UPDATE conflict_triggers SET state = 'skipped', reason = ? WHERE id = ?`. src/db/store.ts:1071 retries only `WHERE state = 'pending'`. src/integrations/github-poller.ts:206 emits another event only when `next.mergeable === "CONFLICTING" && prev?.mergeable !== "CONFLICTING"`; lines 367–374 save that observation before consuming its trigger.
verification.trigger: An open factory PR becomes CONFLICTING while a review round is active. Its conflict trigger becomes skipped. If the review round then fails without changing the head, continued CONFLICTING observations produce no new event, so no conflict round starts.

findings.title: A stale poller snapshot can permanently discard a land trigger
findings.detail: The land path uses any stored GitHub snapshot without refreshing it. `startConflictTrigger` marks the trigger skipped when that snapshot's head differs from the land entry's approved head, even if the snapshot is simply older than the approval. The trigger is then no longer pending, so this landing-queue trigger cannot recover on restart.
findings.suggestion: Refresh or otherwise establish the snapshot's freshness before permanently skipping a land trigger; retain it pending when the observation cannot establish the current head.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller saved head A, the PR advances to B and B is approved before the next poll, and the land queue detects a conflict at B. Processing compares B with the saved A and skips the trigger instead of starting a round.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:21 uses the saved snapshot whenever present. src/db/store.ts:1126–1127 compares its head with the trigger head; lines 1137–1140 execute `UPDATE conflict_triggers SET state = 'skipped', reason = ? WHERE id = ?`. Pending processing selects only `state = 'pending'` (lines 1068–1072).
verification.trigger: Landing B conflicts while the saved snapshot still records A; the B land trigger is permanently skipped instead of starting a round.

findings.title: Retrying comment creation can post duplicate resolution comments
findings.detail: The `gh` wrapper retries transient failures around the entire comment command. If GitHub creates the comment but its response is lost, the retry creates another comment without checking the marker again. The preflight marker lookup only protects a later delivery attempt, not retries within this call.
findings.suggestion: Recheck for the marker after an uncertain comment outcome before issuing another creation request.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub accepts `pr comment`, but the client receives a timeout or connection reset; the retry posts a second comment with the same conflict-round marker.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1894 checks for the marker once, then :1899 calls `await gh(["pr", "comment", prUrl, "--body-file", "-"], ctx.signal, text)`. At :1922, gh wraps each call in `withGitHubRetry(...)`. src/git/repos.ts:55 treats command timeouts as transient; :91–97 retries the same call without repeating the marker lookup.
verification.trigger: GitHub creates the comment but its acknowledgement times out while retry budget remains. Retrying comment creation posts another identical resolution comment, violating the one-comment requirement.

findings.title: Auto-merge is disabled before validating the PR delivery grant
findings.detail: The new auto-merge mutation occurs before `stored()` and `assertFactoryBranchPush` verify that the PR is still open, belongs to the expected branch and repository, and matches the round's current grant. A stale or invalid round can therefore modify the PR even though delivery is subsequently refused.
findings.suggestion: Validate the current grant and PR identity before disabling auto-merge, and revalidate after the mutation before pushing.
findings.failure_scenario: The PR head branch changes while a conflict round runs and auto-merge is enabled. Delivery disables auto-merge, then rejects the changed branch.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1865–1866 executes `if (review.kind === "conflict" && pr.autoMerge) await gh(["pr", "merge", prUrl, "--disable-auto"], ctx.signal)`. Only afterward, :1869–1870 calls `stored()` and `assertFactoryBranchPush(...)`. src/core/delivery.ts:88 rejects a changed branch: `if (pr.headBranch !== branch) return ...`.
verification.trigger: The PR head branch changes during the round and auto-merge is enabled. Delivery disables auto-merge on that PR before rejecting the changed branch.

findings.title: Restart tests do not cover a stale saved observation
findings.detail: The restart tests use either no saved observation or one matching the trigger. They therefore pass while a saved observation for an older head causes a durable land trigger to be skipped permanently, and while an outdated open, non-draft observation can start an ineligible round.
findings.suggestion: Add restart and land-trigger cases with an older saved head and with a PR that became draft or closed after the saved observation. Assert that a current observation governs whether the trigger starts.
findings.failure_scenario: A pending trigger for head B is recovered while the database still contains an open CONFLICTING snapshot for head A; the existing tests never exercise this state.

verification.evidence: test/conflict-rounds.test.ts:330–340 records a trigger and reopens the database without saving an observation. The other startup test uses the same head for both: :517 `recordConflictTrigger(url, await remoteHead(), ...)` and :525 `headRefOid: await remoteHead()`. Neither covers differing heads. src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:21 consumes any saved snapshot; src/db/store.ts:1126–1127 checks `seen.headRefOid !== trigger.head`, then :1139 permanently sets the trigger to `state = 'skipped'`.
verification.trigger: Recover a pending trigger for head B with a saved OPEN/CONFLICTING observation for head A. Recovery skips the trigger; both existing restart tests pass without exercising this state.

findings.title: The non-factory polling case bypasses the poller
findings.detail: The non-factory branch inserts a trigger and calls the store consumer directly, so it does not test whether polling a non-factory PR creates a round. A regression in tracking, event generation, or poller consumption for that case would still pass the test.
findings.suggestion: Exercise a tracked non-factory PR through the same fake GitHub poller path as the other eligibility cases and assert that no conflict round starts.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller erroneously starts a conflict round for a non-factory PR, but the test bypasses the poller and continues to pass.

verification.evidence: test/conflict-rounds.test.ts:365–371 handles `eligibility === "non-factory"` by directly calling `recordConflictTrigger(...)` and `startConflictTrigger(...)`. The `startGitHubPoller(...)` call at :373 is exclusively in the `else` branch. The zero-round assertion at :393 therefore verifies only the direct consumer for this case.
verification.trigger: A regression in polling behavior for non-factory PRs would not be exercised by the non-factory test case, which bypasses the poller and could continue passing.

findings.title: Persisted conflict filenames bypass credential redaction
findings.detail: Conflict paths come from the repository under review and are copied into run state without credential redaction. The state is subsequently persisted by updateRun, so a registered credential embedded in a filename reaches storage even though the later PR comment redacts it.
findings.suggestion: Redact credential-bearing paths before storing them or sending them to any external sink, while retaining whatever representation is needed for local conflict resolution.
findings.failure_scenario: A changed repository contains a conflicting filename that includes a registered token; the token is stored in conflictFiles in the run state.

verification.evidence: src/git/merge.ts:79–83 obtains conflict paths from git stdout and returns them. src/pipeline/engine.ts:2245 assigns `ctx.state.conflictFiles = conflicts`; :2252 persists that state through `ctx.store.updateRun(..., ctx.state)`. src/db/store.ts:1485–1486 stores `json(state)`, and :71–72 defines json using plain `JSON.stringify(v)` without redaction.
verification.trigger: A conflicting filename contains a registered credential of sufficient length for substring redaction. The raw filename is serialized into persisted conflictFiles without credential redaction.

findings.title: Disable auto-merge only after validating the delivery grant and PR head
findings.detail: The new GitHub mutation runs before stored() and assertFactoryBranchPush validate that the grant still holds and that the PR is still open on the expected branch and head. A stale conflict round can therefore change auto-merge settings even when its delivery is subsequently refused.
findings.suggestion: Validate the current grant and PR identity before disabling auto-merge, and recheck state after the mutation before pushing.
findings.failure_scenario: The PR head or round grant changes while a conflict round is running and auto-merge is enabled. Delivery disables auto-merge, then rejects the stale round.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1865–1866 disables auto-merge before :1869 invokes `stored()` and :1870 invokes `assertFactoryBranchPush(...)`. The stored-record change guard at :1851–1857 throws `the round's record changed during delivery`; src/core/delivery.ts:77–80 rejects mismatched remote or PR head SHAs.
verification.trigger: The PR head moves, or the stored round grant changes after initial validation, while auto-merge is enabled. Delivery disables auto-merge before rejecting the stale round.

findings.title: An untrusted PR comment can suppress the resolution comment
findings.detail: The idempotency check accepts the marker in any PR comment without verifying its author. A PR participant can post the predictable marker before delivery, causing the factory to treat the required resolution summary as already published.
findings.suggestion: Tie the checkpoint to a trusted factory-authored comment or another durable publication record rather than trusting arbitrary comment text.
findings.failure_scenario: A PR participant posts `<!-- limitless-conflict-round:<run-id> -->` before the round delivers; the merge is pushed but no factory resolution summary is posted.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1889 marks the round delivered before :1892 fetches PR comments. At :1894, `if (!comments?.some((comment) => comment.body?.includes(marker)))` controls whether the summary is posted. The inspected comment structure at :1893 contains only `body`; no author or factory ownership check is performed.
verification.trigger: A PR participant posts a comment containing the round's marker before delivery. After pushing the merge, the factory treats that comment as its own and skips the required resolution summary.

findings.title: A stale saved snapshot can start a round for a draft PR
findings.detail: When a saved poller snapshot exists, trigger processing uses it without refreshing the PR. A PR can become draft or close without changing its head, so the saved observation still passes the start checks. Delivery eventually checks draft status, but the forbidden round and its model work have already started.
findings.suggestion: Refresh the PR state before starting a pending conflict trigger, and leave the trigger pending if its current state cannot be verified.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller saves an open non-draft PR, the owner converts it to draft, and a land conflict trigger is processed before the next poll. A conflict round starts from the stale snapshot.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:21 starts from the saved snapshot without refreshing it. src/db/store.ts:1099 reads the saved data into `seen`; lines 1124–1125 check only `seen.isDraft`, then lines 1143–1144 create the round with `this.insertRun(...)`. src/pipeline/engine.ts:1864 checks the live draft state during delivery, after creation.
verification.trigger: A saved non-draft snapshot remains after the owner converts the PR to draft. A matching-head land trigger creates a conflict round despite the draft exclusion; the later delivery guard does not prevent that work from starting.

findings.title: A stale poller snapshot permanently discards a land conflict trigger
findings.detail: The request says a landing queue conflict must start a conflict round and that the trigger must survive restart. Whenever any saved PR snapshot exists, this path uses it without refreshing it. If its head predates the approved head, startConflictTrigger marks the trigger skipped as "PR head moved". The later poll updates the snapshot, but the skipped trigger is never reconsidered, so the blocked entry has no round.
findings.suggestion: Refresh the PR observation for a land trigger, or leave a trigger pending when its saved observation is older than the trigger head and retry after a fresh observation.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller last observed head A, the PR advances to B and B is approved before the next poll, then the land queue detects a conflict at B. The saved A snapshot causes the only land trigger to be skipped permanently.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:16–21 prefers saved PR data over `readPrHead`. src/db/store.ts:1126–1127 assigns `"PR head moved"` when the saved head differs from the trigger; lines 1137–1140 durably mark the trigger `skipped`.
verification.trigger: A land conflict at approved head B is processed using saved head A, permanently discarding that land trigger. Recovery depends on a separate future trigger.

findings.title: Auto-merge is disabled before verifying the PR and delivery grant
findings.detail: The new conflict delivery path changes GitHub state before assertFactoryBranchPush validates that the PR is open, still has the authorized head and branch, and still belongs to the expected repository. A stale or invalid round can therefore disable auto-merge on a PR even though its push is subsequently refused. This is an unrequested side effect of a failed delivery.
findings.suggestion: Validate the current grant and PR identity before disabling auto-merge, and revalidate after the asynchronous call before pushing.
findings.failure_scenario: A conflict round finishes after the PR head has moved and auto-merge is enabled. Delivery disables auto-merge, then refuses the push because the head no longer matches the reviewed SHA.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1865–1870 disables auto-merge with `await gh(["pr", "merge", prUrl, "--disable-auto"], ctx.signal)` before `stored()` and `assertFactoryBranchPush(...)`. src/core/delivery.ts:77–80 then throws `head moved` when the remote or PR head differs from the expected SHA.
verification.trigger: A conflict round reaches delivery after another push moved the PR head, with auto-merge enabled. Delivery disables auto-merge, then rejects its push because the head moved, leaving auto-merge disabled despite delivering no resolution.

findings.title: The PR comment does not summarize the resolution
findings.detail: The request requires "one comment summarizing the resolution." The comment reports the base SHA, conflicting file names and resulting SHA, but does not describe how the conflicting changes were reconciled. A reviewer cannot learn the resolution from the comment.
findings.suggestion: Include a concise, checked description of the actual resolution in the idempotent comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A conflict in a shared function is resolved and pushed; the PR comment names that file but gives no account of which behavior was retained or changed.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1895–1899 constructs and posts only `Merged base ${ctx.state.reviewBaseSha}. Conflicted files: ${JSON.stringify(ctx.state.conflictFiles ?? [])}.\nConflict resolved at ${head}; approve the new head to land.` No explanation of the resolution is included.
verification.trigger: A conflict resolution changes shared-function behavior and is delivered. The PR comment lists the base, files and resulting SHA but does not summarize how the conflict was resolved, leaving the explicitly requested resolution summary undelivered.

findings.title: A stale poller snapshot can permanently discard a land conflict
findings.detail: The land-trigger consumer treats any saved GitHub snapshot as current and immediately marks a rejected trigger as skipped. A snapshot can predate the land queue's observation. The poller emits pr.conflicting only on entry into the conflicting state, so a later refresh need not generate another trigger.
findings.suggestion: Verify the land trigger against a fresh PR observation, or retain it pending until a sufficiently recent observation can decide eligibility.
findings.failure_scenario: The saved snapshot says the PR is draft and CONFLICTING. The PR is made ready, then the land queue detects a conflict before the next poll. The trigger is skipped as draft; the next poll still sees CONFLICTING, emits no new conflict event, and no round starts.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:16–21 reads the saved snapshot and immediately calls `if (snapshot) store.startConflictTrigger(trigger.id, snapshot, now())`, without refreshing it. src/db/store.ts:1124–1125 rejects `seen.isDraft` as `"PR is draft"`; :1139 permanently sets `state = 'skipped'`. src/integrations/github-poller.ts:206 emits only when `next.mergeable === "CONFLICTING" && prev?.mergeable !== "CONFLICTING"`, so making the PR ready while it remains conflicting does not emit another trigger.
verification.trigger: The saved observation is draft and CONFLICTING; the PR becomes ready and landing detects a conflict before the next poll. The land trigger is permanently skipped using the stale draft flag, and the next unchanged CONFLICTING observation starts no round.

findings.title: A conflict observed while the owning run is finishing is lost
findings.detail: A poller trigger is permanently skipped unless the owning run has already reached succeeded or needs_human. A factory PR can be open and tracked while its owning run is still finishing delivery. Once skipped, the poller will not emit another pr.conflicting event while mergeability remains CONFLICTING.
findings.suggestion: Keep the trigger pending while the owning run is still delivering, and reconsider it when that run reaches a terminal state.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller observes a newly opened factory PR as CONFLICTING while its owner is still running. The trigger is marked skipped as not a factory PR; the owner subsequently succeeds, but subsequent polls see the same conflicting state and never start a round.

verification.evidence: src/db/store.ts:1111–1112 rejects `!["succeeded", "needs_human"].includes(owner.status)` as `"not a factory PR"`; lines 1137–1141 permanently consume it with `UPDATE conflict_triggers SET state = 'skipped', reason = ? Its trigger is permanently skipped. When the owner succeeds, unchanged CONFLICTING observations do not generate another trigger, leaving the conflict unresolved unless another independent trigger occurs.

findings.title: Failed trigger lookups are not retried during normal operation
findings.detail: A lookup error leaves the trigger pending, but this catch only logs the error. The queue processes pending triggers only at startup or after another land entry blocks. If polling is disabled or does not produce another observation for the PR, a transient `gh` failure leaves the conflict unresolved indefinitely until a restart or unrelated block.

findings.failure_scenario: A land conflict is recorded while `gh pr view` temporarily fails and there is no saved PR snapshot. The command later recovers, but no further land conflict or PR poll occurs, so the pending trigger never starts.

Startup processing is guarded by “if (!this.conflictStartup)” (src/land/queue.ts:128), whose value remains set until stop. findings.title: A stale saved PR observation can start or discard a land trigger
findings.detail: When any saved GitHub snapshot exists, the trigger consumer uses it without checking the current PR. A snapshot from before the land conflict can say the PR is draft or has a different head, causing the durable trigger to be permanently skipped; it can also say the PR is open and ready after it has become draft or closed, starting a round that should not start. findings.suggestion: Verify land and resumed triggers against a current PR observation before consuming them, and test stale snapshots against changed draft, state and head values.
findings.failure_scenario: The last poll recorded head A; the PR advances to head B and the landing queue detects a conflict at B before the next poll. Processing compares B to the saved A and marks the only land trigger skipped, so no conflict round starts from that trigger.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:641 calls `recordConflictTrigger(blocked.prUrl, blocked.approvedSha, "land", ...)`. src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:16–21 loads the saved observation and uses it without a fresh lookup. src/db/store.ts:1126–1127 classifies a snapshot/trigger SHA mismatch as `"PR head moved"`; :1139 updates the trigger to `state = 'skipped'`, excluding it from subsequent pending processing (:1071).

findings.failure_scenario: A PR lookup or stored snapshot omits `isDraft` for a draft PR. The conflict round is admitted and the delivery check sees `false`, allowing a push to the draft branch.

findings.title: Cargo home allowance exposes registry credentials to gate commands
findings.detail: The gate profile grants file reads throughout Cargo home, but neither the built-in deny list nor the later specific-deny rules exclude Cargo's credentials or credentials.toml files. findings.detail: The policy derives the home directory from os.homedir(), which uses HOME when set. The request specifically notes that ssh finds keys through the password database rather than HOME. If the daemon starts with HOME pointing elsewhere, the policy denies credential paths under that alternate directory but leaves the account's password-database home and its SSH keys readable to gates and editors.

An untrusted large patch with many occurrences of a registered multiline value can therefore block the daemon's event loop for a prolonged period, and each page request repeats the work. A targeted invocation of the extracted function took 893 ms for 50,000 lines and 3,514 ms for 100,000 lines, consistent with quadratic growth.
findings.suggestion: Map match offsets to affected ranges using an ordered cursor or binary search, so work grows with the patch size and number of matching lines.

findings.detail: The catch path recomputes preparationMs whenever roundsUsed is absent. findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the initial TLS connection
findings.detail: The initial connection accepts any certificate, and the displayed code is supplied by that connection. A man-in-the-middle can relay the pairing request to the real coordinator, return its code and secret to the worker, and present its own certificate. The owner sees the same code on both sides and approves it; the attacker then observes the claim and issued token. Pinning the attacker's certificate on subsequent requests does not prevent this. The submitted worker certificate fingerprint is never authenticated or used to bind the exchange.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to both endpoints' certificate fingerprints and the pairing exchange, so relaying through a different TLS certificate changes the code or causes verification to fail.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies the real coordinator's pairing response, and forwards the approved claim while terminating both TLS connections.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23-27 sends the initial pairing request with only `{ signal }`; :39 subsequently pins `first.fingerprint`. src/workers/tls.ts:103 uses `rejectUnauthorized: false`, and :114 checks the certificate only when `options.pin !== undefined`. src/db/workers.ts:85-89 claims an approved token using only the pairing secret.
verification.trigger: An active intermediary terminates the initial TLS connection and relays the coordinator's pairing response and code. Owner approval lets the intermediary claim the token; the worker persists the intermediary's certificate fingerprint. The matching code does not authenticate the TLS endpoint.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
findings.detail: Private read protection is an in-memory registry. Pairing releases the token and fingerprint registrations on return, and `runWorker` registers them only in the worker CLI process. A daemon running gates or agents in a separate process therefore does not include those files in its sandbox deny paths. The coordinator TLS key has the same lifetime problem when its listener is disabled after the key has been created. Mode 0600 does not protect files from another process running as the same user.
findings.suggestion: Register the configured worker credential and TLS key paths in every process that constructs agent or gate sandboxes, independent of whether a worker or listener is currently running.
findings.failure_scenario: Pair a worker, then run a factory daemon and a gate on the same machine; the daemon's sandbox is built without the worker token path registered, allowing a gate with access to that path to read the token.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate creation permanently blocks restart
findings.detail: Certificate generation creates the final key path before invoking OpenSSL. If generation fails, times out, or the process stops before both files are complete, the next start either rejects the incomplete pair or tries to parse invalid material. No cleanup or recovery occurs, so the worker listener or pairing command continues to fail on every subsequent start.
findings.suggestion: Generate both files under temporary names, validate them, and publish them only after successful generation; clean up incomplete temporary material on failure.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is stopped after creating the empty key file but before OpenSSL creates the certificate; every later listener start throws `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:18 creates `writeFileSync(keyPath, "", { flag: "wx", mode: 0o600 })` before awaiting OpenSSL. On restart, src/workers/tls.ts:16-17 checks for either missing file and throws `new Error("Incomplete worker TLS material")` if either exists. The catch at :45-47 only calls `release()` and rethrows; it does not remove partial files.
verification.trigger: With workers.listen enabled, interrupt first-time certificate generation after key.pem is created but before cert.pem exists. Every subsequent startup fails until the partial material is repaired manually. The interruption window is unusual and limited to initial generation.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
findings.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker pins the certificate observed on that connection. The displayed code comes from the coordinator but is not bound to that certificate or to an authenticated exchange. An intermediary can relay the pairing request and code unchanged, obtain the pairing secret and issued token, and leave the worker pinned to the intermediary's certificate even though the owner compared matching codes.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate and pairing exchange so a relaying intermediary cannot obtain a usable token or substitute its certificate.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, forwards the request to the real coordinator, and relays its code. The owner approves the matching code; the attacker claims the token and the worker pins the attacker's certificate.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23-27 makes the first request without a pin, :33 prints the returned code, :39 pins the observed first certificate, and :47 persists that fingerprint. src/workers/tls.ts:103 disables certificate authority validation. src/db/workers.ts:85-89 returns the approved token based solely on the secret hash.
verification.trigger: An active intermediary forwards the pairing request to the real coordinator and relays its code. The owner approves the matching code, while the intermediary learns the claim secret, obtains the token, and causes the worker to pin the intermediary's certificate.

findings.title: Permanent TLS and configuration errors are retried silently forever
findings.detail: The heartbeat loop catches every request exception and retries without a deadline or diagnostic. This includes a changed coordinator fingerprint and malformed coordinator URL, neither of which can be repaired by retrying. The worker remains running but never sends another heartbeat, and the owner receives no explanation.
findings.suggestion: Retry only transient transport failures with a bounded policy; propagate permanent validation and certificate-pin failures with their original reason.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing. Every heartbeat fails fingerprint validation, but the worker silently retries indefinitely instead of reporting that it must be paired again.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:114-115 rejects a changed certificate with `new Error("Coordinator certificate fingerprint changed")`. src/workers/client.ts:99-102 catches every request exception and returns `undefined`; :93 loops indefinitely and :106-107 sleeps with a delay capped at 10 seconds. Only HTTP responses below 500 terminate the loop (:104-105).
verification.trigger: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing, or the configured origin is invalid. Each heartbeat throws a permanent error that is discarded, leaving the worker silently retrying forever instead of reporting the necessary repair.

findings.title: Existing TLS key loses sandbox protection when the listener is disabled
findings.detail: The TLS key is registered with the sandbox deny list only when the listener starts. After a listener has created the key, restarting the daemon with workers.listen unset skips registration even though the key remains on disk. Agent sandboxes that can read that data directory can then read the coordinator's private key, contrary to the requirement that it be denied in every agent sandbox.
findings.suggestion: Register protection for existing worker TLS material independently of whether the listener is enabled, and retain it for the daemon lifetime.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the listener once, then disable it and restart the daemon with the data directory outside the default home deny paths. A subsequent agent can read worker-tls/key.pem.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:15–16: `if (!listen) return undefined;` precedes `certificate(join(paths.home, "worker-tls"))`. The key deny is registered only inside that function: src/workers/tls.ts:14: `const release = protectPrivateFile(keyPath);`. Editor denies incorporate that process-local registry at src/harness/read-policy.ts:190: `const denyRead = policySpellings([...credentials, ...privateReadPaths()], true, fs);`.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation prevents future startup
findings.detail: Certificate generation creates the final key path before running openssl, but its error path leaves partial files behind. A timeout, failed openssl invocation, or interruption can therefore leave only the empty key or other incomplete material. Every later start rejects the incomplete material, requiring manual cleanup.
findings.suggestion: Generate both files in temporary paths and publish them only after successful generation, cleaning up partial temporary files on failure.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is interrupted after creating key.pem but before openssl writes cert.pem. Subsequent starts fail with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:18 writes an empty key.pem before `await sh(...)` at :19. src/workers/tls.ts:17 throws `Incomplete worker TLS material` whenever only one TLS file exists. Error handling at :45-47 performs no filesystem cleanup. src/server/workers.ts:16 awaits `certificate(...)`, propagating this failure.
verification.trigger: Interrupt initial certificate generation between creating key.pem and writing cert.pem. Later listener starts repeatedly fail rather than completing generation; manual repair is required. This is a narrow first-start timing window.

findings.title: Credential read protection ends with the pairing process
findings.detail: The worker token and coordinator fingerprint are registered in an in-memory deny list only while `pairWorker` or `runWorker` holds them. Pairing releases both registrations before exiting, and a separately running daemon has its own deny list. Likewise, an existing coordinator TLS key is not registered when the listener is disabled. An agent sandbox created by that daemon therefore does not receive these paths as private-file denies.
findings.suggestion: Register persisted worker credential and TLS-key paths in every process that constructs agent sandbox policies, independently of whether pairing, the worker loop or the listener is currently running.
findings.failure_scenario: Pair a worker, exit the pairing command, and run an agent through a separate daemon using the same data directory: that daemon's private-file deny list does not contain the stored worker token or coordinator fingerprint.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:47-48 registers the persisted fingerprint and token, then :55-57 releases both registrations before pairing returns. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 uses a process-local map. src/harness/read-policy.ts:217 applies the home-wide deny only when `gate` is true; editor credential denies at :150-190 do not include worker files unless dynamically registered.
verification.trigger: After pairing exits, a separate daemon runs an editor agent using the same data directory. The worker token and coordinator fingerprint are absent from its private-file registrations and built-in credential denies, so the editor can read them under the normal editor read policy.

findings.title: Privacy probe masks the cross-process credential protection gap
findings.detail: The real-Seatbelt test creates the TLS material and registers both worker files in the same process that starts the gate, retaining all registrations throughout the probe. It consequently passes even if a daemon started separately after pairing has no credential paths in its in-memory deny list.
findings.suggestion: Add a real-Seatbelt probe that persists credentials, releases the pairing registrations, and launches the gate from an independently initialized daemon or process; cover an existing TLS key with the listener disabled as well.
findings.failure_scenario: The current implementation releases the registrations after pairing, yet this test retains them and reports all three files denied.

verification.evidence: test/workers.test.ts:266 retains registrations with `const protectedFiles = files.slice(1).map((p) => privateFile(p, "synthetic-private-file"));` until releases at lines 295–296, after running gates. Production src/workers/client.ts:55–57 instead executes `cert.release(); for (const release of held) release();` when pairing returns. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 uses a process-local `Map`, and lines 19–21 delete registrations on release. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 derives protection from `privateReadPaths()`; its static credential list does not include worker files.
verification.trigger: The privacy probe runs gates in the same process while explicitly retaining all registrations, so it passes without testing protection after pairing exits or from another factory process. It therefore masks the cross-process registration gap.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
findings.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the displayed code is supplied by that untrusted connection. An active intermediary can forward the request to the real coordinator, relay its code to the worker, and retain the returned pairing secret. The owner and worker see matching codes, but the intermediary can claim the approved token and the worker pins the intermediary's certificate.
findings.suggestion: Bind the human-compared code to both the coordinator certificate fingerprint and the pairing exchange, so relaying a coordinator response through a different TLS certificate changes the code.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies `/worker/pair` to the coordinator, and relays the real code. After the owner approves it, the attacker claims the worker token.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23-28 sends the initial pairing request with only `{ signal }`; lines 35-39 subsequently pin `first.fingerprint`. src/workers/tls.ts:103 sets `rejectUnauthorized: false`, and lines 114-115 verify the certificate only when `options.pin !== undefined`. src/db/workers.ts:83-89 looks up `tokenHash(secret)` and returns the approved token without authenticating the worker certificate.
verification.trigger: An attacker intercepts initial pairing, forwards the request, and relays the coordinator's code and secret. Owner approval succeeds with matching codes; the attacker uses the observed secret to claim the worker token.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
findings.detail: `protectPrivateFile` maintains an in-memory registry. Pairing releases its registrations before exiting, and `runWorker` registers the files only in the worker process. A separately running daemon on the same machine does not receive those registrations when it constructs Claude or Codex sandbox policies, so its agents can read the persistent worker token and coordinator fingerprint. Mode 0600 does not protect them from agents running as the same user.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every daemon process that launches agents, including when the worker is stopped, and cover separate-process sandbox behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine runs both a worker and a factory daemon under the same user. An agent launched by the daemon reads `<data>/worker/token` and impersonates that worker.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:87-88 protects credentials through `privateFile(...)`. src/workers/tls.ts:52 implements this with `protectPrivateFile(path)`. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 stores registrations in a process-local `const privatePaths = new Map<string, number>()`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 builds denials from `credentials` and `privateReadPaths()`; its built-in credential list at lines 150-161 excludes `<data>/worker/`. Lines 217-218 apply the home-wide read restriction only to gates.
verification.trigger: A worker and daemon run as separate processes under the same user. The daemon never registers the worker's token path, so an editor agent can read the mode-0600 token using that user's permissions and impersonate the worker.

findings.title: Disabling the listener leaves its existing TLS key unprotected from agents
findings.detail: The TLS key is added to the process-local private-read registry only when the listener is enabled. After an owner removes `workers.listen` and restarts the daemon, the existing key remains on disk but is no longer included in agent sandbox deny paths. An agent running as the same user can read it, compromising the certificate trusted by already paired workers if the listener is later re-enabled.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent TLS key path independently of whether the listener is currently enabled, or securely remove and rotate the material when disabling it.
findings.failure_scenario: A coordinator previously enabled workers, then starts with the listener disabled. A tool-enabled agent reads `<data>/worker-tls/key.pem` before the listener is enabled again.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:15–16: `if (!listen) return undefined;` skips `certificate(join(paths.home, "worker-tls"))`, whose src/workers/tls.ts:14 calls `protectPrivateFile(keyPath)`. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 initializes protection as an in-memory `const privatePaths = new Map<string, number>();`; it does not survive daemon restarts.
verification.trigger: Restart with workers disabled after TLS material has been created. Unless another configured deny covers the data directory, a tool-enabled editor can read the retained private key before the listener is enabled again.

findings.title: Store untrusted heartbeat fields only after redaction
findings.detail: Heartbeat capabilities are serialized directly into SQLite. Several worker-controlled strings can contain coordinator credentials or private strings, but sanitization occurs only when listing workers. This leaves the unredacted values in persistent storage even though the trust-boundary rules require redaction before storage.
findings.suggestion: Redact and apply private-string policy to worker-supplied capability fields before persisting them, while preserving the fields needed for version matching.
findings.failure_scenario: A paired worker sends a coordinator credential or private string in `osVersion`; the value is written verbatim to the workers table.

verification.evidence: src/workers/protocol.ts:8 accepts `osVersion: z.string().max(128)`. src/server/workers.ts:43–46 parses the heartbeat then calls `workers.heartbeat(current, capabilities)`. src/db/workers.ts:143–144 persists it with `UPDATE workers SET last_heartbeat_at=?,capabilities=? WHERE name=? AND state='approved'` and `.run(this.now(), JSON.stringify(c), w.name)`, without redaction. `this.sanitize(...)` is applied later when listing workers (src/db/workers.ts:124), after persistence.
verification.trigger: An approved worker submits an otherwise valid heartbeat containing a credential or private string of at most 128 characters in osVersion; the coordinator stores that value verbatim in workers.capabilities.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied in the daemon's agent sandboxes
findings.detail: The request requires the worker token and coordinator fingerprint to be read-denied to gates. The deny registry is process-local, but pairing and the worker loop run as separate CLI processes from the daemon. Their registrations are also released when those commands exit. A daemon on the same machine therefore does not add these files to its agent sandbox deny lists; mode 0600 does not protect them from agents running as the same user.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every daemon process that can launch agents and gates, including when the worker command is not running.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine is both a paired worker and a coordinator. An agent launched by its daemon reads the token under the worker data directory and uses it to impersonate the worker.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:55-57 releases pairing-time protections: `cert.release(); for (const release of held) release();`. src/util/private-reads.ts:4,13 maintains only a process-local registration map. src/harness/claude.ts:203-211 derives editor read denials from `writeRoots(...)`; src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 includes only built-in credentials and that process's `privateReadPaths()`, with no built-in worker credential paths.
verification.trigger: A paired machine also runs its coordinator daemon. Pairing registrations are released, and a separately running worker cannot register paths in the daemon. An editor agent launched by the daemon can read the persisted worker token and impersonate it.

findings.title: Disabling the listener removes protection for an existing TLS key
findings.detail: The request says the TLS key is read-denied in every agent sandbox. When the listener is disabled, startup returns before registering the previously generated key with the process-local deny registry. The key remains on disk, and editor sandboxes do not otherwise deny the worker TLS directory.
findings.suggestion: Register the existing key path for the daemon lifetime independently of whether the listener is enabled.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner disables workers after having enabled them, then starts a run. An editor agent can read the retained coordinator TLS private key.

verification.evidence: src/cli/daemon.ts:30 calls `startWorkerListener(factory.workers, factory.cfg.paths, factory.cfg.workers.listen)` before starting integrations. However, src/server/workers.ts:15 returns immediately when disabled, bypassing the key protection at src/workers/tls.ts:14: `const release = protectPrivateFile(keyPath);`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 derives editor denies from `credentials` and `privateReadPaths()`.
verification.trigger: Disable workers after an enabled deployment, restart, then start a run. An editor can read the retained coordinator TLS key when no independent deny covers its location; the default credential list does not include ~/.limitless/worker-tls.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation permanently blocks listener startup
findings.detail: The key file is created before openssl runs, but a failed or interrupted generation leaves it behind. The next start sees incomplete TLS material and throws instead of generating a certificate, so a transient failure prevents the daemon from starting whenever the worker listener is configured.
findings.suggestion: Generate the certificate and key in temporary files and publish them together, cleaning up incomplete generation safely.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is stopped or openssl fails after the empty key file is created but before the certificate is written; every subsequent daemon start fails with "Incomplete worker TLS material".

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:18 creates key.pem before invoking OpenSSL at :19-38; :16-17 rejects a key-only state with `Incomplete worker TLS material`. The catch at :45-47 only releases protection and rethrows. src/cli/daemon.ts:30 awaits listener startup before mounting integrations, and :44-46 propagates startup errors.

findings.title: A changed pinned certificate is retried indefinitely without an explanation
findings.detail: The request requires the coordinator fingerprint to be pinned. Although the transport detects a mismatch, the heartbeat loop catches that error along with transient connection failures and retries forever. The operator receives no indication that the certificate changed and that intervention is required.
findings.suggestion: Surface fingerprint mismatch as a terminal error while retaining retries for transient transport failures.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing. The worker remains running but never sends another heartbeat and never reports the pin mismatch.

findings.title: Initial pairing permits a relay to steal the worker token
findings.detail: The first connection accepts any TLS certificate and receives both the comparison code and the claim secret. An attacker between the worker and coordinator can relay the initial request and response, so the owner and worker see matching codes, while the attacker learns the secret and can claim the approved token. Pinning the attacker's certificate for subsequent requests does not prevent this.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate and the claim secret, or use an authenticated pairing exchange that does not expose the claim credential to an unverified intermediary.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
findings.detail: The token and fingerprint are registered in an in-memory private-path map only in the pairing or worker CLI process, and pairing releases those registrations before exiting. A daemon running on the same machine has a separate map and does not register these persisted files when constructing its agent sandboxes. Thus an agent reader in that daemon can read the worker token and fingerprint; file mode 0600 does not protect against another process running as the same user.
findings.suggestion: Register the persisted worker credential paths in every process that creates agent sandboxes, including when the worker command is not running.

Re-enabling the listener later reuses that key.
findings.suggestion: Register the existing coordinator key path for sandbox denial independently of whether the listener is enabled.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner disables the listener after pairing workers, then runs an agent with read access to the data directory; the agent reads the persisted key and can impersonate the coordinator when the listener is re-enabled.

findings.title: An approved pairing that fails before token storage cannot be retried
findings.detail: An approved name is always rejected by `pair`, even if the worker never received or saved its token. A transient failure after approval therefore leaves the worker unable to pair again until the owner explicitly revokes it.
findings.suggestion: Provide a safe recovery path for an approved but unclaimed pairing, or report the required revoke-and-repair action clearly.
findings.failure_scenario: The owner approves a request, but the worker process exits before its next claim; restarting `limitless worker pair` with the same name receives a refusal.

Restarting begins a new `/worker/pair` request (lines 23-29), which src/db/workers.ts:43-46 rejects for an approved name regardless of expiry.

candidates.title: Initial pairing permits a relay to steal the worker token
candidates.detail: The first connection accepts any TLS certificate and receives both the comparison code and the claim secret. An attacker between the worker and coordinator can relay the initial request and response, so the owner and worker see matching codes, while the attacker learns the secret and can claim the approved token. Pinning the attacker's certificate for subsequent requests does not prevent this.
candidates.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate and the claim secret, or use an authenticated pairing exchange that does not expose the claim credential to an unverified intermediary.
candidates.failure_scenario: A network attacker proxies the initial pairing exchange, forwards the genuine code to the worker, and claims the token after the owner approves that code.

candidates.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
candidates.detail: The token and fingerprint are registered in an in-memory private-path map only in the pairing or worker CLI process, and pairing releases those registrations before exiting. A daemon running on the same machine has a separate map and does not register these persisted files when constructing its agent sandboxes. Thus an agent reader in that daemon can read the worker token and fingerprint; file mode 0600 does not protect against another process running as the same user.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persisted worker credential paths in every process that creates agent sandboxes, including when the worker command is not running.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine runs both a paired worker and a Limitless daemon; an agent launched by the daemon reads the worker token from the data directory and impersonates the worker.

candidates.title: Interrupted certificate generation permanently blocks listener startup
candidates.detail: The key file is created before the asynchronous OpenSSL command completes. If generation fails or the process stops before the certificate is written, the next startup encounters the incomplete pair and always throws. Normal restarts cannot recover without manually deleting the leftover material.
candidates.suggestion: Generate both files under temporary names and publish them only after successful generation, or safely clean up an incomplete first-generation attempt.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon is interrupted after creating key.pem but before OpenSSL writes cert.pem; every subsequent worker-listener startup fails with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

candidates.title: Certificate replacement prevents the documented re-pairing flow
candidates.detail: The guide says a worker must pair again after the coordinator certificate changes, but an approved worker's existing name is always rejected by the pairing route. Re-running the documented pairing command with the default name therefore cannot recover unless the owner first revokes the existing record or chooses another name.
candidates.suggestion: Support an explicit secure re-pairing flow for an existing worker, or document the required revocation before re-pairing.
candidates.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes and an existing worker runs `limitless worker pair` with its original name; the coordinator rejects the request as already paired.

candidates.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
candidates.detail: The first request accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker pins the certificate observed on that connection. An active intermediary can forward the pairing request to the real coordinator, relay the same code to the worker, and use the observed pairing secret to claim the approved token. Comparing the displayed codes does not detect the intermediary because the code is not bound to the TLS connection.
candidates.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate or otherwise authenticate the coordinator before sending the pairing secret.
candidates.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the initial pairing connection, relays the request and code to the real coordinator, and claims the worker token after the owner approves the matching code.

candidates.title: Credential read protection ends when pairing exits
candidates.detail: The private-file deny registry is process-local, and pairing releases both credential paths before exiting. A separate daemon on the worker machine therefore does not register those files in its agent sandbox deny rules; running the worker in another process does not share its registrations either. The same lifecycle problem affects an existing coordinator TLS key when its listener is disabled.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential and TLS key paths in every process that launches agent sandboxes, independently of whether the worker listener or client is running.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine is paired, the pairing command exits, and an agent launched by a separate local daemon reads the worker token from the data directory.

candidates.title: Permanent TLS and configuration failures retry forever
candidates.detail: The catch treats every request error as transient and retries indefinitely without logging the original error. A changed certificate fingerprint, malformed coordinator URL, or invalid stored pin therefore leaves the worker silently looping instead of reporting the failure and requiring corrective action.
candidates.suggestion: Retry only transient transport errors with an appropriate bound, and propagate certificate, pin and configuration errors with their original cause.
candidates.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing; every heartbeat fails fingerprint verification, but the worker remains running indefinitely with no diagnostic.

candidates.title: Interrupted certificate generation prevents future startup
candidates.detail: Certificate generation creates the key path before invoking OpenSSL, but failures leave generated or partial files in place. The next start either rejects the incomplete pair or reads invalid material, so a transient interruption permanently blocks the worker listener until the files are manually removed.
candidates.suggestion: Generate both files in temporary paths, clean them up on failure, and publish the completed pair only after validation.
candidates.failure_scenario: OpenSSL times out or the process stops after creating key.pem but before writing cert.pem; subsequent daemon starts fail with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

candidates.title: Worker credentials lose sandbox protection when pairing exits
candidates.detail: Protection is held in a process-local registry and released when pairing finishes. A separate daemon or agent process does not inherit that registration, even though the token and coordinator fingerprint remain on disk. The real-Seatbelt test explicitly registers synthetic files in the same process that launches the gates, so it does not exercise this lifecycle or cross-process case.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every process that constructs an agent sandbox, and test access from a separately started process after pairing has finished.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine pairs a worker, the pairing command exits, and a separate local factory process launches an agent sandbox that can otherwise reach the worker data directory; the persisted token and fingerprint are absent from that process's private-read registry.

candidates.title: No test covers claiming an approved pairing after coordinator restart
candidates.detail: The implementation reconstructs an issued token from the persistent TLS key so that a worker can claim it after a restart, but the pairing tests approve and claim within one listener lifetime. A regression in key reuse or token reconstruction would leave an approved worker unable to pair without being caught.
candidates.suggestion: Approve a pending request, restart the listener and store, then claim with the original secret and verify that the returned token authenticates a heartbeat.
candidates.failure_scenario: The coordinator restarts after the owner approves a pending request but before the worker claims its token.

candidates.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator certificate
candidates.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the coordinator generates a random code that is unrelated to either endpoint's certificate. A man-in-the-middle can relay the pairing request and response unchanged, present its own certificate to the worker, and relay the subsequent claim. The owner and worker see the same code, but the worker pins the attacker's certificate and sends it the issued token.
candidates.suggestion: Bind the displayed pairing code to the coordinator certificate and pairing exchange, and verify that binding on both sides before issuing or accepting credentials.
candidates.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies requests to the real coordinator, and forwards the unchanged pairing code. After approval, the attacker receives the worker token while the worker pins the attacker's certificate.

candidates.title: Worker credential deny registrations do not protect other processes
candidates.detail: The token and fingerprint are registered in an in-memory, process-local deny list, and pairing releases those registrations before exiting. A separately running daemon or agent process therefore never registers the worker credential paths. Its agent sandbox can consequently lack the explicit denies required for these files, even while the worker is running in another process.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every process that launches agent sandboxes, independently of the worker process and pairing command.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine is both a paired worker and a coordinator with a tool-enabled agent. The worker runs as a separate process, so the coordinator's agent sandbox does not receive the worker token and fingerprint deny entries.

candidates.title: Pairing can be relayed through an attacker-controlled coordinator
candidates.detail: The first connection accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker pins that certificate after receiving the pairing response. An attacker between the worker and coordinator can relay the pair request and the unchanged code to the real coordinator, then relay the claim request after owner approval. The codes match, but the attacker obtains the issued token and the worker pins the attacker's certificate. The submitted worker certificate fingerprint is stored but is never authenticated or used to bind the claim.
candidates.suggestion: Bind approval and token delivery to authenticated coordinator and worker identities so that relaying a matching code cannot disclose the worker token or substitute the pinned coordinator.
candidates.failure_scenario: A worker pairs over a network controlled by an attacker who proxies both pairing endpoints to the real coordinator; the owner sees the same code and approves, after which the proxy receives the worker token.

candidates.title: Worker credentials are not registered for denial in the daemon's sandboxes
candidates.detail: The request requires the worker token and coordinator fingerprint to be read-denied to gates. Their protection is held only in the pairing or worker CLI process's in-memory private-path registry and is released when that process exits. A separate daemon on the same machine does not register these paths when it starts, so its sandbox policy can permit access to them. The real-Seatbelt test creates and protects all files in the same process as the gate, so it does not cover this deployment.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persisted worker credential paths in every process that launches agent or gate sandboxes, independently of whether the worker CLI is running, and test across the actual process boundary.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine is both a worker and a coordinator, with its data directory in a location readable by an agent sandbox; after pairing, a gate launched by the separate daemon reads the worker token and fingerprint.

candidates.title: The coordinator TLS key is unprotected when the listener is disabled
candidates.detail: The request says the TLS key must be read-denied in every agent sandbox. The key path is registered only when the worker listener starts. After a listener has generated the key, disabling `[workers] listen` and restarting leaves the private key on disk without registering it in the daemon's sandbox deny policy. Re-enabling the listener later reuses that key.
candidates.suggestion: Register the existing coordinator key path for sandbox denial independently of whether the listener is enabled.
candidates.failure_scenario: An owner disables the listener after pairing workers, then runs an agent with read access to the data directory; the agent reads the persisted key and can impersonate the coordinator when the listener is re-enabled.

candidates.failure_scenario: The owner approves a request, but the worker process exits before its next claim; restarting `limitless worker pair` with the same name receives a refusal.

findings.title: Treat a worker confinement failure as a terminal failure
findings.detail: A check reporting a confinement failure is rejected as an invalid result, which calls workers.fail. After the retry is exhausted, the LAN executor runs the gates locally and can return a pass. This converts a failed security check into a successful gate result.
findings.suggestion: Preserve confinement failures as a distinct terminal failure and propagate them through the gate result without retrying them into a pass.
findings.failure_scenario: Both worker attempts report a Seatbelt launch failure, but the local fallback executes successfully; the overall gate is reported as passing.

verification.evidence: src/workers/protocol.ts:65 rejects confinement reports: `.refine((r) => !r.confinementError && !launchFailure(r.output), "Worker confinement failed")`. src/server/workers.ts:131-133 routes rejection through `workers.fail(id, ...)`. src/db/workers.ts:260 retries or marks failed with `j.attempt < 2 ? "queued" : "failed"`. src/gates/lan.ts:73-89 handles that failure by executing locally, then `workers.complete(handle.id, run, true); return workers.sanitize(run);`, without preserving the confinement failure in the result.
verification.trigger: Both worker attempts report a Seatbelt launch failure; local execution passes. The returned GateRun passes, erasing the blocking confinement outcome.

findings.title: Do not discard failed checks received before an infrastructure failure
findings.detail: Check events from a worker are persisted and forwarded, but the final result is replaced by the next attempt or local fallback if that worker disconnects before posting its GateRun. A later pass therefore erases an already observed failing check, contrary to the requirement that infrastructure retries never turn a failing check into a pass.
findings.suggestion: Preserve and account for validated failing check results across attempts when producing the final gate outcome.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker posts a failing test check and loses its connection before posting the final result; the retry or local fallback passes, so the run receives a passing GateRun.

verification.evidence: src/gates/lan.ts:68–72 copies stored events into the event stream, then returns only the final result: `events.push(...stored.slice(index));` and `if (job.state === "done" && job.result) return JSON.parse(job.result) as GateRun;`. Local fallback likewise returns its own outcome at src/gates/lan.ts:86–89: `const [run] = await Promise.all([execution.result, stream]); ... return workers.sanitize(run);`. Neither path merges earlier failed checks. src/gates/executor.ts:211–215 forwards check events to hooks but returns `result` unchanged.
verification.trigger: A worker posts a valid failing check event, then disconnects before submitting its GateRun. After retry or local fallback passes that check, the executor returns a passing GateRun despite the recorded failure, violating the explicit requirement that infrastructure retries never turn a failing check into a pass.

findings.title: Do not retry certificate pin failures indefinitely
findings.detail: The catch treats every workerRequest exception as a transient connection error. That includes an invalid coordinator URL or a changed pinned TLS fingerprint, so the worker silently retries forever instead of surfacing the security or configuration failure. The retry has no deadline.
findings.suggestion: Classify request errors and propagate certificate validation and configuration failures; bound retries for transient transport errors.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator presents a certificate whose fingerprint differs from the stored pin. The worker stays running and retries indefinitely without reporting the fingerprint mismatch.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:114-115 rejects a mismatched pin with `new Error("Coordinator certificate fingerprint changed")`. src/workers/client.ts:146-148 catches every request error and returns `undefined`; :139 uses `for (;;)`, and :157-158 sleeps and retries with a delay capped at 10 seconds.
verification.trigger: A coordinator certificate differs from the stored pin while the worker remains un-aborted → the fingerprint error is silently discarded and requests retry indefinitely. Certificate verification still blocks sending credentials.

findings.title: The credential test does not establish worker-side redaction
findings.detail: The worker and coordinator run in the same process and share the credential registry. The test registers the secret globally and checks only the stored coordinator result and events, so coordinator-side sanitization can make it pass even if the worker sends the credential in plaintext.
findings.suggestion: Inspect the outgoing worker event and result bodies before coordinator processing, or run the worker in a separate process with a credential unknown to the coordinator.
findings.failure_scenario: Worker-side redaction is removed and a gate prints a worker-only credential; the shared coordinator registry still redacts the stored output, so this test passes while the credential crosses the connection.

verification.evidence: test/workers.test.ts:659 registers `registerCredential("WORKER_OUTPUT_TEST", secret)` in the shared process; :459 directly calls `runWorker(...)`. Assertions at :681–683 inspect only stored `result` and `events`. Coordinator storage independently redacts: src/db/workers.ts:238 `events.push(this.sanitize(event))` and :291 `JSON.stringify(this.sanitize(run))`; :59 sanitization calls `redactGateData(data)`.
verification.trigger: Worker-side redaction regresses: the shared coordinator credential registry can still sanitize received output before storage, so these assertions pass without proving that the credential was redacted before transmission.

findings.title: The bundle test never exercises distinct head and base commits
findings.detail: The shared request fixture assigns the same commit to headSha and baseSha. Consequently, the end-to-end bundle test cannot detect an implementation that bundles only the head, even though the request requires both commits to be available on the worker.
findings.suggestion: Create distinct base and head commits and have a worker gate verify that both requested commits are present.
findings.failure_scenario: Bundle creation omits baseSha when it differs from headSha; the existing end-to-end test still passes because its two SHAs are identical.

verification.evidence: test/workers.test.ts:123–124 sets `baseSha: sha, headSha: sha`; the end-to-end test at :657 uses `request(true)` and at :677 checks only `output` containing `req.headSha`. Production bundle creation currently includes both via src/server/workers.ts:88 `new Set([request.headSha, request.baseSha].filter(Boolean))`.
verification.trigger: Bundle creation regresses to including only headSha. Because the fixture gives head and base the same SHA, the existing end-to-end test still passes and cannot detect omission of a distinct base commit.

findings.title: Reconcile streamed check failures with the final result
findings.detail: The coordinator validates each check event and the final GateRun independently. It accepts a passing final result even if the same lease previously reported that check as failed. The failed event is stored, but it does not influence the returned GateRun, so an inconsistent worker response can turn an observed failure into a pass.
findings.suggestion: Validate the final run against the check events recorded for the current lease and treat inconsistent results as an infrastructure failure.
