findings.title: Rollback to the previous release does not notify the executor
findings.detail: The executor detects a release change only through the database setting written by this new daemon. The previous release never writes that setting, so rolling back leaves the new release SHA in place. A running new executor continues its job and can continue leasing queued jobs even though the active daemon is now the older release.
findings.suggestion: Use release ownership that the previous release can invalidate or otherwise ensure that a rollback stops the executor before the old daemon resumes work.
findings.failure_scenario: Start an in-place gate on this release, then roll back and start the base-commit daemon. The setting still names this release, so the executor does not cancel the gate as required.

verification.evidence: src/cli/daemon.ts:50 adds `factory.store.setSetting("executor.daemonRelease", factory.bootSha);`; the base daemon has no such write (base src/cli/daemon.ts:50 starts with `detachSlots = await attachSlotPools(...)`). src/gates/inplace.ts:39 detects release changes solely through `store.getSetting("executor.daemonRelease", "") !== releaseSha`. src/db/workers.ts:388 uses the same persisted setting to permit leasing.
verification.trigger: Run an executor gate on this release, then roll back to the base daemon, with no LAN worker polling to invalidate the job. The old daemon leaves executor.daemonRelease unchanged, so the executor continues the gate and can lease remaining queued jobs despite the daemon release changing.

findings.title: Process existence is treated as a fresh executor heartbeat
findings.detail: Executor availability checks only PID and birth identity; there is no heartbeat timestamp. An executor whose event loop is stalled remains eligible indefinitely. Once its lease expires, the daemon marks the job failed, but waitStopped waits indefinitely while that process exists, so it cannot fall back or proceed with the worktree.
findings.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and provide a bounded, safe path for confirming that an unresponsive executor's gate processes have stopped.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor is alive but paused or blocked while running a gate. Its lease expires; the daemon enters waitStopped and never completes the gate or starts the fallback.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:359 identifies availability solely with `return processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth;`. Lease expiry marks the job failed (src/db/workers.ts:671–672), but fallback first calls `await workers.waitStopped(handle.id, controller.signal)` (src/gates/lan.ts:131). In waitStopped, recovery occurs only when `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)` (src/db/workers.ts:370); otherwise it repeatedly sleeps (line 384).
verification.trigger: A leased executor remains alive but stops progressing beyond lease expiry. The job fails, but fallback waits indefinitely until the executor resumes or exits.

findings.title: Targeted and timeout retry jobs cannot reattach
findings.detail: The resume predicate explicitly accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A restart during an in-place targeted or timeout retry therefore cancels the still-running job and repeats work instead of attaching to its matching handle.
findings.suggestion: Persist and restore the retry context needed to validate and reattach matching retry jobs.
findings.failure_scenario: A daemon restarts while a long targeted retry is leased by the executor. On resume, the purpose fails this allowlist and the retry is cancelled or started again.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:30 requires '["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)'; lines 35–43 cancel and clear rejected handles. src/pipeline/engine.ts:1566 runs purpose "timeout", and lines 1592–1595 run "regression-retry-targeted" or "regression-retry". On restart, engine.ts:1536 first calls resumeGateExecution with "initial", rejecting a surviving retry handle.
verification.trigger: The daemon restarts during an in-place targeted or timeout retry. Resume cancels the surviving retry and restarts gate work instead of attaching to its result.

findings.title: LAN configuration bypasses the in-place executor for local fallback
findings.detail: When the gate executor is configured as LAN, this factory always returns the LAN executor, even when the in-place executor is enabled. Its local path for repositories outside the LAN list runs directly in the daemon, so those local gates cannot survive a daemon restart.
findings.suggestion: Route the LAN executor's local path through the in-place executor when it is enabled and available.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the executor, configure LAN gates for one repository, and run a gate in another repository. The gate runs in the daemon and is lost on restart despite a live in-place executor.

verification.evidence: src/gates/executor.ts:77–81 uses the flag only for local routing: `return inplace && workers ? lanExecutor(workers, [], true) : localExecutor();`; the LAN branch returns `lanExecutor(workers, repos)`. src/gates/lan.ts:16 defaults `inplace = false`, and :71 routes excluded repositories directly to `local.start(req, signal)`. That executor stores executions in process-local maps (src/gates/executor.ts:85–90).
verification.trigger: Set gates.executor="lan", enable executor.enabled, configure workers.repos for one repository, and run gates in another with a fresh in-place executor available. Gates run inside the daemon instead of creating durable in-place jobs; a daemon restart loses the execution and repeats the work.

findings.title: Confinement failures are converted into local retries
findings.detail: The executor catches every error from executeGate and records an ordinary failed job. The attaching daemon then reruns every failed in-place job locally. This loses the distinction between an infrastructure failure and a ConfinementError, so a failed isolation check can be followed by a successful gate instead of failing closed.
findings.suggestion: Persist a failure classification and propagate confinement and inspection failures to the daemon without retrying them.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor's confinement preflight throws ConfinementError, but the daemon's subsequent local preflight succeeds; the gate passes despite the original security check failing.

verification.evidence: src/gates/inplace.ts:70–71 catches every error with `workers.fail(job.id, redactCredentials(String(error)))`, losing the ConfinementError type. src/db/workers.ts:626–632 sets in-place jobs to `state='failed'`. src/gates/lan.ts:130–139 handles every failed job by calling `local.start(request, controller.signal)` without checking the failure classification; lines 147–150 complete the job and return the fallback result.
verification.trigger: Executor confinement preflight throws ConfinementError; process cleanup completes; the daemon's local preflight succeeds. The local gate can pass and replace the confinement failure with a successful result.

findings.title: A cleanup failure can leave the run waiting indefinitely
findings.detail: waitStopped only attempts recovery or reports an error after the executor process disappears. If a job finishes with process discovery or cleanup records remaining, the executor deliberately leaves stopped=0 but continues running. waitStopped then polls forever because the executor is still alive, even though that executor will never revisit the completed job.
findings.suggestion: Make the executor publish a terminal cleanup failure, or have waitStopped detect that the job is no longer being cleaned up and fail closed with a clear error.
findings.failure_scenario: A cancelled gate leaves a cleanup record after process cleanup fails; the executor continues polling for other jobs, while the daemon waits forever to start the replacement gate.

verification.evidence: src/gates/inplace.ts:76–80 sets `stopped=1` only when both process discovery and cleanup lists are empty, then returns to the polling loop (line 29). src/db/workers.ts:370 permits recovery only when `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)`; a live executor instead causes repeated sleeps (line 384).
verification.trigger: Cleanup fails and leaves a record after cancellation. The executor continues polling, while the daemon waits for stopped=1. No code retries cleanup or reports the unresolved cleanup to that waiter while the executor remains alive.

findings.title: Executor availability has no heartbeat freshness check
findings.detail: Executor availability is based only on PID and birth identity; the executors table has no heartbeat timestamp. A live but stalled executor is treated as available indefinitely. New gates are enqueued instead of immediately using the requested in-process fallback, and a leased job is not considered disconnected until its lease expires.
findings.suggestion: Record and renew an executor heartbeat and require it to be fresh when selecting an executor and sweeping its jobs.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process remains alive but its event loop stops making progress; the daemon treats it as available and waits for pickup or lease expiry rather than recognizing that no fresh executor is available.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:354 queries executors with fields `id`, `pid`, `birth`, and `release_sha`; availability is `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth` (line 359). src/gates/lan.ts:62 checks `if (!workers.executor())` to choose immediate local fallback. The executor registers once with `INSERT INTO executors (id,pid,birth,release_sha)` (src/gates/inplace.ts:23), with no heartbeat freshness field.
verification.trigger: An executor remains alive with an unresponsive event loop. The daemon considers it available and enqueues work instead of taking the required fallback for an executor without a fresh heartbeat; queued work waits for the pickup timeout.

findings.title: Targeted retry jobs are cancelled on restart instead of reattached

findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while an executor is running a long targeted regression retry; the new engine cancels that job and repeats gate work instead of receiving its result.

findings.title: Executor stores gate output without the daemon’s dynamic credential registrations
findings.detail: Credential registrations are process-local. findings.title: Confinement derives credential paths from the executor environment
findings.detail: The gate receives the daemon’s saved environment, but the executor constructs its read policy from its own process environment. findings.title: Rollback to an older daemon does not stop the executor
findings.detail: The executor detects a release change only through the persistent `executor.daemonRelease` setting. A daemon from before this change never updates that setting, so after rollback it still contains the newer release SHA. The newer executor continues its running job while the older daemon resumes the run without understanding the in-place handle, allowing both releases to operate on the same worktree.
findings.suggestion: Use a coordinator release and liveness mechanism that also detects replacement by a daemon that does not write this setting, and stop the executor's jobs before the older daemon can resume them.
findings.failure_scenario: A new-release in-place gate is running when the daemon is rolled back to the base release. The old daemon leaves the setting unchanged and starts its own recovery or gate while the executor continues.

verification.evidence: src/gates/inplace.ts:39 detects release changes solely with `store.getSetting("executor.daemonRelease", "") !== releaseSha`; lines 52–57 otherwise renew the lease. src/cli/daemon.ts:50 introduces `factory.store.setSetting("executor.daemonRelease", factory.bootSha)`. The base version of startScopedDaemon has no corresponding write, so rollback leaves the new release's value intact.
verification.trigger: Roll back while a new-release executor job is running. The base daemon never updates the release setting, so the executor continues renewing and running instead of cancelling as required.

findings.title: Targeted retries cannot reattach after restart
findings.detail: The resume predicate accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A running `regression-retry-targeted` job therefore gets cancelled on restart even when its stage, round, SHA, environment, release, and lease still match. The stage repeats work instead of attaching to the retry, contrary to the requested coverage of targeted retries.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry progress to resume the targeted retry at its recorded purpose and attach to its matching job.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a long targeted regression retry is running. On resume, the saved handle fails the purpose check and the running job is cancelled.

findings.title: A live but unresponsive executor can block a worktree indefinitely
findings.detail: Executor freshness is determined solely by whether its PID and birth time still match; there is no heartbeat. If the executor is alive but no longer making progress, the sweep eventually fails its lease, but `waitStopped` continues waiting for that same live process to set `stopped`. Consequently the daemon never reaches the in-process fallback or starts another gate in the worktree.
findings.suggestion: Track executor heartbeat freshness and provide a bounded, confirmed process-stop or recovery path before falling back.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor becomes stuck while running a gate but remains alive. Its lease expires, and the daemon waits indefinitely in `waitStopped`.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:359 defines availability as `return processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`. At :366–384, `while (this.job(id)?.stopped === 0)` only attempts recovery when `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)`; otherwise it sleeps without a deadline. src/gates/lan.ts:131 awaits `workers.waitStopped(handle.id, controller.signal)` before fallback.
verification.trigger: An executor stalls while owning a job, remains alive, and stops renewing. Lease expiry fails the job, but stopped remains 0; fallback waits indefinitely unless externally aborted or the executor exits.

findings.title: Confinement failures are converted into a local retry
findings.detail: The executor catches every error from `executeGate`, including `ConfinementError`, and marks the job failed. The daemon treats every failed in-place job as eligible for local fallback in `lan.ts`. A confinement inspection failure can therefore be replaced by a passing second execution, hiding the failed security check and allowing the gate to pass.
findings.suggestion: Preserve the failure classification across the job boundary and propagate confinement failures without retrying them as local gates.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor cannot verify its Seatbelt confinement, but the daemon's subsequent local confinement check succeeds; the local retry passes and the original security failure is lost.

verification.trigger: Executor confinement verification throws, then daemon-side confinement verification succeeds. The fallback can return a passing GateRun despite the original security-check failure; its diagnostic remains stored, but its blocking classification is lost.

findings.title: A live but unresponsive executor is treated as fresh indefinitely
findings.detail: Executor availability checks only PID and birth time; there is no heartbeat or freshness timestamp. If the executor remains alive but stops making progress, new jobs are sent to it and previously leased jobs eventually enter `waitStopped`, which continues waiting as long as that process exists. Lease expiry therefore does not produce a bounded fallback or a completed cancellation.
findings.suggestion: Track executor freshness and provide a bounded, fail-closed recovery path for an unresponsive owner while confirming its gate processes have stopped.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor hangs while running a gate and stops renewing its lease. The sweep marks the job failed, but `waitStopped` waits indefinitely because the executor PID still exists, so the run never falls back or finishes.

findings.title: Executor liveness has no heartbeat freshness check
findings.detail: Executor availability is determined only by whether the recorded PID and birth time still match. The executor table has no heartbeat timestamp, so a live but stalled executor remains available indefinitely. New jobs are sent to it until pickup timeout, and waitStopped can wait indefinitely for a stalled owner after cancellation. The tests cover a dead PID and a release mismatch but never a live executor whose heartbeat stops.
findings.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and test a live but unresponsive executor for both fallback and cancellation behavior.

findings.detail: The pickup test stops after asserting that sweep marks an unclaimed job failed. It never attaches through the gate executor or verifies that the check subsequently runs locally and returns its result, so a regression in the failed-job fallback path would pass.
findings.suggestion: Add a test that leaves an in-place job unclaimed, advances through pickup expiry, and asserts the local check executes and its GateRun is returned.

findings.detail: The subprocess explicitly installs a no-op confinement wrapper, and the parent uses fakeConfinement. Consequently the test can pass even if executor gates run without the daemon's required confinement. Existing output and environment assertions do not exercise this boundary.

findings.detail: Executor availability checks only the PID and birth identity; there is no heartbeat or freshness timestamp. If the executor process remains alive but stops polling or renewing, the daemon continues to consider it available. findings.title: Worktree exclusivity check races with job creation
findings.detail: The scan for existing jobs and the later enqueue are separate operations with awaits between them. Two concurrent starts for the same worktree can both observe no existing job and enqueue distinct jobs, which separate executor processes can lease simultaneously. This defeats the required one-job-per-worktree guarantee.
findings.suggestion: Serialize reservation and enqueue for a worktree with an atomic database constraint or transaction, retaining the reservation until process cleanup is confirmed.

AND state='queued'`, without a cwd exclusion. Thus neither enqueue nor leasing closes the race.
verification.trigger: Two concurrent starts for the same cwd both scan before either attaches and enqueues. With two executors and available gate capacity, both jobs can be leased and run concurrently in that worktree, violating the explicit exclusivity requirement.

findings.title: Restart discards running retry jobs
findings.detail: The request says that a resumed stage whose handle matches its stage, round, purpose, and SHA attaches to it, and explicitly includes the targeted retry. This allowlist rejects timeout and regression retry purposes even when all of those fields match. The stage’s initial resume check also cancels a recorded retry before it can be attached.

Initial gates run again at src/pipeline/engine.ts:1547.

findings.title: Executor availability has no heartbeat freshness
findings.detail: The request requires a fresh executor heartbeat and says the sweep applies freshness timers against it. Executor records contain only process identity and release, so a live but stalled executor remains available indefinitely. After a leased job expires, `waitStopped` also waits indefinitely while that process remains alive, preventing fallback.
findings.suggestion: Track executor heartbeat freshness and provide a safe way to confirm its job processes have stopped when the executor stops responding.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process remains alive but its event loop stops responding while a gate is running. The lease expires, yet the daemon waits indefinitely for `stopped=1` rather than completing the gate or safely failing over.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:359 considers an executor available when `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`, with no freshness check. src/gates/lan.ts:130–131 handles failed jobs with `if (inplace) await workers.waitStopped(handle.id, controller.signal)`. src/db/workers.ts:370–384 performs recovery only for an absent executor and otherwise sleeps without a timeout.
verification.trigger: An executor remains alive but stops servicing its renewal timer during a gate. Lease expiry marks the job failed, yet fallback remains blocked waiting for stopped=1.

findings.title: LAN configuration bypasses the in-place executor for local repositories
findings.detail: The request says that when the executor is enabled and alive, the daemon’s local gate path creates an in-place job. With `[gates] executor = "lan"`, this branch always selects the LAN executor, whose fallback for repositories outside `workers.repos` runs directly in the daemon regardless of `[executor] enabled`.

candidates.title: Rollback to an older daemon does not stop the executor
candidates.detail: The executor detects a release change only through the persistent `executor.daemonRelease` setting. A daemon from before this change never updates that setting, so after rollback it still contains the newer release SHA. The newer executor continues its running job while the older daemon resumes the run without understanding the in-place handle, allowing both releases to operate on the same worktree.
candidates.suggestion: Use a coordinator release and liveness mechanism that also detects replacement by a daemon that does not write this setting, and stop the executor's jobs before the older daemon can resume them.
candidates.failure_scenario: A new-release in-place gate is running when the daemon is rolled back to the base release. The old daemon leaves the setting unchanged and starts its own recovery or gate while the executor continues.

candidates.title: Targeted retries cannot reattach after restart
candidates.detail: The resume predicate accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A running `regression-retry-targeted` job therefore gets cancelled on restart even when its stage, round, SHA, environment, release, and lease still match. The stage repeats work instead of attaching to the retry, contrary to the requested coverage of targeted retries.
candidates.suggestion: Persist enough retry progress to resume the targeted retry at its recorded purpose and attach to its matching job.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a long targeted regression retry is running. On resume, the saved handle fails the purpose check and the running job is cancelled.

candidates.title: A live but unresponsive executor can block a worktree indefinitely
candidates.detail: Executor freshness is determined solely by whether its PID and birth time still match; there is no heartbeat. If the executor is alive but no longer making progress, the sweep eventually fails its lease, but `waitStopped` continues waiting for that same live process to set `stopped`. Consequently the daemon never reaches the in-process fallback or starts another gate in the worktree.
candidates.suggestion: Track executor heartbeat freshness and provide a bounded, confirmed process-stop or recovery path before falling back.
candidates.failure_scenario: An executor becomes stuck while running a gate but remains alive. Its lease expires, and the daemon waits indefinitely in `waitStopped`.

candidates.title: Confinement failures are converted into a local retry
candidates.detail: The executor catches every error from `executeGate`, including `ConfinementError`, and marks the job failed. The daemon treats every failed in-place job as eligible for local fallback in `lan.ts`. A confinement inspection failure can therefore be replaced by a passing second execution, hiding the failed security check and allowing the gate to pass.
candidates.suggestion: Preserve the failure classification across the job boundary and propagate confinement failures without retrying them as local gates.
candidates.failure_scenario: The executor cannot verify its Seatbelt confinement, but the daemon's subsequent local confinement check succeeds; the local retry passes and the original security failure is lost.

candidates.title: A live but unresponsive executor is treated as fresh indefinitely
candidates.detail: Executor availability checks only PID and birth time; there is no heartbeat or freshness timestamp. If the executor remains alive but stops making progress, new jobs are sent to it and previously leased jobs eventually enter `waitStopped`, which continues waiting as long as that process exists. Lease expiry therefore does not produce a bounded fallback or a completed cancellation.
candidates.suggestion: Track executor freshness and provide a bounded, fail-closed recovery path for an unresponsive owner while confirming its gate processes have stopped.
candidates.failure_scenario: An executor hangs while running a gate and stops renewing its lease. The sweep marks the job failed, but `waitStopped` waits indefinitely because the executor PID still exists, so the run never falls back or finishes.

candidates.title: Targeted retry jobs cannot reattach after restart
candidates.detail: The resume whitelist excludes targeted and other retry purposes. When a daemon restarts during a targeted retry, the resumed stage rejects the recorded handle and cancels the surviving job instead of attaching to it. This leaves the requested restart protection incomplete for a gate purpose explicitly named in the request.
candidates.suggestion: Persist enough retry-stage state to resume the matching retry job and attach to it after restart.
candidates.failure_scenario: A long `regression-retry-targeted` job is running when the daemon restarts; the resumed gate stage cancels that job and reruns earlier gate work rather than receiving its result.

candidates.title: Targeted retry jobs cannot reattach after a restart
candidates.detail: Resume is restricted to baseline, initial and rebase purposes. Targeted retries use baseline-retry-targeted or regression-retry-targeted, so a restart rejects their matching durable handle, cancels the running job and starts the stage over. The new restart tests cover only baseline, initial and rebase, leaving this requested behavior untested.
candidates.suggestion: Persist enough retry context to resume the matching targeted job, and add a restart test that verifies the same job completes and its command runs once.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while an executor is running a regression-retry-targeted check at the same SHA; the resumed stage cancels that job instead of attaching to it.

candidates.title: Executor liveness has no heartbeat freshness check
candidates.detail: Executor availability is determined only by whether the recorded PID and birth time still match. The executor table has no heartbeat timestamp, so a live but stalled executor remains available indefinitely. New jobs are sent to it until pickup timeout, and waitStopped can wait indefinitely for a stalled owner after cancellation. The tests cover a dead PID and a release mismatch but never a live executor whose heartbeat stops.
candidates.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and test a live but unresponsive executor for both fallback and cancellation behavior.
candidates.failure_scenario: An executor process remains alive but its event loop stops servicing jobs; the daemon treats it as fresh and a cancellation can remain blocked waiting for its acknowledgement.

candidates.title: Pickup timeout test does not exercise in-process fallback
candidates.detail: The pickup test stops after asserting that sweep marks an unclaimed job failed. It never attaches through the gate executor or verifies that the check subsequently runs locally and returns its result, so a regression in the failed-job fallback path would pass.
candidates.suggestion: Add a test that leaves an in-place job unclaimed, advances through pickup expiry, and asserts the local check executes and its GateRun is returned.
candidates.failure_scenario: The sweep marks the job failed, but the attach loop fails to launch or return the in-process fallback; the existing test still passes.

candidates.title: Executor tests replace the confinement they need to verify
candidates.detail: The subprocess explicitly installs a no-op confinement wrapper, and the parent uses fakeConfinement. Consequently the test can pass even if executor gates run without the daemon's required confinement. Existing output and environment assertions do not exercise this boundary.
candidates.suggestion: Add a platform-gated real confinement probe through the executor that checks both an allowed worktree operation and a denied out-of-scope write.
candidates.failure_scenario: The executor launches a gate without its required confinement; every new executor test still passes because the test fixture disables confinement.

candidates.title: Executor output is redacted with an incomplete credential registry
candidates.detail: Credential registration is process-local. The executor loads configuration, but it does not register credentials acquired by the daemon at runtime, such as its API token, GitHub token, or worker tokens. Gate output is redacted and truncated in the executor and then written to job events and results using that executor's registry. A credential known only to the daemon can therefore be persisted unredacted, and truncation can prevent the daemon from recognizing it later.
candidates.suggestion: Make the executor's redaction policy cover the daemon's dynamically registered credentials before it captures, truncates, or persists gate output.
candidates.failure_scenario: A gate prints a daemon-registered API or GitHub token that is absent from the executor's credential registry; the token appears in the stored gate event or result.

candidates.title: A live but stalled executor is treated as fresh indefinitely
candidates.detail: Executor availability checks only the PID and birth identity; there is no heartbeat or freshness timestamp. If the executor process remains alive but stops polling or renewing, the daemon continues to consider it available. For a leased job, waitStopped also waits indefinitely for that same process instead of reaching a confirmed-stop recovery path.
candidates.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and provide a bounded, fail-closed recovery path for a stale owner.
candidates.failure_scenario: An executor process stalls while running a gate and remains alive. Its lease expires, but the daemon waits indefinitely for stopped to become 1 and cannot fall back or start the next gate.

candidates.title: Worktree exclusivity check races with job creation
candidates.detail: The scan for existing jobs and the later enqueue are separate operations with awaits between them. Two concurrent starts for the same worktree can both observe no existing job and enqueue distinct jobs, which separate executor processes can lease simultaneously. This defeats the required one-job-per-worktree guarantee.
candidates.suggestion: Serialize reservation and enqueue for a worktree with an atomic database constraint or transaction, retaining the reservation until process cleanup is confirmed.
candidates.failure_scenario: Two gate starts for the same cwd run concurrently while two executors are available. Both pass the empty-job scan, enqueue, and execute checks in the same worktree at once.

candidates.title: Restart discards running retry jobs
candidates.detail: The request says that a resumed stage whose handle matches its stage, round, purpose, and SHA attaches to it, and explicitly includes the targeted retry. This allowlist rejects timeout and regression retry purposes even when all of those fields match. The stage’s initial resume check also cancels a recorded retry before it can be attached.
candidates.suggestion: Persist enough retry-stage state to resume the recorded retry, and validate its matching handle without restricting resumption to the first execution.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while an executor runs `regression-retry-targeted`; the resumed stage cancels that job and repeats earlier gates instead of receiving the retry result.

candidates.title: Executor availability has no heartbeat freshness
candidates.detail: The request requires a fresh executor heartbeat and says the sweep applies freshness timers against it. Executor records contain only process identity and release, so a live but stalled executor remains available indefinitely. After a leased job expires, `waitStopped` also waits indefinitely while that process remains alive, preventing fallback.
candidates.suggestion: Track executor heartbeat freshness and provide a safe way to confirm its job processes have stopped when the executor stops responding.
candidates.failure_scenario: An executor process remains alive but its event loop stops responding while a gate is running. The lease expires, yet the daemon waits indefinitely for `stopped=1` rather than completing the gate or safely failing over.

candidates.title: LAN configuration bypasses the in-place executor for local repositories
candidates.detail: The request says that when the executor is enabled and alive, the daemon’s local gate path creates an in-place job. With `[gates] executor = "lan"`, this branch always selects the LAN executor, whose fallback for repositories outside `workers.repos` runs directly in the daemon regardless of `[executor] enabled`.
candidates.suggestion: Route the LAN executor’s local fallback through the enabled in-place executor while retaining LAN dispatch for configured repositories.
candidates.failure_scenario: A coordinator uses LAN gates for one repository and enables the local executor; a different repository’s local gate still runs in the daemon and is lost on restart.

candidates.title: Resume accepts jobs without a held lease
candidates.detail: The request states, “A job is only re-attached while the executor still holds its lease.” `canResume` also accepts queued jobs and completed jobs without checking a held lease. This deviates from the requested restart boundary.
candidates.suggestion: Require a current executor-held lease for reattachment, or explicitly define and implement a separate completed-result recovery rule.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts after saving a handle while the job is still queued; the resumed stage reattaches to that unleased job instead of starting fresh.

Verifier: 8 candidates, 8 checked, 1 refuted.

findings.title: Key validation does not enforce the required owner and mode
findings.detail: The startup check accepts any regular file with the owner-read bit set and no group or world permission bits. It does not check the file's owner, and it accepts modes such as 0700 and 0400 despite requiring mode 0600. A file owned by another user can therefore pass the metadata check even when the daemon cannot read it, deferring failure until a configured repository first needs a token.
findings.suggestion: Check the file owner and enforce the requested mode and readability during configuration loading, with a clear startup error.
findings.failure_scenario: A key file owned by another user has mode 0600. Its metadata passes this check, but the daemon cannot read it and App-authenticated GitHub calls fail later.

verification.evidence: src/config.ts:390 performs only `key = statSync(privateKeyPath)`; src/config.ts:394 checks `!key.isFile() || (key.mode & 0o077) !== 0 || !(key.mode & 0o400)`. Neither verifies effective readability. Actual reading occurs later at src/integrations/github-identity.ts:64: `readFileSync(app.privateKeyPath)`.
verification.trigger: A traversable path contains another user's mode-0600 key. An unprivileged daemon can stat it, so startup accepts it, but App operations subsequently fail to read it.

findings.title: Verify the key is readable by the factory at startup
findings.detail: The permission check inspects mode bits but does not check the file owner or whether the daemon can actually read the file. A mode-0600 key owned by another user passes configuration loading, then fails only when the first App operation tries to read it. The check also accepts modes such as 0400 and 0700 despite requiring mode 0600.
findings.suggestion: Verify the file belongs to the running user, is readable, and has the required mode before accepting the configuration.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured key is a regular mode-0600 file owned by another user. Startup succeeds, but every GitHub operation for an App repository later fails with `cannot read or sign with private key`.

findings.title: Key validation does not enforce the required mode or ownership

It also never checks that the file belongs to the process owner, so a mode-0600 file owned by another user can pass startup validation even when the daemon cannot read it. The failure then occurs later during token acquisition instead of at startup.

findings.title: Key validation tests omit owner-only executable mode and ownership
findings.detail: The permission cases cover group and world bits but do not exercise a mode such as 0700 or a file owned by another user. Consequently they pass with the incomplete startup validation and do not catch the underlying key-file defect.
findings.suggestion: Add a regression case for mode 0700 and a controlled ownership or stat fixture for a key owned by another user, asserting startup refusal.
findings.failure_scenario: A change that checks only group and world permission bits while ignoring owner execute bits and file ownership passes the current key permission tests.

findings.title: An App key outside the config directory can be exposed to agents
findings.detail: The configuration accepts any absolute key path, but the agent read policy automatically denies the config directory, not the configured key file. candidates.failure_scenario: The configured key path points to a 0600 file owned by another user. loadConfig accepts it, but the first App token exchange fails when readFileSync attempts to open it.

candidates.title: Validate the key file's owner and exact permissions
candidates.detail: The startup check only inspects the file type and selected permission bits. It does not verify that the file belongs to the current user, and it accepts modes such as 0400 and 0700 even though the request requires mode 0600. A file owned by another user can pass the check despite being unreadable to the daemon, deferring failure until a GitHub operation.
candidates.suggestion: Require the current user's ownership and mode 0600, and verify that the key is readable at startup.
candidates.failure_scenario: A regular key file owned by another user with mode 0600 passes configuration validation, but the daemon cannot read it when it needs to sign a JWT.

candidates.title: Correct the test that accepts a non-0600 key
candidates.detail: The test explicitly expects a 0400 key to be accepted, asserting behavior contrary to the requested mode 0600 requirement. The permission cases also do not cover ownership or owner execute permissions, so they do not catch the incomplete startup validation.
candidates.suggestion: Expect non-0600 modes to fail and add coverage for a key not owned by the daemon user where the test environment supports it.
candidates.failure_scenario: Changing validation to enforce the requested exact mode causes this test to fail, while the existing incomplete check passes it.

candidates.title: Protect the configured private key outside the config directory
candidates.detail: The configuration accepts an absolute key path or a relative path that escapes the config directory, but the read policy only adds the config directory to its credential deny list. A key at another agent-readable location can therefore be read by an agent or gate running as the same user. The key itself is not registered for output redaction.
candidates.suggestion: Add the resolved key file, including its canonical path and relevant aliases, to the shared read-deny policy used by every agent and gate, or reject paths whose confinement cannot be guaranteed.
candidates.failure_scenario: An operator configures a mode-0600 key at an absolute path inside a checkout. An agent or gate reads that file and can publish the App private key.

candidates.title: Enforce the specified key-file mode and readability at startup
candidates.detail: The mode check accepts owner-executable files such as 0700, and checking the owner-read bit does not establish that the daemon can actually read the file. The request requires a readable mode-0600 file and startup refusal otherwise; an unreadable file currently passes configuration and fails only when an App call is attempted.
candidates.suggestion: Validate the required mode and verify the file can be opened during configuration loading, reporting a clear startup error.
candidates.failure_scenario: A key file has mode 0700, or has mode 0600 but belongs to a different user. Configuration loads even though the required startup validation should refuse it.

candidates.title: Manual landing bypasses the configured App identity
candidates.detail: The request requires “one implementation used by every factory gh invocation for a repository” and says configured repositories use the App. This script invokes gh directly without loading or configuring the identity provider, including for the merge. Consequently manual landing uses the owner's login and can merge even when an App token exchange would fail.
candidates.suggestion: Initialize the configured identity provider in this script and route its repository-scoped gh calls through it.
candidates.failure_scenario: Run scripts/land-pr.sh for an App-configured repository: its private-strings merge step invokes gh with the owner's credentials, so the merge appears owner-authored.

candidates.title: Key validation does not enforce the required mode or readability
candidates.detail: The request says the key must be a regular file with “mode 0600” and that startup refuses otherwise. This check also accepts modes such as 0400 and 0700, and checks the owner-read permission bit without checking whether the process can actually read the file. For example, a 0600 file owned by another user passes startup validation but cannot be read when an App call is attempted.
candidates.suggestion: Enforce the required permission bits and verify that the configured key is readable during startup.
candidates.failure_scenario: Configure a regular private key owned by another user with mode 0600: startup succeeds, but the first App identity request fails to read the key.

candidates.title: Doctor still requires an owner gh login for an App-only configuration
candidates.detail: The request says doctor reports the active identity and whether the App token exchange works. Doctor unconditionally marks gh authentication as failed before checking the App identity, even when every configured repository uses the App and the exchange and installation coverage succeed. This reports a working App-only setup as failed.
candidates.suggestion: Make the gh authentication check reflect whether any configured repository needs the owner's login.
candidates.failure_scenario: With only App-configured repositories and no owner gh login, doctor reports gh authentication failure despite a successful App token exchange and complete repository coverage.

Verifier: 21 candidates, 21 checked, 5 refuted.

findings.title: Lifecycle transitions can disappear between polls
findings.detail: Comments are derived from the current run status, and an event is persisted only when reconciliation observes that status. A run that enters needs_human and is resumed or resolved before the next poll never records or posts that event. Likewise, a second needs_human episode is suppressed by the first episode's done checkpoint. This does not provide a durable side effect for each transition across restarts or polling intervals.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur, with an identity for each status episode, and reconcile those records independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:97–102 reads `run = store.getRun(snapshot.id)` and adds the event only `if (run.status === "needs_human")`. Lines 112–114 skip absent events unless already pending: `if (!events.has(event) && state(effect) !== "pending") continue;`.
verification.trigger: A run enters and leaves needs_human between polls, before its comment becomes pending. Reconciliation never posts the required needs-you reason.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates only run for queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Both the reconciler and its timer are conditional on the issue queue's repository and trusted-account configuration. Runs started through CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers in any other configured repository therefore receive no lifecycle labels or comments, even though the requested behavior covers every start path and does not require queue admission to be enabled.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and select linked issues according to the supported repository settings.
findings.failure_scenario: A repository has the GitHub integration configured but is absent from githubQueue.repos; a CLI run with `Closes #42` produces no lifecycle updates.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10–12 defines lifecycleManaged using `cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; line 43 skips with `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:144 also returns immediately when queue repositories or trusted accounts are absent.
verification.trigger: A CLI run contains Closes #42 in a GitHub-integrated repository outside githubQueue.repos. Its required lifecycle labels and comments are skipped.

findings.title: A partial failure can release an issue before its failure label is applied
findings.detail: The label loop removes in-progress before adding failed. If the add fails, reconciliation logs the failure and queue selection continues in the same poll. The existing latest-run admission check only finds issue-source runs, so it does not protect a failed CLI or MCP run linked through its prompt. The issue can be selected again using its old priority approval before the failed label is retried.
findings.suggestion: Keep admission closed until the failure transition is durably reflected, including for prompt-linked runs; order label writes so a partial transition does not release the issue.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #42` fails; deleting in-progress succeeds but adding failed returns an error. The same poll sees the old priority label and starts a queue run without re-approval.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:13 orders labels as in-progress, needs-you, failed; lines 68–86 delete non-target labels before adding failed and catch write failures at lines 93–95. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 continues into admission after reconciliation. src/db/store.ts:1268 restricts latestIssueRun to `json_extract(runs.source_ref, '$.kind') = 'issue'`, excluding ordinary CLI Closes runs.
verification.trigger: An otherwise eligible issue's CLI run fails. Removing in-progress succeeds but adding failed fails. The failed run no longer claims the issue, and latestIssueRun excludes it, so the same poll can admit a queue run using the old approval.

findings.title: An older run can overwrite a newer run's issue labels
findings.detail: The latest-run map is computed once before any GitHub requests. If another run for the issue is created while a label request is awaiting, the old run remains designated latest and can complete its label transition after the newer run starts. Its completed cursor then prevents correction until the newer run is reconciled on a later poll.
findings.suggestion: Recheck which run owns the issue after awaited operations and before each label mutation and completion checkpoint.
findings.failure_scenario: While reconciliation fetches labels for a failed run, a new run for the same issue starts; the old reconciliation then applies failed and removes in-progress for the active run.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:35–39 builds `latest` once from `store.issueLifecycleRuns()`. Line 56 checks that snapshot before awaiting the labels request at line 60. Lines 63–71 subsequently re-read only `store.getRun(snapshot.id)` and its desired label; they never recheck whether a newer run owns the issue.
verification.trigger: A newer run for the issue is created while the old failed run's labels request is awaiting GitHub. The old reconciliation can then remove in-progress and apply failed despite the newer active run, until a later poll corrects it.

findings.title: Persist lifecycle events when they occur, not only when a poll observes them
findings.detail: The needs-human, failure, and cancellation comments are created only when reconciliation observes the corresponding current status. No pending effect exists until the comment loop reaches that event. A status that changes between polls, or while an earlier comment write is failing, is therefore never recorded or retried. The single done cursor also suppresses a second needs-human episode for the same run.
findings.suggestion: Record each lifecycle event and its publication-safe content durably at the state transition, then let polling deliver each recorded event.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next poll; reconciliation sees the resumed status and never posts the required reason. Similarly, a failed started-comment write can delay processing until after needs_human has ended.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:99–103 derives comment events from current status. Lines 159–161 persist an event only when its comment is reached. The ordered loop at line 110 processes started first, and lines 165–167 execute `failure(error); break;` on a write failure.
verification.trigger: A needs_human episode ends before polling observes it, or a failed started-comment write prevents reaching its needs_human comment before the run resumes. No durable needs_human event exists, so its required reason is permanently omitted. This overlaps C1.

findings.title: Reconcile issue-linked runs outside queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle processing is restricted to repositories listed in githubQueue with a nonempty trusted list, and the reconciler is started only when that queue is enabled. The request applies lifecycle updates to issue-linked runs from every start path; it does not condition those updates on queue admission being enabled for the repository.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and determine the target repository from each linked issue.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner starts a run with Closes #12 in a repository not listed in githubQueue, or with the queue disabled. No lifecycle labels or new lifecycle comments are written for that issue.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10–12 requires `cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length` and membership in `cfg.githubQueue.repos`; line 43 skips other repositories: `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`. src/integrations/index.ts:66–67 starts reconciliation only when `!!queue?.repos.length && !!queue.trusted.length`.
verification.trigger: A new owner-started run contains Closes #12, but its repository is outside githubQueue or queue configuration is disabled. The required lifecycle labels and comments are never reconciled.

findings.title: Prevent re-pick while a failed label write is pending
findings.detail: The new re-approval guard depends on the failed label being visible on GitHub. If that write fails, the queue continues selection in the same poll. The existing latestIssueRun lookup only considers issue source references, so it cannot supply a local failure guard for runs linked through a Closes directive.
findings.suggestion: Use the existing admission and claim check to account for the latest linked run and its failure while the GitHub failure-label effect is pending.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with Closes #12 fails, the GitHub failed-label POST fails, and issue #12 still has its previously trusted priority label. latestIssueRun returns no issue-sourced run, so the queue can immediately select the issue again without re-approval.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:93-95 catches label-write errors with "failure(error)" and continues. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 then proceeds from reconciliation to candidate selection, supplying "latest: factory.store.latestIssueRun(repo, issue.number)" at line 223. src/db/store.ts:1268 restricts that lookup to "json_extract(runs.source_ref, '$.kind') = 'issue'"; issueClaim at lines 1224-1229 considers only active statuses.
verification.trigger: A CLI run containing Closes #12 fails. Reconciliation removes any in-progress label but its failed-label POST errors. With no earlier issue-sourced run, no active claim, and the old trusted priority label still present, the queue admits another run without re-approval.

findings.title: Authenticate the comment used as a delivery checkpoint
findings.detail: A pending comment is considered delivered when any issue comment contains the predictable marker. The code does not verify the comment author or exact body, although issue comments are untrusted data. A third party can therefore make the reconciler mark a failed write as done without the factory ever posting the required comment.
findings.suggestion: Verify that a matching comment was authored by the configured factory identity and matches the recorded body before marking the effect complete.
findings.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails and leaves its effect pending, another issue participant posts a comment containing the run's lifecycle marker. On the next poll the factory treats that comment as its own and permanently skips the real update.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:121–130 reads pending comments using `z.object({ body: z.string() })` and accepts `comments.some((c) => c.body.includes(marker))`, then calls `save(effect, "done")`. No author identity is checked.
verification.trigger: A comment POST fails, leaving its effect pending. Another participant posts the lifecycle marker. The next poll marks delivery complete and permanently suppresses the factory's comment.

findings.title: Lifecycle events can disappear between polls
findings.detail: The reconciler derives needs-human and failure comments only from the current run status. If a run enters one of those states and is resolved or restarted before the next poll, no pending effect was recorded, so that event is never published. The pending-comment tests cover a status change only after a poll has already attempted the comment; they do not cover a transition entirely between polls.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when the transitions occur, and add a test that enters needs_human or failed and leaves it before reconciliation runs.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resolves it before the next queue poll. The issue receives no needs-you comment or label for that event.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101–102 creates the event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; line 113 skips it when `!events.has(event) && state(effect) !== "pending"`. src/db/store.ts:2038 changes resolved runs to `status: "resolved"`.
verification.trigger: A run enters needs_human and is resolved before reconciliation observes it. No pending checkpoint exists, so subsequent polls omit the needs-you comment and label.

findings.title: Encoded credentials can reach public issue comments
findings.detail: The comment body is passed directly to literal credential redaction. The private-string check detects encoded private-string entries, but registered credentials are not necessarily entries in that list. A credential encoded in a run error can therefore be published in a form a reader can decode.
findings.suggestion: Decode supported representations before credential redaction, or reject comment text containing encoded registered credentials before publication.
findings.failure_scenario: A failed run's error contains a percent-encoded registered token that is absent from private-strings.txt; the posted failure comment contains the encoded token.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:134–148 passes the reason directly through `redactCredentials(...)` and checks only `loadPrivateStrings(...)` before posting at line 163. src/util/proc.ts:1234–1236 registers literal and JSON-escaped credential variants, without percent decoding. src/gates/private.ts:120–122 loads private entries solely from file lines.
verification.trigger: A failure reason contains a percent-encoded registered credential whose literal value is absent from private-strings.txt. Literal credential matching misses it, the private-string check passes, and the recoverable credential is persisted and posted publicly.

findings.title: An unrelated comment can satisfy a pending publication checkpoint
findings.detail: Retry reconciliation trusts a marker found in any issue comment without checking its author or body. Issue comments are untrusted input, so a commenter who knows a run ID can make the factory record an effect as completed even though the factory never posted it.
findings.suggestion: Verify the comment belongs to the expected GitHub identity and matches the saved publication body before marking the effect done.
findings.failure_scenario: A user posts the predictable failed-event marker, and the factory's subsequent comment POST fails before reaching GitHub. On the next poll, the user's marker causes the pending failure comment to be marked done.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:120 constructs `<!-- limitless-lifecycle:${run.id}:${event} -->`; lines 128–130 accept any comment containing that marker as completion. Lines 159–163 persist `save(effect, "pending")` before attempting the POST.
verification.trigger: A participant preposts the predictable failed-event marker, then the factory's POST fails before publication. On retry, the unrelated comment satisfies the pending checkpoint and the failure notification is permanently skipped. This is the same underlying defect as C9.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to configured queue repositories
findings.detail: The lifecycle reconciler skips repositories outside githubQueue.repos, and it is not started when the issue queue is disabled. The request requires updates for runs started through CLI, MCP, label, and comment paths as well as the queue; those paths can target repositories that are not configured for automatic issue selection.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and cover all repositories for which linked runs can be created.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #123` targets a configured repository outside githubQueue.repos; it receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10–12 defines lifecycleManaged as `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length && cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; line 43 applies `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`.
verification.trigger: A CLI run containing Closes #123 targets a repository outside githubQueue.repos. Reconciliation skips all lifecycle labels and comments despite the explicit any-start-path requirement.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to queue-configured repositories
findings.detail: The request covers “any start path: queue, `limitless run` with `Closes #n`, MCP, label or comment trigger.” Reconciliation skips repositories outside `githubQueue.repos`, and the reconciler is not started at all when the queue is disabled. Consequently, runs started through those other paths receive no lifecycle labels or the required comments unless their repository also happens to be configured for the issue queue.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and apply it to linked issues from all supported start paths.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #7` starts in a repository with no issue-queue configuration; no in-progress label or start comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:143–144: `const q = factory.cfg.githubQueue; if (!q?.repos.length || !q.trusted.length) return () => {};`. The lifecycle reconciler is called inside this queue's tick at line 191.
verification.trigger: A CLI run containing Closes #7 starts without issue-queue configuration. The lifecycle poller never starts, so no start label or comment is posted.

findings.title: Transient lifecycle events are lost between polls
findings.detail: The request requires each label change and comment to be a recorded side effect with a durable checkpoint. Here needs-human, failed, and cancelled events are discovered only from the current status. If a run enters and leaves one of those states before a poll observes it, no effect is recorded and its comment is permanently lost. The initial in-progress label can likewise be skipped if the run reaches a later state before its first poll.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when the corresponding transitions occur, then reconcile each recorded effect independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll; the reconciler never posts the needs-you reason or applies its label.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101–102 only creates the event when `run.status === "needs_human"`; line 113 skips absent events unless their checkpoint is already pending. src/db/store.ts:2037–2038 permits needs_human to become resolved: `(opts.from ?? ["needs_human", "failed"]).includes(from)` followed by `status: "resolved"`.
verification.trigger: A run reaches needs_human and is resolved before the next lifecycle poll. Although same-run resumption is not supported, this supported transition likewise loses the needs-you label and reason because no event was checkpointed.

findings.title: A failed label write can allow a failed CLI issue to be picked
findings.detail: A lifecycle write failure is caught and queue selection continues, but `latestIssueRun` only finds runs with an issue source reference. A failed CLI or MCP run linked through `Closes #n` has no such reference. Until the failed label is successfully written, the queue therefore sees neither the failure label nor that latest failed run and can select the issue without re-approval.
findings.suggestion: Include all linked-issue runs in the existing eligibility/admission evidence, including runs linked through their prompt.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run for `Closes #7` fails, the GitHub failed-label write errors, and the issue still has its previously approved priority label; the same poll can create a queue run for it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 awaits reconciliation before querying issues. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:93-95 logs label-write errors and continues. Eligibility only checks failure approval when "issue.labels.nodes.some((l) => l.name === 'limitless:failed')" (issue-queue.ts:97). src/db/store.ts:1268 limits latestIssueRun to issue source references, excluding ordinary CLI runs.
verification.trigger: A failed CLI run for Closes #7 has no remaining active claim. If its failed-label POST fails after in-progress removal, GitHub exposes neither blocking lifecycle label. With no issue-sourced history and an existing trusted priority label, the same poll can create another run without fresh approval.

findings.title: Re-approval in the same timestamp second is rejected
findings.detail: The requirement specifies the labeled events' order and actor. Comparing parsed timestamps with strict greater-than rejects a trusted priority event that follows the failure event but has the same timestamp precision, even though the timeline preserves their order.
findings.suggestion: Use the ordered timeline events to determine whether a trusted priority application follows the failure event, including ties in timestamps.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub records the failure label and a subsequent trusted priority label with the same second in `createdAt`; the issue remains ineligible.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:64–68 computes `failedAt` from failure-label timestamps. At :99, re-approval requires `Date.parse(e.createdAt) > failedAt`; otherwise :101 returns `"factory status requires priority re-approval after failure"`. Timeline order is not considered when timestamps tie.
verification.trigger: A failure-label event followed by a trusted priority-label event has identical second-resolution createdAt values. The strict timestamp comparison rejects the later approval, leaving the issue ineligible on subsequent polls.

candidates.title: Lifecycle transitions can disappear between polls
candidates.detail: Comments are derived from the current run status, and an event is persisted only when reconciliation observes that status. A run that enters needs_human and is resumed or resolved before the next poll never records or posts that event. Likewise, a second needs_human episode is suppressed by the first episode's done checkpoint. This does not provide a durable side effect for each transition across restarts or polling intervals.
candidates.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur, with an identity for each status episode, and reconcile those records independently of the current status.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates only run for queue-enabled repositories
candidates.detail: Both the reconciler and its timer are conditional on the issue queue's repository and trusted-account configuration. Runs started through CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers in any other configured repository therefore receive no lifecycle labels or comments, even though the requested behavior covers every start path and does not require queue admission to be enabled.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and select linked issues according to the supported repository settings.
candidates.failure_scenario: A repository has the GitHub integration configured but is absent from githubQueue.repos; a CLI run with `Closes #42` produces no lifecycle updates.

candidates.title: A partial failure can release an issue before its failure label is applied
candidates.detail: The label loop removes in-progress before adding failed. If the add fails, reconciliation logs the failure and queue selection continues in the same poll. The existing latest-run admission check only finds issue-source runs, so it does not protect a failed CLI or MCP run linked through its prompt. The issue can be selected again using its old priority approval before the failed label is retried.
candidates.suggestion: Keep admission closed until the failure transition is durably reflected, including for prompt-linked runs; order label writes so a partial transition does not release the issue.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #42` fails; deleting in-progress succeeds but adding failed returns an error. The same poll sees the old priority label and starts a queue run without re-approval.

candidates.title: A removed priority label can satisfy failure re-approval
candidates.detail: The re-approval check accepts any trusted priority labeled event after failure, without requiring that event to correspond to a currently applied approved priority label. An old, still-present priority label can therefore supply the queue priority while a different, subsequently removed label supplies the purported re-approval.
candidates.suggestion: Require a currently applied trusted priority label whose latest application occurred after the failure event.
candidates.failure_scenario: priority:1 was applied before failure; after failure a trusted user applies and removes priority:9. The issue remains failed with priority:1, but becomes eligible.

candidates.title: An older run can overwrite a newer run's issue labels
candidates.detail: The latest-run map is computed once before any GitHub requests. If another run for the issue is created while a label request is awaiting, the old run remains designated latest and can complete its label transition after the newer run starts. Its completed cursor then prevents correction until the newer run is reconciled on a later poll.
candidates.suggestion: Recheck which run owns the issue after awaited operations and before each label mutation and completion checkpoint.
candidates.failure_scenario: While reconciliation fetches labels for a failed run, a new run for the same issue starts; the old reconciliation then applies failed and removes in-progress for the active run.

candidates.title: Persist lifecycle events when they occur, not only when a poll observes them
candidates.detail: The needs-human, failure, and cancellation comments are created only when reconciliation observes the corresponding current status. No pending effect exists until the comment loop reaches that event. A status that changes between polls, or while an earlier comment write is failing, is therefore never recorded or retried. The single done cursor also suppresses a second needs-human episode for the same run.
candidates.suggestion: Record each lifecycle event and its publication-safe content durably at the state transition, then let polling deliver each recorded event.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next poll; reconciliation sees the resumed status and never posts the required reason. Similarly, a failed started-comment write can delay processing until after needs_human has ended.

candidates.title: Reconcile issue-linked runs outside queue-enabled repositories
candidates.detail: Lifecycle processing is restricted to repositories listed in githubQueue with a nonempty trusted list, and the reconciler is started only when that queue is enabled. The request applies lifecycle updates to issue-linked runs from every start path; it does not condition those updates on queue admission being enabled for the repository.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and determine the target repository from each linked issue.
candidates.failure_scenario: An owner starts a run with Closes #12 in a repository not listed in githubQueue, or with the queue disabled. No lifecycle labels or new lifecycle comments are written for that issue.

candidates.title: Prevent re-pick while a failed label write is pending
candidates.detail: The new re-approval guard depends on the failed label being visible on GitHub. If that write fails, the queue continues selection in the same poll. The existing latestIssueRun lookup only considers issue source references, so it cannot supply a local failure guard for runs linked through a Closes directive.
candidates.suggestion: Use the existing admission and claim check to account for the latest linked run and its failure while the GitHub failure-label effect is pending.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run with Closes #12 fails, the GitHub failed-label POST fails, and issue #12 still has its previously trusted priority label. latestIssueRun returns no issue-sourced run, so the queue can immediately select the issue again without re-approval.

candidates.title: Authenticate the comment used as a delivery checkpoint
candidates.detail: A pending comment is considered delivered when any issue comment contains the predictable marker. The code does not verify the comment author or exact body, although issue comments are untrusted data. A third party can therefore make the reconciler mark a failed write as done without the factory ever posting the required comment.
candidates.suggestion: Verify that a matching comment was authored by the configured factory identity and matches the recorded body before marking the effect complete.
candidates.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails and leaves its effect pending, another issue participant posts a comment containing the run's lifecycle marker. On the next poll the factory treats that comment as its own and permanently skips the real update.

candidates.title: Lifecycle events can disappear between polls
candidates.detail: The reconciler derives needs-human and failure comments only from the current run status. If a run enters one of those states and is resolved or restarted before the next poll, no pending effect was recorded, so that event is never published. The pending-comment tests cover a status change only after a poll has already attempted the comment; they do not cover a transition entirely between polls.
candidates.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when the transitions occur, and add a test that enters needs_human or failed and leaves it before reconciliation runs.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resolves it before the next queue poll. The issue receives no needs-you comment or label for that event.

candidates.title: A removed priority label can satisfy re-approval
candidates.detail: The post-failure check accepts any trusted priority-label application in the timeline, even when that label is no longer present. An older, still-present priority label can separately satisfy the approved-label check, allowing a repick after the post-failure approval was removed. The new tests only use a post-failure event for a priority label that remains on the issue.
candidates.suggestion: Require the qualifying post-failure application to correspond to a currently applied, trusted priority label, and test removal of that label while an older priority label remains.
candidates.failure_scenario: An issue retains priority:1 from before failure. After failure, a trusted user applies priority:2 and then removes it; the issue is still eligible even though its remaining priority label was not re-applied after failure.

candidates.title: Restart-between-effects coverage exercises only the start event
candidates.detail: The restart test interrupts the initial in-progress label and started comment. The table-driven terminal-state tests restart only after both writes have completed, and the PR and merge tests likewise do not interrupt their transitions. Consequently, regressions in recovery between a needs-you, failed, cancellation, or merge label change and its associated comment are not covered as requested.
candidates.suggestion: Exercise interruption during each applicable lifecycle transition, then restart and assert the final label set and exactly one corresponding comment.
candidates.failure_scenario: A future change loses a failed comment after the failed label is written and the daemon restarts; the existing restart test still passes because it covers only the started event.

candidates.title: Encoded credentials can reach public issue comments
candidates.detail: The comment body is passed directly to literal credential redaction. The private-string check detects encoded private-string entries, but registered credentials are not necessarily entries in that list. A credential encoded in a run error can therefore be published in a form a reader can decode.
candidates.suggestion: Decode supported representations before credential redaction, or reject comment text containing encoded registered credentials before publication.
candidates.failure_scenario: A failed run's error contains a percent-encoded registered token that is absent from private-strings.txt; the posted failure comment contains the encoded token.

candidates.title: An unrelated comment can satisfy a pending publication checkpoint
candidates.detail: Retry reconciliation trusts a marker found in any issue comment without checking its author or body. Issue comments are untrusted input, so a commenter who knows a run ID can make the factory record an effect as completed even though the factory never posted it.
candidates.suggestion: Verify the comment belongs to the expected GitHub identity and matches the saved publication body before marking the effect done.
candidates.failure_scenario: A user posts the predictable failed-event marker, and the factory's subsequent comment POST fails before reaching GitHub. On the next poll, the user's marker causes the pending failure comment to be marked done.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to configured queue repositories
candidates.detail: The lifecycle reconciler skips repositories outside githubQueue.repos, and it is not started when the issue queue is disabled. The request requires updates for runs started through CLI, MCP, label, and comment paths as well as the queue; those paths can target repositories that are not configured for automatic issue selection.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and cover all repositories for which linked runs can be created.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #123` targets a configured repository outside githubQueue.repos; it receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

candidates.title: A removed priority label can satisfy re-approval
candidates.detail: The post-failure check accepts any historical trusted priority application, even when that label is no longer present. The separate approved-label check can be satisfied by a different priority label that predates the failure, so the two checks together do not establish that a current priority label was re-applied after failure.
candidates.suggestion: Require the post-failure event to be the latest trusted application of a currently present approved priority label.
candidates.failure_scenario: An issue retains priority:2 from before failure. A trusted user applies and then removes priority:1 after failure; the historical priority:1 event permits the issue to be picked using the stale priority:2 label.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to queue-configured repositories
candidates.detail: The request covers “any start path: queue, `limitless run` with `Closes #n`, MCP, label or comment trigger.” Reconciliation skips repositories outside `githubQueue.repos`, and the reconciler is not started at all when the queue is disabled. Consequently, runs started through those other paths receive no lifecycle labels or the required comments unless their repository also happens to be configured for the issue queue.
