candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #7` starts in a repository with no issue-queue configuration; no in-progress label or start comment is posted.

candidates.title: Transient lifecycle events are lost between polls
candidates.detail: The request requires each label change and comment to be a recorded side effect with a durable checkpoint. Here needs-human, failed, and cancelled events are discovered only from the current status. If a run enters and leaves one of those states before a poll observes it, no effect is recorded and its comment is permanently lost. The initial in-progress label can likewise be skipped if the run reaches a later state before its first poll.
candidates.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when the corresponding transitions occur, then reconcile each recorded effect independently of the current status.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll; the reconciler never posts the needs-you reason or applies its label.

candidates.title: Repeated needs-human episodes share one comment checkpoint
candidates.detail: The comment effect is keyed only by run and event name. Once `comment:needs_human` is done, a later needs-human transition in the same resumed run is suppressed, including its new reason. The request requires a comment when a run reaches needs_human, and the second episode is a distinct transition.
candidates.suggestion: Key lifecycle effects by a durable transition or status-episode identifier.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run asks for human help, resumes after an answer, then needs human help again for a different reason; only the first reason is posted.

candidates.title: A failed label write can allow a failed CLI issue to be picked

A failed CLI or MCP run linked through `Closes #n` has no such reference. Until the failed label is successfully written, the queue therefore sees neither the failure label nor that latest failed run and can select the issue without re-approval.

candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run for `Closes #7` fails, the GitHub failed-label write errors, and the issue still has its previously approved priority label; the same poll can create a queue run for it.

candidates.suggestion: Use the ordered timeline events to determine whether a trusted priority application follows the failure event, including ties in timestamps.

Lines 63–71 reread only `store.getRun(snapshot.id)` and its desired status, without checking whether a newer run now owns the issue.

findings.title: Transient lifecycle events disappear before they are checkpointed

findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human while the started comment write is failing, then is resumed before the next poll. No needs-you comment is ever posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101–102 adds the event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`. The loop processes `"started"` first (line 110), checkpoints only the current event with `save(effect, "pending")` (line 161), and stops on failure with `break` (line 167).

findings.title: A second needs-human episode is treated as already delivered

findings.failure_scenario: A run needs human input, resumes after the owner responds, and later needs human input for a different reason. The second reason is never commented.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:112 uses the run-wide key `const effect = `comment:${event}``; line 114 skips it whenever `state(effect) === "done"`. Line 164 permanently saves that state after the first successful comment.
verification.trigger: A run completes one needs-human episode, resumes, and later needs human input for another reason. The existing comment:needs_human checkpoint suppresses the second comment.

findings.title: Re-approval can come from a priority label that is no longer applied
findings.detail: The post-failure check accepts any trusted priority labeled event, even if that label was subsequently removed. The separate approved check can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before the failure, so the current approval need not be the one applied after failure.

findings.failure_scenario: Priority:2 was applied before failure; a trusted user applies and removes priority:1 after failure. The issue remains eligible using the old priority:2 label despite the later approval having been withdrawn.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:74–81 derives `approved` from current labels, but independently src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:99 checks `events.some((e) => trusts(e.actor?.login) && Date.parse(e.createdAt) > failedAt)`. Those events include historical applications of removed priority labels (lines 61–63).
verification.trigger: Keep trusted priority:2 from before failure; apply and remove priority:1 afterward. The historical priority:1 event supplies re-approval while priority:2 supplies current approval, making the failed issue eligible despite withdrawal.

findings.title: An unrelated comment can impersonate a completed lifecycle write
findings.detail: Recovery treats any issue comment containing the predictable marker as proof that the factory posted its pending comment, without checking its author. An issue participant can supply that marker and cause the actual lifecycle comment to be permanently marked done.
findings.suggestion: Verify the recovered comment was authored by the configured factory identity and matches the pending body before marking the effect done.
findings.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails, another issue participant posts a comment containing the run's marker. On the next poll the factory records the failed comment as delivered and never retries it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:123 parses comments using only `z.object({ body: z.string() })`. Lines 128–130 accept `comments.some((c) => c.body.includes(marker))` and then `save(effect, "done")`, without checking the author or complete body.
verification.trigger: After a failed comment POST leaves a pending checkpoint, another participant posts the predictable marker. Reconciliation treats that unrelated comment as successful delivery and never retries the factory comment.

findings.title: A 404 during label removal is silently recorded as success

findings.failure_scenario: The initial label read succeeds, but the App loses repository access before the DELETE. GitHub returns 404 and the reconciliation cursor records the label set as complete even though the label remains.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:86 swallows any removal error matching HTTP 404: `if (add || !/\bHTTP 404\b/.test(String(error))) throw error;`. It then calls `save(effect, "done")` (line 88) and saves the complete label cursor (line 92). Line 56 skips subsequent reconciliation when that cursor matches.
verification.trigger: During a removal-only transition, label reading succeeds but repository access is lost before DELETE. Its HTTP 404 is recorded as success, leaving the label present without logging or retrying the failed removal.

findings.title: Status transitions between polls never produce their comments
findings.detail: Lifecycle comments are derived from the current run status. A needs_human episode that begins and ends between polls is never recorded as pending, so its required comment is permanently lost. The pending-comment tests cover a transition only after a poll has already observed it.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur and reconcile those records. Add a test that enters and leaves needs_human between polls, then restarts and checks for exactly one comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next issue-queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 invokes `reconcileIssueLifecycle` during polling. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:97 reads the current run, and lines 101–102 generate needs_human only from its current status. Line 113 skips an absent event unless it was already pending.
verification.trigger: A run enters and leaves needs_human between polls. No lifecycle checkpoint captures that episode, so its needs-you comment is never posted.

findings.title: A removed priority label can supply re-approval
findings.detail: The re-approval check accepts any trusted priority-label event after failure, even if that label is no longer present. The separate approved-label check can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before failure. The tests only exercise re-approval using the currently present label and miss this combination.
findings.suggestion: Require a currently applied, trusted priority label whose applicable labeling event is later than the failure event. Add a test with an old current priority and a later trusted priority that has since been removed.
findings.failure_scenario: priority:1 remains from before failure; a trusted user adds and then removes priority:2 after failure. The issue becomes eligible despite having no current priority approval applied after failure.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:99 accepts any trusted priority application after failure: `events.some((e) => trusts(e.actor?.login) && Date.parse(e.createdAt) > failedAt)`. It does not require that event's label to appear among current labels used by `approved` at lines 74–81.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside the issue queue configuration
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation requires the repository to be in githubQueue.repos with trusted accounts configured, and the poller does not start without that configuration. findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation for linked GitHub issues independently of queue admission configuration, and test a CLI or MCP run when queue polling is disabled.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner starts a run with Closes #7 in a GitHub repository that is not enabled for automatic issue picking; the issue receives neither labels nor comments.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10–12 defines lifecycleManaged as `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length && cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; line 43 skips issues with `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:144 also disables the poller without queue repositories and trusted accounts.

findings.title: Restart coverage does not exercise each lifecycle transition
findings.detail: The interruption matrix only interrupts the initial started event. findings.suggestion: Exercise interruption after the label update and before the comment for each applicable transition, then reopen the store and verify the final labels and exactly one comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that loses a failed or needs-human comment after its label write can pass the current restart tests.

verification.evidence: test/issue-queue.test.ts:1275–1298 parameterizes interruption only by `["after label", "after comment"]` for a newly created run and checks `"comment:started"`. verification.trigger: A regression specific to failed or needs-human recovery after the label write but before the comment checkpoint could lose the comment while all existing restart tests pass.

findings.title: Do not accept an arbitrary issue comment as proof of a factory write
findings.detail: Recovery treats any comment containing the predictable lifecycle marker as proof that the factory posted its comment. Issue comments are untrusted: their author is neither retrieved nor checked. An attacker who can comment can therefore suppress a pending lifecycle notification.

findings.failure_scenario: A comment POST fails or the daemon restarts after marking it pending. Another issue participant posts a comment containing `<!-- limitless-lifecycle:<run-id>:failed -->`. On the next poll, reconciliation marks the failed notification done without posting it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:123 parses comments using only `z.object({ body: z.string() })`. Lines 128–130 accept `comments.some((c) => c.body.includes(marker))`, then `save(effect, "done")` and continue without posting.

findings.title: Tie re-approval to a priority label that is still applied

verification.trigger: Retain trusted priority:2 from before failure, then apply and remove priority:1 after failure. The two independent checks succeed using different labels, permitting another run after approval was withdrawn.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only runs when the issue queue has trusted accounts and only processes repositories listed in that queue. Consequently, CLI, MCP, label-triggered, and comment-triggered runs against other repositories receive no lifecycle labels or durable lifecycle comments, even though the request covers any start path.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and include all repositories with linked issues.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both event bodies always contain only a UI link and never inspect the run's reason. The fixed message is required as a fallback when publication checks block the reason, but this code uses it for every run. The new tests explicitly assert that the original reason is absent.

findings.title: A blocked comment is marked done without posting the required fallback
findings.detail: If the publication check rejects a comment, the effect is permanently marked done instead of creating and delivering a fixed safe message. The same suppression happens during the delivery-time recheck. This loses the lifecycle notification permanently.

findings.title: Lifecycle transitions between polls are lost
findings.detail: The poller derives events solely from the current run status and records no transition at the point the status changes. A needs-human or failure state that is resolved before the next poll is never observed, so neither its comment nor its corresponding label is applied. A single effect key per event also prevents a second needs-human episode from producing a comment.
findings.suggestion: Persist lifecycle events with the state transition and reconcile those durable records on subsequent polls.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resolves it before the next queue poll; the issue never receives the needs-you update or reason.

duplicates.title: Transient lifecycle states are lost between polls

This also affects transitions while the daemon is stopped.
duplicates.suggestion: Persist lifecycle events at the corresponding state transitions, then let polling deliver their checkpointed effects.

findings.title: A failed issue can be picked before the failure label is applied
findings.detail: When the failed label is absent, eligibility falls back to accepting any trusted priority event after the run finished. If the lifecycle label write fails, that approval can occur before the failure label exists, yet the next queue poll can select the issue. This violates the required ordering after the failure label was applied.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories
candidates.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only runs when the issue queue has trusted accounts and only processes repositories listed in that queue. Consequently, CLI, MCP, label-triggered, and comment-triggered runs against other repositories receive no lifecycle labels or durable lifecycle comments, even though the request covers any start path.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and include all repositories with linked issues.
candidates.failure_scenario: A repository is configured for GitHub integration but not in githubQueue.repos; `limitless run` with `Closes #7` starts and no in-progress label or start comment is posted.

candidates.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
candidates.detail: Both event bodies always contain only a UI link and never inspect the run's reason. The fixed message is required as a fallback when publication checks block the reason, but this code uses it for every run. The new tests explicitly assert that the original reason is absent.
candidates.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after credential redaction and private-string checking, falling back to fixed text when it cannot be published.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run fails with `error: "tests failed"`; the issue receives only `failed: see ...` and the owner cannot see the requested reason in the comment.

candidates.title: A blocked comment is marked done without posting the required fallback
candidates.detail: If the publication check rejects a comment, the effect is permanently marked done instead of creating and delivering a fixed safe message. The same suppression happens during the delivery-time recheck. This loses the lifecycle notification permanently.
candidates.suggestion: Construct and check a fixed safe fallback and retain a pending effect until it is delivered.
candidates.failure_scenario: A configured private string matches the generated run link or run ID; the start comment is marked done and no comment is ever posted.

candidates.title: Lifecycle transitions between polls are lost
candidates.detail: The poller derives events solely from the current run status and records no transition at the point the status changes. A needs-human or failure state that is resolved before the next poll is never observed, so neither its comment nor its corresponding label is applied. A single effect key per event also prevents a second needs-human episode from producing a comment.
candidates.suggestion: Persist lifecycle events with the state transition and reconcile those durable records on subsequent polls.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resolves it before the next queue poll; the issue never receives the needs-you update or reason.

duplicates.title: Transient lifecycle states are lost between polls
duplicates.detail: The reconciler creates effects only from the current run snapshot. It does not durably record a needs-human transition when it happens, so a transition that is resolved or resumed before the next poll produces neither the required comment nor its label change. This also affects transitions while the daemon is stopped.
duplicates.suggestion: Persist lifecycle events at the corresponding state transitions, then let polling deliver their checkpointed effects.
duplicates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and an owner resumes it before the next queue poll; the issue never receives the needs-you update.

candidates.title: A failed issue can be picked before the failure label is applied
candidates.detail: When the failed label is absent, eligibility falls back to accepting any trusted priority event after the run finished. If the lifecycle label write fails, that approval can occur before the failure label exists, yet the next queue poll can select the issue. This violates the required ordering after the failure label was applied.
candidates.suggestion: Keep failed runs ineligible until the failure label application is observed and a trusted priority event follows it.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run fails, adding `limitless:failed` fails, and a trusted user reapplies priority before the next poll. The issue has no failed label, so the timestamp fallback admits it without a priority event after the failure label.

candidates.title: Failure and needs-you comments omit the reason

candidates.failure_scenario: A run fails with an ordinary, publishable error such as "tests failed"; the issue receives only "failed: see ..." and its watchers cannot see the reason.

candidates.title: Publication errors permanently discard comments

The same permanent suppression occurs when rechecking a pending body at line 248.
candidates.suggestion: Post a checked fixed fallback for a private-string match, and leave unexpected inspection failures pending for a later retry.
candidates.failure_scenario: A private string matches the generated UI link, or the private-strings file is temporarily unreadable; the lifecycle event is recorded as done without any issue comment and remains absent after the condition is corrected.

candidates.title: A failed label write permits re-pick based on an earlier approval
candidates.detail: When the failed label is absent, admission falls back to any trusted priority event after the run finished. The next queue scan can therefore start another run without the required approval after the label.
candidates.suggestion: Keep a failed run ineligible until the failure label has been observed and a trusted priority application is observed after that label.

verification.trigger: A CLI or MCP run closes an issue in a repository absent from githubQueue.repos. Its lifecycle labels and comments are skipped, despite the requirement covering every start path.

findings.title: Failure and needs-you comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both event bodies contain only a generic status and UI link. The requested reason is never read from the run or sanitized for publication, so issue watchers cannot see why the run failed or needs attention.
findings.suggestion: Include the available reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, with a fixed fallback when publication is blocked.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a public error such as `tests failed`; the issue comment says only `failed: see …` and does not report the error.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82–83: `events.set("needs_human", `needs you: see ${link}.`)` and `events.set("failed", `failed: see ${link}.`)`. These bodies include no error or question text.
verification.trigger: A run fails with a publishable reason such as 'tests failed', or reaches needs_human with a public question. The issue comment omits the required reason.

findings.title: A blocked publication check permanently drops the comment
findings.detail: If the private-strings check rejects a generated comment, the effect is marked done without posting anything. The request requires a fixed safe message in this case. Marking it done also prevents a later poll from correcting the omission.
findings.suggestion: Create and deliver a fixed safe fallback body when the original text is blocked, retaining a pending effect until delivery succeeds.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured UI link contains a private string, so `checkBody` throws for a started or terminal comment. The effect is stored as done and no comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:93–100 checks the body, then on error executes `save(effect, "done"); logFailure(...)`. Line 87 skips existing effects: `if (effects.has(effect)) continue;`. No fixed fallback comment is queued.
verification.trigger: A configured UI URL contains a private string and publication checking rejects the comment. The effect becomes permanently done without posting the required fixed fallback message.

findings.title: Failure and needs-you comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both comments use fixed text and never include the run's reason. The request requires a reason, subject to redaction and private-string checking, so an owner watching the issue cannot tell why the run stopped.
findings.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after sanitization and publication checks, using the fixed message when the reason cannot be published.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a gate error or reaches needs_human with a question; the issue comment only says to see the UI.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82–83 constructs only `needs you: see ${link}.` and `failed: see ${link}.`; line 95 wraps that fixed text with the run id. Neither reason nor question is included.
verification.trigger: A gate failure or needs_human question has a publishable explanation. The lifecycle comment directs readers to the UI without reporting the required reason. This duplicates C4.

findings.title: A blocked comment is permanently discarded instead of replaced
findings.detail: When publication checking throws, the effect is marked done without posting. The request explicitly requires a fixed fallback message when private-string checking blocks the text. The delivery-time check similarly marks the effect done on any error, including potentially temporary inspection errors, so it will never be retried.
findings.suggestion: Post a checked fixed fallback for blocked text, and leave effects pending when an inspection failure cannot be resolved safely.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the UI link or comment text, or the private-string check fails temporarily; no lifecycle comment is posted on this or later polls.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:98–100 catches publication rejection with `save(effect, "done"); logFailure(run, repo, number, error);`. Line 87 then skips it forever: `if (effects.has(effect)) continue;`. No fallback is created.
verification.trigger: A private string in the comment or UI URL causes publication validation to throw; the notification is permanently discarded instead of replaced with fixed text.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: The only reconciliation entry point is the issue queue, and lifecycleManaged further restricts writes to its configured repositories. The requested lifecycle applies to all listed start paths, including manual and trigger-created runs, but those runs receive no lifecycle labels when their repository is not in the queue configuration or the queue is disabled.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and include issue-linked runs from all applicable repositories.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #42` in a repository not listed in githubQueue.repos; no in-progress label or lifecycle comment is delivered.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:11–13 requires `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length && cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`. Lines 110 and 116 gate observation and delivery on `lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)`. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:156 also disables the poller when queue configuration is absent.
verification.trigger: A CLI run contains `Closes #42` for a repository outside githubQueue.repos; it receives neither lifecycle labels nor lifecycle comments, despite the requirement covering every start path.

duplicates.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories
duplicates.detail: The request requires updates for “any start path,” but lifecycleManaged only accepts repositories in githubQueue.repos with trusted accounts configured, and the reconciler runs only when the queue is enabled. A CLI, MCP, label-triggered, or comment-triggered run in another configured repository therefore receives no lifecycle labels or durable lifecycle comments.
duplicates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of issue-queue admission configuration and include linked issues from every supported start path.
duplicates.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #12` for a repository not listed in githubQueue.repos; no in-progress label or start comment is posted.

findings.title: Transitions between polls are never recorded
findings.detail: Events are derived solely from the current run snapshot, and each event type has only one effect key. A needs_human state that is resolved before the next poll is invisible; a later needs_human episode is also suppressed if the first was already recorded. This does not provide a durable checkpoint for each lifecycle event.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably at the state transition, with an identity for each occurrence, and let the poller deliver those records.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next poll; the needs-you label and comment are never produced.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82 creates the event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; lines 105–110 observe current runs during reconciliation. src/db/store.ts:2083–2089 updates the current row and publishes it without recording a lifecycle effect. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:307 schedules reconciliation by `q.pollSeconds`.
verification.trigger: A run enters needs_human and resumes between reconciliation polls. The next observation sees the resumed status, so no needs-you comment or label is recorded or delivered.

findings.title: Admission can re-pick a failed issue before its failure label is written
findings.detail: If the failure-label write fails or is deferred, the issue has no current failed label. Eligibility then falls back to accepting any trusted priority application after finishedAt, even though the required failure-label application has not happened. Reconciliation errors are nonfatal and admission proceeds in the same poll.
findings.suggestion: Keep a failed run ineligible until its failure label is confirmed and a trusted priority application follows that label.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, its label write encounters a GitHub error, and a trusted user reapplies priority before the next poll. The queue can start another run without any approval after the failure label.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:88 defines `failed` solely from current GitHub labels. At :117–123, `context.latest.status === "failed" && failed` gates the failure-event ordering check; otherwise a trusted priority event after finishedAt suffices. Admission at :265–269 calls this same eligibility function with `latest: factory.store.latestIssueRun(repo, issue.number)` and adds no pending-label guard. Lifecycle write errors are logged and swallowed at src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:227–234.
verification.trigger: After in-progress removal succeeds and failure-label addition fails, a trusted user reapplies priority after the run finishes. If the failure label remains unwritten during the next scan, admission permits a replacement run without any priority application after the failure label.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both event bodies use fixed text and never include the run's reason, although the request requires a comment with the reason. The tests explicitly assert that the original reason is absent, so they encode the defect rather than catch it.
findings.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, and test both safe and sensitive reasons.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a safe error such as "typecheck failed"; the issue comment only says "failed: see" and links to the UI.

findings.title: A blocked publication is marked done without posting the required fallback
findings.detail: When the private-strings check rejects a comment, the effect is marked done and no comment is posted. The request requires a fixed safe message in this case. The test at test/issue-queue.test.ts:1559 explicitly expects suppression, so it asserts the wrong behavior.
findings.suggestion: Construct and validate a fixed fallback message, post it when the original text is blocked, and test that it is posted exactly once.
findings.failure_scenario: A lifecycle comment contains a configured private string; its checkpoint becomes done and the issue never receives the corresponding notification.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:98–100 marks rejected comments `done` without posting a fallback. findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` for a repository that is not enabled in the issue queue; no label or comment is written.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:11–13: `lifecycleManaged` requires `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length` and membership in `cfg.githubQueue.repos`. Lines 109–116 guard observation and delivery with this predicate. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:156 additionally returns immediately without queue configuration.

findings.detail: The reconciler creates event checkpoints only from the current run status. If a run reaches needs_human or failed and then changes status before the next poll, there is no recorded event to reconcile, so its label and comment are never delivered. The tests change status and poll before changing it again; they do not cover an unobserved intermediate transition.

findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll; the issue never receives the needs-you label or comment.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82: `if (run.status === "needs_human") events.set("needs_human", ...)`. Lines 105–111 observe current run snapshots only. src/db/store.ts:2083–2088 updates the run and publishes it without recording lifecycle effects; reconciliation is invoked by the poll at src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:203.
verification.trigger: A run enters needs_human and resumes between lifecycle polls. The next observation sees the resumed status, so no needs-you label or comment is recorded or delivered.

findings.title: Blocked comments are permanently discarded instead of replaced
findings.detail: When the private-strings check rejects a comment, the effect is marked done without posting the required fixed fallback. The same happens if a pending comment fails its publication check at delivery. The checkpoint prevents a later poll from recovering the missing notification.
findings.suggestion: For a private-text match, checkpoint and publish a fixed safe message; retain a retryable state when the publication check itself cannot be performed.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the UI URL or run ID. A run fails, the failed comment is marked done, and the issue receives no failure comment.

verification.trigger: A configured private string survives sanitization in the UI URL or run ID. Comment validation throws, permanently completing the effect without posting the required fixed replacement message.

findings.title: Needs-human and failure comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both event bodies contain only a generic status and UI link; neither includes the run's reason. The requested fallback is appropriate when text cannot be published safely, but this implementation uses it for every event, including ordinary publishable reasons.
findings.suggestion: Include the relevant reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, falling back to a fixed message when it is blocked.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a non-sensitive error such as a failed build. The issue comment says only that the run failed and does not tell the watcher why.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation is enabled only for repositories listed in githubQueue with trusted accounts configured, and the reconciler is started only when that queue is enabled. findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation for issue-linked runs independently of queue admission configuration, while retaining queue configuration for picking issues.
findings.failure_scenario: A repository uses `limitless run` with `Closes #7` but has no issue queue configured. The run starts and fails without any lifecycle updates to issue 7.

verification.trigger: A repository has no issue queue configured and receives a CLI run with `Closes #7`. The lifecycle reconciler never runs for it, so starting and failing the run produce no lifecycle updates.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: The table requires a “comment with the reason” for both needs_human and failed. Both bodies contain only a generic status and UI link, regardless of the recorded run error or question. The added tests explicitly assert that the original reason is absent.
findings.suggestion: Include the recorded public-safe reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, using the specified fixed fallback when it cannot be published.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a gate error or needs a specific owner decision; issue watchers receive only “failed: see” or “needs you: see” and cannot see why.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82–83 constructs only `events.set("needs_human", `needs you: see ${link}.`)` and `events.set("failed", `failed: see ${link}.`)`. Neither includes the run's reason. test/issue-queue.test.ts:1392 explicitly asserts the comment does `not.toContain("original reason")`.
verification.trigger: A non-discreet linked run fails or needs an owner decision; its comment omits the reason explicitly required by the request.

findings.title: A blocked publication check discards the comment instead of posting a fallback
findings.detail: The request says “If the check blocks the text, post a fixed message without it.” The catch instead marks the comment done without posting anything; the same behavior occurs when a pending body fails its later check. It will never be retried.
findings.suggestion: Checkpoint and post a fixed safe fallback when publication text is blocked, retaining retry behavior for write failures.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the run ID or UI URL used in the comment; the check rejects the body and the issue receives no comment for that event.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:93–100 checks the body, then handles rejection with `save(effect, "done"); logFailure(run, repo, number, error);`, without creating a fallback. The delivery-time check likewise marks it done and skips posting at src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:247–251: `save(effect, "done"); ... continue;`.
verification.trigger: A private string in the constructed comment causes publication validation to reject it; the event is permanently marked done without the required fixed fallback comment.

findings.title: Polling snapshots lose lifecycle transitions between polls
findings.detail: The request requires each lifecycle event to have a durable checkpoint, including across restarts. This code discovers needs_human, failed, and cancelled only from the current run status at reconciliation time. A transition that is resolved or otherwise changed before the next poll is never recorded, and a second needs_human episode is also suppressed by the single `comment:needs_human` key.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur and reconcile those records, with an identity for each applicable episode.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resolved before the next queue poll; no needs-you label or reason comment is ever recorded or posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:105–111 obtains `store.issueLifecycleRuns()` and calls `observe(run, repo, number)` on those snapshots. Event creation requires the current status at :82: `if (run.status === "needs_human")`. src/db/store.ts:2112–2115 permits resolving needs_human and overwrites status with `status: "resolved"`; the lifecycle query at :1244–1256 reads current run fields, not transition history.
verification.trigger: A run enters needs_human and is resolved between lifecycle polls. The next observation sees resolved, so the needs_human event is never checkpointed and its label and comment are never delivered.

findings.title: A failed run can be picked again before its failure label is applied
findings.detail: The request requires “No re-pick after failure without re-approval” after the failure label was applied. When the failure label is absent, the admission check falls back to accepting any trusted priority event after finishedAt. Reconciliation can remove in-progress and then fail or exhaust its call budget before adding failed, while queue admission still proceeds in the same poll.
findings.suggestion: Keep admission closed for a failed run until its failure label has been applied and a trusted priority-label event is observed after that application, using the existing admission check.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, a trusted user applies a priority label before the failed-label write succeeds, and the in-progress label has already been removed. The next candidate check admits the issue without a priority application after the failure label.

candidates.title: A failed run can be picked again before its failure label is applied

Consequently, issue-linked CLI, MCP, label, and comment runs outside that configuration never receive the requested lifecycle labels or comments.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation for issue-linked runs independently of queue admission configuration, while retaining queue configuration for picking issues.
candidates.failure_scenario: A repository uses `limitless run` with `Closes #7` but has no issue queue configured. The run starts and fails without any lifecycle updates to issue 7.

candidates.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
candidates.detail: The table requires a “comment with the reason” for both needs_human and failed. Both bodies contain only a generic status and UI link, regardless of the recorded run error or question. The added tests explicitly assert that the original reason is absent.
candidates.suggestion: Include the recorded public-safe reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, using the specified fixed fallback when it cannot be published.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run fails with a gate error or needs a specific owner decision; issue watchers receive only “failed: see” or “needs you: see” and cannot see why.

candidates.title: A blocked publication check discards the comment instead of posting a fallback
candidates.detail: The request says “If the check blocks the text, post a fixed message without it.” The catch instead marks the comment done without posting anything; the same behavior occurs when a pending body fails its later check. It will never be retried.
candidates.suggestion: Checkpoint and post a fixed safe fallback when publication text is blocked, retaining retry behavior for write failures.
candidates.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the run ID or UI URL used in the comment; the check rejects the body and the issue receives no comment for that event.

candidates.title: Polling snapshots lose lifecycle transitions between polls
candidates.detail: The request requires each lifecycle event to have a durable checkpoint, including across restarts. This code discovers needs_human, failed, and cancelled only from the current run status at reconciliation time. A transition that is resolved or otherwise changed before the next poll is never recorded, and a second needs_human episode is also suppressed by the single `comment:needs_human` key.
candidates.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur and reconcile those records, with an identity for each applicable episode.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resolved before the next queue poll; no needs-you label or reason comment is ever recorded or posted.

candidates.title: A failed run can be picked again before its failure label is applied
candidates.detail: The request requires “No re-pick after failure without re-approval” after the failure label was applied. When the failure label is absent, the admission check falls back to accepting any trusted priority event after finishedAt. Reconciliation can remove in-progress and then fail or exhaust its call budget before adding failed, while queue admission still proceeds in the same poll.
candidates.suggestion: Keep admission closed for a failed run until its failure label has been applied and a trusted priority-label event is observed after that application, using the existing admission check.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run fails, a trusted user applies a priority label before the failed-label write succeeds, and the in-progress label has already been removed. The next candidate check admits the issue without a priority application after the failure label.

findings.title: An initially empty repository discards its first commands
findings.detail: A successful poll with no open issues stores no enable boundary. When an issue and command later appear, that later poll establishes the boundary from their timestamps and skips the command as if it existed at enablement. The added test explicitly expects this loss.
findings.suggestion: Establish a durable GitHub-time boundary on the first successful poll even when there are no open issues.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the queue while the repository has no open issues, then create an issue and post a trusted command before the next poll. No run is ever created for that command.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:272-275 derives `newest` from `issues.nodes` and persists it only with `if (newest) factory.store.githubCommentBoundary(repo, newest)`. Line 282 processes comments only when `boundary` exists; line 301 skips timestamps `<=` that boundary. test/issue-queue.test.ts:3015 explicitly tests that an empty repository stays uninitialized and its subsequent first command never runs.
verification.trigger: An empty successful first poll stores no boundary. The next poll containing the new issue and command establishes a boundary at or after that command, permanently excluding it.

findings.title: Identity lookup failure bypasses the factory-author exclusion
findings.detail: An identity lookup error is converted to null, but slash commands continue to be processed. With no bot login, the factory-author comparison cannot exclude the App's own account. If that account is trusted, its command is admitted and permanently recorded even though the invariant forbids factory-authored commands.
findings.suggestion: Fail closed for comment processing when the factory identity needed to identify its author cannot be established, leaving comments retryable.
findings.failure_scenario: The trusted list includes the App bot, identity lookup temporarily fails, and the bot has posted `/limitless do work` after the boundary. The poll creates a run from the factory's own comment.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:278 catches identity failure with `.catch(() => null)`; line 280 sets `bot` to null. The exclusion at line 298 is only `author.toLowerCase() === bot`, while lines 284-285 still parse slash commands and lines 318-324 invoke `factory.createRun`.
verification.trigger: With an established boundary, a trusted App bot's unedited, marker-free slash command passes the factory-author guard when identity lookup fails and can create a run.

findings.title: Canonicalized names no longer resolve existing mixed-case repository registrations
findings.detail: The queue passes the lowercased repository name into run creation. Repository resolution uses a case-sensitive getRepoBySlug lookup, so an existing mixed-case registration is missed. Resolution then calls GitHub and creates a second repository record with default settings. This can lose the existing registration's merge policy and default branch, and queue admission can fail when the extra GitHub lookup fails.
findings.suggestion: Use canonical keys for comparisons and snapshots while preserving or resolving the registered repository's spelling for run creation.
findings.failure_scenario: A queue configured for Owner/Repo already has a registered Owner/Repo with a custom merge policy. The queue now requests owner/repo, misses that registration, and creates a separate record using the global default policy.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:261 lowercases the repository: `const repo = configuredRepo.toLowerCase()`, then passes it to `issueRunRequest` at :434–436. src/app.ts:398 calls `resolveRepo(this.store, req.repo, this.cfg.githubMerge)`. src/db/store.ts:1222 uses case-sensitive `SELECT * FROM repos WHERE slug = ?`. src/git/repos.ts:209–215 creates the missing registration with `slug` and `mergePolicy: merge`.
verification.trigger: An existing Owner/Repo registration has a custom merge policy. Queue admission resolves owner/repo instead, creating a second registration with the global merge policy.

findings.title: Lowercasing configured repositories bypasses existing registrations
findings.detail: Queue requests now use the lowercased slug, but repository registration and resolveRepo lookups are case-sensitive. An existing registration such as Owner/Repo is therefore not found when the queue creates a run for owner/repo. resolveRepo instead performs a GitHub lookup and creates a second registration with default settings, losing the existing registration's repository-specific settings. If that lookup fails, queue admission fails altogether.
findings.suggestion: Deduplicate using lowercase comparison keys while preserving a configured spelling for repository resolution, or make repository resolution reuse existing registrations case-insensitively.
findings.failure_scenario: A queue configured for Owner/Repo has an existing Owner/Repo registration with a custom merge policy. After upgrade, an approved issue is admitted as owner/repo and resolves to a newly created registration using the default merge policy.

findings.title: Changes before the repository snapshot still invalidate it
findings.detail: The listener records changes from the start of the poll, and the snapshot no longer clears invalidations. A change completed before `latestIssueRuns` is read is therefore treated as if it made that fresh snapshot stale. Repeated changes during lifecycle reconciliation or the repository lookup can defer an otherwise eligible issue on every poll.
findings.suggestion: Track whether each issue already has a snapshot when its linked run changes, while preserving invalidations for earlier candidates when a case-variant repository is read.
findings.failure_scenario: A linked run finishes during each poll's GitHub lookup, before the queue reads the latest run snapshot. The snapshot includes the finished state, but admission still refuses the issue indefinitely.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:251–259 subscribes before awaiting lifecycle reconciliation and adds changed issue keys to `invalidated`. The later snapshot at :318–322 only calls `snapshots.set(repo, latest)`; it does not clear prior invalidations. Admission at :401–404 skips any invalidated issue.
verification.trigger: A decision-relevant linked-run change occurs during GitHub lookup before the snapshot. Although the snapshot contains the new state, an otherwise eligible issue is deferred. Repeating such changes each poll repeats the deferral.

findings.title: No test covers a relevant publication before the snapshot
findings.detail: The new decision-field tests publish during the second repository lookup, after the first repository's snapshot. They do not verify that a change observed before an issue's own snapshot is incorporated into that snapshot and does not defer admission. This gap hides the new indefinite deferral defect.
findings.suggestion: Publish a status or finish-time change during the issue's own lookup on consecutive polls, then assert that the fresh snapshot permits an eligible issue to start.
findings.failure_scenario: A linked run changes before `latestIssueRuns` executes, but the queue rejects the fresh snapshot as invalidated; the added tests still pass because they only change it after the snapshot.

At :401–404, `changedDuringPoll(...)` overrides eligibility and skips admission. test/issue-queue.test.ts:1267 triggers changes only during `name:"b"`, after owner/a's snapshot.

The fresh snapshot permits admission, but the earlier invalidation still defers it. The added tests do not cover this ordering.

findings.title: Lowercasing configured slugs bypasses existing mixed-case registrations
findings.detail: Configuration now rewrites every queue repository to lowercase, but `resolveRepo` and `getRepoBySlug` still look up registered slugs case-sensitively. An existing registration such as `Owner/Repo` is missed when the queue creates a run for `owner/repo`, causing a remote lookup and potentially a second repository registration with different settings. The queue tests use a fake factory and do not exercise this resolution path.

findings.failure_scenario: A deployment already has `Owner/Repo` registered and configured in the queue. After the change, queue admission requests `owner/repo`, misses the registered row, and resolves or creates a separate repository instead.

verification.trigger: Only Owner/Repo is registered before upgrade. Queue admission now requests owner/repo, misses the existing row, and creates a separate repository registration when GitHub resolution succeeds.

findings.title: Avoid resolving every historical run individually on each poll
findings.detail: Every poll loads every run and calls `linkedIssues` for each one; that function performs a recursive ownership query even for ordinary root runs. This introduces a synchronous query per historical run, including runs unrelated to configured queue repositories, and parses every stored prompt. The work grows with the entire database and can again block the daemon on each poll, undermining the stall reduction this follow-up is meant to preserve.

findings.title: Classify the moved tip before discarding a release intent
findings.detail: Every `moved` result from a replay marks the confirmed lease lost and clears the intent without examining the returned tip. findings.detail: Reconciliation delegates a pending release to `reconcileLeaseIntent`, which can replay the release with `client.write` without a GitHub-time sample or `beforeSend` predicate. findings.title: Renewal loop omits recovered confirmed leases
findings.detail: The loop iterates only the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated by writes applied in this manager instance. Confirmed held rows loaded at startup, and acquisitions confirmed by intent reconciliation, never enter that map. Even if `active` would accept their handles, the loop never renews them.
findings.suggestion: Enumerate confirmed held rows when starting or reconciling and make their handles available to the renewal loop.
findings.failure_scenario: A manager restarts with a confirmed held lease and starts the loop. Every tick skips that lease; it expires even though the associated run is active.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:49 initializes `const handles = new Map<string, LeaseHandle>()`. Recovery at :64–70 does not populate it. Registration occurs only on a direct applied write at :192: `handles.set(key(repo, ref), held)`. The renewal loop at :242 iterates only `handles.values()`.

findings.title: A different run cannot reconcile an earlier pending acquisition
findings.detail: The cross-run check returns `refused` before reconciliation whenever the existing row has an intent. This violates the requirement to reconcile pending intents before every operation, and prevents the caller from clearing a dropped first acquisition unless a separate loop happens to run.

candidates.failure_scenario: A release commit is journaled but its ref update is interrupted; the process restarts more than ten minutes later while the old tip remains current. Recovery writes the release without checking whether the generation is still renewable.

candidates.title: Different-run requests skip pending-intent reconciliation
candidates.detail: The early refusal executes before reconciliation whenever another run owns a row with an intent. An unresolved first acquisition that is subsequently proven unchanged remains in the database and prevents the next run from acquiring until a timer happens to reconcile it; if the loop has not started, it blocks indefinitely. The request requires reconciliation before every operation and forgetting an unconfirmed acquisition when dropped.
candidates.suggestion: Reconcile the row before deciding whether its run blocks the request, then re-read the row and apply the ownership checks.
candidates.failure_scenario: Run A leaves an unconfirmed acquisition intent for an absent ref, then ends. GitHub later becomes readable and run B calls acquire before the renewal loop starts; B receives `refused: live` and A’s droppable intent remains.

candidates.title: Recovered and reconciled holdings are never added to the renewal loop
candidates.detail: The loop renews only the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated solely by an immediately applied write in `operate`. Startup recovery and later reconciliation can confirm a held acquisition without populating that map. Such confirmed holdings are never presented to `active` or renewed, so they expire even when the caller considers the run active.
candidates.suggestion: Populate or derive the loop’s handles from confirmed held rows after recovery and reconciliation.
candidates.failure_scenario: An acquisition’s ref update succeeds but its response is unreadable, so acquire returns wait. The next tick reconciles the intent as applied, but subsequent ticks never renew that confirmed generation.

candidates.title: A second moved outcome can mark a non-superseded generation lost
candidates.detail: After two moved outcomes the manager unconditionally calls `lose` for a confirmed row, without checking whether the returned record supersedes that confirmed ownership. A moved result can instead contain an older generation or a malformed record. This violates the requirement that only a superseding record establishes loss and clears the confirmed ownership on an uncertain result.
candidates.suggestion: Classify the second moved tip against the confirmed run, member and generation before marking loss; return a non-loss result when it does not establish supersession.
candidates.failure_scenario: A confirmed generation 2 write encounters two concurrent ref movements, and the second returned tip is malformed or generation 1. The manager marks generation 2 lost and calls `onLost` even though the returned tip does not establish a superseding generation.

candidates.title: An exception in the renewal timer becomes an unhandled rejection
candidates.detail: The async interval callback has no rejection handler. A thrown database, clock, client, or hook error rejects the callback, stops processing the remaining leases for that tick, and can terminate the process under an unhandled-rejection policy. There is no reporting or controlled retry of the failure.
candidates.suggestion: Handle and report failures from timer work explicitly, and ensure one failed ref does not silently prevent the other refs from being processed.
candidates.failure_scenario: A clock read throws while renewing the first active lease. The timer callback rejects and later active leases are skipped for that tick; the rejection may terminate the daemon.

candidates.title: A different run is refused before the pending intent is reconciled
candidates.detail: The cross-run guard runs before reconciliation, so a pending intent returns `refused` rather than `wait` and cannot be resolved by that acquisition. The test for a pending old run explicitly expects this behavior, masking the violation of the requirement to reconcile pending intents before every operation.
candidates.suggestion: Reconcile first, return wait while the intent remains pending, and only then evaluate the confirmed row and fresh tip. Test both unresolved and dropped intents when a different run acquires.
candidates.failure_scenario: Run A has an unconfirmed first acquisition whose intent can now be dropped; run B calls acquire before the loop runs and is refused instead of reconciling and acquiring.

candidates.title: The renewal loop omits confirmed leases recovered without an in-memory handle
candidates.detail: The loop iterates only handles created by an applied write in this manager instance. Recovery and intent reconciliation can confirm a held row without adding a handle, so that lease is never passed to `active` or renewed. The recovery tests cover loss and an update on an already registered handle, but do not cover a recovered or reconciled acquisition becoming eligible for renewal.
candidates.suggestion: Populate or derive renewal handles from confirmed held rows after recovery and reconciliation, and test a recovered acquisition through a renewal tick.
candidates.failure_scenario: An acquisition returns unconfirmed, then the loop reconciles its intent as applied; subsequent ticks never renew that confirmed lease because no handle was inserted into `handles`.

candidates.title: Mutation tests expect the broken two-winner result

candidates.failure_scenario: The fake allows both concurrent writes unconditionally; both acquisitions report held at the same generation, yet the mutant test passes.

candidates.title: Replayed release bypasses the lease-time send check
candidates.detail: The manager delegates pending-intent reconciliation to `reconcileLeaseIntent`, which replays a release using `client.write` without a `beforeSend` hook or a fresh GitHub-time sample. A release interrupted before its ref update can therefore be sent after the confirmed generation has expired. That violates the same-generation send-time check and can publish a released tip after the holder's authority has ended.
candidates.suggestion: Require the same fresh-time decision and immediate pre-send revalidation when replaying a release, and leave the intent pending when that authority cannot be confirmed.
candidates.failure_scenario: A release commit is journaled before its ref update, the process stops for longer than the lease expiry, and reconciliation finds the old held tip unchanged. It replays the release without checking expiry; a different run can then acquire the released tip.

candidates.title: Renewal loop omits recovered confirmed leases
candidates.detail: The loop renews only handles inserted into the in-memory `handles` map by an applied write in this manager instance. candidates.failure_scenario: An acquisition updates GitHub but returns `unconfirmed`; the next tick reconciles its intent to applied. Subsequent ticks never renew that confirmed lease because no handle was added to `handles`.

candidates.title: Different-run acquisition skips pending-intent reconciliation

candidates.failure_scenario: Run A leaves an unconfirmed first-acquisition intent whose GitHub ref is still absent. Run B calls acquire before the loop reconciles it and receives `refused: live` instead of reconciling the dropped intent and acquiring the absent ref.

candidates.title: Reconcile another run’s pending intent before refusing

candidates.title: Restore confirmed handles for the renewal loop

candidates.failure_scenario: A manager restarts with a confirmed held lease, or an unconfirmed acquisition is confirmed on a later tick. Even with `active` returning true, subsequent ticks never renew that lease and it expires.

candidates.title: Revalidate time before replaying a pending release
candidates.detail: The request requires that “Immediately before the `updateRefs` send” the manager revalidate the applicable time predicate. `reconcileLeaseIntent` can replay a release by calling `client.write` without a `beforeSend` hook or a GitHub-time check; this path is also invoked during initial recovery. findings.detail: The engine labels the browser available whenever a preview exists and no `browser_unavailable` event was recorded. findings.title: A superseded unsent question set can never be published later
findings.detail: An unsent question effect is permanently marked done when its run temporarily stops waiting. If the run later returns to waiting with the same unanswered question IDs, observe() sees the existing effect and never creates another publication. The same problem occurs after recovery establishes that a stale POST was not accepted. The run can therefore remain waiting indefinitely without its questions appearing on the issue.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish a superseded effect with no confirmed publication from a completed publication, and allow a fresh eligible waiting episode to publish the set after any uncertain prior POST has been recovered.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters waiting_input with question 42, but its pending comment has not been posted. The run temporarily changes to running, so reconciliation marks the effect done. It returns to waiting_input with question 42 still unanswered; subsequent polls and restarts never post the question.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:355–358: `let stale = pending.state === "recovering" || !eligible(); if (stale && !pending.page) { save(effect, "done"); continue; }`. At :129, publication creation requires `!effects.has(`comment:questions:${ids}`)`, so the completed checkpoint prevents recreation even without a comment.
verification.trigger: An unsent question set becomes ineligible while the run is running. Reconciliation permanently marks it done; returning to waiting_input with the same unanswered IDs never publishes it, including after restart.

findings.title: Retired unsent question sets cannot be published if they become eligible again
findings.detail: Superseding an unsent question effect marks it done, and observe() will never create that effect again because it already exists. A temporary linkage or status change can therefore permanently suppress a question set that was never posted.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish superseded unsent effects from completed publications and allow the same set to be scheduled again when it becomes eligible.
findings.failure_scenario: A waiting run has a pending question publication, loses its issue link before the POST, and later regains the same link while the question remains open. The effect is done without a comment, so subsequent polls never publish that question set.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:206–208 makes eligibility depend on the current issue link. At :356–358, an ineligible unsent effect is saved as `"done"`. At :129, `!effects.has(`comment:questions:${ids}`)` prevents recreating that effect when the same link returns. src/db/store.ts:1468 selects question work only with `state IN ('pending','recovering')`.
verification.trigger: Remove an issue link while its question publication is unsent and reconcile, then restore the same link. The existing done checkpoint permanently suppresses publication of the still-open set.

findings.title: Privacy reinspection can close an uncertain POST without recovery
findings.detail: The pending body is reinspected before marker recovery, and any inspection failure immediately marks the effect done. For a checkpoint with page set, GitHub may already have accepted the POST; closing it without checking the marker violates the required recovery behavior and loses the recorded outcome.
findings.suggestion: Recover an uncertain POST using its independently generated marker and checkpointed identity before closing the effect, even when the stored body can no longer pass publication inspection. Keep any new POST suppressed if inspection fails.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub accepts a question comment but the response is lost. Before the next poll, private-string configuration becomes unreadable or changes to match the stored body. Reinspection fails, the checkpoint is marked done, and the accepted comment is never recovered.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:365–369 runs `body = checkBody(run, pending.body, markerFor(run.id, task, repo, number))` and on failure executes `save(effect, "done")` and `continue`. Recovery starts only afterward at :371: `if (pending.page)`. At :426–427, the checkpoint records `page: 1` before issuing POST.
verification.trigger: GitHub accepts a POST whose response is lost. Before recovery, private-string inspection fails or newly matches its stored body. The checkpoint closes without searching for or acknowledging the accepted comment, violating the required recovery-before-closure behavior.

findings.title: Publication failures log exception output instead of a fixed code
findings.detail: The delivery catch passes the exception to logFailure, which logs its text. The subprocess error can include the full command and stderr, and credential redaction does not remove configured private strings. This violates the requirement that publication diagnostics contain fixed codes and never exception output. The new privacy tests inject fixed errors and do not exercise an exception containing withheld content.
findings.suggestion: Log a fixed delivery-failure code without the exception text, and add a fake gh failure whose error contains protected question or reason text.
findings.failure_scenario: A failed GitHub POST or recovery request returns an error containing a configured private string or withheld field; that string is written to lifecycle diagnostics.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:442 passes the caught exception to `logFailure(run, repo, number, error)`. At :62–64, that helper logs `redactCredentials(`Issue lifecycle ${repo}#${number} run ${run.id}: ${String(error)}`)`. It neither replaces exception output with a fixed code nor checks configured private strings.
verification.trigger: A POST or recovery exception contains a configured private string that is not a registered credential. Its text reaches lifecycle diagnostics unchanged; exception diagnostics also violate the explicit fixed-code requirement.
