findings.title: A dirty worktree can bypass detection of a cancelled worker's push
findings.detail: When reconciliation rejects an open job, the executor cancels it and calls prepare(). If the coordinator worktree is dirty, prepare() returns null before checking the remote branch, so the executor runs the local session even if the cancelled worker already pushed an unreported commit. The request requires that case to end NeedsHuman.
findings.suggestion: Check the cancelled job's remote branch for an unreported push before falling back to local execution, including when preparation cannot proceed because the worktree is dirty.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker pushes W but has not reported it; after restart the coordinator worktree is dirty. Reconciliation cancels the leased job, prepare() returns null, and a local session starts instead of reporting the unaccepted push.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1138-1139 requires HEAD to match and `(await clean())` for resume. src/pipeline/lan-agent.ts:89-91 then executes `workers.cancelAgentJob(id)` and `id = undefined` when resume fails. Preparation at src/pipeline/engine.ts:1149 returns early with `if (!(await clean())) return null;`, before `const remote = await remoteSha()` at :1150. src/pipeline/lan-agent.ts:110 executes `if (!prepared) return fallback();`; fallback at :51 calls `local()` unless aborted.
verification.trigger: A handled, leased worker job has pushed W without an accepted report, and the coordinator worktree is dirty at restart. Reconciliation cancels the job, then preparation returns null before checking the remote branch. A local session starts instead of raising NeedsHuman for the unaccepted push.

findings.title: A fenced pending report no longer renews its lease
findings.detail: The new result request survives the fence, but the fence aborts the job controller and heldJobs() consequently omits the job from heartbeats. Those heartbeats no longer renew its lease. If result requests remain unavailable while heartbeat requests succeed, the lease expires despite the worker continuing to retry the accepted-report request, and the coordinator rejects the eventual report.
findings.suggestion: Keep a pushed job in the heartbeat's held-job list while its independently bounded result report is pending, until the result is accepted or the lease is explicitly lost.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker pushes during an outage and its fence fires. After restart, heartbeats succeed but result requests fail transiently for longer than the remaining lease or restart grace. The coordinator expires the job; a later result receives 409 and the pushed commit cannot be adopted.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:503 filters held jobs with `job.reported && !job.controller.signal.aborted`; the fence aborts those controllers at :565-567. Heartbeats send `jobs: heldJobs()` (:546), while pushed reports continue with an independent timeout signal (:857-862). src/db/workers.ts:242-252 renews leases only for IDs in `c.jobs`; :415-420 fails expired leases. src/server/workers.ts:202-203 rejects reports without a held lease with 409.
verification.trigger: A pushed report remains pending when the fence fires. After restart, heartbeats recover but omit the aborted job. If result requests keep failing beyond the remaining lease/restart grace, the lease expires and the eventual report is rejected, preventing adoption of the pushed commit.

findings.title: Late result retries can prevent worker shutdown
findings.detail: The late-result signal excludes the worker's shutdown signal as well as the job cancellation and fence signals. If the coordinator is unreachable, `call()` keeps retrying until the attempt deadline, while `runWorker` waits for every job task in its shutdown cleanup. Stopping the worker can therefore hang for the remainder of the agent attempt, potentially many minutes.
findings.suggestion: Combine the attempt-deadline signal with the worker's shutdown signal while continuing to exclude the job controller used by cancellation and the fence.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker pushes a commit, begins retrying its result during a coordinator outage, and then receives a shutdown signal. Its result request remains active and `runWorker` does not finish until the attempt deadline expires.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:861 gives pushed reports only `AbortSignal.timeout(Math.max(0, deadline - Date.now()))`, excluding the worker shutdown signal. The retry loop continues until its supplied signal aborts (:508-525). Shutdown calls `stop.abort()` and aborts job controllers (:984-986), then awaits every job task with `await Promise.allSettled(...)` (:987-991).
verification.trigger: A worker pushes and retries its report during a coordinator outage, then receives shutdown. Shutdown cannot abort the report request or retry sleeps, and runWorker waits for the task until reporting succeeds, receives a refusal, or reaches the attempt deadline.

findings.title: Queued restart test completes the job before the scheduler resumes
findings.detail: The queued case leases and reports the job before calling resumed.start(), so the resumed executor sees a done job. It does not exercise reattachment to a queued job followed by pickup and completion after restart.
findings.suggestion: Start the resumed factory while the job is still queued, observe reattachment, then lease and complete that same ID and assert that no second row is created.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that replaces a stored queued job on resume could pass this integration case because the stored job has already become done.

verification.evidence: test/pipeline-lan-agent.test.ts:940 leases the old job, then :943 executes `await report(resumed, job, request(job), await publish(bare, request(job)));` before :945 calls `resumed.start();`.
verification.trigger: The queued integration case completes the stored job before scheduler reconciliation. A regression replacing queued jobs while preserving done-job reuse could pass this case.

findings.title: Already-adopted recovery lacks negative verification cases
findings.detail: The checkpoint test exercises recovery with a valid commit and clean worktree, but does not verify that the new HEAD-already-at-result path rejects a dirty worktree or a commit that fails the shared commit-object checks. Existing adoptWorkerCommit tests exercise the ordinary adoption path.
findings.suggestion: Add recovery cases with HEAD already at the reported SHA and either a dirty worktree or an invalid commit shape, and assert that recovery refuses adoption.
findings.failure_scenario: Removing the cleanliness or commit verification from the already-moved path would still allow the new successful recovery test to pass.

verification.evidence: test/pipeline-lan-agent.test.ts:477 publishes a valid commit; :488 checks `expect(await headSha(state.worktreePath)).toBe(first.result_sha);`, and :497-498 restarts and expects success without introducing dirt or an invalid commit. src/pipeline/engine.ts:1201-1203 separately calls `verifyWorkerCommit(...)` and checks `!(await clean())` on this path.
verification.trigger: Removing verification or cleanliness checks specifically from the already-moved adoption path would leave the successful recovery cases passing; they contain no negative inputs exercising those guards.

findings.title: Late-report coverage does not test the attempt deadline
findings.detail: The pushed and fenced cases verify that a report survives a restart and fence, but neither holds the coordinator offline until the attempt deadline. The new independent report signal must also stop retrying at that deadline.
findings.suggestion: Add a controlled deadline case that keeps result delivery unavailable through expiry and checks that retries terminate without an accepted result.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression using an unbounded signal for pushed results would still pass the current restart cases and could leave a worker retrying indefinitely.

verification.evidence: test/pipeline-lan-agent.test.ts:850-853 waits for publication and optionally invokes `fence();`; :870 restores `offline = false` before completion. It never expires the attempt deadline. The distinct production bound is src/workers/client.ts:861: `sha === req.parentSha ? jobSignal : AbortSignal.timeout(Math.max(0, deadline - Date.now()))`.
verification.trigger: Replacing the pushed-result timeout signal with an unbounded signal would still pass the restart and fence scenarios, leaving indefinite result retries during a prolonged outage untested.

findings.title: Restart grace expires after heartbeat freshness, before one lease period
findings.detail: The request says “a worker that stays unreachable for one lease period after the restart is retried on another worker.” Although the lease-expiry calculation grants 60 seconds, this freshness check fails the job after 30 seconds without a heartbeat. That can discard a worker’s pushed result before the promised lease period has elapsed. The requested freshness formula also specifies this 30-second behavior, so the requirements conflict and need to be reconciled.
findings.suggestion: Resolve the conflicting requirements and make the retry timing and documentation agree; add a test covering an unreachable worker between the freshness and lease deadlines.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker pushes while the coordinator is down and remains unreachable for 31 seconds after restart. The next sweep fails its job as disconnected, even though the 60-second restart lease grace has not elapsed; a subsequent result is rejected.

verification.evidence: src/workers/protocol.ts:104-105 sets `fresh: 30_000` and `lease: 60_000`. Although src/db/workers.ts:415-418 extends lease expiry to `resumedAt + this.times.lease`, lines 422-425 independently check `now - Math.max(w.last_heartbeat_at ?? 0, this.resumedAt ?? Number.NEGATIVE_INFINITY) > this.times.fresh` and call `this.failAgentJob(j.id, "Worker disconnected")`. src/db/workers.ts:347 calls `this.sweepAgentJobs()` before checking lease ownership; src/server/workers.ts:202-203 rejects results without ownership with HTTP 409.
verification.trigger: An approved worker has a leased job with an unexpired attempt deadline and a pre-restart heartbeat. It remains unreachable until 31 seconds after restart. A sweep then removes its lease as disconnected, despite the 60-second restart lease extension; its subsequent pushed-commit report is rejected, losing the surviving session's result.

findings.title: Operational failures leave the CLI with a successful exit status

Automation relying on the exit status can therefore treat a generator run that produced nothing as successful.
candidates.suggestion: Distinguish expected case exclusions from operational errors and set a nonzero process exit status when operational errors occur, while still printing all rows.
candidates.failure_scenario: The gh command fails authentication for every requested PR; the table contains errors, but the generator exits with status 0.

candidates.title: The command never looks up production complexity
candidates.detail: The command-line entry point supplies no `lookupRun` dependency, so `replayProduction` always defaults complexity to medium even when the report identifies a run whose record is available locally. This loses the requested production difficulty signal and can put cases in the wrong evaluation complexity cell.
candidates.suggestion: Connect the command-line entry point to the production run store and pass a lookup that retrieves the identified run's complexity.
candidates.failure_scenario: Generate a replay for a factory PR whose run record has complexity `small`: the generated case records `medium` and says lookup was not configured.

candidates.title: The complexity test injects a lookup absent from the real command
candidates.detail: The success fixture always provides a fake `lookupRun`, while the production entry point never provides one. Consequently, the assertion that the generated case has the run's complexity passes without exercising the wiring users invoke and does not catch the missing production lookup.
candidates.suggestion: Add a test of the command's production dependency wiring using a local run record with non-medium complexity, and assert that the resulting case preserves it.
candidates.failure_scenario: A regression or omission in the CLI's run-store wiring leaves every generated case at medium, while the existing fake-injected test still passes.

candidates.title: The generator cannot run without the implement dataset
candidates.detail: The request requires the command to add cases to `evals/implement/cases.json`, but this checkout has no `evals` directory or implement dataset. The unconditional read fails before any PR is processed, so the documented command cannot generate a case in this repository.
candidates.suggestion: Provide the existing implement dataset in the checkout or initialize the required dataset envelope and directory when it is absent, while preserving existing cases when present.
candidates.failure_scenario: Running the documented generator command in this checkout fails with an ENOENT when it reads `evals/implement/cases.json`.

candidates.title: The CLI never looks up available production complexity
candidates.detail: The request requires “the production run's triage complexity, when it can be found.” Although the generator accepts an injected lookup, the actual CLI never supplies one. Consequently every CLI-generated case is assigned medium even when its run footer identifies a locally stored run with a different complexity.
candidates.suggestion: Wire the CLI to a read-only run-record lookup and use the recorded complexity when available.
candidates.failure_scenario: A merged factory PR identifies a locally stored run whose triage complexity is small; the documented CLI generates a medium case and records that lookup was not configured.

Verifier: 18 candidates, 18 checked, 0 refuted.

findings.title: Rollback to the previous release does not notify the executor
findings.detail: The executor detects a release change only through the database setting written by this new daemon. The previous release never writes that setting, so rolling back leaves the new release SHA in place. A running new executor continues its job and can continue leasing queued jobs even though the active daemon is now the older release.
findings.suggestion: Use release ownership that the previous release can invalidate or otherwise ensure that a rollback stops the executor before the old daemon resumes work.
findings.failure_scenario: Start an in-place gate on this release, then roll back and start the base-commit daemon. The setting still names this release, so the executor does not cancel the gate as required.

verification.evidence: src/cli/daemon.ts:50 introduces `factory.store.setSetting("executor.daemonRelease", factory.bootSha);`; the base-commit daemon has no corresponding write. src/gates/inplace.ts:39 detects changes only through `store.getSetting("executor.daemonRelease", "") !== releaseSha`, and lines 53–57 otherwise renew the lease. src/db/workers.ts:388 likewise gates leasing on that persisted setting. Base src/util/proc.ts:74 preserves live process owners with `return birth === ownerBirth;`, so startup recovery does not stop the executor's gates.
verification.trigger: Run an in-place gate on HEAD, then roll back to the base-release daemon while leaving the executor running, with no LAN worker polling to sweep the job. The release setting remains HEAD's SHA; the executor continues its gate and remains eligible to lease queued HEAD jobs despite the daemon running another release.

findings.title: Process existence is treated as a fresh executor heartbeat
findings.detail: Executor availability checks only PID and birth identity; there is no heartbeat timestamp. An executor whose event loop is stalled remains eligible indefinitely. Once its lease expires, the daemon marks the job failed, but waitStopped waits indefinitely while that process exists, so it cannot fall back or proceed with the worktree.
findings.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and provide a bounded, safe path for confirming that an unresponsive executor's gate processes have stopped.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor is alive but paused or blocked while running a gate. Its lease expires; the daemon enters waitStopped and never completes the gate or starts the fallback.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:359: `return processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth;`; src/db/workers.ts:671–672: expired leases call `this.fail(j.id, "Lease expired")`; src/gates/lan.ts:131: `if (inplace) await workers.waitStopped(handle.id, controller.signal);`. In src/db/workers.ts:370–384, recovery occurs only when `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)`; otherwise the loop repeats `await Bun.sleep(this.times.tick)` without a deadline.
verification.trigger: An executor remains paused or blocked after its leased job expires. Process identity still matches, so the failed job waits indefinitely for stopped=1 and never reaches fallback unless the executor resumes, exits, or the wait is aborted.

findings.title: Targeted and timeout retry jobs cannot reattach
findings.detail: The resume predicate explicitly accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A restart during an in-place targeted or timeout retry therefore cancels the still-running job and repeats work instead of attaching to its matching handle.
findings.suggestion: Persist and restore the retry context needed to validate and reattach matching retry jobs.
findings.failure_scenario: A daemon restarts while a long targeted retry is leased by the executor. On resume, the purpose fails this allowlist and the retry is cancelled or started again.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1566 runs purpose "timeout"; :1595 selects "regression-retry-targeted" for targeted retries. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:30 requires '["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)' to resume. Lines 35–43 cancel a rejected handle and clear persisted state. On stage restart, engine.ts:1536 first requests resume with purpose "initial", also rejecting either retry handle.
verification.trigger: Daemon restarts while an in-place targeted or timeout retry is running. The resumed gates stage rejects and cancels its durable handle, then repeats gate work instead of attaching to the surviving retry.

findings.title: LAN configuration bypasses the in-place executor for local fallback
findings.detail: When the gate executor is configured as LAN, this factory always returns the LAN executor, even when the in-place executor is enabled. Its local path for repositories outside the LAN list runs directly in the daemon, so those local gates cannot survive a daemon restart.
findings.suggestion: Route the LAN executor's local path through the in-place executor when it is enabled and available.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the executor, configure LAN gates for one repository, and run a gate in another repository. The gate runs in the daemon and is lost on restart despite a live in-place executor.

verification.evidence: src/gates/executor.ts:77–81 uses the flag only for local configuration: `return inplace && workers ? lanExecutor(workers, [], true) : localExecutor();`; the LAN branch instead returns `lanExecutor(workers, repos)`. src/gates/lan.ts:16 defaults `inplace = false`, and :71 routes unlisted repositories directly to the daemon: `else if (!repos.includes(req.repo)) return local.start(req, signal);`. At :79, local handles attach through `local.attach(...)`.
verification.trigger: Set gates.executor="lan" and executor.enabled=true, configure repository A for LAN gates, then run gates for repository B with a live in-place executor. Repository B's gates run in the daemon, bypassing the executor; a daemon restart interrupts them and requires repeated work.

findings.title: Confinement failures are converted into local retries
findings.detail: The executor catches every error from executeGate and records an ordinary failed job. The attaching daemon then reruns every failed in-place job locally. This loses the distinction between an infrastructure failure and a ConfinementError, so a failed isolation check can be followed by a successful gate instead of failing closed.
findings.suggestion: Persist a failure classification and propagate confinement and inspection failures to the daemon without retrying them.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor's confinement preflight throws ConfinementError, but the daemon's subsequent local preflight succeeds; the gate passes despite the original security check failing.

verification.evidence: src/gates/inplace.ts:70–71 catches every error: `catch (error) { workers.fail(job.id, redactCredentials(String(error))); }`. src/db/workers.ts:626–632 marks in-place failures `state='failed'` without preserving their type. src/gates/lan.ts:130–139 handles every failed job by calling `local.start(request, controller.signal)` and `local.attach(...)`.
verification.trigger: The executor preflight throws ConfinementError and cleanup completes. The daemon retries locally; if its preflight and checks succeed, it returns a passing GateRun despite the original confinement failure.

findings.title: A cleanup failure can leave the run waiting indefinitely
findings.detail: waitStopped only attempts recovery or reports an error after the executor process disappears. If a job finishes with process discovery or cleanup records remaining, the executor deliberately leaves stopped=0 but continues running. waitStopped then polls forever because the executor is still alive, even though that executor will never revisit the completed job.
findings.suggestion: Make the executor publish a terminal cleanup failure, or have waitStopped detect that the job is no longer being cleaned up and fail closed with a clear error.
findings.failure_scenario: A cancelled gate leaves a cleanup record after process cleanup fails; the executor continues polling for other jobs, while the daemon waits forever to start the replacement gate.

verification.evidence: src/gates/inplace.ts:75–80 only sets `stopped=1` when both `!store.listProcessDiscoveries(undefined, req.cwd).length` and `!store.listProcessCleanups(undefined, req.cwd).length`; execution then returns to the polling loop at line 29. src/db/workers.ts:370 permits recovery only under `!worker || !this.executor(worker, false)`, while lines 366–384 otherwise keep waiting. src/gates/lan.ts:49 awaits this wait during discard.
verification.trigger: Cleanup fails and leaves a discovery or cleanup record. The executor remains alive and proceeds to polling, without retrying that job's cleanup or acknowledging its stop. Replacement execution waits indefinitely, even if the leftover processes subsequently exit.

findings.title: Worktree exclusion is not atomic across concurrent starts
findings.detail: The query for existing jobs and the later enqueue are separate operations. Two daemon-side starts for the same worktree can both observe no existing job and enqueue independently. With two executor processes, each can lease one job and run both gates in the same worktree.
findings.suggestion: Enforce worktree exclusivity atomically in the database when creating or leasing an in-place job.
findings.failure_scenario: Two concurrent gate starts for the same cwd pass the existing-job query before either enqueues, and two executors lease their jobs concurrently.

verification.evidence: src/gates/lan.ts:54–59 queries existing jobs and waits for them, but src/gates/lan.ts:72 then does `await releaseGateSlotScope()` before allocating a handle. The row is only inserted later at src/gates/lan.ts:80–81: `workers.enqueue(req, handle.id, true)`. Thus concurrent starts can both observe no existing job. src/db/workers.ts:400 leases with `WHERE id=? AND state='queued'`, without checking for another active job in the same cwd.
verification.trigger: Two concurrent starts for the same cwd both finish the existing-job query before either attaches. Both subsequently enqueue distinct jobs; two executor processes with available gate slots can lease and run them simultaneously in that worktree.

findings.title: Targeted retry jobs cannot reattach after a restart
findings.detail: The resume predicate accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A durable in-place handle for a targeted retry is therefore cancelled even when its stage, round, SHA, environment, and lease all match. The retry is restarted instead of receiving the surviving job's result.
findings.suggestion: Provide a resume path for targeted retry purposes and preserve the state needed to resume them.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a long targeted retry is running; resume rejects its matching handle, cancels the executor job, and runs the retry again.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1595 assigns targeted jobs purpose "regression-retry-targeted". src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–30 requires matching purpose and '["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)'; lines 35–43 cancel and clear rejected handles. engine.ts:1536 resumes the stage with purpose "initial".
verification.trigger: Daemon restarts during an in-place targeted retry. Resume rejects the saved retry handle, cancels that job and repeats gate work.

findings.title: Executor availability has no heartbeat freshness check
findings.detail: Executor availability is based only on PID and birth identity; the executors table has no heartbeat timestamp. A live but stalled executor is treated as available indefinitely. New gates are enqueued instead of immediately using the requested in-process fallback, and a leased job is not considered disconnected until its lease expires.
findings.suggestion: Record and renew an executor heartbeat and require it to be fresh when selecting an executor and sweeping its jobs.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process remains alive but its event loop stops making progress; the daemon treats it as available and waits for pickup or lease expiry rather than recognizing that no fresh executor is available.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:354 queries executor fields `id`, `pid`, `birth`, and `release_sha`; line 359 determines availability with `return processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth;`. src/gates/lan.ts:61–69 selects immediate local fallback only when `!workers.executor()`. src/db/workers.ts:656–657 instead fails an unpicked queued job after `this.times.pickup`.
verification.trigger: An executor's event loop stops progressing while its process identity remains valid. The daemon still selects it as available, enqueues work, and waits for pickup timeout rather than immediately using the local fallback. A previously leased job additionally encounters the unbounded stop wait.

findings.title: Targeted retry jobs are cancelled on restart instead of reattached
findings.detail: Resume accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A recorded `baseline-retry-targeted` or `regression-retry-targeted` handle therefore fails the resume check even when its stage, round, SHA, environment, and executor lease match. The live job is cancelled and the stage starts over, contrary to the requested restart behavior for targeted retries.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry state to resume the targeted retry and accept its matching handle during stage recovery.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while an executor is running a long targeted regression retry; the new engine cancels that job and repeats gate work instead of receiving its result.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1595 uses "regression-retry-targeted" for targeted regression retries. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:30 permits only '["baseline", "initial", "rebase"]'; lines 35–43 cancel rejected jobs and clear their handles. engine.ts:1536 enters resume with purpose "initial".
verification.trigger: A long targeted regression retry survives a daemon restart in the executor. The new engine rejects and cancels its handle instead of receiving its result, repeating gate work.

findings.title: Restart coverage omits targeted retries
findings.detail: The engine restart cases cover baseline, initial, and rebase gates, but none interrupts a targeted baseline or regression retry. Consequently the tests do not catch the resume-purpose restriction that cancels those jobs.
findings.suggestion: Add a restart test that pauses a targeted retry, resumes the engine, and asserts that the same job completes and its command ran once.
findings.failure_scenario: A targeted retry is running when the daemon stops; the current suite passes without checking whether the resumed engine reattaches to it.

verification.evidence: test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:487–494 parameterizes restart coverage only with "baseline", "initial", and "rebase". src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:30 explicitly restricts resumption to `["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)`.
verification.trigger: The daemon stops during a targeted retry. No in-place executor restart test covers that purpose, so the suite does not detect cancellation and repeated work instead of reattachment.

findings.title: Pickup timeout test never verifies in-process fallback
findings.detail: The pickup test stops after asserting that the queued job becomes failed. It does not attach a daemon-side execution or assert that the check subsequently runs locally and returns its result, so a regression in the failed-job fallback path would pass.
findings.suggestion: Exercise an attached in-place job that is never leased, sweep it past pickup timeout, and assert that the local check runs and its result reaches the caller.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor remains alive but does not pick up a queued job, and the daemon fails to start the local fallback after the sweep marks it failed.

verification.evidence: test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:319–324 ends after `later.sweep()`, `expect(later.job(missed)?.state).toBe("failed")`, and the attempt assertion. It never attaches or observes a local check. The fallback it leaves untested calls `local.start(request, controller.signal)` at src/gates/lan.ts:137–139.
verification.trigger: An alive executor leaves a job queued until pickup expires. Removing or breaking the subsequent local fallback would still pass this timeout test.

findings.title: Gate result comparison discards most of the result shape
findings.detail: The purported in-process comparison projects each result down to name, ok, and exitCode, while the event assertion checks only names. It would still pass if executor results or events lost output, command, timing, failure metadata, or other fields required by consumers. The test also does not compare the produced gate artifacts.
findings.suggestion: Compare representative complete result and event structures, excluding only nondeterministic values, and verify the corresponding artifact contents.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor drops a check's output or failure metadata while preserving its name and exit code; this test still passes although the reported gate data changed.

verification.evidence: test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts:114–115 projects results to `({ name, ok, exitCode })`; line 144 compares only those projections. Line 146 separately checks only the environment check's output, and lines 152–154 compare event names only.
verification.trigger: The executor loses another check's output, command, or failure metadata while retaining its name, status, and exit code. The result comparison still passes.

findings.title: Executor stores gate output without the daemon’s dynamic credential registrations
findings.detail: Credential registrations are process-local. The executor loads configured provider credentials, but it does not receive credentials registered dynamically by the daemon, such as GitHub installation tokens and worker tokens. It redacts and persists check events and results using its own incomplete registry before the daemon sees them, so the daemon’s later redaction cannot remove the copies already stored in gate_jobs.
findings.suggestion: Ensure the executor has the daemon’s complete current redaction set before processing output, or defer persistence of output to a boundary that has that set while preserving restart-safe event handling.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon registers a GitHub installation token during operation, and a gate prints that token. An in-place executor that never registered the token stores it unredacted in the job’s events or result.

verification.evidence: src/util/proc.ts:1216–1224 keeps registered credentials in process-local Sets. src/gates/inplace.ts:65 writes check events through `workers.event(...)`, and line 69 calls `workers.complete(job.id, run)`. src/db/workers.ts:612 and :717 persist `this.sanitize(...)`; its sanitizer (:129–133) uses local redaction and privacy filters. src/util/private-output.ts:11 consults `registeredCredentials()`, with no daemon-registration synchronization.
verification.trigger: A token registered dynamically only in the daemon appears in gate output and is absent from the executor’s configured private strings. The executor does not recognize it and persists it unredacted in gate_jobs events/result.

findings.title: Confinement derives credential paths from the executor environment
findings.detail: The gate receives the daemon’s saved environment, but the executor constructs its read policy from its own process environment. The policy uses environment variables such as AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE, GH_CONFIG_DIR, and CARGO_HOME to deny credential paths. When those variables differ between the daemon and executor, a credential path known to the daemon can be omitted from the executor’s deny list, weakening the confinement applied to untrusted gate commands.
findings.suggestion: Build the gate’s confinement policy from the same trusted environment used by the daemon, including its credential-path variables, and refuse execution if that policy cannot be reconstructed.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon has AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE pointing to a credential file under an otherwise allowed toolchain path, while the executor lacks that variable. A gate can read the file through the in-place executor even though the daemon’s local confinement would deny it.

verification.evidence: src/gates/inplace.ts:27 runs under `readPolicyScope.run(cfg.readPolicy, ...)`. src/config.ts:455 constructs that policy with `configureReadPolicy(raw.sandbox, configDir)`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:44–62 snapshots the configuring process’s environment, including `AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE`; :144 uses `options.environment ?? process.env`, and :169 adds that variable to credential denies. The executor passes `req.env` to executeGate (:64), but does not use the daemon’s read policy.
verification.trigger: The daemon specifies a custom credential file under an otherwise readable toolchain path, while the separately started executor lacks that environment variable. Its policy omits the credential denial, allowing gate code to read the file despite the daemon’s policy protecting it.

findings.title: Targeted retries cannot reattach after restart
findings.detail: The request says the local executor covers “the targeted retry” and that a resumed stage with the same stage, round, purpose and SHA attaches to its job. The purpose whitelist excludes both regression retry purposes and baseline retry purposes. On resume, the surrounding stage first asks to resume its initial gate, so it cancels the still-running retry and starts the stage's gate work again.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry context to resume the recorded retry at its original point, and include its purpose in the resume validation.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while an executor is running `regression-retry-targeted`; the resumed stage treats the handle as a mismatch, cancels the retry and reruns gate work instead of receiving that job's result.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1595 records purpose "regression-retry-targeted". src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–30 requires a matching purpose in '["baseline", "initial", "rebase"]', excluding that retry. Lines 35–43 cancel the rejected job and clear its handle; engine.ts:1536 resumes with "initial".
verification.trigger: Daemon restarts while the executor runs regression-retry-targeted. The resumed stage treats its persisted handle as a mismatch, cancels the retry and reruns gate work.

findings.title: Executor liveness is process existence, not a fresh heartbeat
findings.detail: The request requires fallback when no executor has a fresh heartbeat and requires the sweep to apply freshness timers against that heartbeat. Executor rows contain no heartbeat timestamp; this method only checks whether the PID and birth time still exist. In addition, `waitStopped` waits indefinitely while that process exists, even after its job lease expires.
findings.suggestion: Record and check a bounded executor heartbeat, and make the stop/fallback path handle an unresponsive owner without assuming that process existence proves progress or safe cleanup.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process becomes unresponsive while its gate is running. Its lease expires, but the daemon regards the executor as alive and waits indefinitely for `stopped` rather than reaching a safe fallback.

verification.evidence: src/db/workers.ts:359 accepts an executor solely when `processBirthSync(e.pid) === e.birth`. Although lines 671–672 fail an expired lease, src/gates/lan.ts:131 then awaits `workers.waitStopped(handle.id, controller.signal)`. src/db/workers.ts:366–384 loops while `stopped === 0`, skipping recovery whenever the executor process still exists, with no stop deadline.
verification.trigger: An executor becomes persistently unresponsive during a gate but remains alive. Lease expiry fails the job, yet fallback remains blocked waiting for the executor's stop acknowledgement. This is the same failure as C2.

findings.title: Rollback to an older release does not notify the executor
findings.detail: The request says that when the daemon's release changes, including a rollback, the executor stops leasing and cancels its running jobs. The release marker is written only by this new daemon code. A rollback to the previous release starts a daemon that does not write that marker, so the executor continues to see its own SHA in the database and does not detect the release change.
findings.suggestion: Use a release identity that remains observable across rollback to the previous release, and test an actual old-daemon/new-executor transition.

candidates.title: Rollback to the previous release does not notify the executor
candidates.detail: The executor detects a release change only through the database setting written by this new daemon. The previous release never writes that setting, so rolling back leaves the new release SHA in place. A running new executor continues its job and can continue leasing queued jobs even though the active daemon is now the older release.
candidates.suggestion: Use release ownership that the previous release can invalidate or otherwise ensure that a rollback stops the executor before the old daemon resumes work.

candidates.title: Process existence is treated as a fresh executor heartbeat
candidates.detail: Executor availability checks only PID and birth identity; there is no heartbeat timestamp. An executor whose event loop is stalled remains eligible indefinitely. Once its lease expires, the daemon marks the job failed, but waitStopped waits indefinitely while that process exists, so it cannot fall back or proceed with the worktree.
candidates.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and provide a bounded, safe path for confirming that an unresponsive executor's gate processes have stopped.
candidates.failure_scenario: An executor is alive but paused or blocked while running a gate. Its lease expires; the daemon enters waitStopped and never completes the gate or starts the fallback.

candidates.title: Targeted and timeout retry jobs cannot reattach
candidates.detail: The resume predicate explicitly accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A restart during an in-place targeted or timeout retry therefore cancels the still-running job and repeats work instead of attaching to its matching handle.
candidates.suggestion: Persist and restore the retry context needed to validate and reattach matching retry jobs.
candidates.failure_scenario: A daemon restarts while a long targeted retry is leased by the executor. On resume, the purpose fails this allowlist and the retry is cancelled or started again.

candidates.title: LAN configuration bypasses the in-place executor for local fallback
candidates.detail: When the gate executor is configured as LAN, this factory always returns the LAN executor, even when the in-place executor is enabled. Its local path for repositories outside the LAN list runs directly in the daemon, so those local gates cannot survive a daemon restart.
candidates.suggestion: Route the LAN executor's local path through the in-place executor when it is enabled and available.
candidates.failure_scenario: Enable the executor, configure LAN gates for one repository, and run a gate in another repository. The gate runs in the daemon and is lost on restart despite a live in-place executor.

candidates.title: Confinement failures are converted into local retries
candidates.detail: The executor catches every error from executeGate and records an ordinary failed job. The attaching daemon then reruns every failed in-place job locally. This loses the distinction between an infrastructure failure and a ConfinementError, so a failed isolation check can be followed by a successful gate instead of failing closed.
candidates.suggestion: Persist a failure classification and propagate confinement and inspection failures to the daemon without retrying them.
candidates.failure_scenario: The executor's confinement preflight throws ConfinementError, but the daemon's subsequent local preflight succeeds; the gate passes despite the original security check failing.

candidates.title: A cleanup failure can leave the run waiting indefinitely
candidates.detail: waitStopped only attempts recovery or reports an error after the executor process disappears. If a job finishes with process discovery or cleanup records remaining, the executor deliberately leaves stopped=0 but continues running. waitStopped then polls forever because the executor is still alive, even though that executor will never revisit the completed job.
candidates.suggestion: Make the executor publish a terminal cleanup failure, or have waitStopped detect that the job is no longer being cleaned up and fail closed with a clear error.
candidates.failure_scenario: A cancelled gate leaves a cleanup record after process cleanup fails; the executor continues polling for other jobs, while the daemon waits forever to start the replacement gate.

candidates.title: Worktree exclusion is not atomic across concurrent starts
candidates.detail: The query for existing jobs and the later enqueue are separate operations. Two daemon-side starts for the same worktree can both observe no existing job and enqueue independently. With two executor processes, each can lease one job and run both gates in the same worktree.
candidates.suggestion: Enforce worktree exclusivity atomically in the database when creating or leasing an in-place job.
candidates.failure_scenario: Two concurrent gate starts for the same cwd pass the existing-job query before either enqueues, and two executors lease their jobs concurrently.

candidates.title: Targeted retry jobs cannot reattach after a restart
candidates.detail: The resume predicate accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A durable in-place handle for a targeted retry is therefore cancelled even when its stage, round, SHA, environment, and lease all match. The retry is restarted instead of receiving the surviving job's result.
candidates.suggestion: Provide a resume path for targeted retry purposes and preserve the state needed to resume them.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a long targeted retry is running; resume rejects its matching handle, cancels the executor job, and runs the retry again.

candidates.title: Executor availability has no heartbeat freshness check
candidates.detail: Executor availability is based only on PID and birth identity; the executors table has no heartbeat timestamp. A live but stalled executor is treated as available indefinitely. New gates are enqueued instead of immediately using the requested in-process fallback, and a leased job is not considered disconnected until its lease expires.
candidates.suggestion: Record and renew an executor heartbeat and require it to be fresh when selecting an executor and sweeping its jobs.
candidates.failure_scenario: An executor process remains alive but its event loop stops making progress; the daemon treats it as available and waits for pickup or lease expiry rather than recognizing that no fresh executor is available.

candidates.title: Targeted retry jobs are cancelled on restart instead of reattached
candidates.detail: Resume accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A recorded `baseline-retry-targeted` or `regression-retry-targeted` handle therefore fails the resume check even when its stage, round, SHA, environment, and executor lease match. The live job is cancelled and the stage starts over, contrary to the requested restart behavior for targeted retries.
candidates.suggestion: Persist enough retry state to resume the targeted retry and accept its matching handle during stage recovery.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while an executor is running a long targeted regression retry; the new engine cancels that job and repeats gate work instead of receiving its result.

candidates.title: Restart coverage omits targeted retries
candidates.detail: The engine restart cases cover baseline, initial, and rebase gates, but none interrupts a targeted baseline or regression retry. Consequently the tests do not catch the resume-purpose restriction that cancels those jobs.
candidates.suggestion: Add a restart test that pauses a targeted retry, resumes the engine, and asserts that the same job completes and its command ran once.
candidates.failure_scenario: A targeted retry is running when the daemon stops; the current suite passes without checking whether the resumed engine reattaches to it.

candidates.title: Pickup timeout test never verifies in-process fallback
candidates.detail: The pickup test stops after asserting that the queued job becomes failed. It does not attach a daemon-side execution or assert that the check subsequently runs locally and returns its result, so a regression in the failed-job fallback path would pass.
candidates.suggestion: Exercise an attached in-place job that is never leased, sweep it past pickup timeout, and assert that the local check runs and its result reaches the caller.
candidates.failure_scenario: An executor remains alive but does not pick up a queued job, and the daemon fails to start the local fallback after the sweep marks it failed.

candidates.title: Gate result comparison discards most of the result shape
candidates.detail: The purported in-process comparison projects each result down to name, ok, and exitCode, while the event assertion checks only names. It would still pass if executor results or events lost output, command, timing, failure metadata, or other fields required by consumers. The test also does not compare the produced gate artifacts.
candidates.suggestion: Compare representative complete result and event structures, excluding only nondeterministic values, and verify the corresponding artifact contents.
candidates.failure_scenario: The executor drops a check's output or failure metadata while preserving its name and exit code; this test still passes although the reported gate data changed.

candidates.title: Executor stores gate output without the daemon’s dynamic credential registrations
candidates.detail: Credential registrations are process-local. The executor loads configured provider credentials, but it does not receive credentials registered dynamically by the daemon, such as GitHub installation tokens and worker tokens. It redacts and persists check events and results using its own incomplete registry before the daemon sees them, so the daemon’s later redaction cannot remove the copies already stored in gate_jobs.

candidates.title: Confinement derives credential paths from the executor environment
candidates.detail: The gate receives the daemon’s saved environment, but the executor constructs its read policy from its own process environment. The policy uses environment variables such as AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE, GH_CONFIG_DIR, and CARGO_HOME to deny credential paths. When those variables differ between the daemon and executor, a credential path known to the daemon can be omitted from the executor’s deny list, weakening the confinement applied to untrusted gate commands.

findings.detail: The startup check accepts any regular file with the owner-read bit set and no group or world permission bits. findings.title: An App key outside the config directory can be exposed to agents
findings.detail: The configuration accepts any absolute key path, but the agent read policy automatically denies the config directory, not the configured key file. findings.title: Lifecycle transitions can disappear between polls
findings.detail: Comments are derived from the current run status, and an event is persisted only when reconciliation observes that status. A run that enters needs_human and is resumed or resolved before the next poll never records or posts that event. Likewise, a second needs_human episode is suppressed by the first episode's done checkpoint. This does not provide a durable side effect for each transition across restarts or polling intervals.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur, with an identity for each status episode, and reconcile those records independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101–102: `if (run.status === "needs_human") events.set("needs_human", ...)`; :113: `if (!events.has(event) && state(effect) !== "pending") continue;`. Events are derived from the current status, without recording intervening transitions.
verification.trigger: A run enters needs_human and resumes between polls. No pending event exists, so its needs-you comment and reason are permanently omitted.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates only run for queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Both the reconciler and its timer are conditional on the issue queue's repository and trusted-account configuration. Runs started through CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers in any other configured repository therefore receive no lifecycle labels or comments, even though the requested behavior covers every start path and does not require queue admission to be enabled.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and select linked issues according to the supported repository settings.
findings.failure_scenario: A repository has the GitHub integration configured but is absent from githubQueue.repos; a CLI run with `Closes #42` produces no lifecycle updates.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10–12 requires `cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; :43 skips with `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:144 also returns immediately when queue configuration is absent.
verification.trigger: A CLI run contains Closes #42 in a GitHub-integrated repository outside githubQueue.repos. It receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

findings.title: A partial failure can release an issue before its failure label is applied
findings.detail: The label loop removes in-progress before adding failed. If the add fails, reconciliation logs the failure and queue selection continues in the same poll. The existing latest-run admission check only finds issue-source runs, so it does not protect a failed CLI or MCP run linked through its prompt. The issue can be selected again using its old priority approval before the failed label is retried.
findings.suggestion: Keep admission closed until the failure transition is durably reflected, including for prompt-linked runs; order label writes so a partial transition does not release the issue.

findings.title: Status transitions between polls are lost
findings.detail: Comments and labels are derived only from the run's current status. No durable event is recorded when a run enters needs_human or failed, so a transition that ends before the next poll cannot be reconstructed. The single comment key for each status also suppresses later occurrences of the same status.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle transitions durably when they occur and reconcile each recorded occurrence independently.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll. The poll sees running and never posts the needs-you comment or applies its label. A second needs_human episode after an observed first episode also receives no new comment.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101–102: `if (run.status === "needs_human") events.set("needs_human", ...)`; :112–114: `const effect = `comment:${event}`; if (!events.has(event) && state(effect) !== "pending") continue; if (state(effect) === "done") continue;`. Labels likewise derive from current status (:15–25), without recording intervening transitions.
verification.trigger: A run enters and leaves needs_human between polls: neither its needs-you label nor comment is published. After one observed episode completes its comment checkpoint, subsequent needs_human episodes never receive another comment.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside queue-configured repositories
findings.detail: The reconciler skips every repository that is absent from githubQueue.repos or has no trusted queue accounts, and it is not started at all when the queue is disabled. The requested lifecycle applies to runs started through every entry point; it is not limited to repositories enabled for automatic issue picking.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration for linked issues.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` in a repository that has no issue queue configured. The run receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10–12: `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length && cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; :43: `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`. src/integrations/index.ts:65–67 starts the queue only when `!!queue?.repos.length && !!queue.trusted.length`.
verification.trigger: A CLI run containing Closes #7 targets a repository without issue-queue configuration. Lifecycle reconciliation never runs for that repository, so the required labels and comments are absent.

findings.title: A failed label write can allow a failed manual run to be re-picked
findings.detail: The transition removes in-progress before adding failed, and a write failure is caught before the queue continues to query candidates. The queue's latestIssueRun lookup only recognizes issue source references, so a terminal CLI or MCP run linked through `Closes #n` supplies no local re-approval guard.
findings.suggestion: Make admission account for terminal runs linked through all supported start paths, including while lifecycle writes are pending.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run for `Closes #7` fails. Removing in-progress succeeds, adding failed fails, and the issue still has its old trusted priority label. The same poll can pick it again without a new approval.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:13 orders labels as `["limitless:in-progress", "limitless:needs-you", "limitless:failed"]`; :68–86 removes non-target labels before adding failed, catching write errors at :93–94. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:97 checks re-approval only when the failed label exists. src/db/store.ts:1268 restricts latestIssueRun to `json_extract(runs.source_ref, '$.kind') = 'issue'`; :1225 restricts claims to active statuses. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 reconciles before selecting candidates.
verification.trigger: A failed CLI Closes #7 run has no issue sourceRef. Removing in-progress succeeds but adding failed fails. With its old trusted priority label intact, no active claim and no issue-sourced history, the same poll can admit another run without re-approval.

findings.title: An older run can overwrite labels after a newer run starts
findings.detail: The latest-run map is computed once before any GitHub awaits. Re-reading the old run's status does not check whether another run has since claimed the same issue, so an in-flight reconciliation can apply an old terminal label after a newer run has started.
findings.suggestion: Recheck issue ownership after awaited operations and before each label mutation, coordinating it with run admission.
findings.failure_scenario: While reconciliation of an old failed run is awaiting its label read, a new run for the same issue starts. The old reconciliation then removes in-progress or adds failed based on its stale latest-run map.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:35–39 builds `latest` once from `store.issueLifecycleRuns()`. The ownership check at :56 precedes the awaited label read at :60. Subsequent checks at :63–71 only reload `store.getRun(snapshot.id)` and compare `desiredLabel(run) !== target`; they never refresh issue ownership.
verification.trigger: A newer run for the issue is created while an old failed run awaits its label read. The old reconciliation retains ownership in its stale map and can remove in-progress or add failed after the newer run starts, until a subsequent poll corrects the labels.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation skips every repository absent from githubQueue.repos, and the reconciler itself is started only when the queue has configured repositories and trusted accounts. The request requires lifecycle updates for every start path, including CLI and MCP runs, with gh as the fallback identity.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and handle linked issues for all applicable repositories.
findings.failure_scenario: A user runs `limitless run` with `Closes #7` for a repository that is not in githubQueue.repos. No lifecycle label or comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10–12 requires `cfg.githubQueue.repos.some((r) => r.toLowerCase() === repo.toLowerCase())`; :43 skips the issue when this condition fails: `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`.
verification.trigger: A CLI run containing Closes #7 targets a repository absent from githubQueue.repos. Its lifecycle labels and comments are skipped. This duplicates C2.

findings.title: Transient lifecycle events disappear before they are checkpointed
findings.detail: Events are inferred only from the current run snapshot. A needs_human or failed state that begins and ends between polls is never recorded. The same loss occurs when an earlier comment fails: the loop breaks before saving later events as pending, so a status change before the next poll erases them.
findings.suggestion: Durably record each lifecycle transition when it occurs, then reconcile its effects independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human while the started comment write is failing, then is resumed before the next poll. No needs-you comment is ever posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:110 processes "started" before "needs_human"; :159–161 checkpoints only the current event; :165–167 catches a write failure and executes "break". At :101–102, needs_human is reconstructed only when "run.status === \"needs_human\"".
verification.trigger: The started comment fails while the run needs human input. Processing stops before checkpointing needs_human; the run resumes before another poll, so that event disappears and its comment is never posted.

findings.title: A second needs-human episode is treated as already delivered
findings.detail: Comment checkpoints are keyed only by run and event name. Once a needs_human comment is marked done, a resumed run that later reaches needs_human again cannot post its new reason. Label reconciliation can still switch back to needs-you, leaving the issue with a stale explanation.
findings.suggestion: Key lifecycle effects by a durable transition or status episode rather than only by event type.
findings.failure_scenario: A run needs human input, resumes after the owner responds, and later needs human input for a different reason. The second reason is never commented.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:112 uses "const effect = `comment:${event}`"; :114 skips "if (state(effect) === \"done\") continue"; :164 saves that effect as "done". The key contains no episode identifier.
verification.trigger: The first needs_human comment succeeds. After resuming, the same run needs human input for another reason; its existing comment:needs_human checkpoint suppresses the second comment.

findings.title: Re-approval can come from a priority label that is no longer applied
findings.detail: The post-failure check accepts any trusted priority labeled event, even if that label was subsequently removed. The separate approved check can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before the failure, so the current approval need not be the one applied after failure.
findings.suggestion: Require a currently applied, trusted priority label whose latest application occurred after the failure label.
findings.failure_scenario: Priority:2 was applied before failure; a trusted user applies and removes priority:1 after failure. The issue remains eligible using the old priority:2 label despite the later approval having been withdrawn.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:74–81 builds `approved` from current labels and checks `trusts(last?.actor?.login)`, without requiring application after failure. Lines 97–99 separately accept `!events.some((e) => trusts(e.actor?.login) && Date.parse(e.createdAt) > failedAt)` as the rejection condition; `events` includes historical priority applications (lines 61–63), including removed labels.
verification.trigger: Trusted priority:2 remains from before failure. Trusted priority:1 is applied after failure and then removed. The historical priority:1 event satisfies re-approval while priority:2 supplies current approval, allowing the failed issue to be picked again.

findings.title: An unrelated comment can impersonate a completed lifecycle write
findings.detail: Recovery treats any issue comment containing the predictable marker as proof that the factory posted its pending comment, without checking its author. An issue participant can supply that marker and cause the actual lifecycle comment to be permanently marked done.
findings.suggestion: Verify the recovered comment was authored by the configured factory identity and matches the pending body before marking the effect done.
findings.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails, another issue participant posts a comment containing the run's marker. On the next poll the factory records the failed comment as delivered and never retries it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:123 parses comments as "z.object({ body: z.string() })"; :128–130 accepts "comments.some((c) => c.body.includes(marker))" and calls "save(effect, \"done\")" without checking the author or full body.
verification.trigger: After a failed comment POST, another participant posts a comment containing the predictable run/event marker. Reconciliation treats it as the factory's completed write and suppresses the intended comment.

findings.title: A 404 during label removal is silently recorded as success
findings.detail: The catch treats every HTTP 404 as an already-removed label. GitHub can also return 404 for an inaccessible repository or issue, so a permission or installation failure can be checkpointed as a successful label transition and will not be retried.
findings.suggestion: Confirm the label is absent with a successful fresh read before recording the removal as complete; otherwise log and retry the error.
findings.failure_scenario: The initial label read succeeds, but the App loses repository access before the DELETE. GitHub returns 404 and the reconciliation cursor records the label set as complete even though the label remains.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:86 throws only "if (add || !/\bHTTP 404\b/.test(String(error)))"; :88 then saves the removal effect as "done", and :92 saves the complete label cursor. At :56, a matching cursor skips further reconciliation.
verification.trigger: The initial label read succeeds, but repository access disappears before DELETE and GitHub returns HTTP 404 while retaining the label. The failure is swallowed and checkpointed as success; restoring access does not retry removal while the desired state remains unchanged.

findings.title: Status transitions between polls never produce their comments
findings.detail: Lifecycle comments are derived from the current run status. A needs_human episode that begins and ends between polls is never recorded as pending, so its required comment is permanently lost. The pending-comment tests cover a transition only after a poll has already observed it.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur and reconcile those records. Add a test that enters and leaves needs_human between polls, then restarts and checks for exactly one comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next issue-queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 invokes "await reconcileIssueLifecycle(...)" from the polling tick. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:97–102 reads the current run and adds needs_human only if "run.status === \"needs_human\"". src/db/store.ts:2012–2017 updates the run row and publishes it without recording a lifecycle event.
verification.trigger: A run enters needs_human and resumes between polls. Reconciliation observes only the resumed status, so it never checkpoints or posts the needs-you comment.

findings.title: A removed priority label can supply re-approval
findings.detail: The re-approval check accepts any trusted priority-label event after failure, even if that label is no longer present. The separate approved-label check can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before failure. The tests only exercise re-approval using the currently present label and miss this combination.
findings.suggestion: Require a currently applied, trusted priority label whose applicable labeling event is later than the failure event. Add a test with an old current priority and a later trusted priority that has since been removed.
findings.failure_scenario: priority:1 remains from before failure; a trusted user adds and then removes priority:2 after failure. The issue becomes eligible despite having no current priority approval applied after failure.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:61–63 collects all historical priority `LabeledEvent`s. Lines 74–81 independently approve current labels. Lines 97–99 require only `events.some((e) => trusts(e.actor?.login) && Date.parse(e.createdAt) > failedAt)`, with no current-label membership check.
verification.trigger: Trusted priority:1 remains from before failure; trusted priority:2 is applied after failure and removed. The removed label's event passes the failure guard, so the issue remains eligible without a currently applied post-failure approval.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside the issue queue configuration
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation requires the repository to be in githubQueue.repos with trusted accounts configured, and the poller does not start without that configuration. The request requires updates for linked runs from all start paths. The new test explicitly asserts no updates for disabled or unlisted repositories, thereby protecting this omission.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation for linked GitHub issues independently of queue admission configuration, and test a CLI or MCP run when queue polling is disabled.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner starts a run with Closes #7 in a GitHub repository that is not enabled for automatic issue picking; the issue receives neither labels nor comments.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10-12 requires `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length && cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; line 43 skips issues with `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`. src/integrations/index.ts:65-67 starts reconciliation's queue only when queue repositories and trusted accounts are configured.
verification.trigger: Start a new CLI run containing Closes #7 in a repository outside githubQueue.repos, or with the queue disabled. No lifecycle labels or comments are written.

findings.title: Restart coverage does not exercise each lifecycle transition
findings.detail: The interruption matrix only interrupts the initial started event. The needs-human, failure, cancellation, PR, and merge tests restart after their writes have completed, so they do not establish that a restart between each transition's label change and comment preserves the required effect.
findings.suggestion: Exercise interruption after the label update and before the comment for each applicable transition, then reopen the store and verify the final labels and exactly one comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that loses a failed or needs-human comment after its label write can pass the current restart tests.

verification.evidence: test/issue-queue.test.ts:1275 parameterizes interruption only by ["after label", "after comment"]; its assertions at :1295–1298 cover only "limitless:in-progress" and "comment:started". The terminal-transition test checks `expect(h.comments.get(7)).toHaveLength(2)` at :1225 before `h.stop()` at :1228. The additional failed/needs_human restart cases already require `comment:${status}` to be "pending" at :1347 before restarting at :1349–1350.
verification.trigger: A regression affecting failed or needs_human recovery specifically between the label write and creation of the comment checkpoint could pass these tests: only the started transition is interrupted in that window. Terminal-transition tests restart after the comment is completed or already pending.

findings.title: Do not accept an arbitrary issue comment as proof of a factory write
findings.detail: Recovery treats any comment containing the predictable lifecycle marker as proof that the factory posted its comment. Issue comments are untrusted: their author is neither retrieved nor checked. An attacker who can comment can therefore suppress a pending lifecycle notification.
findings.suggestion: Authenticate the author of a matching comment against the GitHub identity used for the write, and require an exact, validated marker before recording the effect as done.
findings.failure_scenario: A comment POST fails or the daemon restarts after marking it pending. Another issue participant posts a comment containing `<!-- limitless-lifecycle:<run-id>:failed -->`. On the next poll, reconciliation marks the failed notification done without posting it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:123 parses comments as `z.object({ body: z.string() })`, without author identity. Lines 128-130 accept `comments.some((c) => c.body.includes(marker))` and execute `save(effect, "done"); continue;`.
verification.trigger: A lifecycle comment remains pending after a failed POST or restart. Another participant posts its predictable run/event marker. Reconciliation accepts that comment and permanently suppresses the factory notification.

findings.title: Tie re-approval to a priority label that is still applied
findings.detail: The post-failure check accepts any historical trusted priority-label event, even if that label has since been removed. The separately computed `approved` set can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before the failure, so a withdrawn re-approval still permits the issue to run.
findings.suggestion: Require the latest trusted application of a currently applied priority label to be later than the failure event.
findings.failure_scenario: An issue retains `priority:2` from before failure. A trusted account applies `priority:1` after failure and subsequently removes it to withdraw approval. The old `priority:2` satisfies `approved`, while the historical `priority:1` event satisfies this check, so the failed issue is picked again.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:74–81 validates current priority labels using `return trusts(last?.actor?.login)`. findings.title: Canonicalized names no longer resolve existing mixed-case repository registrations
findings.detail: The queue passes the lowercased repository name into run creation. Repository resolution uses a case-sensitive getRepoBySlug lookup, so an existing mixed-case registration is missed. findings.title: Classify the moved tip before discarding a release intent
findings.detail: Every `moved` result from a replay marks the confirmed lease lost and clears the intent without examining the returned tip. The claim client can return `moved` for a malformed record or a valid record that does not meet the supersession conditions.
