findings.title: An exception in the renewal timer becomes an unhandled rejection
findings.detail: The async interval callback has no rejection handler. A thrown database, clock, client, or hook error rejects the callback, stops processing the remaining leases for that tick, and can terminate the process under an unhandled-rejection policy. There is no reporting or controlled retry of the failure.
findings.suggestion: Handle and report failures from timer work explicitly, and ensure one failed ref does not silently prevent the other refs from being processed.
findings.failure_scenario: A clock read throws while renewing the first active lease. The timer callback rejects and later active leases are skipped for that tick; the rejection may terminate the daemon.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:239-243 installs `timer.set(async () => { ... for (const h of handles.values()) if (current(h) && next.active(h)) await manager.update(h, {}); }, LEASE.renewMs)` without catching rejection. The renewal path calls `clock.sample()` at :146. src/util/claim-clock.ts:64 explicitly throws on zero clock readings.
verification.trigger: A clock read throws during renewal of the first active lease. The interval callback rejects without a handler, and remaining leases are skipped for that tick. Process termination depends on runtime rejection handling.

findings.title: A different run is refused before the pending intent is reconciled
findings.detail: The cross-run guard runs before reconciliation, so a pending intent returns `refused` rather than `wait` and cannot be resolved by that acquisition. The test for a pending old run explicitly expects this behavior, masking the violation of the requirement to reconcile pending intents before every operation.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile first, return wait while the intent remains pending, and only then evaluate the confirmed row and fresh tip. Test both unresolved and dropped intents when a different run acquires.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A has an unconfirmed first acquisition whose intent can now be dropped; run B calls acquire before the loop runs and is refused instead of reconciling and acquiring.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:107 returns early when `row && row.runId !== want.run && (row.intent || row.confirmed?.state === "held")`; reconciliation occurs afterward at :108. At :91, reconciliation would forget a dropped, never-confirmed row: `if (result === "dropped" && !store.leaseRow(repo, ref)?.confirmed) store.forgetLease(repo, ref);`.
verification.trigger: Run A leaves an unconfirmed first-acquisition intent that is now droppable. Run B calls acquire before a reconciliation tick and receives refused: live without reconciliation, despite the ref being available.

findings.title: The renewal loop omits confirmed leases recovered without an in-memory handle
findings.detail: The loop iterates only handles created by an applied write in this manager instance. Recovery and intent reconciliation can confirm a held row without adding a handle, so that lease is never passed to `active` or renewed. The recovery tests cover loss and an update on an already registered handle, but do not cover a recovered or reconciled acquisition becoming eligible for renewal.
findings.suggestion: Populate or derive renewal handles from confirmed held rows after recovery and reconciliation, and test a recovered acquisition through a renewal tick.
findings.failure_scenario: An acquisition returns unconfirmed, then the loop reconciles its intent as applied; subsequent ticks never renew that confirmed lease because no handle was inserted into `handles`.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/lease-store.ts:132-134 confirms a reconciled intent with `confirm(tip.sha); return "applied";`. src/integrations/leases.ts:87-92 does not add a handle after that result, while :242 renews only `handles.values()`. Handles are inserted solely in the direct applied-write branch at :192.
verification.trigger: An acquisition returns unconfirmed and a later tick reconciles it as applied. The newly confirmed lease has no in-memory handle, so subsequent ticks omit renewal even when the active hook would accept it. This duplicates C6.

findings.title: Mutation tests expect the broken two-winner result
findings.detail: The unconditional-ref-write cases explicitly expect two winners and therefore pass when the single-holder invariant is broken. The request requires the concurrent-create and takeover tests to fail against that mutant; these cases instead assert the mutant's defect as success.
findings.suggestion: Use the same one-winner assertions for the normal implementation and mutation check, and verify that running them with the unconditional-write mutant fails.
findings.failure_scenario: The fake allows both concurrent writes unconditionally; both acquisitions report held at the same generation, yet the mutant test passes.

verification.evidence: test/leases.test.ts:138 asserts `expect(winners).toHaveLength(unconditional ? 2 : 1)`, and line 140 skips the refused-loser assertion when unconditional. Lines 143–147 run both races with the mutant enabled. test/claim-github-fake.ts:125–129 bypasses conflict checks when `this.unconditional` and applies the write.
verification.trigger: Enable the unconditional-ref-write mutant during concurrent create or takeover: both managers report held at the same generation, and the assertions accept two winners instead of failing the required single-holder invariant. Targeted execution was blocked by an unrelated `floors.prefault is not a function` initialization error.

findings.title: Replayed release bypasses the lease-time send check
findings.detail: The manager delegates pending-intent reconciliation to `reconcileLeaseIntent`, which replays a release using `client.write` without a `beforeSend` hook or a fresh GitHub-time sample. A release interrupted before its ref update can therefore be sent after the confirmed generation has expired. That violates the same-generation send-time check and can publish a released tip after the holder's authority has ended.
findings.suggestion: Require the same fresh-time decision and immediate pre-send revalidation when replaying a release, and leave the intent pending when that authority cannot be confirmed.
findings.failure_scenario: A release commit is journaled before its ref update, the process stops for longer than the lease expiry, and reconciliation finds the old held tip unchanged. It replays the release without checking expiry; a different run can then acquire the released tip.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:89 calls `reconcileLeaseIntent({ client, store, signal }, repo, ref)` without time validation; startup also invokes `recoverLeases({ client, store })` at line 65. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:118-121 replays releases using `client.write(..., { signal, onCommit: ... })` without `beforeSend`. src/integrations/claim-ref.ts:206-208 only aborts when `opts.beforeSend?.()` returns `false`.
verification.trigger: A pending release survives a restart longer than lease expiry, while GitHub still has the confirmed held tip. Recovery sends and confirms the expired generation's release without checking renewable time; a terminal-status release then permits another run to acquire.

findings.title: Renewal loop omits recovered confirmed leases
findings.detail: The loop renews only handles inserted into the in-memory `handles` map by an applied write in this manager instance. Creation and reconciliation do not populate that map for previously confirmed held rows or for an acquisition whose unconfirmed intent is later reconciled as applied. Those leases never receive automatic renewal unless another operation happens to write them first.
findings.suggestion: Populate or derive loop handles from confirmed held rows, including rows confirmed during recovery and reconciliation.
findings.failure_scenario: An acquisition updates GitHub but returns `unconfirmed`; the next tick reconciles its intent to applied. Subsequent ticks never renew that confirmed lease because no handle was added to `handles`.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:49 initializes `handles = new Map<string, LeaseHandle>()`. Its only insertion is `handles.set(key(repo, ref), held)` at line 192, after an immediate applied write. The reconciliation wrapper at lines 87-92 never registers handles. Lines 240-242 reconcile pending rows, then renew only `handles.values()`.
verification.trigger: A first acquisition reaches GitHub but returns unconfirmed. A tick reconciles it to confirmed held ownership, but no handle enters the renewal map. Later ticks skip the lease even when active returns true, allowing it to expire.

findings.title: Different-run acquisition skips pending-intent reconciliation
findings.detail: The early different-run check returns `refused` whenever the row has an intent, before reconciliation runs. An unresolved intent is required to yield `wait`, and a dropped never-confirmed acquisition must be forgotten so another run can acquire. This path does neither; without a running renewal loop, the stale intent can block the next run indefinitely.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile the row before classifying a different-run acquisition, returning wait while unresolved and applying the normal dropped-intent cleanup.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A leaves an unconfirmed first-acquisition intent whose GitHub ref is still absent. Run B calls acquire before the loop reconciles it and receives `refused: live` instead of reconciling the dropped intent and acquiring the absent ref.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:107 returns refused when `row.runId !== want.run && (row.intent || row.confirmed?.state === "held")`, before `await reconcile(repo, ref, signal)` at line 108. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:113-116 drops an acquisition intent when the ref is absent; src/integrations/leases.ts:91 would then forget its never-confirmed row.
verification.trigger: Run A leaves an unconfirmed acquisition intent, but its write did not create the ref. Run B acquires before a loop reconciliation and gets refused: live without reconciling and clearing A's failed acquisition.

findings.title: Reconcile another run’s pending intent before refusing
findings.detail: The request says, “Before every operation, under the ref mutex, a row's pending intent goes through #952's reconcileLeaseIntent” and unresolved intents return `wait`. This early return instead refuses a different run without attempting reconciliation, even when the pending acquisition can be dropped and its never-confirmed row forgotten.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile the row before deciding whether its run or confirmed ownership prevents the acquisition.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A has an unconfirmed first acquisition whose write did not move the ref. Run B acquires the same ref after it becomes readable; it receives `refused: live` rather than reconciling A's dropped intent and proceeding.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:107 checks another run's `row.intent` and immediately returns refused; reconciliation occurs only at line 108. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:113-116 would drop the failed acquisition when a readable ref is absent, and src/integrations/leases.ts:91 would forget the unconfirmed row.
verification.trigger: GitHub becomes readable after run A's unconfirmed first acquisition failed to move the ref. Run B still receives refused: live because A's pending intent prevents the reconciliation that would clear it and permit acquisition. This duplicates C14.

findings.title: Restore confirmed handles for the renewal loop
findings.detail: The request requires the loop to update “each confirmed `held` handle whose `active` hook is true.” The loop only visits the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated by writes applied in this manager instance. Existing confirmed rows after restart, and acquisitions confirmed by intent reconciliation, never enter that map.
findings.suggestion: Populate or derive renewal handles from confirmed held rows after recovery and reconciliation.
findings.failure_scenario: A manager restarts with a confirmed held lease, or an unconfirmed acquisition is confirmed on a later tick. Even with `active` returning true, subsequent ticks never renew that lease and it expires.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:49 creates an empty handles map. Startup recovery at lines 64-70 handles superseded losses but never restores held handles. Only the immediate applied-write path inserts a handle at line 192. The loop at lines 240-242 reconciles intents and renews exclusively from `handles.values()`.
verification.trigger: A restarted manager has a persisted confirmed held lease, or recovery confirms an unconfirmed acquisition. Without another successful explicit acquisition, the renewal map remains empty for that lease; active returning true cannot cause renewal, so it expires.

findings.title: Revalidate time before replaying a pending release
findings.detail: The request requires that “Immediately before the `updateRefs` send” the manager revalidate the applicable time predicate. `reconcileLeaseIntent` can replay a release by calling `client.write` without a `beforeSend` hook or a GitHub-time check; this path is also invoked during initial recovery. A release intent left before its send can consequently be written after the generation has expired.
findings.suggestion: Ensure release replay obtains and revalidates the same-generation time authorization before sending, including during recovery.
findings.failure_scenario: A release is journaled, the process stops before updating the ref, and recovery runs more than ten minutes later while the ref is unchanged. Recovery sends the stale same-generation release without checking whether renewal is still permitted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:65 calls `recoverLeases({ client, store })`; line 89 likewise calls `reconcileLeaseIntent({ client, store, signal }, repo, ref)` without time validation. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:118-121 replays a release using `client.write(..., { signal, onCommit: ... })`, omitting `beforeSend`. src/integrations/claim-ref.ts:206-208 aborts only when `opts.beforeSend?.()` returns false.
verification.trigger: A pending release survives a restart exceeding the lease lifetime, with the ref still at its confirmed tip. Recovery sends and confirms the expired generation's release without a fresh GitHub-time decision or send-time revalidation.

findings.title: Do not mark ownership lost for every second moved result
findings.detail: The request says “Only `moved` to a superseding record means lost.” After two non-matching `moved` outcomes, this branch marks any confirmed row lost without checking whether the second tip supersedes its generation and identity.
findings.suggestion: Classify the returned tip against confirmed ownership before marking the lease lost; return a non-loss result when it does not supersede it.
findings.failure_scenario: A confirmed generation encounters two moved results whose final tip is malformed or has a lower generation. The manager marks the confirmed lease lost and calls `onLost` despite having no superseding record.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:202-208 checks `mine`, then executes `if (++moved < 2) continue; if (row?.confirmed && row.runId === want.run) { lose(row, result.tip); return { kind: "superseded", tip: result.tip }; }`. It does not validate the final tip's generation or malformed status. The called `lose` performs `store.markLeaseLost(row.repo, row.ref)` and `hooks?.onLost(h, tip)` at lines 60-62.
verification.trigger: An acquisition with confirmed ownership receives two non-same-holder moved outcomes. For example, the first points to a lower-generation released record, allowing another acquisition attempt, and the second is malformed. The second outcome marks ownership lost and reports supersession despite containing no superseding record.

candidates.title: Reconcile a pending intent before refusing another run
candidates.detail: The different-run check returns `refused` before reconciliation whenever an intent exists. An unresolved intent must produce `wait`, and a resolvable failed first acquisition must be dropped and forgotten before the next run is considered. This ordering can leave the next run refused even though the first run never acquired the ref.
candidates.suggestion: Reconcile the row first, return `wait` if it remains pending, and then evaluate ownership using the refreshed row.
candidates.failure_scenario: Run A's first acquisition leaves an unconfirmed intent. Run B calls acquire before the renewal loop reconciles it; B receives `refused: live` without a GitHub read, even if reconciliation would establish that A's write did not happen.

candidates.title: Release replay bypasses lease-time revalidation

candidates.suggestion: Make release reconciliation apply the same fresh-time decision and send-time predicate as other same-generation writes.
candidates.failure_scenario: A release intent is persisted before its ref update, the process stops, and recovery runs after the lease window and renewable period have elapsed while the old tip remains unchanged. Recovery sends the release anyway.

candidates.title: Renewal loop omits confirmed leases recovered from storage
candidates.detail: The loop only visits the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated by an immediately applied write in this manager instance. Startup recovery and later reconciliation can confirm held leases without adding a handle, and existing confirmed rows also do not populate the map. Such leases never reach the `active` hook or get renewed by the loop.
candidates.suggestion: Populate or derive renewal handles from confirmed held rows after recovery and reconciliation, while retaining the generation checks.
candidates.failure_scenario: An acquisition is applied on GitHub but returns unconfirmed; a later loop tick reconciles it to held. No handle was added to `handles`, so subsequent ticks do not renew it and the lease expires.

candidates.title: Replaying a release bypasses lease-time validation
candidates.detail: Reconciliation can replay a pending release through `reconcileLeaseIntent`, whose write has no `beforeSend` time check. This path runs before the manager samples GitHub time or checks the lease window, including during startup recovery and loop ticks. A release interrupted before its ref update can therefore mutate a generation after its lease has expired.
candidates.suggestion: Make release replay use the manager’s fresh time decision and send-time revalidation, or leave the intent pending until it can be replayed safely.

candidates.detail: The early refusal executes before reconciliation whenever another run owns a row with an intent. An unresolved first acquisition that is subsequently proven unchanged remains in the database and prevents the next run from acquiring until a timer happens to reconcile it; if the loop has not started, it blocks indefinitely. The request requires reconciliation before every operation and forgetting an unconfirmed acquisition when dropped.
candidates.suggestion: Reconcile the row before deciding whether its run blocks the request, then re-read the row and apply the ownership checks.
candidates.failure_scenario: Run A leaves an unconfirmed acquisition intent for an absent ref, then ends. GitHub later becomes readable and run B calls acquire before the renewal loop starts; B receives `refused: live` and A’s droppable intent remains.

candidates.title: Recovered and reconciled holdings are never added to the renewal loop
candidates.detail: The loop renews only the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated solely by an immediately applied write in `operate`. Startup recovery and later reconciliation can confirm a held acquisition without populating that map. Such confirmed holdings are never presented to `active` or renewed, so they expire even when the caller considers the run active.
candidates.suggestion: Populate or derive the loop’s handles from confirmed held rows after recovery and reconciliation.
candidates.failure_scenario: An acquisition’s ref update succeeds but its response is unreadable, so acquire returns wait. The next tick reconciles the intent as applied, but subsequent ticks never renew that confirmed generation.

candidates.title: A second moved outcome can mark a non-superseded generation lost
candidates.detail: After two moved outcomes the manager unconditionally calls `lose` for a confirmed row, without checking whether the returned record supersedes that confirmed ownership. A moved result can instead contain an older generation or a malformed record. This violates the requirement that only a superseding record establishes loss and clears the confirmed ownership on an uncertain result.
candidates.suggestion: Classify the second moved tip against the confirmed run, member and generation before marking loss; return a non-loss result when it does not establish supersession.
candidates.failure_scenario: A confirmed generation 2 write encounters two concurrent ref movements, and the second returned tip is malformed or generation 1. The manager marks generation 2 lost and calls `onLost` even though the returned tip does not establish a superseding generation.

findings.title: A superseded unsent question set can never be published later
findings.detail: An unsent question effect is permanently marked done when its run temporarily stops waiting. If the run later returns to waiting with the same unanswered question IDs, observe() sees the existing effect and never creates another publication. The same problem occurs after recovery establishes that a stale POST was not accepted. The run can therefore remain waiting indefinitely without its questions appearing on the issue.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish a superseded effect with no confirmed publication from a completed publication, and allow a fresh eligible waiting episode to publish the set after any uncertain prior POST has been recovered.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters waiting_input with question 42, but its pending comment has not been posted. The run temporarily changes to running, so reconciliation marks the effect done. It returns to waiting_input with question 42 still unanswered; subsequent polls and restarts never post the question.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:355–358: `let stale = pending.state === "recovering" || !eligible(); if (stale && !pending.page) { save(effect, "done"); continue; }`. At :129, creation requires `!effects.has(`comment:questions:${ids}`)`; at :353, delivery accepts only `"pending", "recovering"`. A retired effect is never reopened.
verification.trigger: An unsent question set becomes ineligible while the run is running, then the run returns to waiting_input with the same unanswered IDs. Its durable done checkpoint prevents publication on every subsequent poll and restart.

findings.title: Retired unsent question sets cannot be published if they become eligible again
findings.detail: Superseding an unsent question effect marks it done, and observe() will never create that effect again because it already exists. A temporary linkage or status change can therefore permanently suppress a question set that was never posted.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish superseded unsent effects from completed publications and allow the same set to be scheduled again when it becomes eligible.

findings.title: A stale poller snapshot can permanently discard a land conflict
findings.detail: A land trigger is immediately evaluated against any saved poller snapshot, even if that snapshot predates the approved head. `startConflictTrigger` marks the trigger skipped when the saved head differs, and a later poll cannot reconsider it. The queue has already blocked the entry, so the requested conflict round never starts.
findings.suggestion: Refresh the PR observation before rejecting a land trigger for a stale head, or retain the trigger pending until a current observation can decide it.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller last observed head A; a review round pushes head B and B is approved before the next poll. Landing B conflicts with the base, but the saved snapshot still says A, so the B trigger is permanently skipped as `PR head moved`.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/review-round.ts:185–196 reads the live head and records approval without updating github_prs. src/land/queue.ts:293 calls mergeBase; :641 records the conflicting approved SHA; :266 calls processConflictTriggers. src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:21 uses the saved snapshot without refreshing it. src/db/store.ts:1126–1127 checks 'seen.headRefOid !== trigger.head' → 'PR head moved'; :1139 permanently updates the trigger to "state = 'skipped'".
verification.trigger: Snapshot contains A; a review round delivers B and B receives approval before polling refreshes the snapshot. Landing B conflicts, but processing permanently skips its durable land trigger against A. A later poll may create a separate trigger; it does not recover this land trigger.

findings.title: A conflict observed during another round is lost permanently
findings.detail: An active review or conflict round causes the trigger to be marked skipped. The poller emits `pr.conflicting` only on entry into the conflicting state, so if the active round fails or ends without changing the head, subsequent polls do not create another trigger. The unresolved conflict therefore never gets its own round.
findings.suggestion: Keep the trigger pending while another round is active and reconsider it when that round terminates, subject to a fresh PR observation and the daily cap.
findings.failure_scenario: A review round is in flight when the poller first observes the PR as CONFLICTING. The trigger is skipped; the review round later fails without pushing, and every subsequent poll still sees CONFLICTING, so no conflict round starts.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/review-round.ts:199 creates an ordinary review round via `store.createReviewRound(...)`. When a conflict is observed, src/integrations/github-poller.ts:372-374 saves the observation and calls `store.startConflictTrigger(trigger.id, snap, now())`. src/db/store.ts:1130-1140 checks `rounds.some((r) => !TERMINAL_STATUSES.includes(r.status))`, assigns `"round in flight"`, and executes `UPDATE conflict_triggers SET state = 'skipped', reason = ? WHERE id = ?`. Only `state = 'pending'` triggers are retried (src/db/store.ts:1071). The ordinary review round can then abort without delivery: src/pipeline/engine.ts:589-594 aborts a conflicting merge and throws `NeedsHumanError`. Subsequent unchanged observations cannot recreate the trigger because src/integrations/github-poller.ts:206 emits only when `next.mergeable === "CONFLICTING" && prev?.mergeable !== "CONFLICTING"`.
verification.trigger: An open, non-draft factory PR has an ordinary review round in flight when polling first observes CONFLICTING. Its conflict trigger becomes permanently skipped. The review round ends without pushing, leaving the same conflicting head; subsequent polls and restarts never start a conflict round unless another independent trigger occurs.

findings.title: A transient PR lookup failure leaves a trigger idle until another event or restart
findings.detail: When no poller snapshot exists, a failed `readPrHead` leaves the trigger pending, but both queue processing calls only log the error. The startup worker is not scheduled again, and the blocked land entry is no longer pumped. If the PR is not subsequently observed by the poller, the durable trigger remains pending indefinitely.
findings.suggestion: Arrange for pending triggers to be retried through an existing periodic consumer after transient lookup failures.
findings.failure_scenario: A land entry conflicts before its first poller snapshot exists, and the initial `gh pr view` fails transiently. GitHub recovers, but no new land block or daemon restart occurs; the entry stays blocked and no round starts.

verification.evidence: With polling disabled, src/integrations/index.ts:38-40 uses `factory.cfg.githubPoll ? startGitHubPoller(...) : () => {}`. src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:23-30 explicitly leaves lookup failures pending: `// Lookup failures leave the durable trigger pending for startup to try again` followed by `lookupError ??= error; continue;`. The land-block attempt runs once at src/land/queue.ts:266, and startup processing is guarded by `if (!this.conflictStartup)` at src/land/queue.ts:128. With polling enabled, recovery does exist: src/integrations/github-poller.ts:373-374 calls `store.startConflictTrigger(trigger.id, snap, now())` for pending triggers on subsequent observations.
verification.trigger: With the supported configuration `[github] poll = false`, a land conflict creates a pending trigger without a saved snapshot, and its initial `gh pr view` fails transiently. Recovery of GitHub alone does not retry it; the round remains idle until another processing event or restart. With default polling enabled, the claim is prevented by subsequent poll observations.

findings.title: A stale poller snapshot can permanently discard a land trigger
findings.detail: The land path uses any stored GitHub snapshot without refreshing it. `startConflictTrigger` marks the trigger skipped when that snapshot's head differs from the land entry's approved head, even if the snapshot is simply older than the approval. The trigger is then no longer pending, so this landing-queue trigger cannot recover on restart.
findings.suggestion: Refresh or otherwise establish the snapshot's freshness before permanently skipping a land trigger; retain it pending when the observation cannot establish the current head.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller saved head A, the PR advances to B and B is approved before the next poll, and the land queue detects a conflict at B. Processing compares B with the saved A and skips the trigger instead of starting a round.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/review-round.ts:195–196 records approval for the live reviewed SHA. src/land/queue.ts:201–204 accepts that approval; :641 records blocked.approvedSha as the conflict trigger. src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:21 passes the saved snapshot. src/db/store.ts:1126–1127 classifies a snapshot/trigger SHA mismatch as 'PR head moved', and :1139 sets "state = 'skipped'". Pending selection at :1071 excludes skipped triggers.
verification.trigger: B is approved while github_prs still contains A. A land conflict at B produces a trigger that is permanently skipped rather than started or retained for a fresh observation.

findings.title: Retrying comment creation can post duplicate resolution comments
findings.detail: The `gh` wrapper retries transient failures around the entire comment command. If GitHub creates the comment but its response is lost, the retry creates another comment without checking the marker again. The preflight marker lookup only protects a later delivery attempt, not retries within this call.
findings.suggestion: Recheck for the marker after an uncertain comment outcome before issuing another creation request.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub accepts `pr comment`, but the client receives a timeout or connection reset; the retry posts a second comment with the same conflict-round marker.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1921-1922 wraps each gh call in `withGitHubRetry(async () => (await runner(args, signal, stdin)) ?? "", { budget, signal })`. The marker lookup occurs separately at :1892-1894, followed at :1899 by `await gh(["pr", "comment", prUrl, "--body-file", "-"], ctx.signal, text)`. src/git/repos.ts:55 treats command timeouts as transient; :91-97 retries the same call without repeating the marker lookup.
verification.trigger: A successful conflict round reaches delivery; GitHub creates its resolution comment but the command times out with retry budget remaining. The retry posts the same comment again.

findings.title: Restart tests do not cover a stale saved observation

Neither exercises different saved and triggered heads. src/db/store.ts:1126–1127 handles that difference with `seen.headRefOid !== trigger.head ? "PR head moved"`.

findings.title: The non-factory polling case bypasses the poller
findings.detail: The non-factory branch inserts a trigger and calls the store consumer directly, so it does not test whether polling a non-factory PR creates a round. A regression in tracking, event generation, or poller consumption for that case would still pass the test.

findings.title: Persisted conflict filenames bypass credential redaction
findings.detail: Conflict paths come from the repository under review and are copied into run state without credential redaction. The state is subsequently persisted by updateRun, so a registered credential embedded in a filename reaches storage even though the later PR comment redacts it.

findings.title: A stale saved snapshot can start a round for a draft PR

findings.detail: The land-trigger consumer treats any saved GitHub snapshot as current and immediately marks a rejected trigger as skipped. A snapshot can predate the land queue's observation. findings.detail: A lookup error leaves the trigger pending, but this catch only logs the error. The queue processes pending triggers only at startup or after another land entry blocks. If polling is disabled or does not produce another observation for the PR, a transient `gh` failure leaves the conflict unresolved indefinitely until a restart or unrelated block.

findings.failure_scenario: A land conflict is recorded while `gh pr view` temporarily fails and there is no saved PR snapshot. The command later recovers, but no further land conflict or PR poll occurs, so the pending trigger never starts.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:23–30 explicitly leaves failed lookups pending: “Lookup failures leave the durable trigger pending for startup to try again”; the catch sets “lookupError ??= error” and continues. src/land/queue.ts:266–268 catches that failure and only logs it. findings.title: Missing draft state is treated as permission to proceed

findings.failure_scenario: A PR lookup or stored snapshot omits `isDraft` for a draft PR. The conflict round is admitted and the delivery check sees `false`, allowing a push to the draft branch.

findings.title: Cargo home allowance exposes registry credentials to gate commands
findings.detail: The gate profile grants file reads throughout Cargo home, but neither the built-in deny list nor the later specific-deny rules exclude Cargo's credentials or credentials.toml files. findings.title: Line-by-line redaction can expose partial holdout quotations
findings.detail: The new redactor withholds only lines that independently match a catalogued detail. A report can include both a complete verifier observation and a shorter quotation of it; the complete line is withheld, but the partial quotation can remain visible when it contains no separately catalogued literal. Previously, a match caused the entire report value to be withheld. This exposes holdout-only verifier prose to the reviewer and potentially to the next implementer.
findings.suggestion: Protect partial quotations of private verifier observations, or withhold the containing report when safe separation cannot be established. Add a regression test with a complete observation and a shorter quotation on separate lines.
findings.failure_scenario: A private criterion has evidence "Verifier saw the amber lantern glow." A report contains that sentence on one line and "The amber lantern glow was observed" on another. The first line matches the catalogued prose, while the second has no independently harvested syntax-shaped literal and is returned.

Lines 347–355 filter each line independently using `pattern.test(line)`, `encoded(line)`, and `privateMatches(line, distinctive)`. src/gates/private.ts:70–71 requires the complete protected value: `if (layer.includes(protectedText)) return true; if (!truncated) return false;`. Report output uses this filter at src/integrations/mcp-change.ts:514–523.

findings.detail: The request says that “any report line that quotes” holdout test text stays withheld. The catalogue generally records complete scenario phrases and syntax-shaped literals, so a report line quoting only an ordinary fragment of a longer scenario can pass every match and be returned. This limitation predates the diff, but remains an unmet privacy requirement of the change.

findings.title: Repeated credential matches make patch filtering quadratic
findings.detail: Every occurrence scans every line range synchronously before paging. An untrusted large patch with many occurrences of a registered multiline value can therefore block the daemon's event loop for a prolonged period, and each page request repeats the work. A targeted invocation of the extracted function took 893 ms for 50,000 lines and 3,514 ms for 100,000 lines, consistent with quadratic growth.
findings.suggestion: Map match offsets to affected ranges using an ordered cursor or binary search, so work grows with the patch size and number of matching lines.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the initial TLS connection
findings.detail: The initial connection accepts any certificate, and the displayed code is supplied by that connection. A man-in-the-middle can relay the pairing request to the real coordinator, return its code and secret to the worker, and present its own certificate. The owner sees the same code on both sides and approves it; the attacker then observes the claim and issued token. Pinning the attacker's certificate on subsequent requests does not prevent this. The submitted worker certificate fingerprint is never authenticated or used to bind the exchange.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to both endpoints' certificate fingerprints and the pairing exchange, so relaying through a different TLS certificate changes the code or causes verification to fail.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies the real coordinator's pairing response, and forwards the approved claim while terminating both TLS connections.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23-27 calls the initial pairing request with only `{ signal }`; src/workers/tls.ts:103 sets `rejectUnauthorized: false`, and :114 checks the certificate only when `options.pin !== undefined`. src/workers/client.ts:33 prints the returned code and :39 pins `first.fingerprint`. src/db/workers.ts:83-89 issues the approved token solely from the pairing secret: `return w.state === "approved" ? { token: this.issued(w) } : { pending: true };`.
verification.trigger: An active interceptor terminates the initial TLS connection and relays the real pairing response and subsequent claims. The owner sees matching codes, while the interceptor obtains the token and the worker pins the interceptor's certificate.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
findings.detail: Private read protection is an in-memory registry. Pairing releases the token and fingerprint registrations on return, and `runWorker` registers them only in the worker CLI process. A daemon running gates or agents in a separate process therefore does not include those files in its sandbox deny paths. The coordinator TLS key has the same lifetime problem when its listener is disabled after the key has been created. Mode 0600 does not protect files from another process running as the same user.
findings.suggestion: Register the configured worker credential and TLS key paths in every process that constructs agent or gate sandboxes, independent of whether a worker or listener is currently running.
findings.failure_scenario: Pair a worker, then run a factory daemon and a gate on the same machine; the daemon's sandbox is built without the worker token path registered, allowing a gate with access to that path to read the token.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:47-48 registers the persisted files temporarily, then :55-57 executes `for (const release of held) release();`. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 stores protections in a process-local `Map`, and :21 deletes released entries. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 derives explicit denies from `credentials` and `privateReadPaths()`. Its gate-wide protection at :217 covers the OS home, whereas src/config.ts:160 permits `overrides.home ?? process.env.LIMITLESS_HOME` outside that home. src/harness/sandbox.ts:53 uses `(allow default)`.
verification.trigger: Pair with a data directory outside the OS home, then start a separate daemon using it. A gate can read the worker token because the daemon never registered its path and the general home denial does not cover it. Default data directories under the OS home remain protected from gates by the broader denial.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate creation permanently blocks restart
findings.detail: Certificate generation creates the final key path before invoking OpenSSL. If generation fails, times out, or the process stops before both files are complete, the next start either rejects the incomplete pair or tries to parse invalid material. No cleanup or recovery occurs, so the worker listener or pairing command continues to fail on every subsequent start.

findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is stopped after creating the empty key file but before OpenSSL creates the certificate; every later listener start throws `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:18 creates `writeFileSync(keyPath, "", { flag: "wx", mode: 0o600 })` before awaiting OpenSSL at lines 19–39. Line 17 rejects the resulting partial state with `throw new Error("Incomplete worker TLS material")`. Lines 45–47 perform no file cleanup. src/server/workers.ts:15–16 invokes certificate creation for a configured listener, and src/cli/daemon.ts:30 propagates its failure during startup.
verification.trigger: Interrupting initial TLS generation after key.pem creation but before cert.pem creation leaves persistent partial material. Subsequent listener and daemon starts fail until manual repair. The brief, first-start-only interruption window makes this medium severity.

findings.title: Credential read protection ends with the pairing process
findings.detail: The worker token and coordinator fingerprint are registered in an in-memory deny list only while `pairWorker` or `runWorker` holds them. Pairing releases both registrations before exiting, and a separately running daemon has its own deny list. Likewise, an existing coordinator TLS key is not registered when the listener is disabled. An agent sandbox created by that daemon therefore does not receive these paths as private-file denies.
findings.suggestion: Register persisted worker credential and TLS-key paths in every process that constructs agent sandbox policies, independently of whether pairing, the worker loop or the listener is currently running.
findings.failure_scenario: Pair a worker, exit the pairing command, and run an agent through a separate daemon using the same data directory: that daemon's private-file deny list does not contain the stored worker token or coordinator fingerprint.

verification.evidence: src/cli/main.ts:359-366 runs pairing as a separate command. src/workers/client.ts:47-48 writes the token and fingerprint, then :55-57 releases their protection. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 declares a process-local `Map`. src/cli/daemon.ts:15 registers the API token and :30 starts the coordinator listener, without loading worker credential files. src/harness/scratch.ts:136 defaults editor confinement to `gate = false`; src/harness/read-policy.ts:217 adds the whole-home denial only for gates, while :190 includes only credential paths and process-local registrations.
verification.trigger: Pair a worker, exit the pairing command, and start a separate daemon with the same data directory. Editor agents lack explicit denies for the stored worker token and fingerprint; the gate-only whole-home denial does not protect these files from editors.

findings.title: Privacy probe masks the cross-process credential protection gap
findings.detail: The real-Seatbelt test creates the TLS material and registers both worker files in the same process that starts the gate, retaining all registrations throughout the probe. It consequently passes even if a daemon started separately after pairing has no credential paths in its in-memory deny list.
findings.suggestion: Add a real-Seatbelt probe that persists credentials, releases the pairing registrations, and launches the gate from an independently initialized daemon or process; cover an existing TLS key with the listener disabled as well.
findings.failure_scenario: The current implementation releases the registrations after pairing, yet this test retains them and reports all three files denied.

verification.evidence: test/workers.test.ts:266 creates registrations with `files.slice(1).map((p) => privateFile(p, "synthetic-private-file"))`, runs gates at :274, and releases registrations only at :295–296. Production pairing instead releases them before returning: src/workers/client.ts:55–57, `finally { cert.release(); for (const release of held) release(); }`. Registrations are process-local (src/util/private-reads.ts:4, `const privatePaths = new Map<string, number>()`), and release deletes entries (:21). Although runWorker registers token and fingerprint in its own process (src/workers/client.ts:85–86), this does not register them in a separate daemon running agents.
verification.trigger: Run the privacy probe: all three files remain registered in the same process that constructs the gate sandbox, so it passes without testing protection after pairing exits or from a separate daemon. The cross-process protection gap remains untested.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
findings.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the displayed code is supplied by that untrusted connection. An active intermediary can forward the request to the real coordinator, relay its code to the worker, and retain the returned pairing secret. The owner and worker see matching codes, but the intermediary can claim the approved token and the worker pins the intermediary's certificate.
findings.suggestion: Bind the human-compared code to both the coordinator certificate fingerprint and the pairing exchange, so relaying a coordinator response through a different TLS certificate changes the code.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies `/worker/pair` to the coordinator, and relays the real code. After the owner approves it, the attacker claims the worker token.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23-27 sends the initial pairing request with only `{ signal }`; src/workers/tls.ts:103 uses `rejectUnauthorized: false`. Subsequent claims pin that first connection's certificate (`{ pin: first.fingerprint, signal }`, src/workers/client.ts:39). The listener returns the pending secret (src/server/workers.ts:33-35), and `claim(secret)` returns `{ token: this.issued(w) }` once approved (src/db/workers.ts:83-89), without authenticating the worker certificate.
verification.trigger: During the documented initial pairing, an active network interceptor terminates TLS and proxies the pairing request. Relaying the real code satisfies the owner's comparison, while the interceptor learns the claim secret and can retrieve the approved worker token.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
findings.detail: `protectPrivateFile` maintains an in-memory registry. Pairing releases its registrations before exiting, and `runWorker` registers the files only in the worker process. A separately running daemon on the same machine does not receive those registrations when it constructs Claude or Codex sandbox policies, so its agents can read the persistent worker token and coordinator fingerprint. Mode 0600 does not protect them from agents running as the same user.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every daemon process that launches agents, including when the worker is stopped, and cover separate-process sandbox behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine runs both a worker and a factory daemon under the same user. An agent launched by the daemon reads `<data>/worker/token` and impersonates that worker.

verification.evidence: The CLI stores pairing credentials in `join(cfg.paths.home, "worker")` (src/cli/main.ts:359-365). `privateFile` calls `protectPrivateFile(path)` (src/workers/tls.ts:51-52), whose registry is a module-local `const privatePaths = new Map<string, number>()` (src/util/private-reads.ts:4). Daemon startup registers its API token and listener, then mounts integrations, without registering worker credentials (src/cli/daemon.ts:15-31). Editor sandboxes call `writeRoots(..., false, ...)` (src/harness/claude.ts:203); the home is denied wholesale only when `gate` is true (src/harness/read-policy.ts:217).
verification.trigger: Run the supported worker CLI and factory daemon as separate processes under the same user with the default data directory. The daemon's editor sandbox lacks the worker process's private-file registrations, allowing agent-controlled code to read the worker token despite its 0600 mode and impersonate the worker.

findings.title: Disabling the listener leaves its existing TLS key unprotected from agents
findings.detail: The TLS key is added to the process-local private-read registry only when the listener is enabled. After an owner removes `workers.listen` and restarts the daemon, the existing key remains on disk but is no longer included in agent sandbox deny paths. An agent running as the same user can read it, compromising the certificate trusted by already paired workers if the listener is later re-enabled.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent TLS key path independently of whether the listener is currently enabled, or securely remove and rotate the material when disabling it.
findings.failure_scenario: A coordinator previously enabled workers, then starts with the listener disabled. A tool-enabled agent reads `<data>/worker-tls/key.pem` before the listener is enabled again.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:15-16: `if (!listen) return undefined;` precedes `const tls = await certificate(join(paths.home, "worker-tls"));`. Protection is registered inside that skipped function: src/workers/tls.ts:14, `const release = protectPrivateFile(keyPath);`. src/cli/daemon.ts:30-31 subsequently mounts integrations. Editor deny policy includes `privateReadPaths()` at src/harness/read-policy.ts:190, but denies the entire home only for gates at line 217.
verification.trigger: Restart with workers disabled after previously generating TLS material. A tool-enabled editor can read the retained key because startup never registers its private-file protection, provided no separate configured denial covers it.

findings.title: Store untrusted heartbeat fields only after redaction
findings.detail: Heartbeat capabilities are serialized directly into SQLite. Several worker-controlled strings can contain coordinator credentials or private strings, but sanitization occurs only when listing workers. This leaves the unredacted values in persistent storage even though the trust-boundary rules require redaction before storage.
findings.suggestion: Redact and apply private-string policy to worker-supplied capability fields before persisting them, while preserving the fields needed for version matching.
findings.failure_scenario: A paired worker sends a coordinator credential or private string in `osVersion`; the value is written verbatim to the workers table.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:42-46 accepts authenticated POST /worker/heartbeat, parses `Heartbeat.parse(await req.json())`, then calls `workers.heartbeat(current, capabilities)`. src/workers/protocol.ts:8 permits `osVersion: z.string().max(128)`. src/db/workers.ts:143-144 persists it directly: `.query("UPDATE workers SET last_heartbeat_at=?,capabilities=? WHERE name=? AND state='approved'").run(this.now(), JSON.stringify(c), w.name)`. Redaction occurs only when listing: src/db/workers.ts:123-124 reads stored capabilities and calls `this.sanitize(...)`.
verification.trigger: With the worker listener enabled, an approved worker sends a valid heartbeat containing a credential or private string in osVersion. The coordinator stores that value verbatim in workers.capabilities; later list-response sanitization does not remove the persisted secret.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied in the daemon's agent sandboxes
findings.detail: The request requires the worker token and coordinator fingerprint to be read-denied to gates. The deny registry is process-local, but pairing and the worker loop run as separate CLI processes from the daemon. Their registrations are also released when those commands exit. A daemon on the same machine therefore does not add these files to its agent sandbox deny lists; mode 0600 does not protect them from agents running as the same user.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every daemon process that can launch agents and gates, including when the worker command is not running.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine is both a paired worker and a coordinator. An agent launched by its daemon reads the token under the worker data directory and uses it to impersonate the worker.

verification.evidence: Pairing explicitly removes its registrations on return: `cert.release(); for (const release of held) release();` (src/workers/client.ts:55-57). `runWorker` registers token and pin only in its own process (src/workers/client.ts:85-89; src/util/private-reads.ts:4-13). Coordinator daemon startup registers the API token and starts the worker listener but never protects `<data>/worker/token` (src/cli/daemon.ts:15-31). Sandbox read denies combine credential paths and the current process's `privateReadPaths()` (src/harness/read-policy.ts:190); whole-home denial applies only to gates (src/harness/read-policy.ts:217).
verification.trigger: A paired worker machine also runs a coordinator daemon. An editor agent launched by that daemon can read the persisted worker token because neither pairing's released registrations nor the separate worker process's registrations protect the daemon's sandbox. This duplicates C11's underlying defect.

findings.title: Disabling the listener removes protection for an existing TLS key
findings.detail: The request says the TLS key is read-denied in every agent sandbox. When the listener is disabled, startup returns before registering the previously generated key with the process-local deny registry. The key remains on disk, and editor sandboxes do not otherwise deny the worker TLS directory.
findings.suggestion: Register the existing key path for the daemon lifetime independently of whether the listener is enabled.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner disables workers after having enabled them, then starts a run. An editor agent can read the retained coordinator TLS private key.

verification.evidence: src/cli/daemon.ts:30-31 starts the optional listener before mounting integrations. With no listener address, src/server/workers.ts:15 returns immediately, bypassing `certificate(...)` at line 16 and therefore `protectPrivateFile(keyPath)` at src/workers/tls.ts:14. Editors use `writeRoots(..., false, ...)` (src/harness/claude.ts:203); src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 includes registered private paths, and line 217 makes whole-home denial conditional on `gate`.
verification.trigger: Disable workers after using them, restart the daemon, then start an editor run. The existing coordinator key remains on disk but loses its specific sandbox read denial, allowing the editor to read it unless another deny path covers it.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation permanently blocks listener startup
findings.detail: The key file is created before openssl runs, but a failed or interrupted generation leaves it behind. The next start sees incomplete TLS material and throws instead of generating a certificate, so a transient failure prevents the daemon from starting whenever the worker listener is configured.
findings.suggestion: Generate the certificate and key in temporary files and publish them together, cleaning up incomplete generation safely.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is stopped or openssl fails after the empty key file is created but before the certificate is written; every subsequent daemon start fails with "Incomplete worker TLS material".

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:18 writes an empty key before OpenSSL runs; lines 45–47 only `release(); throw error;` on failure. src/util/proc.ts:650–651 throws for unsuccessful or timed-out commands. On subsequent calls, src/workers/tls.ts:17 throws `Incomplete worker TLS material` when the key exists without the certificate. src/cli/daemon.ts:30 awaits this through src/server/workers.ts:16 before continuing startup.
verification.trigger: With the listener enabled, interruption or OpenSSL failure during initial generation can leave key.pem without cert.pem. All later daemon starts reject that state until manual repair. Medium because this requires unusual initial-generation timing or an OpenSSL failure.

findings.title: A changed pinned certificate is retried indefinitely without an explanation
findings.detail: The request requires the coordinator fingerprint to be pinned. Although the transport detects a mismatch, the heartbeat loop catches that error along with transient connection failures and retries forever. The operator receives no indication that the certificate changed and that intervention is required.
findings.suggestion: Surface fingerprint mismatch as a terminal error while retaining retries for transient transport failures.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing. The worker remains running but never sends another heartbeat and never reports the pin mismatch.

verification.evidence: The worker CLI enters `runWorker` (src/cli/main.ts:373). A changed certificate rejects with `new Error("Coordinator certificate fingerprint changed")` (src/workers/tls.ts:114-115), but the heartbeat request catches every rejection and returns `undefined` unless aborted (src/workers/client.ts:95-102). Its `for (;;)` then sleeps and retries with delay capped at 10 seconds (src/workers/client.ts:93-107), without reporting the error.
verification.trigger: Replace the coordinator certificate after pairing. Every heartbeat fails the pin check, but the worker silently retries indefinitely and never explains that pairing must be repeated.

findings.title: Initial pairing permits a relay to steal the worker token
findings.detail: The first connection accepts any TLS certificate and receives both the comparison code and the claim secret. An attacker between the worker and coordinator can relay the initial request and response, so the owner and worker see matching codes, while the attacker learns the secret and can claim the approved token. Pinning the attacker's certificate for subsequent requests does not prevent this.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate and the claim secret, or use an authenticated pairing exchange that does not expose the claim credential to an unverified intermediary.
findings.failure_scenario: A network attacker proxies the initial pairing exchange, forwards the genuine code to the worker, and claims the token after the owner approves that code.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23-27 sends the initial pairing request with only `{ signal }`, then :39 pins `first.fingerprint`. src/workers/tls.ts:103 sets `rejectUnauthorized: false`. src/db/workers.ts:61 returns `{ code, secret, expiresAt }`; :83-89 releases `{ token: this.issued(w) }` based solely on the secret and approval. src/server/workers.ts:37-38 exposes that claim before authentication.
verification.trigger: An attacker terminates TLS during initial pairing and relays the genuine coordinator response, including its code and secret. The owner approves the matching code; the attacker uses the secret to obtain the worker token. The submitted worker fingerprint requires no proof of possession.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
findings.detail: The token and fingerprint are registered in an in-memory private-path map only in the pairing or worker CLI process, and pairing releases those registrations before exiting. A daemon running on the same machine has a separate map and does not register these persisted files when constructing its agent sandboxes. Thus an agent reader in that daemon can read the worker token and fingerprint; file mode 0600 does not protect against another process running as the same user.
findings.suggestion: Register the persisted worker credential paths in every process that creates agent sandboxes, including when the worker command is not running.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine runs both a paired worker and a Limitless daemon; an agent launched by the daemon reads the worker token from the data directory and impersonates the worker.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:85-88 registers `<data>/worker/token` only inside runWorker. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 uses a module-local `privatePaths = new Map<string, number>()`; :30 returns only that map's keys. src/config.ts:160 defaults data to `~/.limitless`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:150-161 lists credential directories without `.limitless/worker`; :190 adds only locally registered private paths. src/harness/codex.ts:300-305 builds the editor profile with `["/", "read"]` plus those denies. src/cli/daemon.ts:15-31 registers the API token and listener, but no worker-client files.
verification.trigger: A paired worker and a separate daemon run as the same user with the default data directory. The daemon's editor sandbox lacks the worker process's private-path registrations, so an editor can read the mode-0600 worker token and impersonate that worker.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation permanently blocks listener startup
findings.detail: The key file is created before the asynchronous OpenSSL command completes. If generation fails or the process stops before the certificate is written, the next startup encounters the incomplete pair and always throws. Normal restarts cannot recover without manually deleting the leftover material.
findings.suggestion: Generate both files under temporary names and publish them only after successful generation, or safely clean up an incomplete first-generation attempt.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is interrupted after creating key.pem but before OpenSSL writes cert.pem; every subsequent worker-listener startup fails with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:18 creates key.pem before awaiting OpenSSL: `writeFileSync(keyPath, "", { flag: "wx", mode: 0o600 })`. Lines 45–47 only `release(); throw error;`, leaving the file behind. On restart, line 17 throws `new Error("Incomplete worker TLS material")` when only one file exists. src/server/workers.ts:15–16 calls certificate when listen is configured; src/cli/daemon.ts:30 awaits that listener before starting the daemon.
verification.trigger: With workers.listen enabled, interruption during initial certificate generation after key.pem creation but before cert.pem creation leaves persistent incomplete material. Every subsequent startup fails until manual repair. The initial-generation timing window is unusual.

findings.title: Certificate replacement prevents the documented re-pairing flow
findings.detail: The guide says a worker must pair again after the coordinator certificate changes, but an approved worker's existing name is always rejected by the pairing route. Re-running the documented pairing command with the default name therefore cannot recover unless the owner first revokes the existing record or chooses another name.
findings.suggestion: Support an explicit secure re-pairing flow for an existing worker, or document the required revocation before re-pairing.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes and an existing worker runs `limitless worker pair` with its original name; the coordinator rejects the request as already paired.

verification.evidence: docs/GUIDE.md:236 says, “Changing the coordinator's certificate requires pairing again.” However, src/db/workers.ts:43–46 rejects an existing worker when `existing.state === "approved"`, throwing `"Worker name already paired or pending"`, regardless of fingerprint or expiry. src/workers/client.ts:23–29 always starts with `/worker/pair` and throws `Pairing refused` on a non-200 response.
verification.trigger: Replace the coordinator certificate while retaining its workers database, then re-run pairing with an approved worker's original name. Pairing is refused; recovery requires explicitly revoking the worker first or choosing another name.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
findings.detail: The first request accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker pins the certificate observed on that connection. An active intermediary can forward the pairing request to the real coordinator, relay the same code to the worker, and use the observed pairing secret to claim the approved token. Comparing the displayed codes does not detect the intermediary because the code is not bound to the TLS connection.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate or otherwise authenticate the coordinator before sending the pairing secret.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the initial pairing connection, relays the request and code to the real coordinator, and claims the worker token after the owner approves the matching code.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23-27 makes the first request without a pin; :33 prints the returned code; :39 trusts the first connection's fingerprint. src/workers/tls.ts:103 disables CA verification. src/server/workers.ts:37-38 allows unauthenticated claims, and src/db/workers.ts:83-89 returns the approved token to anyone supplying the pairing secret.
verification.trigger: An attacker intercepts initial TLS, forwards the real pairing request and matching code, and retains the returned secret. Approval authenticates the relayed pending request without authenticating the worker's coordinator connection, allowing the attacker to claim the token. This duplicates C1.

findings.title: Credential read protection ends when pairing exits
findings.detail: The private-file deny registry is process-local, and pairing releases both credential paths before exiting. A separate daemon on the worker machine therefore does not register those files in its agent sandbox deny rules; running the worker in another process does not share its registrations either. The same lifecycle problem affects an existing coordinator TLS key when its listener is disabled.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential and TLS key paths in every process that launches agent sandboxes, independently of whether the worker listener or client is running.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine is paired, the pairing command exits, and an agent launched by a separate local daemon reads the worker token from the data directory.

The default data directory is `~/.limitless` (src/config.ts:160), outside the built-in credential directories in src/harness/read-policy.ts:150-161.
verification.trigger: After the pairing command exits, the persisted token remains readable by the same user. A separate daemon does not register that token path, so its editor can read it even before the worker loop starts. This shares C2's missing cross-process protection.

findings.title: Permanent TLS and configuration failures retry forever
findings.detail: The catch treats every request error as transient and retries indefinitely without logging the original error. A changed certificate fingerprint, malformed coordinator URL, or invalid stored pin therefore leaves the worker silently looping instead of reporting the failure and requiring corrective action.
findings.suggestion: Retry only transient transport errors with an appropriate bound, and propagate certificate, pin and configuration errors with their original cause.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing; every heartbeat fails fingerprint verification, but the worker remains running indefinitely with no diagnostic.

verification.evidence: src/cli/main.ts:373 invokes runWorker with the supplied coordinator URL. src/workers/tls.ts:114-115 rejects a changed fingerprint with `Error("Coordinator certificate fingerprint changed")`. src/workers/client.ts:93-107 catches every request exception, returns `undefined`, and retries indefinitely with delay capped at 10 seconds; only received HTTP statuses below 500 terminate the loop.
verification.trigger: After coordinator certificate replacement, a paired worker repeatedly encounters a permanent fingerprint mismatch. The exception is discarded without a diagnostic, and the worker retries forever until externally cancelled. Invalid coordinator origins are swallowed the same way.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation prevents future startup
findings.detail: Certificate generation creates the key path before invoking OpenSSL, but failures leave generated or partial files in place. The next start either rejects the incomplete pair or reads invalid material, so a transient interruption permanently blocks the worker listener until the files are manually removed.
findings.suggestion: Generate both files in temporary paths, clean them up on failure, and publish the completed pair only after validation.
findings.failure_scenario: OpenSSL times out or the process stops after creating key.pem but before writing cert.pem; subsequent daemon starts fail with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

findings.detail: Protection is held in a process-local registry and released when pairing finishes. A separate daemon or agent process does not inherit that registration, even though the token and coordinator fingerprint remain on disk. The real-Seatbelt test explicitly registers synthetic files in the same process that launches the gates, so it does not exercise this lifecycle or cross-process case.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every process that constructs an agent sandbox, and test access from a separately started process after pairing has finished.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine pairs a worker, the pairing command exits, and a separate local factory process launches an agent sandbox that can otherwise reach the worker data directory; the persisted token and fingerprint are absent from that process's private-read registry.

findings.title: No test covers claiming an approved pairing after coordinator restart
findings.detail: The implementation reconstructs an issued token from the persistent TLS key so that a worker can claim it after a restart, but the pairing tests approve and claim within one listener lifetime. A regression in key reuse or token reconstruction would leave an approved worker unable to pair without being caught.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator certificate
findings.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the coordinator generates a random code that is unrelated to either endpoint's certificate. A man-in-the-middle can relay the pairing request and response unchanged, present its own certificate to the worker, and relay the subsequent claim. The owner and worker see the same code, but the worker pins the attacker's certificate and sends it the issued token.

findings.title: Worker credential deny registrations do not protect other processes
findings.detail: The token and fingerprint are registered in an in-memory, process-local deny list, and pairing releases those registrations before exiting. A separately running daemon or agent process therefore never registers the worker credential paths. Its agent sandbox can consequently lack the explicit denies required for these files, even while the worker is running in another process.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every process that launches agent sandboxes, independently of the worker process and pairing command.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine is both a paired worker and a coordinator with a tool-enabled agent. The worker runs as a separate process, so the coordinator's agent sandbox does not receive the worker token and fingerprint deny entries.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:87–88 registers token and fingerprint through `privateFile(...)` only inside `runWorker`. src/workers/tls.ts:52 calls `protectPrivateFile(path)`, backed by the module-local Map at src/util/private-reads.ts:4. src/cli/daemon.ts:15 and :30 register the daemon API credential and listener TLS material, without registering worker credentials. src/harness/claude.ts:203 constructs editor roots with `writeRoots(..., false, ...)`; src/harness/read-policy.ts:217 applies whole-home denial only when `gate` is true.

findings.title: Pairing can be relayed through an attacker-controlled coordinator
findings.detail: The first connection accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker pins that certificate after receiving the pairing response. An attacker between the worker and coordinator can relay the pair request and the unchanged code to the real coordinator, then relay the claim request after owner approval. The codes match, but the attacker obtains the issued token and the worker pins the attacker's certificate. The submitted worker certificate fingerprint is stored but is never authenticated or used to bind the claim.
findings.suggestion: Bind approval and token delivery to authenticated coordinator and worker identities so that relaying a matching code cannot disclose the worker token or substitute the pinned coordinator.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker pairs over a network controlled by an attacker who proxies both pairing endpoints to the real coordinator; the owner sees the same code and approves, after which the proxy receives the worker token.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23–27 makes an unpinned initial request, :33 displays `pending.code`, and :35–39 sends the pairing secret while pinning the initially observed certificate. src/workers/tls.ts:103 sets `rejectUnauthorized: false`; :114 only verifies an explicitly supplied pin. src/server/workers.ts:36–37 serves claims using only the supplied secret; src/db/workers.ts:89 returns `{ token: this.issued(w) }` after approval.
verification.trigger: An attacker-controlled TLS endpoint transparently relays both pairing endpoints. Comparing the printed code succeeds because the attacker forwards it unchanged. Once approved, the proxy receives the worker token.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not registered for denial in the daemon's sandboxes
findings.detail: The request requires the worker token and coordinator fingerprint to be read-denied to gates. Their protection is held only in the pairing or worker CLI process's in-memory private-path registry and is released when that process exits. A separate daemon on the same machine does not register these paths when it starts, so its sandbox policy can permit access to them. The real-Seatbelt test creates and protects all files in the same process as the gate, so it does not cover this deployment.
findings.suggestion: Register the persisted worker credential paths in every process that launches agent or gate sandboxes, independently of whether the worker CLI is running, and test across the actual process boundary.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine is both a worker and a coordinator, with its data directory in a location readable by an agent sandbox; after pairing, a gate launched by the separate daemon reads the worker token and fingerprint.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:47–48 registers the persisted files, then :57 releases those registrations. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 stores registrations in a process-local Map. src/cli/daemon.ts:15–31 registers API/listener credentials but never the worker files. src/config.ts:160 permits relocation through `process.env.LIMITLESS_HOME`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:217 denies the actual home for gates, but has no unconditional worker-directory denial.
verification.trigger: With LIMITLESS_HOME relocated to a system location readable by gates, a separately running daemon lacks the worker token and fingerprint deny entries. A gate can read those files. Default data under the user’s home remains covered by whole-home denial; exploitation requires the unusual readable data location described in the claim.

findings.title: The coordinator TLS key is unprotected when the listener is disabled
findings.detail: The request says the TLS key must be read-denied in every agent sandbox. The key path is registered only when the worker listener starts. After a listener has generated the key, disabling `[workers] listen` and restarting leaves the private key on disk without registering it in the daemon's sandbox deny policy. Re-enabling the listener later reuses that key.
findings.suggestion: Register the existing coordinator key path for sandbox denial independently of whether the listener is enabled.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner disables the listener after pairing workers, then runs an agent with read access to the data directory; the agent reads the persisted key and can impersonate the coordinator when the listener is re-enabled.

Only certificate() registers the key deny: src/workers/tls.ts:12-14, `keyPath = join(home, "key.pem")` and `const release = protectPrivateFile(keyPath)`. findings.title: An approved pairing that fails before token storage cannot be retried
findings.detail: An approved name is always rejected by `pair`, even if the worker never received or saved its token. A transient failure after approval therefore leaves the worker unable to pair again until the owner explicitly revokes it.
findings.suggestion: Provide a safe recovery path for an approved but unclaimed pairing, or report the required revoke-and-repair action clearly.
findings.failure_scenario: The owner approves a request, but the worker process exits before its next claim; restarting `limitless worker pair` with the same name receives a refusal.

Restarting pairing calls `/worker/pair` again (lines 23–26), but src/db/workers.ts:43–46 rejects every existing approved name. The approved-state rejection has no expiry condition.
