candidates.title: Initial pairing permits a relay to steal the worker token
candidates.detail: The first connection accepts any TLS certificate and receives both the comparison code and the claim secret. An attacker between the worker and coordinator can relay the initial request and response, so the owner and worker see matching codes, while the attacker learns the secret and can claim the approved token. Pinning the attacker's certificate for subsequent requests does not prevent this.
candidates.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate and the claim secret, or use an authenticated pairing exchange that does not expose the claim credential to an unverified intermediary.
candidates.failure_scenario: A network attacker proxies the initial pairing exchange, forwards the genuine code to the worker, and claims the token after the owner approves that code.

candidates.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
candidates.detail: The token and fingerprint are registered in an in-memory private-path map only in the pairing or worker CLI process, and pairing releases those registrations before exiting. A daemon running on the same machine has a separate map and does not register these persisted files when constructing its agent sandboxes. Thus an agent reader in that daemon can read the worker token and fingerprint; file mode 0600 does not protect against another process running as the same user.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persisted worker credential paths in every process that creates agent sandboxes, including when the worker command is not running.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine runs both a paired worker and a Limitless daemon; an agent launched by the daemon reads the worker token from the data directory and impersonates the worker.

candidates.title: Interrupted certificate generation permanently blocks listener startup
candidates.detail: The key file is created before the asynchronous OpenSSL command completes. If generation fails or the process stops before the certificate is written, the next startup encounters the incomplete pair and always throws. Normal restarts cannot recover without manually deleting the leftover material.
candidates.suggestion: Generate both files under temporary names and publish them only after successful generation, or safely clean up an incomplete first-generation attempt.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon is interrupted after creating key.pem but before OpenSSL writes cert.pem; every subsequent worker-listener startup fails with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

candidates.title: Certificate replacement prevents the documented re-pairing flow
candidates.detail: The guide says a worker must pair again after the coordinator certificate changes, but an approved worker's existing name is always rejected by the pairing route. Re-running the documented pairing command with the default name therefore cannot recover unless the owner first revokes the existing record or chooses another name.
candidates.suggestion: Support an explicit secure re-pairing flow for an existing worker, or document the required revocation before re-pairing.
candidates.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes and an existing worker runs `limitless worker pair` with its original name; the coordinator rejects the request as already paired.

candidates.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
candidates.detail: The first request accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker pins the certificate observed on that connection. An active intermediary can forward the pairing request to the real coordinator, relay the same code to the worker, and use the observed pairing secret to claim the approved token. Comparing the displayed codes does not detect the intermediary because the code is not bound to the TLS connection.
candidates.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate or otherwise authenticate the coordinator before sending the pairing secret.
candidates.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the initial pairing connection, relays the request and code to the real coordinator, and claims the worker token after the owner approves the matching code.

candidates.title: Credential read protection ends when pairing exits
candidates.detail: The private-file deny registry is process-local, and pairing releases both credential paths before exiting. A separate daemon on the worker machine therefore does not register those files in its agent sandbox deny rules; running the worker in another process does not share its registrations either. The same lifecycle problem affects an existing coordinator TLS key when its listener is disabled.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential and TLS key paths in every process that launches agent sandboxes, independently of whether the worker listener or client is running.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine is paired, the pairing command exits, and an agent launched by a separate local daemon reads the worker token from the data directory.

candidates.title: Permanent TLS and configuration failures retry forever
candidates.detail: The catch treats every request error as transient and retries indefinitely without logging the original error. A changed certificate fingerprint, malformed coordinator URL, or invalid stored pin therefore leaves the worker silently looping instead of reporting the failure and requiring corrective action.
candidates.suggestion: Retry only transient transport errors with an appropriate bound, and propagate certificate, pin and configuration errors with their original cause.
candidates.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing; every heartbeat fails fingerprint verification, but the worker remains running indefinitely with no diagnostic.

candidates.title: Interrupted certificate generation prevents future startup
candidates.detail: Certificate generation creates the key path before invoking OpenSSL, but failures leave generated or partial files in place. The next start either rejects the incomplete pair or reads invalid material, so a transient interruption permanently blocks the worker listener until the files are manually removed.
candidates.suggestion: Generate both files in temporary paths, clean them up on failure, and publish the completed pair only after validation.
candidates.failure_scenario: OpenSSL times out or the process stops after creating key.pem but before writing cert.pem; subsequent daemon starts fail with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

candidates.title: Worker credentials lose sandbox protection when pairing exits
candidates.detail: Protection is held in a process-local registry and released when pairing finishes. A separate daemon or agent process does not inherit that registration, even though the token and coordinator fingerprint remain on disk. The real-Seatbelt test explicitly registers synthetic files in the same process that launches the gates, so it does not exercise this lifecycle or cross-process case.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every process that constructs an agent sandbox, and test access from a separately started process after pairing has finished.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine pairs a worker, the pairing command exits, and a separate local factory process launches an agent sandbox that can otherwise reach the worker data directory; the persisted token and fingerprint are absent from that process's private-read registry.

candidates.title: No test covers claiming an approved pairing after coordinator restart
candidates.detail: The implementation reconstructs an issued token from the persistent TLS key so that a worker can claim it after a restart, but the pairing tests approve and claim within one listener lifetime. A regression in key reuse or token reconstruction would leave an approved worker unable to pair without being caught.
candidates.suggestion: Approve a pending request, restart the listener and store, then claim with the original secret and verify that the returned token authenticates a heartbeat.
candidates.failure_scenario: The coordinator restarts after the owner approves a pending request but before the worker claims its token.

candidates.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator certificate
candidates.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the coordinator generates a random code that is unrelated to either endpoint's certificate. A man-in-the-middle can relay the pairing request and response unchanged, present its own certificate to the worker, and relay the subsequent claim. The owner and worker see the same code, but the worker pins the attacker's certificate and sends it the issued token.
candidates.suggestion: Bind the displayed pairing code to the coordinator certificate and pairing exchange, and verify that binding on both sides before issuing or accepting credentials.
candidates.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies requests to the real coordinator, and forwards the unchanged pairing code. After approval, the attacker receives the worker token while the worker pins the attacker's certificate.

candidates.title: Worker credential deny registrations do not protect other processes
candidates.detail: The token and fingerprint are registered in an in-memory, process-local deny list, and pairing releases those registrations before exiting. A separately running daemon or agent process therefore never registers the worker credential paths. Its agent sandbox can consequently lack the explicit denies required for these files, even while the worker is running in another process.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every process that launches agent sandboxes, independently of the worker process and pairing command.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine is both a paired worker and a coordinator with a tool-enabled agent. The worker runs as a separate process, so the coordinator's agent sandbox does not receive the worker token and fingerprint deny entries.

candidates.title: Pairing can be relayed through an attacker-controlled coordinator
candidates.detail: The first connection accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker pins that certificate after receiving the pairing response. An attacker between the worker and coordinator can relay the pair request and the unchanged code to the real coordinator, then relay the claim request after owner approval. The codes match, but the attacker obtains the issued token and the worker pins the attacker's certificate. The submitted worker certificate fingerprint is stored but is never authenticated or used to bind the claim.
candidates.suggestion: Bind approval and token delivery to authenticated coordinator and worker identities so that relaying a matching code cannot disclose the worker token or substitute the pinned coordinator.
candidates.failure_scenario: A worker pairs over a network controlled by an attacker who proxies both pairing endpoints to the real coordinator; the owner sees the same code and approves, after which the proxy receives the worker token.

candidates.title: Worker credentials are not registered for denial in the daemon's sandboxes
candidates.detail: The request requires the worker token and coordinator fingerprint to be read-denied to gates. Their protection is held only in the pairing or worker CLI process's in-memory private-path registry and is released when that process exits. A separate daemon on the same machine does not register these paths when it starts, so its sandbox policy can permit access to them. The real-Seatbelt test creates and protects all files in the same process as the gate, so it does not cover this deployment.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persisted worker credential paths in every process that launches agent or gate sandboxes, independently of whether the worker CLI is running, and test across the actual process boundary.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine is both a worker and a coordinator, with its data directory in a location readable by an agent sandbox; after pairing, a gate launched by the separate daemon reads the worker token and fingerprint.

candidates.title: The coordinator TLS key is unprotected when the listener is disabled
candidates.detail: The request says the TLS key must be read-denied in every agent sandbox. The key path is registered only when the worker listener starts. After a listener has generated the key, disabling `[workers] listen` and restarting leaves the private key on disk without registering it in the daemon's sandbox deny policy. Re-enabling the listener later reuses that key.
candidates.suggestion: Register the existing coordinator key path for sandbox denial independently of whether the listener is enabled.
candidates.failure_scenario: An owner disables the listener after pairing workers, then runs an agent with read access to the data directory; the agent reads the persisted key and can impersonate the coordinator when the listener is re-enabled.

candidates.title: An approved pairing that fails before token storage cannot be retried
candidates.detail: An approved name is always rejected by `pair`, even if the worker never received or saved its token. A transient failure after approval therefore leaves the worker unable to pair again until the owner explicitly revokes it.
candidates.suggestion: Provide a safe recovery path for an approved but unclaimed pairing, or report the required revoke-and-repair action clearly.
candidates.failure_scenario: The owner approves a request, but the worker process exits before its next claim; restarting `limitless worker pair` with the same name receives a refusal.

findings.title: Treat a worker confinement failure as a terminal failure
findings.detail: A check reporting a confinement failure is rejected as an invalid result, which calls workers.fail. After the retry is exhausted, the LAN executor runs the gates locally and can return a pass. This converts a failed security check into a successful gate result.
findings.suggestion: Preserve confinement failures as a distinct terminal failure and propagate them through the gate result without retrying them into a pass.
findings.failure_scenario: Both worker attempts report a Seatbelt launch failure, but the local fallback executes successfully; the overall gate is reported as passing.

verification.evidence: The configured production path uses `gateExecutorFor(cfg.gateExecutor, this.workers, cfg.workers.repos)` (src/app.ts:176). Workers execute `runLocalGates` and post each result to `/events` (src/workers/client.ts:215-224). The schema rejects confinement failures with `.refine((r) => !r.confinementError && !launchFailure(r.output), "Worker confinement failed")` (src/workers/protocol.ts:65), but the listener handles that rejection with `workers.fail(id, ...)` (src/server/workers.ts:131-133). That transition uses `j.attempt < 2 ? "queued" : "failed"` (src/db/workers.ts:260). The failed job then runs locally and returns only the fallback result: `workers.complete(handle.id, run, true); return workers.sanitize(run);` (src/gates/lan.ts:73-89).

findings.title: Do not discard failed checks received before an infrastructure failure
findings.detail: Check events from a worker are persisted and forwarded, but the final result is replaced by the next attempt or local fallback if that worker disconnects before posting its GateRun. A later pass therefore erases an already observed failing check, contrary to the requirement that infrastructure retries never turn a failing check into a pass.
findings.suggestion: Preserve and account for validated failing check results across attempts when producing the final gate outcome.

"queued" : "failed"`. However, src/gates/lan.ts:72 returns `JSON.parse(job.result) as GateRun` directly; local fallback similarly returns `workers.sanitize(run)` at :89. A replacement worker or eventual local fallback passes the check. The returned GateRun contains the passing result without preserving the observed failure, violating the requirement that infrastructure retries never turn failing checks into passes.

findings.title: Do not retry certificate pin failures indefinitely
findings.detail: The catch treats every workerRequest exception as a transient connection error. That includes an invalid coordinator URL or a changed pinned TLS fingerprint, so the worker silently retries forever instead of surfacing the security or configuration failure. The retry has no deadline.

findings.title: The credential test does not establish worker-side redaction
findings.detail: The worker and coordinator run in the same process and share the credential registry. The test registers the secret globally and checks only the stored coordinator result and events, so coordinator-side sanitization can make it pass even if the worker sends the credential in plaintext.
findings.suggestion: Inspect the outgoing worker event and result bodies before coordinator processing, or run the worker in a separate process with a credential unknown to the coordinator.
findings.failure_scenario: Worker-side redaction is removed and a gate prints a worker-only credential; the shared coordinator registry still redacts the stored output, so this test passes while the credential crosses the connection.

verification.evidence: test/workers.test.ts:659 registers `registerCredential("WORKER_OUTPUT_TEST", secret)`; :459 starts `runWorker(...)` in the same process. Assertions at :681–683 inspect only stored `result` and `events`. Coordinator storage independently redacts: src/db/workers.ts:238 uses `events.push(this.sanitize(event))`, :291 stores `JSON.stringify(this.sanitize(run))`, and :59 calls `redactGateData(data)`. Thus coordinator redaction masks missing worker redaction.
verification.trigger: Worker-side redaction regresses; the shared credential registry lets coordinator sanitization remove the credential before storage assertions, so the test passes without establishing that transmission was redacted.

findings.title: The bundle test never exercises distinct head and base commits
findings.detail: The shared request fixture assigns the same commit to headSha and baseSha. Consequently, the end-to-end bundle test cannot detect an implementation that bundles only the head, even though the request requires both commits to be available on the worker.
findings.suggestion: Create distinct base and head commits and have a worker gate verify that both requested commits are present.
findings.failure_scenario: Bundle creation omits baseSha when it differs from headSha; the existing end-to-end test still passes because its two SHAs are identical.

verification.evidence: test/workers.test.ts:123–124 sets both `baseSha: sha` and `headSha: sha`; the end-to-end test at :657 uses `request(true)`. Production bundle creation at src/server/workers.ts:88 deduplicates `[request.headSha, request.baseSha]`, then :95 creates the bundle using `...names`. The fixture therefore exercises only one distinct commit and cannot detect omission of a distinct base.
verification.trigger: Bundle creation regresses to include only headSha; the existing end-to-end test still passes because baseSha equals headSha and never checks availability of a separate base commit.

findings.title: Reconcile streamed check failures with the final result
findings.detail: The coordinator validates each check event and the final GateRun independently. It accepts a passing final result even if the same lease previously reported that check as failed. The failed event is stored, but it does not influence the returned GateRun, so an inconsistent worker response can turn an observed failure into a pass.
findings.suggestion: Validate the final run against the check events recorded for the current lease and treat inconsistent results as an infrastructure failure.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker posts a valid failed event for a requested check, then posts a valid GateRun reporting that same check as passed; the coordinator completes the job with the passing result.

verification.evidence: The listener independently validates events and final results using `validCheck(request, event.data.result, event.data.phase)` and `validRun(request, result.data.run)` (src/server/workers.ts:123-130), then executes `workers.event(id, event.data)` or `workers.complete(id, result.data.run)` (src/server/workers.ts:135-136). Neither validation compares the final result with stored events; `validRun` receives only the request and run (src/workers/validation.ts:25-49). Completion stores the supplied run directly (src/db/workers.ts:288-291), and the executor returns it (src/gates/lan.ts:72).
verification.trigger: An authenticated worker holding a lease submits a schema-valid failed check event, then a schema-valid passing final result for the same requested check and SHA. The coordinator accepts the passing result. This requires inconsistent worker input: the provided worker normally streams and returns the same result objects (src/gates/run.ts:183-187).

findings.title: Coordinator-only credentials can be truncated before redaction
findings.detail: runLocalGates truncates output on the worker after redacting only credentials registered on that worker. The coordinator subsequently redacts the already-truncated value using its own credentials. If the tail boundary cuts through a coordinator credential that the worker does not know, the coordinator sees only a fragment and literal credential redaction cannot remove it before the event or result is stored.
findings.suggestion: Ensure coordinator-only credentials cannot be cut before coordinator-side redaction, such as by sending bounded raw output with enough overlap for coordinator redaction before applying the final output limit.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate prints a coordinator credential unknown to the worker, followed by enough output that the 6,000-character tail starts in the middle of that credential. The credential suffix is sent to and stored by the coordinator.

verification.evidence: src/gates/run.ts:74 defines `OUTPUT_TAIL = 6_000`; line 126 returns `combined.slice(-OUTPUT_TAIL)` after worker-local redaction. src/workers/client.ts:233 sends that result using `redactGateData({ run, sha })`. Coordinator completion stores `JSON.stringify(this.sanitize(run))` (src/db/workers.ts:291). findings.title: A failed check from a lost lease can become a pass
findings.detail: The request says infrastructure retries must “never turn a failing check into a pass.” Check events from an attempt are streamed to hooks, but after that attempt loses its lease the final verdict uses only the later worker's GateRun. A failed check already reported by the first worker is therefore discarded for verdict purposes.
findings.suggestion: Retain completed check failures across infrastructure attempts and ensure a later passing result cannot erase them.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker posts a failing check event, disconnects before posting its GateRun, and the replacement worker reports that check as passing. The returned GateRun marks it as passing.

verification.evidence: src/app.ts:176 selects the configured executor, and src/gates/lan.ts:29-30 queues LAN jobs for opted-in repositories. src/server/workers.ts:135 records check events. src/db/workers.ts:277 detects stale heartbeats with `this.fail(j.id, "Worker disconnected")`; :254 excludes the previous worker, and :260 requeues the first failed attempt. findings.title: Restart discards leased retry and timeout jobs
findings.detail: The request says `attach` waits for the stored result so “a coordinator restart re-attaches without enqueueing again.” Resume is restricted to baseline, initial and rebase purposes. A persisted timeout or retry job is cancelled and replaced when its stage resumes, even if the worker is still running or has completed it.
findings.suggestion: Provide durable resume handling for every LAN gate execution purpose, preserving the original job identity and any state needed to consume its result.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a LAN timeout rerun or regression retry is leased. On resume the pending handle fails the purpose whitelist, is cancelled, and a new job is enqueued.

findings.title: Restart discards in-flight LAN retry jobs

A shutdown during a timeout rerun or a baseline or regression retry leaves its durable LAN job running, but resume treats its handle as stale, cancels it, and enqueues another execution. This repeats work that had already been leased or completed and defeats durable reattachment for these gate executions.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry context to reattach the matching durable handle on resume, including timeout and targeted retry purposes.

findings.title: Home-relative paths and file URLs bypass sanitization
findings.detail:
The sanitizer compares link destinations only against literal filesystem roots. A home-relative link such as the one in the request is left broken, and a file URL containing the absolute worktree path is published unchanged, including the owner's username. The direct check below returned both inputs unchanged.

Command: bun -e 'let s=await Bun.file("src/gates/publication.ts").text(); let f=new Function(s.slice(s.indexOf("export function sanitizePublication"),s.indexOf("/** Check both")).replace("export function","function").replace(/: string( \| undefined)?/g,"")+";return sanitizePublication")(); for(let x of ["[file](~/.limitless/work/run/a.ts)","[file](file:///Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts)","[/Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts](a.ts)"]) console.log(f(x,"/Users/alice/.limitless/work/run","/Users/alice/.limitless"))'
Output:
[file](~/.limitless/work/run/a.ts)
[file](file:///Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts)
[/Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts](a.ts)

findings.title: Dot segments classify paths outside the worktree as inside it
findings.detail: Classification uses a string prefix without resolving dot segments. The sanitizer turns `[file](/factory/data/work/run/../other/log)` into `[../other/log](../other/log)`, although the destination is outside the worktree and should be rendered as a data-directory placeholder.
findings.suggestion: Normalize path segments before deciding which root contains a local destination.
findings.failure_scenario: A report links to a data-directory file using an absolute path containing `work/run/../other/log`.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:8 classifies paths using literal prefix matching without normalizing dot segments. Lines 10-11 strip the worktree prefix and return the remainder as a relative path; line 25 creates a link from it. Isolated execution transformed `[log](/Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/../other/log)` into `[../other/log](../other/log)`.
verification.trigger: A data-directory link spells a sibling run's file using `/work/run/../other/log`. It is incorrectly treated as inside the current worktree and published as a repository-relative link instead of plain `<data>/work/other/log` text.

findings.title: File-URL links retain the absolute local path
findings.detail: The link destination is compared directly with the filesystem roots, so a file:// URL never matches. The fallback bare-path matcher also excludes a path preceded by a slash. The publication therefore retains the username and factory layout, or is blocked when those strings are configured as private.
findings.suggestion: Recognize local file URLs and normalize their filesystem path before applying the same root checks.
findings.failure_scenario: [file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts) remains unchanged when the worktree is /factory/data/work/run.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:8 matches only `path === root || path.startsWith(`${root}/`)`; lines 23–24 return the original link when rewriting leaves its destination unchanged. Reproduced output: `[file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts)` remains unchanged.
verification.trigger: A report uses a file:// URL into the worktree. The scheme prevents root matching, leaving the absolute local destination intact.

findings.title: Nested parentheses prevent data-directory links from becoming plain text
findings.detail: The Markdown link expression accepts only one level of parentheses in a destination. For a destination with nested parentheses, the bare-path alternative rewrites only part of the destination and leaves the surrounding link intact, contrary to the requested plain-text output.
findings.suggestion: Handle valid Markdown destinations with nested parentheses before applying the bare-path replacement.
findings.failure_scenario: [log](/factory/data/runs/a(b(c)).log) becomes [log](<data>/runs/a(b(c)).log) instead of plain text.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:13 accepts only one parenthesis nesting level via `\([^()\n]*\)`. The bare-path alternative at line 17 excludes parentheses. Reproduced output: `[log](<data>/runs/a(b(c)).log)`.
verification.trigger: A data-directory link destination contains nested parentheses. Only its bare path prefix is rewritten, retaining Markdown link syntax instead of producing plain text.

findings.title: Publication tests omit file URLs and nested-parenthesis destinations
findings.detail: The sanitizer tests cover absolute path links but do not exercise local file URLs or valid destinations with nested parentheses. Consequently, they miss both the retained private path and the data-directory link that remains Markdown.
findings.suggestion: Add independent expected-output cases for a file:// worktree link and a data-directory link whose destination contains nested parentheses.
findings.failure_scenario: The existing tests pass without detecting that [file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts) retains the absolute path or that a nested-parenthesis log link remains a link.

verification.evidence: test/publication-text.test.ts:7–16 covers absolute paths, HTTP URLs and angle-bracket destinations, but neither file URLs nor nested-parenthesis destinations. src/gates/publication.ts:8–9 requires `path === root || path.startsWith(`${root}/`)`, so a `file:///...` destination remains unchanged. The link regex at line 13 permits only one parenthesis level (`\([^()\n]*\)`); deeper nesting falls through to bare-path replacement. Executing the extracted helper returned `[file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts)` unchanged and converted the nested log example to `[logs](<data>/runs/a(b(c)).log)`, retaining its link syntax. Direct module execution was blocked by the missing `entities` dependency.
verification.trigger: The omitted inputs `[file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts)` and `[logs](/factory/data/runs/a(b(c)).log)` bypass the intended transformations without being covered by the publication tests.

findings.title: Paths in Markdown link labels and titles bypass sanitization
findings.detail: The link alternative consumes the entire Markdown link, but the callback examines only its destination. If the destination is relative or remote, it returns the entire match unchanged, including any absolute local path in the label or title. That path can therefore be published or cause delivery to be blocked once the username is added to private-strings.txt.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize path-bearing link labels and titles as well as destinations, without leaving the consumed text unchecked.
findings.failure_scenario: A report contains `[See /Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts](a.ts)`. The destination is unchanged, so the absolute path in the visible label is published unchanged.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:21 selects only the destination (`const path = angle ?? bare`); line 24 returns the entire original match when that destination is unchanged. src/pipeline/engine.ts:1952 applies this sanitizer to publication text, and lines 2353–2358 pass the resulting report to publication checks. Reproduced output preserves `[See /factory/data/work/run/a.ts](a.ts)` unchanged.
verification.trigger: Model report text puts an absolute worktree path in a link label or title while using a relative destination. The sanitizer preserves that path; publication either exposes it when no private entry matches or is blocked once the username is listed.

findings.title: Sanitizing after clipping can publish a partial private path
findings.detail: Blocked-round evidence is clipped to 300 characters and the complete comment is clipped to 60,000 characters before publicationText sees it. If either cut falls within the data-directory prefix, the sanitizer cannot match the full root, leaving the beginning of the absolute path in the published comment. The report renderer also clips text before the new publication sanitizer runs.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize path-bearing source text before truncation at each publication path, while preserving any full-source privacy checks.
findings.failure_scenario: Blocked evidence consists of 290 characters followed by `/Users/alice/.limitless/runs/log`. The 300-character cut retains `/Users/ali`, which no longer matches the configured data-directory root and can be published.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:2129–2131 clips evidence before path sanitization: `redactGateOutput(redactHoldoutText(c.evidence, ...)).slice(0, 300)`. Only afterward, at :2139–2141, it calls `text = publicationText(ctx, text)` and publishes through `gh(["pr", "comment", ...], ctx.signal, text)`. src/gates/publication.ts:8–9 requires a complete root: `path === root || path.startsWith(`${root}/`)`; unmatched text remains unchanged. src/gates/output.ts:24–25 only strips terminal formatting and credentials.
verification.trigger: An environment-blocked review round has public criterion evidence containing 290 characters followed by `/Users/alice/.limitless/runs/log`, with that data root configured. Clipping retains `/Users/ali`; sanitization cannot recognize the incomplete root, and publication proceeds unless a configured private string independently matches it. The precise truncation position is an unusual trigger.

findings.title: Parent-directory segments are classified under the wrong root
findings.detail: The sanitizer classifies paths by lexical prefix without resolving `..` segments. A path that starts in the worktree but resolves into the factory data directory is emitted as a repository-relative path rather than a `<data>` placeholder.
findings.suggestion: Normalize local path segments before deciding which configured root contains the destination.
findings.failure_scenario: With worktree `/factory/data/work/run`, `/factory/data/work/run/../../runs/log` becomes `../../runs/log` instead of `<data>/runs/log`.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:8 classifies paths using literal prefix matching, then lines 10–11 slice off the matched root without resolving parent segments. Reproduced output for `/factory/data/work/run/../../runs/log` is `../../runs/log`.
verification.trigger: A path lexically starts under the worktree but traverses outside it into the data directory. It becomes a relative repository link/path instead of `<data>/runs/log`.

findings.title: Paths in Markdown link labels bypass rewriting
findings.detail: The request requires rewriting “links and bare paths that point into the run's worktree.” The link alternative consumes the entire Markdown link, but the callback only examines its destination. Consequently, an absolute path in the visible label survives whenever the destination is relative or otherwise unchanged. Once the username is in private-strings.txt, the privacy check can block delivery; until then, the path can be published.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize path occurrences in link labels as well as destinations while preserving ordinary link targets.
findings.failure_scenario: With worktree /factory/data/work/run, the input [`/factory/data/work/run/a.ts`](docs/a.md) is returned unchanged. A standalone invocation of sanitizePublication produced that exact unchanged output.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:13 matches the entire Markdown link, but lines 21–24 examine only its destination: `const path = angle ?? bare; ... if (result === path) return match;`. Consequently, an unchanged relative destination preserves the absolute path in the label. Reproducing the candidate input with the extracted sanitizer returned it unchanged. Publication is reachable through src/pipeline/report.ts:138–139 (`state.implementerReport` becomes the summary), src/pipeline/engine.ts:2354 (`publicationText(ctx, stripReportManifest(rendered.report))`), and lines 2413–2417 (`createPullRequest(... { ... body, ... })`).
verification.trigger: An implementer report contains [`/factory/data/work/run/a.ts`](docs/a.md), with worktree /factory/data/work/run. The absolute label survives sanitization and can publish private directory information, or block delivery if the username is denylisted.

findings.title: File URI links retain absolute local paths
findings.detail: The request covers links pointing into the worktree and factory data directory, but rewrite only recognizes destinations beginning directly with a configured filesystem root. A file:// destination is consumed as a Markdown link and returned unchanged, exposing the local path or causing the private-strings check to block delivery.
findings.suggestion: Recognize local file URI destinations, decode them as appropriate, and apply the same worktree and data-directory rewriting.
findings.failure_scenario: With worktree /factory/data/work/run, [file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts) is returned unchanged. A standalone invocation of sanitizePublication produced that exact unchanged output.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:8–9 recognizes only `path === root || path.startsWith(`${root}/`)` and otherwise returns the original path. Lines 23–24 then preserve the whole link: `const result = rewrite(path); if (result === path) return match;`. A `file:///...` destination never starts with the configured absolute root. Reproducing the candidate input with the extracted sanitizer returned it unchanged. src/pipeline/report.ts:138–139 includes implementer text in reports; src/pipeline/engine.ts:2354 sanitizes that report and lines 2413–2417 pass its body to `createPullRequest`.
verification.trigger: A report contains [file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts), with worktree /factory/data/work/run. The file URI retains its absolute local path. The bypass is proven, but this URI format's occurrence in normal factory reports is not established.

findings.title: Appending a round section rewrites the existing PR body
findings.detail: The request lists “Rewriting already published PR bodies” as out of scope. Sanitizing pr.body together with the new section changes existing published text, including text a user may have edited, whenever it contains a matching path.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize the newly generated round section before appending it, without transforming the existing body.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing PR body contains a worktree path and a new review round is appended; the edit replaces the path in the previously published body as well as adding the round section.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:2145–2151 sanitizes the new section, then sanitizes the entire existing body again: `const text = publicationText(ctx, section)`; `if (!pr.body.includes(marker)) { const body = publicationText(ctx, pr.body + text); ... await gh(["pr", "edit", prUrl, "--body-file", "-"], ctx.signal, body); }`. At :1952, `publicationText` calls `sanitizePublication` with the current worktree and factory data directory.
verification.trigger: A successful ordinary review round appends a section to a PR whose existing body contains a path matching the current worktree or factory data directory. The edit also rewrites that previously published content, contrary to the stated scope exclusion. Paths belonging to older worktrees under the same data directory become `<data>` placeholders.

findings.title: Recheck ownership inside the merge helper before each merge command
findings.detail: The ownership check precedes mergePullRequest, but that helper awaits a GitHub PR lookup before issuing gh pr merge and can repeat that sequence on retry. A reclaim during the lookup is invisible until the heartbeat, so the old worker can still issue a merge after losing its claim.
findings.suggestion: Pass an ownership guard into the helper and check it immediately before each merge command, including retries.
findings.failure_scenario: The old worker enters mergePullRequest, its PR view request is deferred, another owner reclaims the entry, and the view returns before the old heartbeat fires. The old worker then runs gh pr merge.

A reclaim during any of those awaits leaves the old worker able to push before its heartbeat notices.

findings.title: Do not discard a checkout reused by the new claimant
findings.detail: All attempts for an entry use the same land-<id> worktree path. After a reclaim, the old worker reaches this unconditional cleanup even when a new worker has already recreated and started using that path. It can remove the new worker's worktree and cause its checks or merge to fail.
findings.suggestion: Isolate checkout paths by claim or otherwise ensure cleanup cannot remove a newer claimant's checkout.
findings.failure_scenario: A CI response is deferred, the entry is reclaimed and the new worker creates its checkout, then the old response returns. The old worker detects the lost claim but its finally block removes the new worker's checkout.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:393 awaits CI, while :397 unconditionally executes `await this.discard(repo, cwd)` in `finally`. verification.trigger: Another daemon reclaims an expired entry and recreates its checkout while the old worker awaits CI. When the old response returns, the ownership exception runs unconditional cleanup, deleting the new worker's checkout and disrupting its land attempt.

findings.title: A rejected rerun can remain pending forever after claim loss
findings.detail: The rerun claim is persisted before the POST. If ownership changes while the POST is in flight, the new guard discards its response, including an explicit rejection. The replacement worker sees the existing rerun_requested record, but only resolves it when GitHub reports a later workflow attempt. A rejected request creates no later attempt, so CI remains pending and the land cannot complete or report the failure.
findings.suggestion: Provide a recovery path for an unconfirmed rerun request that lets the current owner resolve a rejected or absent rerun without allowing the old owner to write after losing its claim.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker claims a CI rerun, GitHub returns HTTP 422 after another worker reclaims the land entry, and the old worker discards the response. The replacement repeatedly observes the original workflow attempt and retains rerun_requested indefinitely.

findings.title: Encoded credentials in filenames escape diagnostic redaction
findings.detail: The new publication diagnostic passes a Git-controlled path to `redactCredentials` without decoding it first. That function replaces only literal credential variants, so a percent-encoded credential remains recoverable in the error message. The new audit filename handling in `src/gates/audit.ts` has the same issue: `redactGateOutput` also performs literal credential redaction. These diagnostics can be stored as events or sent back to an implementer.
findings.suggestion: Decode supported filename encodings before credential redaction, or suppress the filename when its decoded forms contain a credential. Apply the same handling to both audit findings and publication diagnostics.
findings.failure_scenario: A new file is named with a percent-encoded registered credential and contains text that triggers the publication decoding refusal. findings.title: Audit warnings use the cumulative diff rather than the current round
findings.detail: The new warnings inspect the diff from the run's original base, so a file newly added in a later round can appear as a modification instead of an addition. In that case neither scratch warning fires, even though that round commits the file into publication history.
findings.suggestion: Evaluate the new addition warnings against the current round's commit diff and preserve the cumulative diff for checks that need it.
findings.failure_scenario: A tracked file exists at the base, an earlier round deletes it, and a later round recreates it under a root hidden directory with oversized scratch output. The cumulative diff reports M, so the new A-only checks produce no warning or next-round feedback.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1214-1217 sets `baseSha = ctx.state.verification?.baseSha ?? (ctx.run.baseSha as string)` and calls `diffSince(cwd, baseSha, ...)`. src/git/repos.ts:571 constructs `${baseSha}${threeDot ? "..." : ".."}HEAD`, and line 577 obtains `--name-status` for that range. src/gates/audit.ts:292 guards both new warnings with `if (f.status.startsWith("A"))`. A file present at base and recreated with different contents therefore appears as M and receives neither warning.
verification.trigger: A base-tracked file is deleted in one implementation round and recreated with oversized scratch text in a later round. The cumulative audit reports a modification and omits the round-addition warning and subsequent advisory feedback. This requires an unusual delete-and-recreate sequence.

findings.detail: The diagnostic redacts only literal credential variants. A percent-encoded credential in a path survives redactCredentials, and redactPrivate does not remove it unless it is also in the private-string list. The resulting publication error exposes the recoverable credential. The new test covers only a literal credential in the path.

verification.evidence: src/git/repos.ts:758 constructs the diagnostic with `privacy.redactPrivate(redactCredentials(path), entries)`. src/util/proc.ts:846-847 redacts literal variants using `text.split(secret).join("[redacted]")`; registration at :839 includes only literal and JSON-escaped variants. src/gates/private.ts:102 permits an empty private-string list: `return []`. findings.title: Encoded credentials in diagnosed paths escape redaction
findings.detail: The new diagnostic passes the raw filename to `redactCredentials`, which only matches literal credential variants. `redactPrivate` checks encoded forms only against the private-strings entries, not registered credentials. The same issue affects the new audit filename handling in `src/gates/audit.ts`. An encoded credential can therefore be stored in an audit event, sent in round feedback, or included in a publication refusal.
findings.suggestion: Decode or otherwise recognize encoded credential variants before emitting filenames, and redact the complete diagnostic before it reaches logs, events, or prompts. Cover both audit feedback and publication refusals.
findings.failure_scenario: A registered credential `secret-token-value` appears in an added filename as `%73ecret-token-value`. A scratch warning or decoding-limit refusal includes that filename unchanged, disclosing a readily decodable credential.

verification.evidence: src/git/repos.ts:758 applies `privacy.redactPrivate(redactCredentials(path), entries)`. src/util/proc.ts:839 registers only `secret` and `JSON.stringify(secret).slice(1, -1)`; :847 replaces literal matches. Consequently `%73ecret-token-value` does not match registered `secret-token-value`. src/gates/private.ts:183-186 checks configured private strings separately; an absent list returns `[]` at :102. Production delivery invokes this scan at src/pipeline/engine.ts:2101 and propagates its error at :2110-2111.

findings.detail: The diagnosed path is inserted into the refusal without stripping terminal control characters. Git permits such characters in filenames, so untrusted filenames can inject control sequences or forged lines into displayed or logged errors. The audit path uses `redactGateOutput`, which strips these characters, but the new publication diagnostic does not.
findings.suggestion: Apply terminal-control normalization to the path before including it in the diagnostic, while retaining credential and private-string redaction.
findings.failure_scenario: An added file whose name contains a newline or ANSI escape sequence also contains content exceeding the decoding limit. The resulting refusal displays the untrusted control sequence as part of its message.

At :767 it becomes the diagnostic location; src/gates/private.ts:181 interpolates that location directly into `${location} exceeds the private text decoding limit; publication blocked`. A real-Git probe confirmed that the raw filename retains newline and ANSI bytes even though Git quotes them in patch headers.
verification.trigger: Add a filename containing a newline or ANSI sequence and content exceeding the decoding limit, with no matching private-string entry. The diagnostic error contains the raw control characters.

findings.suggestion: Also inspect rename destinations that introduce a path beneath a root hidden directory.

findings.title: Review eval calls are attributed to one provider and counted as one invocation
findings.detail: Review systems can invoke several finders, samples, and verifiers, including models on different providers. Their trial totals combine those calls, but the fallback creates one record using the trial's primary provider and model. This assigns other providers' tokens and costs to the primary provider and undercounts invocations.
findings.suggestion: Aggregate individual stored call evidence where available, and represent unattributable combined work explicitly rather than assigning it all to the primary provider.
findings.failure_scenario: A review eval calls provider A as its primary reviewer and provider B as a verifier. The report shows one invocation and the combined spend under A, with no invocation or spend under B.

verification.evidence: src/evals/runner.ts:641 sets `trial.details.provider = model.provider`; :1111-1115 selects another verifier target and calls `sendTo(request, to, ...)`. src/pipeline/review.ts:926 returns `result: combined(results, last, ...)`, whose implementation at :541-547 sums costs and tokens across calls. src/db/stats.ts:269-275 assigns the combined trial metrics to `details.provider` and `t.model_id`; :179 counts `invocations: rows.length`.
verification.trigger: A review eval panel invokes primary provider A and verifier provider B. Statistics count one trial as one invocation and attribute its combined spend to A, omitting B's work.

findings.title: Implementation evals lose stored cache token totals
findings.detail: Every eval with rounds is assigned null cache-read and cache-write tokens, even when the trial contains those accumulated measurements and has only one round. Because the summation returns null if any row is unknown, one implementation eval also makes the corresponding provider totals unknown.
findings.suggestion: Use the stored trial cache totals when they can be attributed, including single-round trials, and preserve known aggregate totals where per-round splits cannot be recovered.
findings.failure_scenario: A single-round implementation trial stores 100 cache-read tokens and 20 cache-write tokens. Its model and provider statistics report both values as null, including when it is the only eval for that provider.

verification.evidence: src/evals/runner.ts:1143-1144 stores `trial.details.cacheReadTokens` and `cacheWriteTokens`; :1173-1175 adds round evidence whenever `"hidden" in item`, including single-round implementation trials. src/db/stats.ts:280-281 uses `rounds?.length ? null : ...` for both cache metrics, and :292-293 returns those null values.
verification.trigger: A single-round implementation eval records 100 cache-read and 20 cache-write tokens plus its round evidence. Its provider and model aggregates return null for both cache totals.

findings.title: Eval round totals attribute multiple provider calls to one model
findings.detail: A recorded eval round can include retries or panel calls, but its stored tokens and costs are the combined trial delta while its provider and model identify the round target. Treating that round as one invocation assigns all of the combined work to that target and omits the other calls from their providers and models.
findings.suggestion: Use individually attributed call records where available; otherwise expose the attribution as unknown rather than presenting combined spend as belonging to the target.
findings.failure_scenario: An eval panel calls a reviewer on provider A and a verifier on provider B. The resulting round reports both calls' cost and tokens under A and reports no work for B.

verification.evidence: src/evals/runner.ts:1051 invokes `runReview`; :1111-1115 chooses and invokes the verifier's target. src/pipeline/review.ts:926 returns `combined(results, last, ...)`, summing both calls' costs and tokens at :541-547. src/db/stats.ts:265-275 assigns these totals to one provider/model. Review panels take the trial fallback here: round evidence is persisted only inside `if ("hidden" in item)` at src/evals/runner.ts:1173-1175.
verification.trigger: A review panel calls reviewer A and verifier B. Its combined costs and tokens appear under A's model, with no corresponding work under B. The attribution failure occurs through the trial fallback rather than persisted round records.

findings.title: Discarding eval cache splits makes available totals unknown
findings.detail: When rounds exist, the code forces cache-read and cache-write values to null even though the enclosing trial stores accumulated cacheReadTokens and cacheWriteTokens. Consequently a single ordinary multi-round trial makes its provider's aggregate cache and uncached input totals null, despite those totals being available in stored data.
findings.suggestion: Preserve trial-level cache totals for aggregates that can be attributed accurately, and mark only unavailable per-round breakdowns unknown.
findings.failure_scenario: A completed multi-round eval has cacheReadTokens and cacheWriteTokens in its details. Its eval totals nevertheless return null for both cache metrics and inputTokens.

verification.evidence: src/evals/runner.ts:1143-1144 accumulates cache-read/write totals in trial details, and :1173-1175 persists implementation rounds. src/db/stats.ts:265-266 selects those rounds, :280-281 unconditionally replaces their cache metrics with null, and :291 consequently sets `inputTokens` to null. The summarizer at :171-173 returns null whenever any constituent metric is null.
verification.trigger: A completed multi-round implementation eval contains stored trial cache totals. Its round-based statistics discard those totals, returning null for cacheReadTokens, cacheWriteTokens and inputTokens even when the trial totals are available.

findings.title: Count a running eval trial before any provider invocation exists
findings.detail: A running trial with no recorded rounds is converted into a workload record even when it is still preparing and has no invocation status or usage. This silently reports an invocation and an unsuccessful share for work that may never reach a provider.
findings.suggestion: Only count a trial fallback when persisted evidence establishes that a provider call occurred; represent in-progress preparation separately if needed.
findings.failure_scenario: An eval trial is persisted as running while its workspace is being prepared, with zero usage and no rounds or invocationStatus. The statistics report one failed eval invocation before any model call.

verification.evidence: src/db/stats.ts:246 selects `t.status != 'queued'`; the exclusion at :258 requires `(t.status === "skipped" || details.preparationFailed)`. At :271 fallback status is `details.invocationStatus ?? String(t.status)`, and :179-180 count every row, with only `"ok"` successful. However, workspace preparation occurs in src/evals/runner.ts:688-715 before :931 persists `status: "running"`; dispatch follows at :975 (`return to.harness(...)`).
verification.trigger: A zero-usage running record observed between its persistence and provider dispatch would count as one unsuccessful invocation. The claimed extended workspace-preparation window is not established: workspace preparation precedes the running checkpoint.

findings.title: Eval successful share can reflect grading failures instead of provider results
findings.detail: For implementation evals, the runner can change a round's status from `ok` to `error` or `timeout` when grading fails, even though the provider invocation succeeded. This aggregation uses that modified round status as the provider invocation status, understating the successful share.
findings.suggestion: Preserve and aggregate the provider invocation status separately from the grading outcome.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementation model returns successfully, but its grading process times out. The eval provider statistics count the invocation as unsuccessful.

verification.evidence: src/evals/implement.ts:292-295 assigns `hidden.timedOut || gateTimeout ? "timeout" : launchFailed ? "error"`. src/evals/runner.ts:1201-1203 calls `gradeImplement` after `result.status === "ok"`; :1209-1212 then changes `roundEvidence.status = grade.implement.reason`. Implementation rounds are stored at :1174-1175. src/db/stats.ts:265-266 selects those rounds, :287 uses `status: r.status`, and :180 counts only `r.status === "ok"` as successful.
verification.trigger: An implementation provider returns successfully, but hidden-test or gate grading times out or encounters an operational error. Its recorded round becomes unsuccessful in provider statistics despite the successful provider result.

findings.title: Eval aggregation tests do not exercise runner-produced round evidence
findings.detail: The eval test constructs round records directly and assumes their status and duration describe provider calls. The runner can modify round status after grading and records duration through grading, so this fixture does not catch the resulting misclassification of provider success.
findings.suggestion: Add a test using runner-produced eval evidence where the provider succeeds but grading fails or times out, and assert the provider success share.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression or existing defect that treats a grading timeout as a failed provider invocation passes the manually seeded round test.

verification.evidence: test/provider-workload.test.ts:478–482 manually seeds `rounds: [{ ...round, provider: "alpha" }, { ...round, round: 1, provider: "beta", status: "timeout", durationMs: 150 }]`, then asserts `successfulShare: 0` at lines 521–524. Runner-produced evidence differs: src/evals/runner.ts:1209–1212 changes an originally successful invocation's round status when grading fails: `result.status === "ok" && (grade?.implement?.reason === "error" || grade?.implement?.reason === "timeout")` → `roundEvidence.status = grade.implement.reason`. src/db/stats.ts:265–266 selects these rounds, line 287 uses `status: r.status`, and line 180 counts success only for `r.status === "ok"`.
verification.trigger: A provider invocation succeeds, then hidden-test or gate grading times out. The runner stores the round as timeout, so provider statistics count it as unsuccessful. The manually seeded aggregation test passes without exercising or detecting this distinction.

findings.title: Multi-call eval trials are attributed to one provider and counted as one invocation
findings.detail: The request asks for workload “per provider and model” with “eval invocations shown separately.” A review eval can invoke multiple panel members or samples, including providers other than the trial target. The runner combines their usage and costs into the trial, but this code attributes the entire combined record to the trial target and counts it once. The resulting provider, model, invocation-count, and success figures are misleading.
findings.suggestion: Aggregate individual persisted call evidence where available, and explicitly represent measurements that cannot be attributed from existing records rather than assigning all combined usage to the target.
findings.failure_scenario: A panel eval invokes a target on provider A and a verifier on provider B. Its combined cost and tokens are reported as one invocation for A, while B receives no eval workload.

verification.evidence: src/evals/runner.ts:750-756 resolves panel finder/verifier targets independently. At :1111-1115 it selects a verifier and calls `sendTo(request, to, ...)`; :1033-1038 invokes that target and appends its result to `spent`. src/pipeline/review.ts:926 returns `combined(results, last, ...)`; :541-547 sums all costs and token usage. src/evals/runner.ts:1139-1144 adds combined usage to the trial. src/db/stats.ts:268-275 creates one fallback record using `provider: details.provider`, `modelId: String(t.model_id)` and whole-trial usage.
verification.trigger: A panel eval uses a target on provider A and a verifier on provider B. The combined trial usage becomes one eval record attributed to A; B's invocation and usage are absent from its eval workload.

findings.title: Eval rounds discard stored cached-token totals
findings.detail: The request requires input, output, and cached-token statistics. For every trial with rounds, this code sets both cache fields to null even though the runner accumulates cacheReadTokens and cacheWriteTokens on the trial. Because summarize returns null when any contributing value is unknown, one such trial makes the entire provider's eval cache and uncached-input totals unknown.
findings.suggestion: Use the stored trial-level cache totals for aggregations where they can be attributed without double counting, and preserve unknown values only for breakdowns that cannot be reconstructed.
findings.failure_scenario: An implement eval has one recorded round and stored cacheReadTokens of 500. Its provider's eval totals report cacheReadTokens and inputTokens as null instead of reporting the available values.

verification.evidence: src/evals/runner.ts:1143-1144 persists aggregate cache usage with `trial.details.cacheReadTokens = ... + result.usage.cacheRead` and the corresponding cache-write total. Implementation rounds are recorded at :1174-1175. src/db/stats.ts:280-281 nevertheless assigns `const read = rounds?.length ? null : (details.cacheReadTokens ?? null)` and likewise for write; :291 consequently assigns `inputTokens` null.
verification.trigger: An implementation eval has one recorded round and known trial cache totals, including 500 cache-read tokens. Its eval statistics discard those available totals and report cache-read and uncached-input tokens as null.

findings.title: Historical workload omits stored concierge calls
findings.detail: The request asks for long-term provider workload numbers computed from stored invocations. Historical production reads only the invocations table, while stored concierge calls live in chat_calls and are already counted by the existing provider workload calculation. Consequently the new long-term provider and model totals omit that work even when a provider appears in the legacy today and seven-day fields.
findings.suggestion: Include stored chat calls in the historical workload with an appropriate role and their stored model, status, usage, cost, and duration.
findings.failure_scenario: A provider has a completed concierge call and no pipeline invocations. Its existing today count is one, but the new production totals report zero invocations and zero usage.

verification.evidence: src/concierge.ts:293 invokes the harness and :331 calls `store.recordChatCall(...)`. src/db/store.ts:1015-1024 stores its provider, model, full result, cost and duration in `chat_calls`. Historical production instead reads only `'invocation' AS unit FROM invocations` at :241, and :312 builds `production` solely from those rows.

findings.title: Cross-origin requests can trigger unbounded historical aggregation
findings.detail: The existing GET endpoint now synchronously loads and aggregates every stored invocation and eval trial when no cutoff is supplied. GET requests are exempt from the origin check, so a web page can repeatedly trigger this work against a local daemon even though it cannot read the response. As history grows, each request consumes increasing CPU and memory and blocks the daemon's event loop.
findings.suggestion: Bound or protect the historical computation against unsolicited cross-origin requests, and avoid loading the entire history synchronously for the existing workload endpoint.
findings.failure_scenario: A user with a large invocation history visits a page that repeatedly loads the local /api/stats/providers URL; each request runs the full historical aggregation and can make the daemon unresponsive.

findings.title: A dirty worktree can bypass detection of a cancelled worker's push
findings.detail: When reconciliation rejects an open job, the executor cancels it and calls prepare(). If the coordinator worktree is dirty, prepare() returns null before checking the remote branch, so the executor runs the local session even if the cancelled worker already pushed an unreported commit. The request requires that case to end NeedsHuman.
findings.suggestion: Check the cancelled job's remote branch for an unreported push before falling back to local execution, including when preparation cannot proceed because the worktree is dirty.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker pushes W but has not reported it; after restart the coordinator worktree is dirty. Reconciliation cancels the leased job, prepare() returns null, and a local session starts instead of reporting the unaccepted push.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1138-1139 requires HEAD to match and `(await clean())` for resume. When this fails, src/pipeline/lan-agent.ts:89-91 calls `workers.cancelAgentJob(id)` and clears `id`. It then calls `publication.prepare()` at line 97. But src/pipeline/engine.ts:1149 returns early with `if (!(await clean())) return null;`, before checking `remoteSha()` at line 1150. Consequently src/pipeline/lan-agent.ts:110 takes `if (!prepared) return fallback();`, whose definition at line 51 calls `local()` when not aborted.
verification.trigger: A resumed implement call has a handled, leased job that pushed W without an accepted report, and the coordinator worktree is dirty. Reconciliation cancels the job, then starts a local session without checking the remote branch or raising NeedsHuman. The dirty coordinator worktree requires an additional unusual state whose production source is not established.

findings.title: A fenced pending report no longer renews its lease
findings.detail: The new result request survives the fence, but the fence aborts the job controller and heldJobs() consequently omits the job from heartbeats. Those heartbeats no longer renew its lease. If result requests remain unavailable while heartbeat requests succeed, the lease expires despite the worker continuing to retry the accepted-report request, and the coordinator rejects the eventual report.
findings.suggestion: Keep a pushed job in the heartbeat's held-job list while its independently bounded result report is pending, until the result is accepted or the lease is explicitly lost.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker pushes during an outage and its fence fires. After restart, heartbeats succeed but result requests fail transiently for longer than the remaining lease or restart grace. The coordinator expires the job; a later result receives 409 and the pushed commit cannot be adopted.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:565-567: the fence executes `for (const job of agentJobs.values()) job.controller.abort()`. src/workers/client.ts:501-504: `heldJobs()` includes only `job.reported && !job.controller.signal.aborted`; heartbeat sends `jobs: heldJobs()` (line 546). src/db/workers.ts:242-252 renews leases only `for (const id of c.jobs)`. Its sweep fails jobs when `max(lease_expires_at, resumedAt + lease) <= now` (lines 415-420). src/server/workers.ts:202-203 rejects the subsequent report with `409` when `!workers.holdsAgentJob(id, worker.name)`.
verification.trigger: A pushed job's fence fires during an outage. After restart, heartbeats recover but result requests continue failing beyond the remaining lease/restart grace. The aborted controller permanently excludes the pending report from lease renewal, so its lease expires and the eventual report is rejected.

findings.title: Late result retries can prevent worker shutdown
findings.detail: The late-result signal excludes the worker's shutdown signal as well as the job cancellation and fence signals. If the coordinator is unreachable, `call()` keeps retrying until the attempt deadline, while `runWorker` waits for every job task in its shutdown cleanup. Stopping the worker can therefore hang for the remainder of the agent attempt, potentially many minutes.
findings.suggestion: Combine the attempt-deadline signal with the worker's shutdown signal while continuing to exclude the job controller used by cancellation and the fence.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker pushes a commit, begins retrying its result during a coordinator outage, and then receives a shutdown signal. Its result request remains active and `runWorker` does not finish until the attempt deadline expires.

verification.evidence: src/cli/main.ts:383-384 maps SIGINT and SIGTERM to `controller.abort()`, passing that signal to `runWorker` at line 399. For a pushed commit, src/workers/client.ts:861 instead uses `AbortSignal.timeout(Math.max(0, deadline - Date.now()))` for reporting, excluding the shutdown signal. The retry loop continues on network errors and 5xx responses with `await sleep(delay, undefined, { signal: requestSignal })` (lines 505-526). Shutdown aborts job controllers but then awaits `...allJobs().map(([, j]) => j.task)` (lines 984-991).
verification.trigger: A worker pushes a commit and retries its report during a coordinator outage, then receives SIGTERM or SIGINT. Shutdown cannot abort the report request or its retry sleeps, and runWorker remains pending until reporting succeeds, is refused, or the attempt deadline expires.

findings.title: Queued restart test completes the job before the scheduler resumes
findings.detail: The queued case leases and reports the job before calling resumed.start(), so the resumed executor sees a done job. It does not exercise reattachment to a queued job followed by pickup and completion after restart.
findings.suggestion: Start the resumed factory while the job is still queued, observe reattachment, then lease and complete that same ID and assert that no second row is created.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that replaces a stored queued job on resume could pass this integration case because the stored job has already become done.

verification.evidence: test/pipeline-lan-agent.test.ts:940 leases the old id, then :943 awaits `report(resumed, job, request(job), await publish(...))` before :945 `resumed.start()`. The report helper at :329 calls `completeAgentJob`. Thus scheduler recovery sees a done job. Separate queued executor coverage exists at test/lan-agent.test.ts:505-511, but does not exercise this integration sequence.
verification.trigger: A regression specific to scheduler recovery of stored queued jobs could pass this integration case because the job finishes before recovery begins.

findings.title: Already-adopted recovery lacks negative verification cases
findings.detail: The checkpoint test exercises recovery with a valid commit and clean worktree, but does not verify that the new HEAD-already-at-result path rejects a dirty worktree or a commit that fails the shared commit-object checks. Existing adoptWorkerCommit tests exercise the ordinary adoption path.
findings.suggestion: Add recovery cases with HEAD already at the reported SHA and either a dirty worktree or an invalid commit shape, and assert that recovery refuses adoption.
findings.failure_scenario: Removing the cleanliness or commit verification from the already-moved path would still allow the new successful recovery test to pass.

verification.evidence: test/pipeline-lan-agent.test.ts:488 asserts HEAD already equals `first.result_sha`, then :497-498 starts recovery and expects success without introducing dirt or invalid commit metadata. The distinct recovery guards are src/pipeline/engine.ts:1201 `await verifyWorkerCommit(...)` and :1202 `if ((await headSha(cwd)) !== sha || !(await clean()))`. Existing negative tests in test/adopt-worker-commit.test.ts exercise `adoptWorkerCommit`, not this engine branch.
verification.trigger: Removing verification or cleanliness checks specifically from the already-moved recovery branch would leave the successful recovery cases passing.

findings.title: Late-report coverage does not test the attempt deadline
findings.detail: The pushed and fenced cases verify that a report survives a restart and fence, but neither holds the coordinator offline until the attempt deadline. The new independent report signal must also stop retrying at that deadline.
findings.suggestion: Add a controlled deadline case that keeps result delivery unavailable through expiry and checks that retries terminate without an accepted result.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression using an unbounded signal for pushed results would still pass the current restart cases and could leave a worker retrying indefinitely.

verification.evidence: test/pipeline-lan-agent.test.ts:774 tests `['running', 'pushed', 'fenced']`; :851-853 fires the fence, while :870 restores connectivity and :879 expects a done job. It never expires the attempt deadline. The deadline protection under test would be src/workers/client.ts:861: `sha === req.parentSha ? jobSignal : AbortSignal.timeout(Math.max(0, deadline - Date.now()))`.

findings.title: Validate hidden tests under the same cleanup conditions as grading
findings.detail: Validation runs the hidden command immediately after setup, leaving untracked setup artifacts in the worktree.
