Verifier: 21 candidates, 21 checked, 5 refuted.

findings.title: Lifecycle transitions can disappear between polls
findings.detail: Comments are derived from the current run status, and an event is persisted only when reconciliation observes that status. A run that enters needs_human and is resumed or resolved before the next poll never records or posts that event. Likewise, a second needs_human episode is suppressed by the first episode's done checkpoint. This does not provide a durable side effect for each transition across restarts or polling intervals.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur, with an identity for each status episode, and reconcile those records independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:97–102 reads `run = store.getRun(snapshot.id)` and only creates the event `if (run.status === "needs_human")`. Lines 113–114 preserve only already-pending events. src/server/http.ts:614–620 exposes owner resolution; src/db/store.ts:2037–2040 permits needs_human → resolved. src/config.ts:427 defaults queue polling to 180 seconds.
verification.trigger: A needs_human run is resolved by the owner before the next poll. Its needs-you comment and reason are never recorded or posted. The concrete supported transition is resolution; retry creates a separate run.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates only run for queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Both the reconciler and its timer are conditional on the issue queue's repository and trusted-account configuration. Runs started through CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers in any other configured repository therefore receive no lifecycle labels or comments, even though the requested behavior covers every start path and does not require queue admission to be enabled.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and select linked issues according to the supported repository settings.
findings.failure_scenario: A repository has the GitHub integration configured but is absent from githubQueue.repos; a CLI run with `Closes #42` produces no lifecycle updates.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10–12 requires `cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; line 43 skips issues failing that check. src/integrations/index.ts:65–67 starts the lifecycle-owning queue only when queue repositories and trusted accounts exist. src/db/store.ts:356–357 recognizes non-GitHub prompts containing Closes references independently of queue configuration.
verification.trigger: A CLI run containing `Closes #42` targets a GitHub-integrated repository absent from githubQueue.repos. Required lifecycle labels and comments are skipped.

findings.title: A partial failure can release an issue before its failure label is applied
findings.detail: The label loop removes in-progress before adding failed. If the add fails, reconciliation logs the failure and queue selection continues in the same poll. The existing latest-run admission check only finds issue-source runs, so it does not protect a failed CLI or MCP run linked through its prompt. The issue can be selected again using its old priority approval before the failed label is retried.
findings.suggestion: Keep admission closed until the failure transition is durably reflected, including for prompt-linked runs; order label writes so a partial transition does not release the issue.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #42` fails; deleting in-progress succeeds but adding failed returns an error. The same poll sees the old priority label and starts a queue run without re-approval.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:13 orders labels as in-progress, needs-you, failed; lines 68–86 delete in-progress before adding failed, and lines 93–95 catch write errors. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191–195 continues from reconciliation into issue selection. Its failure guard at lines 97–101 requires the failed label. src/db/store.ts:361–367 excludes failed runs from claims, and lines 1266–1271 restrict `latestIssueRun` to `source_ref.kind = 'issue'`, excluding ordinary CLI Closes runs.
verification.trigger: An otherwise eligible issue has an old trusted priority approval. Its CLI Closes run fails; removing in-progress succeeds and adding failed fails. Selection in the same poll sees neither a blocking label nor a claim or latest issue-source run, and starts another run without re-approval.

findings.title: An older run can overwrite a newer run's issue labels
findings.detail: The latest-run map is computed once before any GitHub requests. If another run for the issue is created while a label request is awaiting, the old run remains designated latest and can complete its label transition after the newer run starts. Its completed cursor then prevents correction until the newer run is reconciled on a later poll.

Verifier: 19 candidates, 19 checked, 5 refuted.

findings.title: Status transitions between polls are lost
findings.detail: Comments and labels are derived only from the run's current status. No durable event is recorded when a run enters needs_human or failed, so a transition that ends before the next poll cannot be reconstructed. The single comment key for each status also suppresses later occurrences of the same status.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle transitions durably when they occur and reconcile each recorded occurrence independently.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll. The poll sees running and never posts the needs-you comment or applies its label. A second needs_human episode after an observed first episode also receives no new comment.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101–102 adds the event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`. Lines 112–114 use `const effect = `comment:${event}`` and `if (state(effect) === "done") continue;`, so checkpoints cannot distinguish repeated episodes. src/config.ts:427 defaults polling to `q.poll_seconds ?? 180`. However, a production path resuming the same needs_human run to running was not established.
verification.trigger: If the same run leaves needs_human between polls, its unobserved episode is lost. If it enters needs_human again after a completed comment, the existing checkpoint suppresses another comment.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside queue-configured repositories
findings.detail: The reconciler skips every repository that is absent from githubQueue.repos or has no trusted queue accounts, and it is not started at all when the queue is disabled. The requested lifecycle applies to runs started through every entry point; it is not limited to repositories enabled for automatic issue picking.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration for linked issues.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` in a repository that has no issue queue configured. The run receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/index.ts:65–67 starts the queue only when `!!queue?.repos.length && !!queue.trusted.length`. Its tick calls lifecycle reconciliation at src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191. Independently, src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10–12 requires membership in `cfg.githubQueue.repos`, and line 43 executes `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`. src/db/store.ts:356–357 recognizes non-GitHub prompt closing directives.
verification.trigger: A new CLI run with `Closes #7` in a repository without queue configuration receives no lifecycle labels or comments, despite the requirement covering any start path.

findings.title: A failed label write can allow a failed manual run to be re-picked
findings.detail: The transition removes in-progress before adding failed, and a write failure is caught before the queue continues to query candidates. The queue's latestIssueRun lookup only recognizes issue source references, so a terminal CLI or MCP run linked through `Closes #n` supplies no local re-approval guard.
findings.suggestion: Make admission account for terminal runs linked through all supported start paths, including while lifecycle writes are pending.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run for `Closes #7` fails. Removing in-progress succeeds, adding failed fails, and the issue still has its old trusted priority label. The same poll can pick it again without a new approval.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:13 orders in-progress before failed; lines 80–86 perform DELETE/POST and throw on a failed addition, while lines 93–94 only log the error. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 reconciles before selecting candidates at lines 219–225. Its failed-label guard at lines 96–101 requires the label to exist. src/db/store.ts:1268 restricts `latestIssueRun` to `json_extract(runs.source_ref, '$.kind') = 'issue'`, excluding ordinary CLI Closes runs; lines 361–367 exclude failed runs from active claims.
verification.trigger: An otherwise eligible issue retains its trusted priority label after its manual Closes run fails. Reconciliation removes in-progress but fails to add failed. With no issue-sourced run history or open closing PR, queue admission can immediately create another run without re-approval.

findings.title: An older run can overwrite labels after a newer run starts
findings.detail: The latest-run map is computed once before any GitHub awaits. Re-reading the old run's status does not check whether another run has since claimed the same issue, so an in-flight reconciliation can apply an old terminal label after a newer run has started.
findings.suggestion: Recheck issue ownership after awaited operations and before each label mutation, coordinating it with run admission.
findings.failure_scenario: While reconciliation of an old failed run is awaiting its label read, a new run for the same issue starts. The old reconciliation then removes in-progress or adds failed based on its stale latest-run map.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:35–39 builds `latest` once from `store.issueLifecycleRuns()`. Line 56 checks that snapshot before the awaited label read at line 60. Lines 63–71 subsequently re-read only `store.getRun(snapshot.id)` and compare its desired status; they never refresh issue ownership. src/app.ts:431–443 allows retrying a run through `this.createRun(...)` with its original source reference.
verification.trigger: A retry or manual replacement starts while an old failed run awaits GitHub's label response. The old run can continue removing in-progress or adding failed because its cached ownership map still names it. The overlap is timing-dependent; a later poll can reconcile the newer run.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation skips every repository absent from githubQueue.repos, and the reconciler itself is started only when the queue has configured repositories and trusted accounts. The request requires lifecycle updates for every start path, including CLI and MCP runs, with gh as the fallback identity.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and handle linked issues for all applicable repositories.
findings.failure_scenario: A user runs `limitless run` with `Closes #7` for a repository that is not in githubQueue.repos. No lifecycle label or comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10–12 defines management as `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length && cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; line 43 skips every linked issue outside that set. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 is the lifecycle reconciliation caller, and src/integrations/index.ts:65–67 mounts it only for an enabled issue queue.
verification.trigger: A CLI run containing `Closes #7` targets a repository absent from githubQueue.repos. Lifecycle reconciliation skips it, producing no labels or comments. This duplicates C2.

findings.title: Transient lifecycle events disappear before they are checkpointed
findings.detail: Events are inferred only from the current run snapshot. A needs_human or failed state that begins and ends between polls is never recorded. The same loss occurs when an earlier comment fails: the loop breaks before saving later events as pending, so a status change before the next poll erases them.
findings.suggestion: Durably record each lifecycle transition when it occurs, then reconcile its effects independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human while the started comment write is failing, then is resumed before the next poll. No needs-you comment is ever posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101–102 creates the event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; :110 processes `"started"` first; :165–167 handles its failure with `failure(error); break;`, before the needs-human checkpoint at :159–162. src/db/store.ts:2037–2040 permits needs_human → resolved. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 calls reconciliation on polls, scheduled at :295 using `q.pollSeconds * 1000`.
verification.trigger: In an enabled queue repository, the started comment fails while the run needs human input. The owner resolves the run before the next successful poll. No needs-human effect was checkpointed, so its comment disappears. Resolution is the supported equivalent of the candidate's assumed resume.

findings.title: An unrelated comment can impersonate a completed lifecycle write
findings.detail: Recovery treats any issue comment containing the predictable marker as proof that the factory posted its pending comment, without checking its author. An issue participant can supply that marker and cause the actual lifecycle comment to be permanently marked done.
findings.suggestion: Verify the recovered comment was authored by the configured factory identity and matches the pending body before marking the effect done.
findings.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails, another issue participant posts a comment containing the run's marker. On the next poll the factory records the failed comment as delivered and never retries it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:120 builds `<!-- limitless-lifecycle:${run.id}:${event} -->`. On retry, :123 parses comments as `z.object({ body: z.string() })`, and :128–130 accepts `comments.some((c) => c.body.includes(marker))`, then saves the effect as `"done"`. No author or body-authenticity check occurs.
verification.trigger: A comment POST fails after the pending checkpoint. Another participant posts the predictable marker. The next poll treats that unrelated comment as successful delivery and suppresses the factory's retry.

findings.title: A 404 during label removal is silently recorded as success
findings.detail: The catch treats every HTTP 404 as an already-removed label. GitHub can also return 404 for an inaccessible repository or issue, so a permission or installation failure can be checkpointed as a successful label transition and will not be retried.
findings.suggestion: Confirm the label is absent with a successful fresh read before recording the removal as complete; otherwise log and retry the error.
findings.failure_scenario: The initial label read succeeds, but the App loses repository access before the DELETE. GitHub returns 404 and the reconciliation cursor records the label set as complete even though the label remains.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:83 issues the label DELETE. Its catch at :86 throws only when `add || !/\bHTTP 404\b/.test(String(error))`; :88 then saves `"done"`, and :92 saves the complete label cursor. At :56 a matching cursor skips further reconciliation. src/integrations/github.ts:19–21 routes production calls through `githubSh`.
verification.trigger: The label read succeeds, repository access disappears before a removal, and DELETE returns HTTP 404 while the label remains. For a removal-only transition, the reconciler records completion without logging or retrying. This requires an unusual access-change timing window.

findings.title: Status transitions between polls never produce their comments
findings.detail: Lifecycle comments are derived from the current run status. A needs_human episode that begins and ends between polls is never recorded as pending, so its required comment is permanently lost. The pending-comment tests cover a transition only after a poll has already observed it.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur and reconcile those records. Add a test that enters and leaves needs_human between polls, then restarts and checks for exactly one comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next issue-queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 invokes `reconcileIssueLifecycle(...)` during polling; :295 schedules the next poll. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:97–102 reads current state and adds needs_human only for the current status; :113 skips absent events unless already pending. src/db/store.ts:2037–2040 permits needs_human → resolved, exposed through `store.resolveRun(...)` at src/server/http.ts:620. The notifier delegates managed issue comments to the queue at src/integrations/github-notifier.ts:298–299.
verification.trigger: An enabled queue's linked run reaches needs_human and is resolved through the owner API before the next poll. No event was captured, so no needs-you comment is posted. The code supports resolution rather than the candidate's assumed same-run resume.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside the issue queue configuration
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation requires the repository to be in githubQueue.repos with trusted accounts configured, and the poller does not start without that configuration. The request requires updates for linked runs from all start paths. The new test explicitly asserts no updates for disabled or unlisted repositories, thereby protecting this omission.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation for linked GitHub issues independently of queue admission configuration, and test a CLI or MCP run when queue polling is disabled.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner starts a run with Closes #7 in a GitHub repository that is not enabled for automatic issue picking; the issue receives neither labels nor comments.

verification.evidence: src/db/store.ts:356-357 links non-GitHub runs using `closedIssues(run.prompt)`. However, src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10-12 requires `cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`, and line 43 skips the issue when that check fails. src/integrations/index.ts:65-67 starts reconciliation only when the issue queue is enabled.
verification.trigger: An owner-created run contains `Closes #7` for a repository outside githubQueue.repos, or automatic issue picking is disabled. Its issue receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

findings.title: Restart coverage does not exercise each lifecycle transition
findings.detail: The interruption matrix only interrupts the initial started event. The needs-human, failure, cancellation, PR, and merge tests restart after their writes have completed, so they do not establish that a restart between each transition's label change and comment preserves the required effect.
findings.suggestion: Exercise interruption after the label update and before the comment for each applicable transition, then reopen the store and verify the final labels and exactly one comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that loses a failed or needs-human comment after its label write can pass the current restart tests.

verification.evidence: test/issue-queue.test.ts:1225 asserts `expect(h.comments.get(7)).toHaveLength(2)` before `h.stop()` at line 1228, so transition tests restart only after comments complete. The interruption test at lines 1275–1298 exercises initial startup only, asserting `"comment:started"`. The failed/needs_human restart tests at lines 1346–1349 first assert `comment:${status}` is `"pending"`, then stop; they do not interrupt between the label write and creation of that comment checkpoint.
verification.trigger: A regression affecting failed or needs_human comment recovery specifically after its label write but before its comment checkpoint could pass these tests: that interruption window is exercised only for the started event.

findings.title: Do not accept an arbitrary issue comment as proof of a factory write
findings.detail: Recovery treats any comment containing the predictable lifecycle marker as proof that the factory posted its comment. Issue comments are untrusted: their author is neither retrieved nor checked. An attacker who can comment can therefore suppress a pending lifecycle notification.
findings.suggestion: Authenticate the author of a matching comment against the GitHub identity used for the write, and require an exact, validated marker before recording the effect as done.

candidates.title: Status transitions between polls are lost
candidates.detail: Comments and labels are derived only from the run's current status. No durable event is recorded when a run enters needs_human or failed, so a transition that ends before the next poll cannot be reconstructed. The single comment key for each status also suppresses later occurrences of the same status.
candidates.suggestion: Record lifecycle transitions durably when they occur and reconcile each recorded occurrence independently.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll. The poll sees running and never posts the needs-you comment or applies its label. A second needs_human episode after an observed first episode also receives no new comment.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside queue-configured repositories
candidates.detail: The reconciler skips every repository that is absent from githubQueue.repos or has no trusted queue accounts, and it is not started at all when the queue is disabled. The requested lifecycle applies to runs started through every entry point; it is not limited to repositories enabled for automatic issue picking.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration for linked issues.
candidates.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` in a repository that has no issue queue configured. The run receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

candidates.title: A failed label write can allow a failed manual run to be re-picked
candidates.detail: The transition removes in-progress before adding failed, and a write failure is caught before the queue continues to query candidates. The queue's latestIssueRun lookup only recognizes issue source references, so a terminal CLI or MCP run linked through `Closes #n` supplies no local re-approval guard.
candidates.suggestion: Make admission account for terminal runs linked through all supported start paths, including while lifecycle writes are pending.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run for `Closes #7` fails. Removing in-progress succeeds, adding failed fails, and the issue still has its old trusted priority label. The same poll can pick it again without a new approval.

candidates.title: An older run can overwrite labels after a newer run starts
candidates.detail: The latest-run map is computed once before any GitHub awaits. Re-reading the old run's status does not check whether another run has since claimed the same issue, so an in-flight reconciliation can apply an old terminal label after a newer run has started.
candidates.suggestion: Recheck issue ownership after awaited operations and before each label mutation, coordinating it with run admission.
candidates.failure_scenario: While reconciliation of an old failed run is awaiting its label read, a new run for the same issue starts. The old reconciliation then removes in-progress or adds failed based on its stale latest-run map.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside queue-enabled repositories
candidates.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation skips every repository absent from githubQueue.repos, and the reconciler itself is started only when the queue has configured repositories and trusted accounts. The request requires lifecycle updates for every start path, including CLI and MCP runs, with gh as the fallback identity.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and handle linked issues for all applicable repositories.
candidates.failure_scenario: A user runs `limitless run` with `Closes #7` for a repository that is not in githubQueue.repos. No lifecycle label or comment is posted.

candidates.title: Transient lifecycle events disappear before they are checkpointed
candidates.detail: Events are inferred only from the current run snapshot. A needs_human or failed state that begins and ends between polls is never recorded. The same loss occurs when an earlier comment fails: the loop breaks before saving later events as pending, so a status change before the next poll erases them.
candidates.suggestion: Durably record each lifecycle transition when it occurs, then reconcile its effects independently of the current status.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human while the started comment write is failing, then is resumed before the next poll. No needs-you comment is ever posted.

candidates.title: A second needs-human episode is treated as already delivered
candidates.detail: Comment checkpoints are keyed only by run and event name. Once a needs_human comment is marked done, a resumed run that later reaches needs_human again cannot post its new reason. Label reconciliation can still switch back to needs-you, leaving the issue with a stale explanation.
candidates.suggestion: Key lifecycle effects by a durable transition or status episode rather than only by event type.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run needs human input, resumes after the owner responds, and later needs human input for a different reason. The second reason is never commented.

candidates.title: Re-approval can come from a priority label that is no longer applied
candidates.detail: The post-failure check accepts any trusted priority labeled event, even if that label was subsequently removed. The separate approved check can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before the failure, so the current approval need not be the one applied after failure.
candidates.suggestion: Require a currently applied, trusted priority label whose latest application occurred after the failure label.
candidates.failure_scenario: Priority:2 was applied before failure; a trusted user applies and removes priority:1 after failure. The issue remains eligible using the old priority:2 label despite the later approval having been withdrawn.

candidates.title: An unrelated comment can impersonate a completed lifecycle write
candidates.detail: Recovery treats any issue comment containing the predictable marker as proof that the factory posted its pending comment, without checking its author. An issue participant can supply that marker and cause the actual lifecycle comment to be permanently marked done.
candidates.suggestion: Verify the recovered comment was authored by the configured factory identity and matches the pending body before marking the effect done.
candidates.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails, another issue participant posts a comment containing the run's marker. On the next poll the factory records the failed comment as delivered and never retries it.

candidates.title: A 404 during label removal is silently recorded as success
candidates.detail: The catch treats every HTTP 404 as an already-removed label. GitHub can also return 404 for an inaccessible repository or issue, so a permission or installation failure can be checkpointed as a successful label transition and will not be retried.
candidates.suggestion: Confirm the label is absent with a successful fresh read before recording the removal as complete; otherwise log and retry the error.
candidates.failure_scenario: The initial label read succeeds, but the App loses repository access before the DELETE. GitHub returns 404 and the reconciliation cursor records the label set as complete even though the label remains.

candidates.title: Status transitions between polls never produce their comments

candidates.title: A removed priority label can supply re-approval

findings.title: A blocked comment is marked done without posting the required fallback

findings.title: Lifecycle transitions between polls are lost
findings.detail: The poller derives events solely from the current run status and records no transition at the point the status changes. A needs-human or failure state that is resolved before the next poll is never observed, so neither its comment nor its corresponding label is applied. A single effect key per event also prevents a second needs-human episode from producing a comment.

findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resolves it before the next queue poll; the issue never receives the needs-you update or reason.

No lifecycle effect is recorded by updateRun (src/db/store.ts:2070–2090).

duplicates.title: Transient lifecycle states are lost between polls

findings.title: A failed issue can be picked before the failure label is applied
findings.detail: When the failed label is absent, eligibility falls back to accepting any trusted priority event after the run finished. If the lifecycle label write fails, that approval can occur before the failure label exists, yet the next queue poll can select the issue. This violates the required ordering after the failure label was applied.
findings.suggestion: Keep failed runs ineligible until the failure label application is observed and a trusted priority event follows it.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, adding `limitless:failed` fails, and a trusted user reapplies priority before the next poll. The issue has no failed label, so the timestamp fallback admits it without a priority event after the failure label.

The catch at :227-232 only calls 'logFailure(...)'. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:203 awaits reconciliation and then continues querying candidates. At :117-123, 'context.latest.status === "failed" && failed' selects failure-label ordering only when the label exists; otherwise a trusted event with 'Date.parse(e.createdAt) > ...finishedAt' suffices. findings.title: Failure and needs-you comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both terminal comments always use a fixed UI reference and never include the run's reason. The request requires a comment with the reason, using a fixed message when the private-strings check blocks that text. The added tests explicitly assert that the reason is absent.

findings.title: Publication errors permanently discard comments
findings.detail: Any exception while preparing or checking a comment marks the effect done. This includes transient inspection errors as well as a private-string match, so no later poll retries it and the required fixed fallback is never posted. The same permanent suppression occurs when rechecking a pending body at line 248.

findings.failure_scenario: A private string matches the generated UI link, or the private-strings file is temporarily unreadable; the lifecycle event is recorded as done without any issue comment and remains absent after the condition is corrected.

findings.title: A failed label write permits re-pick based on an earlier approval

findings.suggestion: Keep a failed run ineligible until the failure label has been observed and a trusted priority application is observed after that label.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, the owner reapplies a priority label, and posting `limitless:failed` fails. The same or a later poll sees the post-finish priority event and selects the issue despite there being no post-failure-label approval.

verification.trigger: A trusted owner reapplies priority after a run finishes unsuccessfully but before the failure label is delivered. findings.title: Lifecycle events between polls are never recorded

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories

findings.title: Lifecycle writes are restricted to repositories enabled for the issue queue

candidates.suggestion: Capture the reason in the durable event body, redact and check it, and use fixed fallback text when the check blocks it.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run fails with error "tests failed"; the issue receives only "failed: see <UI link>" and does not tell watchers why it failed.

duplicates.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
duplicates.detail: Both rows require a “comment with the reason,” but the generated messages contain only a generic status and UI link. The run's error or other reason is never included, even when it passes publication checks.
duplicates.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after redaction and private-string checking, with the requested fixed fallback when it cannot be published.
duplicates.failure_scenario: A run fails with a specific gate error; the issue only receives “failed: see [UI link]” and does not explain the failure.

candidates.title: Tests require the requested reason to be omitted
candidates.detail: The restart test explicitly asserts that the original reason is absent, and the privacy test expects fixed text even when a reason could be redacted. These assertions encode the implementation defect instead of verifying that safe reasons are posted and unsafe reasons are sanitized or replaced.
candidates.suggestion: Assert that a safe original reason survives a restart, and separately exercise a credential and a private string in the reason.
candidates.failure_scenario: Removing reason handling entirely still passes the tests, while implementing the requested safe reason would fail the current assertion.

candidates.title: Transitions between polls are never recorded
candidates.detail: Events are created only from the run's current snapshot during reconciliation. A needs-human or failed state that is resolved before the next poll leaves no durable event to deliver, contrary to the requirement that each transition be a recorded side effect.
candidates.suggestion: Record lifecycle transitions durably when they occur, then have polling deliver those records. Add a test that transitions through needs-human or failed and resolves before reconciliation runs.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and an owner resolves it before the next queue poll; no needs-you label or comment is ever recorded or posted.

candidates.title: Blocked publication permanently drops the comment
candidates.detail: When the private-strings check rejects a generated body, the effect is marked done without posting the required fixed fallback. The test named "private lifecycle bodies are suppressed durably" explicitly expects this behavior.
candidates.suggestion: Create and check a fixed fallback body and keep its delivery pending until it is posted; test that the fallback is posted once.
candidates.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the generated UI link or run identifier; the issue receives no lifecycle comment and no later poll retries it.

candidates.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
candidates.detail: Both terminal comments contain only a status and UI link. The request requires a comment with the reason, and the tests explicitly assert that the original reason is absent. Readers cannot tell from the issue why the run failed or what needs attention.
candidates.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, using a fixed fallback when it cannot be published.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human with an actionable question or fails with an error; the issue receives only “needs you: see …” or “failed: see …”.

candidates.title: Blocked publication text permanently suppresses the comment
candidates.detail: When the private-strings check rejects a comment, the effect is marked done without posting the required fixed message. The same happens when a pending body fails its check before delivery. This permanently loses the lifecycle notification rather than providing the safe fallback required by the request.
candidates.suggestion: Prepare and publish a fixed, checked fallback message when the original text is blocked, and retain the effect as pending until delivery succeeds.
candidates.failure_scenario: The configured UI URL or run ID contains a private string. The label is updated, but no lifecycle comment is ever posted, including after subsequent polls or restarts.

candidates.title: Lifecycle writes are restricted to repositories enabled for the issue queue
candidates.detail: Reconciliation accepts only repositories listed in githubQueue with trusted accounts, and the only caller is the queue poller, which does not start without that configuration. Runs started directly, through MCP, or through GitHub triggers for other repositories therefore receive no lifecycle labels or durable comments, although the request covers any start path.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and cover linked issues for all supported start paths.
candidates.failure_scenario: A configured repository has no issue queue enabled and an owner starts `limitless run` with `Closes #123`; issue 123 never receives the in-progress label or lifecycle comments.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to configured queue repositories
candidates.detail: The request requires updates for “any start path,” but lifecycleManaged requires the repository to be in githubQueue.repos with trusted accounts configured. The reconciler itself is started only when the issue queue is enabled. CLI, MCP, and trigger runs against other repositories therefore receive no lifecycle labels or durable comments.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and include every linked issue from the supported start paths.
candidates.failure_scenario: A user starts a CLI run with Closes #42 in a repository not listed in githubQueue.repos; no in-progress label or start comment is posted.

candidates.title: Blocked publication text silently discards the comment
candidates.detail: The request says “If the check blocks the text, post a fixed message without it.” Instead, a publication check failure marks the effect done without posting anything. The same behavior occurs when a pending body fails its later check.
candidates.suggestion: Checkpoint and deliver a fixed, safe fallback comment when the original body is blocked.
candidates.failure_scenario: The configured UI URL or another generated comment field contains a private string; the check rejects the body and the lifecycle comment is permanently skipped.

candidates.title: A failed run can be re-picked before its failure label is applied
candidates.detail: When the latest run failed but the failed label is absent, admission falls back to accepting a trusted priority event after the run's finish time. If the failure-label write is delayed or fails, this permits re-pick before the required failure label and subsequent approval exist.
candidates.suggestion: For a failed latest run, require evidence that its failure label was applied and that a trusted priority application followed that label.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run fails, its GitHub label write fails, and a trusted user reapplies a priority label before the next poll. The next admission check can start another run without any priority application after the failure label.

findings.title: Canonicalized names no longer resolve existing mixed-case repository registrations
findings.detail: The queue passes the lowercased repository name into run creation. Repository resolution uses a case-sensitive getRepoBySlug lookup, so an existing mixed-case registration is missed. Resolution then calls GitHub and creates a second repository record with default settings. This can lose the existing registration's merge policy and default branch, and queue admission can fail when the extra GitHub lookup fails.
findings.suggestion: Use canonical keys for comparisons and snapshots while preserving or resolving the registered repository's spelling for run creation.

A change completed before `latestIssueRuns` is read is therefore treated as if it made that fresh snapshot stale. Repeated changes during lifecycle reconciliation or the repository lookup can defer an otherwise eligible issue on every poll.

findings.title: Classify the moved tip before discarding a release intent
findings.detail: Every `moved` result from a replay marks the confirmed lease lost and clears the intent without examining the returned tip. The claim client can return `moved` for a malformed record or a valid record that does not meet the supersession conditions. The recovery rules require malformed content to remain pending, and only a higher generation or the same generation under another holder or run establishes supersession. Clearing the journal also makes the row forgettable, losing confirmed ownership history and the final release record.
findings.suggestion: Classify `result.tip` using the same recovery rules as the initial read; retain the intent for malformed or otherwise unclassifiable tips, and mark it lost only when the tip establishes supersession.

The client returns `moved` with that malformed tip, and recovery returns `superseded`, marks the confirmed lease lost, and deletes the pending release instead of returning `pending`.

findings.title: Release-intent replay bypasses lease-time validation
findings.detail: Reconciliation delegates a pending release to `reconcileLeaseIntent`, which can replay the release with `client.write` without a GitHub-time sample or `beforeSend` predicate. findings.failure_scenario: A release intent is journaled, the process stops before sending it, and recovery runs more than ten minutes later while the old tip remains current. Recovery writes the expired generation's release without checking whether it is renewable.

findings.title: A second moved result marks ownership lost without checking for supersession
findings.detail: After two moved outcomes that are not classified as same-holder writes, the code marks any confirmed row lost regardless of the moved tip's generation or identity. The invariant permits loss only when a moved record supersedes confirmed ownership. A malformed tip or an older-generation tip does not establish that the confirmed generation was superseded.
findings.suggestion: Classify the second moved tip against the confirmed generation and identity before marking the row lost; preserve ownership when supersession is not established.
findings.failure_scenario: A confirmed generation 2 write encounters two moved responses whose tips are malformed or generation 1. The manager marks generation 2 lost and calls `onLost` despite having no superseding record.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:202-208 checks only same-holder contention before counting moved results: `if (mine) continue; if (++moved < 2) continue; if (row?.confirmed && row.runId === want.run) { lose(row, result.tip); return { kind: "superseded", tip: result.tip }; }`. It does not require the second tip to supersede confirmed ownership.
verification.trigger: With valid generation-2 reads before each write, two moved outcomes containing malformed or older records reach the unconditional loss branch. Ownership is marked lost and onLost runs without supersession evidence. This requires unusual ref movement; the manager is currently unwired.

A moved result can instead contain an older generation or a malformed record. This violates the requirement that only a superseding record establishes loss and clears the confirmed ownership on an uncertain result.
findings.suggestion: Classify the second moved tip against the confirmed run, member and generation before marking loss; return a non-loss result when it does not establish supersession.
findings.failure_scenario: A confirmed generation 2 write encounters two concurrent ref movements, and the second returned tip is malformed or generation 1. The manager marks generation 2 lost and calls `onLost` even though the returned tip does not establish a superseding generation.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:201–208 checks `mine = ours && next.generation === record.generation ? record.generation : undefined`, then `if (++moved < 2) continue`, followed by `if (row?.confirmed && row.runId === want.run) { lose(row, result.tip); ... }`. This branch never checks whether the second tip supersedes confirmed ownership. claim-ref.ts:229 can return `moved` with any differing tip, including malformed records.
verification.trigger: A confirmed generation 2 operation encounters two non-same-holder moved outcomes, with an intervening readable tip permitting another write. If the second outcome contains malformed data or generation 1, the manager still persists loss and calls onLost. This requires unusual ref movement.

findings.title: An exception in the renewal timer becomes an unhandled rejection
findings.detail: The async interval callback has no rejection handler. A thrown database, clock, client, or hook error rejects the callback, stops processing the remaining leases for that tick, and can terminate the process under an unhandled-rejection policy. There is no reporting or controlled retry of the failure.
findings.suggestion: Handle and report failures from timer work explicitly, and ensure one failed ref does not silently prevent the other refs from being processed.
findings.failure_scenario: A clock read throws while renewing the first active lease. The timer callback rejects and later active leases are skipped for that tick; the rejection may terminate the daemon.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:239–243 installs `timer.set(async () => { ... await manager.update(h, {}); }, LEASE.renewMs)` without rejection handling. Renewal calls `windowOpen(a, clock.sample())` at line 146. src/util/claim-clock.ts:47 explicitly throws on a failed native clock read.
verification.trigger: A clock read throws during the first active lease's renewal. The async timer callback rejects without a handler and skips remaining leases for that tick. Daemon termination is not established, and the manager is currently unwired.

findings.title: A different run is refused before the pending intent is reconciled
findings.detail: The cross-run guard runs before reconciliation, so a pending intent returns `refused` rather than `wait` and cannot be resolved by that acquisition. The test for a pending old run explicitly expects this behavior, masking the violation of the requirement to reconcile pending intents before every operation.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile first, return wait while the intent remains pending, and only then evaluate the confirmed row and fresh tip. Test both unresolved and dropped intents when a different run acquires.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A has an unconfirmed first acquisition whose intent can now be dropped; run B calls acquire before the loop runs and is refused instead of reconciling and acquiring.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:107 returns refused when `row.runId !== want.run && (row.intent || row.confirmed?.state === "held")`, before `await reconcile(repo, ref, signal)` at line 108. lease-store.ts:113–116 can drop an unsuccessful acquisition intent; leases.ts:91 then forgets a never-confirmed row.
verification.trigger: Run A leaves an unconfirmed initial acquisition that is now reconcilable as dropped. Before a timer tick settles it, run B acquires the same ref and receives refused instead of reconciling, forgetting A's row, and proceeding. The manager currently has no production callers.

findings.title: The renewal loop omits confirmed leases recovered without an in-memory handle
findings.detail: The loop iterates only handles created by an applied write in this manager instance. Recovery and intent reconciliation can confirm a held row without adding a handle, so that lease is never passed to `active` or renewed. The recovery tests cover loss and an update on an already registered handle, but do not cover a recovered or reconciled acquisition becoming eligible for renewal.
findings.suggestion: Populate or derive renewal handles from confirmed held rows after recovery and reconciliation, and test a recovered acquisition through a renewal tick.
findings.failure_scenario: An acquisition returns unconfirmed, then the loop reconciles its intent as applied; subsequent ticks never renew that confirmed lease because no handle was inserted into `handles`.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:49 initializes `handles` empty; line 192 populates it only after a directly applied write. Lines 240–242 reconcile pending rows and then renew only `handles.values()`. lease-store.ts:132–134 confirms reconciled ownership in SQLite without registering an in-memory handle.
verification.trigger: An initial acquisition returns unconfirmed and a later tick reconciles it as applied. Its confirmed generation remains absent from handles and receives no later renewal. This duplicates C6; the manager is currently unwired.

findings.title: Mutation tests expect the broken two-winner result
findings.detail: The unconditional-ref-write cases explicitly expect two winners and therefore pass when the single-holder invariant is broken. The request requires the concurrent-create and takeover tests to fail against that mutant; these cases instead assert the mutant's defect as success.
findings.suggestion: Use the same one-winner assertions for the normal implementation and mutation check, and verify that running them with the unconditional-write mutant fails.
findings.failure_scenario: The fake allows both concurrent writes unconditionally; both acquisitions report held at the same generation, yet the mutant test passes.

verification.evidence: test/leases.test.ts:138 asserts `expect(winners).toHaveLength(unconditional ? 2 : 1)`, and :139 checks both winners have the same generation. Lines 143–147 explicitly run the unconditional mutant for create and takeover. test/claim-github-fake.ts:125–129 bypasses both CAS and fast-forward checks when `unconditional` is true, then applies the write. Targeted execution was blocked during import by `TypeError: floors.prefault is not a function`.
verification.trigger: Run either concurrent test with the unconditional-ref-write mutant: two holders at the same generation satisfy the assertion instead of failing the required single-holder invariant.

findings.title: Replayed release bypasses the lease-time send check
findings.detail: The manager delegates pending-intent reconciliation to `reconcileLeaseIntent`, which replays a release using `client.write` without a `beforeSend` hook or a fresh GitHub-time sample. A release interrupted before its ref update can therefore be sent after the confirmed generation has expired. That violates the same-generation send-time check and can publish a released tip after the holder's authority has ended.
findings.suggestion: Require the same fresh-time decision and immediate pre-send revalidation when replaying a release, and leave the intent pending when that authority cannot be confirmed.
findings.failure_scenario: A release commit is journaled before its ref update, the process stops for longer than the lease expiry, and reconciliation finds the old held tip unchanged. It replays the release without checking expiry; a different run can then acquire the released tip.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:68 calls `recoverLeases({ client, store })`; :89 calls `reconcileLeaseIntent({ client, store, signal }, repo, ref)`. For an unchanged release tip, src/integrations/lease-store.ts:114-121 calls `client.write(..., { signal, onCommit: ... })` without `beforeSend`. src/integrations/claim-ref.ts:206-208 only aborts when `opts.beforeSend?.()` returns false.
verification.trigger: A pending release survives beyond expiry while GitHub still has its confirmed predecessor. Recovery replays the expired generation's release without a time check, permitting another run to acquire if its status allows. The manager currently has no production callers.

findings.title: Renewal loop omits recovered confirmed leases
findings.detail: The loop renews only handles inserted into the in-memory `handles` map by an applied write in this manager instance. Creation and reconciliation do not populate that map for previously confirmed held rows or for an acquisition whose unconfirmed intent is later reconciled as applied. Those leases never receive automatic renewal unless another operation happens to write them first.
findings.suggestion: Populate or derive loop handles from confirmed held rows, including rows confirmed during recovery and reconciliation.
findings.failure_scenario: An acquisition updates GitHub but returns `unconfirmed`; the next tick reconciles its intent to applied. Subsequent ticks never renew that confirmed lease because no handle was added to `handles`.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:49 initializes `handles = new Map<string, LeaseHandle>()`; :196 populates it only after a directly applied write. Reconciliation at :89 never registers handles. The timer at :240-242 reconciles pending rows, then renews only `for (const h of handles.values())`. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:132-134 confirms a matching intent and returns `"applied"`.
verification.trigger: A first acquisition applies remotely but returns unconfirmed. A tick later confirms it, but subsequent ticks omit renewal because its handle was never registered. The manager currently has no production callers.

findings.title: Different-run acquisition skips pending-intent reconciliation
findings.detail: The early different-run check returns `refused` whenever the row has an intent, before reconciliation runs. An unresolved intent is required to yield `wait`, and a dropped never-confirmed acquisition must be forgotten so another run can acquire. This path does neither; without a running renewal loop, the stale intent can block the next run indefinitely.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile the row before classifying a different-run acquisition, returning wait while unresolved and applying the normal dropped-intent cleanup.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A leaves an unconfirmed first-acquisition intent whose GitHub ref is still absent. Run B calls acquire before the loop reconciles it and receives `refused: live` instead of reconciling the dropped intent and acquiring the absent ref.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:107 returns `refused` when `row.runId !== want.run && (row.intent || row.confirmed?.state === "held")`, before reconciliation at :108. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:113-116 drops a first-acquisition intent when the ref is absent; src/integrations/leases.ts:91 would then `forgetLease` the never-confirmed row.
verification.trigger: Run A leaves an unconfirmed first-acquisition intent with an absent ref. Run B acquires before a reconciliation tick and receives refused instead of dropping A's intent and proceeding. The manager currently has no production callers.

findings.title: Reconcile another run’s pending intent before refusing
findings.detail: The request says, “Before every operation, under the ref mutex, a row's pending intent goes through #952's reconcileLeaseIntent” and unresolved intents return `wait`. This early return instead refuses a different run without attempting reconciliation, even when the pending acquisition can be dropped and its never-confirmed row forgotten.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile the row before deciding whether its run or confirmed ownership prevents the acquisition.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A has an unconfirmed first acquisition whose write did not move the ref. Run B acquires the same ref after it becomes readable; it receives `refused: live` rather than reconciling A's dropped intent and proceeding.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:107 checks another run's `row.intent` and immediately returns `refused`; `await reconcile(repo, ref, signal)` follows at :108. For a readable absent ref, src/integrations/lease-store.ts:113-116 would call `store.dropLeaseIntent(repo, ref)`; src/integrations/leases.ts:91 would forget the unconfirmed row.
verification.trigger: Run A's unconfirmed acquisition did not create the ref. Once reads recover, Run B still receives refused until another operation or tick reconciles A's intent. This duplicates C14. The manager currently has no production callers.

findings.title: Restore confirmed handles for the renewal loop
findings.detail: The request requires the loop to update “each confirmed `held` handle whose `active` hook is true.” The loop only visits the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated by writes applied in this manager instance. Existing confirmed rows after restart, and acquisitions confirmed by intent reconciliation, never enter that map.
findings.suggestion: Populate or derive renewal handles from confirmed held rows after recovery and reconciliation.
findings.failure_scenario: A manager restarts with a confirmed held lease, or an unconfirmed acquisition is confirmed on a later tick. Even with `active` returning true, subsequent ticks never renew that lease and it expires.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:49 creates an empty `handles` map. Startup :67-73 recovers intents and records losses but restores no handles. The only `handles.set(...)` is :196 after a directly applied write. The renewal loop at :242 iterates exclusively over `handles.values()`.
verification.trigger: Restart with a confirmed held lease, or reconcile a previously unconfirmed acquisition. Even when active returns true, ticks never renew that lease unless a subsequent explicit acquisition or mutation registers its handle. The manager currently has no production callers.

findings.title: Revalidate time before replaying a pending release
findings.detail: The request requires that “Immediately before the `updateRefs` send” the manager revalidate the applicable time predicate. `reconcileLeaseIntent` can replay a release by calling `client.write` without a `beforeSend` hook or a GitHub-time check; this path is also invoked during initial recovery. A release intent left before its send can consequently be written after the generation has expired.
findings.suggestion: Ensure release replay obtains and revalidates the same-generation time authorization before sending, including during recovery.
findings.failure_scenario: A release is journaled, the process stops before updating the ref, and recovery runs more than ten minutes later while the ref is unchanged. Recovery sends the stale same-generation release without checking whether renewal is still permitted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:65 calls `recoverLeases({ client, store })`; line 89 likewise calls `reconcileLeaseIntent({ client, store, signal }, repo, ref)`. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:113–121 replays an intent when `intent.op === "release"` and `intent.before === confirmed?.tip`, calling `client.write(..., { signal, onCommit: ... })` without time validation or `beforeSend`. src/integrations/claim-ref.ts:206–208 aborts only when the optional hook returns false: `const allowed = opts.beforeSend?.(); ... if (allowed === false) return unchanged;`.
verification.trigger: A pending release survives a restart beyond lease expiry while GitHub still has the confirmed tip. Manager initialization replays and confirms the same-generation release without checking renewable time. Rated medium because this slice remains unwired in production.

findings.title: Do not mark ownership lost for every second moved result
findings.detail: The request says “Only `moved` to a superseding record means lost.” After two non-matching `moved` outcomes, this branch marks any confirmed row lost without checking whether the second tip supersedes its generation and identity.
findings.suggestion: Classify the returned tip against confirmed ownership before marking the lease lost; return a non-loss result when it does not supersede it.
findings.failure_scenario: A confirmed generation encounters two moved results whose final tip is malformed or has a lower generation. The manager marks the confirmed lease lost and calls `onLost` despite having no superseding record.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:201–208 reads `const next = result.tip.record`, excludes matching held ownership through `mine`, then executes `if (++moved < 2) continue; if (row?.confirmed && row.runId === want.run) { lose(row, result.tip); return { kind: "superseded", tip: result.tip }; }`. This branch never checks the `supersedes` predicate defined at lines 124–127. Lines 60–62 implement loss as `store.markLeaseLost(row.repo, row.ref)` followed by `hooks?.onLost(h, tip)`.
verification.trigger: Two writes return nonmatching moved tips, with the intervening fresh read still allowing another write; the second moved tip is malformed or lower-generation. The manager marks confirmed ownership lost and reports superseded without a superseding record. This requires unusual external ref changes or inconsistent observations.

findings.title: Treat browser availability as a positive setup outcome
findings.detail: The engine labels the browser available whenever a preview exists and no `browser_unavailable` event was recorded. That event only covers failures while constructing the MCP configuration; it does not establish that the MCP server or Chromium subsequently started successfully.
