findings.title: A stale poller snapshot can permanently discard a land conflict
findings.detail: A land trigger is immediately evaluated against any saved poller snapshot, even if that snapshot predates the approved head. `startConflictTrigger` marks the trigger skipped when the saved head differs, and a later poll cannot reconsider it. The queue has already blocked the entry, so the requested conflict round never starts.
findings.suggestion: Refresh the PR observation before rejecting a land trigger for a stale head, or retain the trigger pending until a current observation can decide it.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller last observed head A; a review round pushes head B and B is approved before the next poll. Landing B conflicts with the base, but the saved snapshot still says A, so the B trigger is permanently skipped as `PR head moved`.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:641 records the approved head with `recordConflictTrigger(blocked.prUrl, blocked.approvedSha, "land", this.now(), id)`; :266 calls `processConflictTriggers`. src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:21 uses `if (snapshot) store.startConflictTrigger(trigger.id, snapshot, now())`, without refreshing it. src/db/store.ts:1126–1127 checks `seen.headRefOid !== trigger.head ? "PR head moved"`; :1139 persists `state = 'skipped'`. Only `state = 'pending'` is selected at :1071.
verification.trigger: The saved snapshot contains A, while a review round has delivered B and B has been approved. Landing B conflicts before the next poll. The processor compares B against saved A and permanently skips that land trigger. A subsequent poll may create a separate trigger, but cannot recover this one.

findings.title: A conflict observed during another round is lost permanently
findings.detail: An active review or conflict round causes the trigger to be marked skipped. The poller emits `pr.conflicting` only on entry into the conflicting state, so if the active round fails or ends without changing the head, subsequent polls do not create another trigger. The unresolved conflict therefore never gets its own round.
findings.suggestion: Keep the trigger pending while another round is active and reconsider it when that round terminates, subject to a fresh PR observation and the daily cap.
findings.failure_scenario: A review round is in flight when the poller first observes the PR as CONFLICTING. The trigger is skipped; the review round later fails without pushing, and every subsequent poll still sees CONFLICTING, so no conflict round starts.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/github-poller.ts:206 emits only on transition: `if (next.mergeable === "CONFLICTING" && prev?.mergeable !== "CONFLICTING") add("pr.conflicting");`. src/db/store.ts:2609-2612 records a trigger from that event: `if (item.kind === "pr.conflicting" && pr)` then `this.recordConflictTrigger(...)`. The poller consumes pending triggers immediately (src/integrations/github-poller.ts:373-374). src/db/store.ts:1130-1131 rejects any active round: `rounds.some((r) => !TERMINAL_STATUSES.includes(r.status)) ? "round in flight"`; lines 1137-1141 permanently consume that trigger with `UPDATE conflict_triggers SET state = 'skipped', reason = ? WHERE id = ?`. Subsequent processing selects only `WHERE state = 'pending'` (src/db/store.ts:1071).
verification.trigger: An eligible open factory PR first becomes CONFLICTING while a review round is active. Its conflict trigger is marked skipped. If the review round fails without pushing and subsequent polls retain CONFLICTING on the same head, no new event or pending trigger exists, so automatic conflict resolution never starts for that episode.

findings.title: A stale poller snapshot can permanently discard a land trigger
findings.detail: The land path uses any stored GitHub snapshot without refreshing it. `startConflictTrigger` marks the trigger skipped when that snapshot's head differs from the land entry's approved head, even if the snapshot is simply older than the approval. The trigger is then no longer pending, so this landing-queue trigger cannot recover on restart.
findings.suggestion: Refresh or otherwise establish the snapshot's freshness before permanently skipping a land trigger; retain it pending when the observation cannot establish the current head.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller saved head A, the PR advances to B and B is approved before the next poll, and the land queue detects a conflict at B. Processing compares B with the saved A and skips the trigger instead of starting a round.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:641 records `blocked.approvedSha` as the land trigger's head, and :266 processes it. src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:16–21 reads `store.githubPrData(trigger.prUrl)` and immediately passes the existing snapshot to `startConflictTrigger`. src/db/store.ts:1126–1127 classifies a differing saved head as `"PR head moved"`; :1139 writes `state = 'skipped'`. The pending query at :1071 excludes skipped triggers.
verification.trigger: A saved poller snapshot still names A when approved head B encounters a land conflict. The land trigger for B is permanently consumed as skipped instead of starting a round. Later polling can independently retrigger, but does not retry the skipped land trigger.

findings.title: Retrying comment creation can post duplicate resolution comments
findings.detail: The `gh` wrapper retries transient failures around the entire comment command. If GitHub creates the comment but its response is lost, the retry creates another comment without checking the marker again. The preflight marker lookup only protects a later delivery attempt, not retries within this call.
findings.suggestion: Recheck for the marker after an uncertain comment outcome before issuing another creation request.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub accepts `pr comment`, but the client receives a timeout or connection reset; the retry posts a second comment with the same conflict-round marker.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1921-1922 wraps each gh command in `withGitHubRetry(async () => (await runner(args, signal, stdin)) ?? "", { budget, signal })`. The marker check at :1894 precedes `await gh(["pr", "comment", prUrl, "--body-file", "-"], ctx.signal, text)` at :1899. src/git/repos.ts:55 classifies `error.timedOut` as transient, and :84-97 retries `call` without repeating the marker lookup.
verification.trigger: A successful conflict round reaches delivery; GitHub creates the comment but its acknowledgement times out, with retry budget remaining. The command retries directly and creates a duplicate resolution comment.

findings.title: Auto-merge is disabled before validating the PR delivery grant
findings.detail: The new auto-merge mutation occurs before `stored()` and `assertFactoryBranchPush` verify that the PR is still open, belongs to the expected branch and repository, and matches the round's current grant. A stale or invalid round can therefore modify the PR even though delivery is subsequently refused.
findings.suggestion: Validate the current grant and PR identity before disabling auto-merge, and revalidate after the mutation before pushing.
findings.failure_scenario: The PR head branch changes while a conflict round runs and auto-merge is enabled. Delivery disables auto-merge, then rejects the changed branch.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1863-1870 reads the PR, then executes `if (review.kind === "conflict" && pr.autoMerge) await gh(["pr", "merge", prUrl, "--disable-auto"], ctx.signal)` before `stored()` and `assertFactoryBranchPush(...)`. src/core/delivery.ts:88 rejects a changed branch: `if (pr.headBranch !== branch) return ...`. Successful rounds call this path at src/pipeline/engine.ts:2136.
verification.trigger: The PR head branch changes during a conflict round while auto-merge is enabled. Delivery disables auto-merge before rejecting the changed branch, silently changing PR behavior despite refusing delivery.

findings.title: Restart tests do not cover a stale saved observation
findings.detail: The restart tests use either no saved observation or one matching the trigger. They therefore pass while a saved observation for an older head causes a durable land trigger to be skipped permanently, and while an outdated open, non-draft observation can start an ineligible round.
findings.suggestion: Add restart and land-trigger cases with an older saved head and with a PR that became draft or closed after the saved observation. Assert that a current observation governs whether the trigger starts.
findings.failure_scenario: A pending trigger for head B is recovered while the database still contains an open CONFLICTING snapshot for head A; the existing tests never exercise this state.

verification.evidence: test/conflict-rounds.test.ts:330–340 records a trigger and reopens the database without saving an observation. The other startup test uses matching heads: line 517 records `await remoteHead()` and line 525 saves `headRefOid: await remoteHead()`. Neither exercises stale A versus trigger B. src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:21 consumes any saved snapshot: `if (snapshot) store.startConflictTrigger(trigger.id, snapshot, now());`. src/db/store.ts:1126–1140 classifies a mismatch as `"PR head moved"` and persists `state = 'skipped'`.
verification.trigger: Recover a pending land trigger for head B with a saved open CONFLICTING observation for head A. Recovery permanently skips the trigger; the restart tests cover only absent or matching snapshots and miss this outcome.

findings.title: The non-factory polling case bypasses the poller
findings.detail: The non-factory branch inserts a trigger and calls the store consumer directly, so it does not test whether polling a non-factory PR creates a round. A regression in tracking, event generation, or poller consumption for that case would still pass the test.
findings.suggestion: Exercise a tracked non-factory PR through the same fake GitHub poller path as the other eligibility cases and assert that no conflict round starts.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller erroneously starts a conflict round for a non-factory PR, but the test bypasses the poller and continues to pass.

verification.evidence: test/conflict-rounds.test.ts:365–371 handles `eligibility === "non-factory"` by directly calling `recordConflictTrigger(...)` and `startConflictTrigger(...)`. The actual `startGitHubPoller(...)` call is exclusively in the `else` branch at lines 372–373. The assertion at line 393 therefore checks direct consumer behavior for this case.
verification.trigger: A regression in the poller's handling of non-factory PRs would not execute in the non-factory test case. The test could continue passing because it only verifies the store consumer's refusal.

findings.title: Persisted conflict filenames bypass credential redaction
findings.detail: Conflict paths come from the repository under review and are copied into run state without credential redaction. The state is subsequently persisted by updateRun, so a registered credential embedded in a filename reaches storage even though the later PR comment redacts it.
findings.suggestion: Redact credential-bearing paths before storing them or sending them to any external sink, while retaining whatever representation is needed for local conflict resolution.
findings.failure_scenario: A changed repository contains a conflicting filename that includes a registered token; the token is stored in conflictFiles in the run state.

verification.evidence: src/git/merge.ts:79-83 returns filenames from `git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U -z`. src/pipeline/engine.ts:2243-2252 assigns `ctx.state.conflictFiles = conflicts` and immediately persists through `ctx.store.updateRun(..., ctx.state)`. src/db/store.ts:1484-1486 writes `state_json` using `values.push(json(state))` without credential redaction. The redaction at src/pipeline/engine.ts:1895 only covers the later comment text.
verification.trigger: A merge conflict involves a filename containing a registered credential. Conflict preparation stores that credential verbatim in the run's persisted conflictFiles array.

findings.title: Disable auto-merge only after validating the delivery grant and PR head
findings.detail: The new GitHub mutation runs before stored() and assertFactoryBranchPush validate that the grant still holds and that the PR is still open on the expected branch and head. A stale conflict round can therefore change auto-merge settings even when its delivery is subsequently refused.
findings.suggestion: Validate the current grant and PR identity before disabling auto-merge, and recheck state after the mutation before pushing.
findings.failure_scenario: The PR head or round grant changes while a conflict round is running and auto-merge is enabled. Delivery disables auto-merge, then rejects the stale round.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1865-1870 executes `--disable-auto` before `const { grant, run } = stored()` and `assertFactoryBranchPush(...)`. The stored-record check at :1851-1857 throws when the round record changes. src/core/delivery.ts:77-80 throws when the remote or observed PR head differs from the expected head. src/pipeline/engine.ts:2136 invokes this delivery path for successful rounds.
verification.trigger: The PR head advances, or the stored delivery grant changes after the initial delivery check, while auto-merge remains enabled. Delivery disables auto-merge and then rejects the stale round, leaving an unintended PR mutation.

findings.title: An untrusted PR comment can suppress the resolution comment
findings.detail: The idempotency check accepts the marker in any PR comment without verifying its author. A PR participant can post the predictable marker before delivery, causing the factory to treat the required resolution summary as already published.
findings.suggestion: Tie the checkpoint to a trusted factory-authored comment or another durable publication record rather than trusting arbitrary comment text.
findings.failure_scenario: A PR participant posts `<!-- limitless-conflict-round:<run-id> -->` before the round delivers; the merge is pushed but no factory resolution summary is posted.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1889 records delivery with `ctx.store.markRoundDelivered(ctx.run.id, head)`. At :1891-1894 it constructs `<!-- limitless-conflict-round:${ctx.run.id} -->`, reads comments as `{ body?: string }[]`, and skips publication whenever `comments?.some((comment) => comment.body?.includes(marker))`. No author or summary-content check authenticates the matching comment.
verification.trigger: A PR participant posts a comment containing the predictable round marker before delivery. The resolution merge is pushed, but that comment suppresses the factory's resolution summary.

findings.title: A stale saved snapshot can start a round for a draft PR
findings.detail: When a saved poller snapshot exists, trigger processing uses it without refreshing the PR. A PR can become draft or close without changing its head, so the saved observation still passes the start checks. Delivery eventually checks draft status, but the forbidden round and its model work have already started.
findings.suggestion: Refresh the PR state before starting a pending conflict trigger, and leave the trigger pending if its current state cannot be verified.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller saves an open non-draft PR, the owner converts it to draft, and a land conflict trigger is processed before the next poll. A conflict round starts from the stale snapshot.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:21 starts from the existing snapshot without fetching current PR state. src/db/store.ts:1099 also derives `seen` from `this.githubPrData(trigger.prUrl)`; :1124–1125 rejects only `seen.isDraft`. When this saved flag is false, :1144 calls `this.insertRun` and :1168 inserts the conflict round. src/pipeline/engine.ts:1864 checks `pr.isDraft` at delivery, which prevents pushing but does not prevent starting the round.
verification.trigger: An eligible open PR is saved as non-draft, then becomes draft while its approved head remains unchanged. A land conflict is processed before the next poll. The stale non-draft snapshot permits a conflict round to start, violating the draft exclusion and potentially wasting model work before delivery rejects it.

findings.title: A stale poller snapshot permanently discards a land conflict trigger
findings.detail: The request says a landing queue conflict must start a conflict round and that the trigger must survive restart. Whenever any saved PR snapshot exists, this path uses it without refreshing it. If its head predates the approved head, startConflictTrigger marks the trigger skipped as "PR head moved". The later poll updates the snapshot, but the skipped trigger is never reconsidered, so the blocked entry has no round.
findings.suggestion: Refresh the PR observation for a land trigger, or leave a trigger pending when its saved observation is older than the trigger head and retry after a fresh observation.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller last observed head A, the PR advances to B and B is approved before the next poll, then the land queue detects a conflict at B. The saved A snapshot causes the only land trigger to be skipped permanently.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:641 records a land conflict using `blocked.approvedSha`; :266 invokes the processor. src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:21 immediately uses an existing saved snapshot. src/db/store.ts:1126–1127 returns `"PR head moved"` when that snapshot's head differs from the trigger; :1139 permanently updates the trigger to `state = 'skipped'`. src/db/store.ts:1071 selects only pending triggers.
verification.trigger: The saved observation names A, but B has since been delivered and approved. A conflict while landing B creates its land trigger, which is permanently skipped against A. A later independent poller trigger may recover the work; the land trigger itself is never retried.

findings.title: Auto-merge is disabled before verifying the PR and delivery grant
findings.detail: The new conflict delivery path changes GitHub state before assertFactoryBranchPush validates that the PR is open, still has the authorized head and branch, and still belongs to the expected repository. A stale or invalid round can therefore disable auto-merge on a PR even though its push is subsequently refused. This is an unrequested side effect of a failed delivery.
findings.suggestion: Validate the current grant and PR identity before disabling auto-merge, and revalidate after the asynchronous call before pushing.
findings.failure_scenario: A conflict round finishes after the PR head has moved and auto-merge is enabled. Delivery disables auto-merge, then refuses the push because the head no longer matches the reviewed SHA.

verification.evidence: Successful rounds call deliverReviewRound at src/pipeline/engine.ts:2134–2136. Inside it, src/pipeline/engine.ts:1865–1866 executes `if (review.kind === "conflict" && pr.autoMerge) await gh(["pr", "merge", prUrl, "--disable-auto"], ctx.signal);` before `stored()` and `assertFactoryBranchPush(...)` at lines 1869–1870. The latter rejects moved heads: src/core/delivery.ts:77–80 checks `remoteHead !== at` and `pr.headSha !== at` and throws `head moved`.
verification.trigger: A conflict round passes checks while another actor updates the PR branch and enables auto-merge. Delivery disables auto-merge before detecting the changed head and refusing its push, leaving the newer head's requested auto-merge disabled.

findings.title: The PR comment does not summarize the resolution
findings.detail: The request requires "one comment summarizing the resolution." The comment reports the base SHA, conflicting file names and resulting SHA, but does not describe how the conflicting changes were reconciled. A reviewer cannot learn the resolution from the comment.
findings.suggestion: Include a concise, checked description of the actual resolution in the idempotent comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A conflict in a shared function is resolved and pushed; the PR comment names that file but gives no account of which behavior was retained or changed.

verification.evidence: After successful delivery, src/pipeline/engine.ts:1895–1899 constructs and posts only `${marker}\nMerged base ${ctx.state.reviewBaseSha}. Conflicted files: ${JSON.stringify(ctx.state.conflictFiles ?? [])}.\nConflict resolved at ${head}; approve the new head to land.` No description of the resolution's behavior is included.
verification.trigger: A conflict resolution changes a shared function's behavior and is delivered successfully. Its PR comment lists the base, files and resulting SHA but does not explain which behavior the resolution retained or changed.

findings.title: A stale poller snapshot can permanently discard a land conflict
findings.detail: The land-trigger consumer treats any saved GitHub snapshot as current and immediately marks a rejected trigger as skipped. A snapshot can predate the land queue's observation. The poller emits pr.conflicting only on entry into the conflicting state, so a later refresh need not generate another trigger.
findings.suggestion: Verify the land trigger against a fresh PR observation, or retain it pending until a sufficiently recent observation can decide eligibility.
findings.failure_scenario: The saved snapshot says the PR is draft and CONFLICTING. The PR is made ready, then the land queue detects a conflict before the next poll. The trigger is skipped as draft; the next poll still sees CONFLICTING, emits no new conflict event, and no round starts.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:265-266 blocks the entry and calls `processConflictTriggers`; :641 records `blocked.approvedSha`. src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:21 uses `if (snapshot) store.startConflictTrigger(trigger.id, snapshot, now())` without refreshing it. src/db/store.ts:1124-1125 rejects `seen.isDraft` as `"PR is draft"`; :1139 permanently sets `state = 'skipped'`. findings.title: A conflict observed while the owning run is finishing is lost
findings.detail: A poller trigger is permanently skipped unless the owning run has already reached succeeded or needs_human. A factory PR can be open and tracked while its owning run is still finishing delivery. Once skipped, the poller will not emit another pr.conflicting event while mergeability remains CONFLICTING.
findings.suggestion: Keep the trigger pending while the owning run is still delivering, and reconsider it when that run reaches a terminal state.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller observes a newly opened factory PR as CONFLICTING while its owner is still running. The trigger is marked skipped as not a factory PR; the owner subsequently succeeds, but subsequent polls see the same conflicting state and never start a round.

findings.title: A stale poller snapshot can permanently discard a land conflict trigger
findings.detail: The request says a landing-queue entry blocked by a conflict starts a conflict round and that the trigger survives restart. If any saved PR snapshot exists, processing uses it without refreshing it. When that snapshot has an older head than the land entry's approved head, startConflictTrigger marks the trigger skipped as "PR head moved". It is then no longer pending, so a later poll of the correct head cannot recover it.
findings.suggestion: Refresh the PR observation before deciding eligibility for a land trigger, or retain the trigger pending until a current observation can be checked.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller last observed head A, the PR advances to B and B is approved for landing before the next poll, and the land queue finds a base conflict. The trigger records B but is permanently skipped against the saved snapshot of A.

Only pending triggers are retried (:1071).

Its trigger is permanently skipped because the saved A differs from B. findings.title: Failed trigger lookups are not retried during normal operation
findings.detail: A lookup error leaves the trigger pending, but this catch only logs the error. The queue processes pending triggers only at startup or after another land entry blocks. If polling is disabled or does not produce another observation for the PR, a transient `gh` failure leaves the conflict unresolved indefinitely until a restart or unrelated block.
findings.suggestion: Arrange a bounded, durable retry for pending lookups during normal operation, without depending on another land failure or daemon restart.
findings.failure_scenario: A land conflict is recorded while `gh pr view` temporarily fails and there is no saved PR snapshot. The command later recovers, but no further land conflict or PR poll occurs, so the pending trigger never starts.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:639-641 persists the blocked entry and trigger: `this.finish(id, "blocked", reason)` and `this.store.recordConflictTrigger(...)`. Its immediate processing attempt only logs failure (src/land/queue.ts:266-267). src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:23-30 explicitly leaves lookup failures pending: `// Lookup failures leave the durable trigger pending for startup to try again.` followed by `lookupError ??= error; continue;`. Startup processing runs once behind `if (!this.conflictStartup)` (src/land/queue.ts:128-135). Poll observations can recover pending triggers (src/integrations/github-poller.ts:373-374), but the poller is optional: `factory.cfg.githubPoll ? startGitHubPoller(...) : () => {}` (src/integrations/index.ts:38-40).
verification.trigger: With supported `[github] poll = false`, a land conflict records a pending trigger without a saved PR snapshot. Its `gh pr view` lookup temporarily fails. After GitHub recovers, no further land failure invokes processing, so the resolution round remains unstarted until a daemon restart or another processing event.

findings.title: A stale saved PR observation can start or discard a land trigger
findings.detail: When any saved GitHub snapshot exists, the trigger consumer uses it without checking the current PR. A snapshot from before the land conflict can say the PR is draft or has a different head, causing the durable trigger to be permanently skipped; it can also say the PR is open and ready after it has become draft or closed, starting a round that should not start. Poller startup likewise consumes pending triggers from the saved snapshot before polling. The restart test supplies a current snapshot and therefore does not cover this case.
findings.suggestion: Verify land and resumed triggers against a current PR observation before consuming them, and test stale snapshots against changed draft, state and head values.
findings.failure_scenario: The last poll recorded head A; the PR advances to head B and the landing queue detects a conflict at B before the next poll. Processing compares B to the saved A and marks the only land trigger skipped, so no conflict round starts from that trigger.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:265-266 records the conflict and immediately processes triggers; :641 records the approved SHA B. src/pipeline/conflict-round.ts:16-21 reads `store.githubPrData(trigger.prUrl)` and uses any existing snapshot without a fresh lookup. src/db/store.ts:1126-1127 rejects saved head A against trigger head B as `"PR head moved"`; :1139 writes `state = 'skipped'`, excluding it from the pending-only retry query at :1071.
verification.trigger: An approved PR advances from saved head A to B before polling refreshes the snapshot. The land queue encounters a conflict at B, but processing permanently discards that land trigger against A, so no round starts from it. Polling may later recover through a separate trigger for B; it never retries the discarded land trigger.

findings.detail: The non-factory branch manually inserts and consumes a trigger instead of running the poller. It verifies the store's refusal but cannot catch a regression in how polling handles a conflicting non-factory PR, despite the test name and the requested poller acceptance case.

findings.title: Missing draft state is treated as permission to proceed
findings.detail: The PR lookup converts a missing or invalid `isDraft` field to false. Conflict delivery therefore proceeds when GitHub's response does not establish that the PR is ready for review. The poller admission path likewise treats an absent `isDraft` as false. This fails open at a condition the request explicitly requires.

findings.detail: The new delivery path changes the PR's auto-merge setting before checking that the PR is still open, belongs to the expected repository and branch, and remains at the reviewed head. A stale round can therefore mutate a PR even though the subsequent delivery guard rejects it.
findings.suggestion: Validate the stored grant and current PR identity before disabling auto-merge, then revalidate after the awaited mutation and before pushing.

candidates.title: Auto-merge is disabled before validating the current PR head
candidates.detail: The new delivery path changes the PR's auto-merge setting before checking that the PR is still open, belongs to the expected repository and branch, and remains at the reviewed head. A stale round can therefore mutate a PR even though the subsequent delivery guard rejects it.

candidates.failure_scenario: The PR head changes while a conflict round runs and a user enables auto-merge for the new head. The stale round disables auto-merge, then fails its head check without pushing.

candidates.title: The PR comment does not summarize the resolution
candidates.detail: The request requires that "The PR gets one comment summarizing the resolution." The comment reports the base SHA and conflicted file names, but contains no account of how the conflicting changes were reconciled. A reader cannot assess the resolution from it.
candidates.suggestion: Include a concise, reviewed summary of the actual resolution in the comment, with the existing publication and redaction checks.
candidates.failure_scenario: A conflict in a file is resolved by combining two behavioral changes; the resulting comment names the file and commit but does not explain the combined behavior.

findings.title: Cached first attempts lose the workspace needed by retries after restart
findings.detail: A completed first attempt is reused from state after restart, but the resumed stage cleans the checkout before reaching this line. A pending or newly started retry therefore runs without the build output or other files produced by that first attempt. Previously, a resumed gate stage reran the first attempt and recreated those files before retrying.
findings.suggestion: Preserve the workspace required by a pending retry, or replay the local first attempt before performing the retry after restart.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate setup creates an ignored build directory, a check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts before or during its retry. On resume, checkoutCommitted removes the directory, the cached initial result is reused, and the retry fails because its build output is missing.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1157-1159 calls `await checkoutCommitted(...)` before `runGateExecution(..., "initial", ...)`. src/git/repos.ts:476 runs `git clean -ffdxq`. src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:23 returns `if (results[purpose]) return results[purpose]`, skipping initial setup. src/pipeline/engine.ts:1192-1193 then invokes the regression retry; src/gates/run.ts:280 supplies `runner({ ...cfg, setup: [], checks: selected })`.
verification.trigger: Setup creates ignored build output; an eligible transient regression enters a retry, and the daemon restarts before its result is checkpointed. Resume deletes the output, reuses the initial result without setup, and reruns the check without its required artifacts, producing a false blocking failure.

findings.title: Executor events are never consumed
findings.detail: The shared execution path awaits only `result` and never reads `execution.events`. Gate reporting and landing logs currently work only because the local executor calls hooks directly; an executor implementing the advertised interface has no way to deliver its streamed check events to those consumers.
findings.suggestion: Consume the event stream in the shared execution path and forward events to the appropriate gate and landing reporting hooks, coordinating stream completion and errors with the result.

The retry therefore runs without files created by the initial attempt, despite the existing requirement that retries see the same build output. Prepare likewise discards changes before resuming its baseline retry.
findings.suggestion: Preserve or reconstruct the first attempt's required workspace state before resuming a local retry, with restart coverage for checks that depend on generated files.
findings.failure_scenario: A setup or initial check creates an untracked build artifact, a later check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts during its retry. The resumed retry cannot find the artifact and produces a different verdict.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1157 unconditionally calls `await checkoutCommitted(cwd, undefined, Boolean(ctx.state.implementerIssue))` before retrieving the initial result. src/git/repos.ts:476 executes `["git", "clean", "-ffdxq"]`, deleting untracked and ignored build output. On resume, src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:23 returns the persisted initial result via `if (results[purpose]) return results[purpose]`, so its setup and successful checks do not recreate those files. The engine then invokes the pending `"regression-retry"` at src/pipeline/engine.ts:1192-1193. Its request omits setup and preceding checks: src/gates/run.ts:280 uses `runner({ ...cfg, setup: [], checks: selected })`. findings.title: A checkpoint failure leaves started work uncancelled
findings.detail: The executor starts work before persisting its handle, but if persistence rejects, execution exits without attaching or cancelling. An executor whose start actually launches work can continue indefinitely without a durable handle, and a subsequent attempt can start duplicate work.
findings.suggestion: On persistence failure, attach to the returned handle and cancel the execution before propagating the failure, while preserving the original error.

Cancellation is installed only afterward at :141–144: `cancellation ??= execution.cancel()`. A persistence rejection therefore exits before any cleanup is installed. The shipped local executor starts actual checks in attach (:78), so it does not leave a running suite in this case.

findings.title: Redacting the local handle changes the request replayed after restart
findings.detail: The local handle contains the gate request, including commands and paths, but the persisted copy is transformed by `redactGateData`. On restart, local attach executes that transformed request rather than the trusted gate configuration. Credential redaction or terminal-control stripping can change a valid command or path, so the resumed run can check different behavior or fail unexpectedly.
findings.suggestion: Keep sensitive request data out of the persisted handle and reconstruct the local request from trusted run state when reattaching, without transforming executable input.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured gate command contains a registered credential or a terminal control character; after a restart, the local executor runs the redacted or stripped command.

Attachment executes the sanitized command instead of the original, potentially changing its result. The command content is an unusual prerequisite.

candidates.detail: A completed first attempt is reused from state after restart, but the resumed stage cleans the checkout before reaching this line. A pending or newly started retry therefore runs without the build output or other files produced by that first attempt. Previously, a resumed gate stage reran the first attempt and recreated those files before retrying.

candidates.title: Executor events are never consumed
candidates.detail: The shared execution path awaits only `result` and never reads `execution.events`. Gate reporting and landing logs currently work only because the local executor calls hooks directly; an executor implementing the advertised interface has no way to deliver its streamed check events to those consumers.
candidates.suggestion: Consume the event stream in the shared execution path and forward events to the appropriate gate and landing reporting hooks, coordinating stream completion and errors with the result.
candidates.failure_scenario: An injected executor yields check events and returns a valid GateRun. The stage verdict is computed, but no per-check pipeline events or landing check output are recorded.

candidates.title: Restarting a retry removes the first attempt's build output
candidates.detail: A resumed gates stage cleans the checkout before retrieving its saved initial result and attaching to the pending retry. The retry therefore runs without files created by the initial attempt, despite the existing requirement that retries see the same build output. Prepare likewise discards changes before resuming its baseline retry.
candidates.suggestion: Preserve or reconstruct the first attempt's required workspace state before resuming a local retry, with restart coverage for checks that depend on generated files.
candidates.failure_scenario: A setup or initial check creates an untracked build artifact, a later check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts during its retry. The resumed retry cannot find the artifact and produces a different verdict.

candidates.title: A checkpoint failure leaves started work uncancelled
candidates.detail: The executor starts work before persisting its handle, but if persistence rejects, execution exits without attaching or cancelling. An executor whose start actually launches work can continue indefinitely without a durable handle, and a subsequent attempt can start duplicate work.
candidates.suggestion: On persistence failure, attach to the returned handle and cancel the execution before propagating the failure, while preserving the original error.
candidates.failure_scenario: A remote executor starts a gate suite and the state save fails because the database write fails; the run fails while the untracked suite continues.

candidates.title: Redacting the local handle changes the request replayed after restart
candidates.detail: The local handle contains the gate request, including commands and paths, but the persisted copy is transformed by `redactGateData`. On restart, local attach executes that transformed request rather than the trusted gate configuration. Credential redaction or terminal-control stripping can change a valid command or path, so the resumed run can check different behavior or fail unexpectedly.
candidates.suggestion: Keep sensitive request data out of the persisted handle and reconstruct the local request from trusted run state when reattaching, without transforming executable input.
candidates.failure_scenario: A configured gate command contains a registered credential or a terminal control character; after a restart, the local executor runs the redacted or stripped command.

candidates.title: Executor event streams are never consumed
candidates.detail: The shared execution path awaits only the result and never reads `execution.events`. The local executor invokes hooks directly, masking the issue, but an injected executor that reports progress and check results through the interface loses those events; landing logs and pipeline gate events are absent.
candidates.suggestion: Consume the event stream while awaiting the result and route events to the appropriate hooks, propagating stream failures according to the executor contract.
candidates.failure_scenario: An executor yields check events and returns a GateRun without invoking local hooks. The gate completes but its check events and landing log output are silently missing.

candidates.title: Persisting a sanitized local request can change the command replayed after restart
candidates.detail: The local handle contains the complete request, but redactGateData transforms every string before the handle is stored. A restart attaches using that transformed request, so a gate command or working directory containing a registered credential or terminal control character can differ from the original. The initial attachment uses the unsanitized handle, making behavior depend on whether the daemon restarted.
candidates.suggestion: Persist a replayable request without storing secrets, for example by reconstructing the local request from trusted run state on resume, and keep redaction at the storage boundary.
candidates.failure_scenario: A base gate command contains a string registered for credential redaction. The daemon stops after saving the handle; on resume, local attachment executes the command with that string replaced by the redaction marker.

candidates.title: Restart tests do not exercise replay of a persisted local request
candidates.detail: The restart cases use a fake LAN executor whose handle has no request, while the local replay test serializes a handle directly without passing it through the persistence redaction path. Consequently they cannot catch a local request being changed before restart.
candidates.suggestion: Add a restart test using the local executor and a request containing a value transformed by redaction, then verify the resumed check executes the original command.
candidates.failure_scenario: A persisted local handle has a gate command altered by redaction; all current restart and local-attachment tests still pass.

candidates.title: Legacy resume test cannot distinguish local selection from injected selection
candidates.detail: The legacy-state test resumes with no injected executor, so local is the only available choice. It does not test the stated compatibility rule when another executor is selected. The selection code uses the injected executor whenever there is no stored handle.
candidates.suggestion: Resume a pre-change run with a non-local fake executor configured and assert that the legacy gate runs locally without starting the fake.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run created before handles existed resumes with a non-local executor injected and starts that executor instead of local; the current test still passes.

candidates.title: Redacting the local handle changes the command replayed after restart
candidates.detail: The local handle embeds the gate request, including its working directory and base-configured commands. Redacting the entire handle before persistence changes any command or path containing a registered credential and strips terminal control sequences. On restart, `localExecutor.attach` executes that altered request rather than the original trusted gate configuration. A resumed gate can therefore test different conditions and report a pass for a check that would have failed.
candidates.suggestion: Persist only the local execution identity and reconstruct its request from the trusted base configuration and current run context on resume, or otherwise preserve execution semantics without storing secret-bearing values.
candidates.failure_scenario: A base gate command compares a value against a registered credential. The daemon restarts while that gate is pending; the persisted command contains the redaction marker instead of the original value, so the replay evaluates a different condition and can pass incorrectly.

candidates.title: Resumed retries reuse results after their build output has been removed
candidates.detail: The request says regression retries and baseline retries do not change, and the surrounding code requires retries to see the first attempt's build output. After a restart during a retry, this returns the saved initial result without rerunning the initial gate, while prepare has already called discardChanges and the gates stage has called checkoutCommitted. A local retry therefore runs in a cleaned checkout without the files produced by its initial attempt, potentially changing a pass into a failure or vice versa.
candidates.suggestion: Restore the first attempt's required workspace state on local resume, or rerun the initial local execution before retrying while preserving the stored handle semantics for executors that can reattach.
candidates.failure_scenario: A setup command generates an untracked build artifact, an initial check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts during its retry. On resume the artifact is cleaned, the saved initial result is reused, and the retry fails because the artifact is missing.

candidates.title: Landing checks discard the execution handle
candidates.detail: The request requires that the caller persist the handle before awaiting the execution and that landing queue checks use the executor. This call supplies neither a stored handle nor a persistence callback, so executeGate uses its no-op default. A restart during landing checks starts another execution instead of attaching to the existing one, leaving remote work duplicated and its result unobserved.
candidates.suggestion: Persist the landing execution handle in durable queue state before attaching, and restore it when resuming the checks.
candidates.failure_scenario: A landing check is running on an executor whose work survives daemon restart. The daemon restarts before the result arrives; the queue starts a second execution because the first handle was never stored.

candidates.title: Executor events are never consumed
candidates.detail: The requested Execution exposes events and the local executor is to preserve gate events. executeGate awaits only result and never reads execution.events; existing progress and landing logs work only because the local implementation calls injected hooks directly. Any executor implementing the advertised interface emits events that are silently discarded, and landing logs contain no command output.
candidates.suggestion: Consume the execution event stream in the shared path and translate its events into the existing hooks, including setup and status events as needed.

findings.suggestion: For local work, restore the pre-change resume behavior by re-running the initial suite before retrying, or otherwise restore the initial suite’s required build state.
findings.failure_scenario: A setup command creates an untracked build artifact, a check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts during its retry. On resume the persisted initial result is reused after the worktree is cleaned; the retry fails because the artifact is missing.

findings.title: Repeated credential matches make patch filtering quadratic
findings.detail: Every occurrence scans every line range synchronously before paging. An untrusted large patch with many occurrences of a registered multiline value can therefore block the daemon's event loop for a prolonged period, and each page request repeats the work. A targeted invocation of the extracted function took 893 ms for 50,000 lines and 3,514 ms for 100,000 lines, consistent with quadratic growth.
findings.suggestion: Map match offsets to affected ranges using an ordered cursor or binary search, so work grows with the patch size and number of matching lines.
findings.failure_scenario: A changed file contains hundreds of thousands of repetitions of a two-line registered credential; requesting its change view monopolizes the daemon event loop for minutes.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/mcp-change.ts:80–84 calls `withhold(start, start + literal.length)` for every occurrence; lines 73–76 implement each call with `for (const range of ranges)`. Lines 617–629 filter the complete Git patch before paging at line 693. src/util/proc.ts:603 permits `SH_OUTPUT_LIMIT = 50_000_000`. Targeted probes measured 20,000 repetitions at 629 ms and 40,000 at 2,690 ms, consistent with quadratic growth.
verification.trigger: A change request selects an added file containing hundreds of thousands of repetitions of a registered two-line credential, within the Git output limit. The adjacent-pair check does not cover a credential that starts in the middle of a patch line, so a deleted or added line containing that credential fragment remains visible.
findings.suggestion: Map clipped matches to every affected patch line, including additions and deletions, and cover credentials embedded within surrounding line text.

findings.title: Keep reviewer execution time out of failed-trial preparation timing
findings.detail: The catch path recomputes preparationMs whenever roundsUsed is absent. Review trials never set roundsUsed, so an exception after the reviewer starts overwrites the already-recorded preparation duration with elapsed time including the reviewer invocation. The reported preparation and trial times are no longer separate for that failure.
findings.suggestion: Record the preparation duration once, and only calculate it in the catch path if preparation did not finish.
findings.failure_scenario: A review invocation runs for several minutes and then throws, for example on an origin-exclusion failure. Its preparationMs includes those minutes even though setup had already completed.

verification.evidence: src/evals/runner.ts:689–690 records completed preparation: `const preparationMs = Date.now() - preparationStarted; ... trial.details.preparationMs = preparationMs`. However, src/evals/runner.ts:1101–1104 sets `roundsUsed` only inside `if ("hidden" in item)` (implementation trials). For review trials, the outer catch at src/evals/runner.ts:1201–1202 therefore overwrites the recorded value with `preparationMs: Date.now() - preparationStarted`. An origin failure reaches this catch through `if (originFailure) throw originFailure` at src/evals/runner.ts:1073.
verification.trigger: A review trial finishes setup, spends time waiting or reviewing, then encounters an exception that reaches the outer catch, such as an origin-exclusion failure during a later panel invocation. Its preparationMs includes the elapsed reviewer execution and waiting time.

findings.title: Setup variants can make routing policy select the wrong trial arm
findings.detail: The request says production is unchanged and gives the setup-enabled standard prompt a separate cache identity. That identity also makes a setup-enabled system and an otherwise identical system valid in the same eval. Policy selection assumes at most one standard system per target, however, and generatePolicy takes only the first summary. It therefore silently ignores one arm, with the selected evidence depending on system ordering.
findings.suggestion: Define which standard arm is eligible for routing policy and update policy selection to handle both configurations explicitly.
findings.failure_scenario: An eval contains standard systems for the same target with and without setup. Both pass configuration validation, but policy generation uses only the first system's results even if the other arm has different outcomes.

findings.failure_scenario: Setup completes in one second and the reviewer throws after several minutes; the failed trial records those minutes as preparation time.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the initial TLS connection
findings.detail: The initial connection accepts any certificate, and the displayed code is supplied by that connection. A man-in-the-middle can relay the pairing request to the real coordinator, return its code and secret to the worker, and present its own certificate. The owner sees the same code on both sides and approves it; the attacker then observes the claim and issued token. Pinning the attacker's certificate on subsequent requests does not prevent this. The submitted worker certificate fingerprint is never authenticated or used to bind the exchange.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to both endpoints' certificate fingerprints and the pairing exchange, so relaying through a different TLS certificate changes the code or causes verification to fail.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes

findings.title: Interrupted certificate creation permanently blocks restart
findings.detail: Certificate generation creates the final key path before invoking OpenSSL. If generation fails, times out, or the process stops before both files are complete, the next start either rejects the incomplete pair or tries to parse invalid material. No cleanup or recovery occurs, so the worker listener or pairing command continues to fail on every subsequent start.

findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is stopped after creating the empty key file but before OpenSSL creates the certificate; every later listener start throws `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

verification.evidence: src/cli/daemon.ts:30 awaits startWorkerListener before starting integrations or HTTP; src/server/workers.ts:15-16: `if (!listen) return undefined; const tls = await certificate(join(paths.home, "worker-tls"));`. src/workers/tls.ts:18 creates `writeFileSync(keyPath, "", { flag: "wx", mode: 0o600 })` before awaiting OpenSSL. findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
findings.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker pins the certificate observed on that connection. The displayed code comes from the coordinator but is not bound to that certificate or to an authenticated exchange. An intermediary can relay the pairing request and code unchanged, obtain the pairing secret and issued token, and leave the worker pinned to the intermediary's certificate even though the owner compared matching codes.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate and pairing exchange so a relaying intermediary cannot obtain a usable token or substitute its certificate.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, forwards the request to the real coordinator, and relays its code. The owner approves the matching code; the attacker claims the token and the worker pins the attacker's certificate.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23-27 makes the initial request without a pin; src/workers/tls.ts:103 sets `rejectUnauthorized: false`. src/workers/client.ts:33 prints the server-supplied code and :47 saves `first.fingerprint`. src/db/workers.ts:85-89 looks up `pairing_secret_hash` and returns the approved token without binding the claim to a TLS peer certificate.

findings.title: Permanent TLS and configuration errors are retried silently forever
findings.detail: The heartbeat loop catches every request exception and retries without a deadline or diagnostic. This includes a changed coordinator fingerprint and malformed coordinator URL, neither of which can be repaired by retrying. The worker remains running but never sends another heartbeat, and the owner receives no explanation.

findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing. Every heartbeat fails fingerprint validation, but the worker silently retries indefinitely instead of reporting that it must be paired again.

verification.evidence: src/cli/main.ts:372 starts `runWorker(values.coordinator, cfg, sha, controller.signal)`. src/workers/tls.ts:114-115 rejects a changed certificate with `Coordinator certificate fingerprint changed`. src/workers/client.ts:99-102 catches every request exception and returns `undefined`; :103-107 retries indefinitely with a delay capped at 10 seconds, without logging the exception.
verification.trigger: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing, or the worker receives an invalid coordinator origin. Every heartbeat throws a permanent error, but the worker remains running and silently retries forever instead of exposing the configuration or re-pairing problem.

findings.title: Existing TLS key loses sandbox protection when the listener is disabled
findings.detail: The TLS key is registered with the sandbox deny list only when the listener starts. After a listener has created the key, restarting the daemon with workers.listen unset skips registration even though the key remains on disk. Agent sandboxes that can read that data directory can then read the coordinator's private key, contrary to the requirement that it be denied in every agent sandbox.
findings.suggestion: Register protection for existing worker TLS material independently of whether the listener is enabled, and retain it for the daemon lifetime.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the listener once, then disable it and restart the daemon with the data directory outside the default home deny paths. A subsequent agent can read worker-tls/key.pem.

verification.evidence: src/cli/daemon.ts:30-31 calls `startWorkerListener(...)` before mounting integrations. src/server/workers.ts:15-16 returns at `if (!listen) return undefined;` before `certificate(join(paths.home, "worker-tls"))`. The skipped function registers protection at src/workers/tls.ts:14: `const release = protectPrivateFile(keyPath);`. Registration is process-local: src/util/private-reads.ts:4 declares `const privatePaths = new Map<string, number>();`. Editors otherwise permit reads: src/harness/codex.ts:302 sets `["/", "read"]`, with exceptions from `denyRead` at line 305.
verification.trigger: Enable workers to create the retained TLS key, disable the listener, then restart with the data directory outside other denied paths. The new process never registers the key's read denial, so a subsequent editor agent can read the private key despite mode 0600 because it runs as the same user.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation prevents future startup
findings.detail: Certificate generation creates the final key path before running openssl, but its error path leaves partial files behind. A timeout, failed openssl invocation, or interruption can therefore leave only the empty key or other incomplete material. Every later start rejects the incomplete material, requiring manual cleanup.
findings.suggestion: Generate both files in temporary paths and publish them only after successful generation, cleaning up partial temporary files on failure.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is interrupted after creating key.pem but before openssl writes cert.pem. Subsequent starts fail with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:15-16 calls `certificate(join(paths.home, "worker-tls"))` whenever the listener is configured. src/workers/tls.ts:18 creates the empty key before OpenSSL runs at lines 19-39. Line 17 rejects an existing key without a certificate with `throw new Error("Incomplete worker TLS material")`. Lines 45-47 release protection and rethrow without deleting the partial material. src/cli/daemon.ts:30,44-46 propagates this failure out of daemon startup.
verification.trigger: With workers.listen enabled, stopping the daemon during initial certificate generation after key.pem creation and before cert.pem creation causes all subsequent daemon startups to fail pending manual repair. The interruption must hit the narrow initial-generation window.

findings.title: Credential read protection ends with the pairing process
findings.detail: The worker token and coordinator fingerprint are registered in an in-memory deny list only while `pairWorker` or `runWorker` holds them. Pairing releases both registrations before exiting, and a separately running daemon has its own deny list. Likewise, an existing coordinator TLS key is not registered when the listener is disabled. An agent sandbox created by that daemon therefore does not receive these paths as private-file denies.
findings.suggestion: Register persisted worker credential and TLS-key paths in every process that constructs agent sandbox policies, independently of whether pairing, the worker loop or the listener is currently running.
findings.failure_scenario: Pair a worker, exit the pairing command, and run an agent through a separate daemon using the same data directory: that daemon's private-file deny list does not contain the stored worker token or coordinator fingerprint.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:47-48 writes the fingerprint and token, then :55-57 releases their protection. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 uses a process-local registry. src/cli/daemon.ts:15-30 does not register existing worker credentials. src/harness/read-policy.ts:150-190 has no built-in worker-directory deny. src/harness/codex.ts:292 describes editor reads as `Everything readable`; its deny list comes from `writeRoots(..., spec.denyRead)` at :300.
verification.trigger: After pairing exits, a separate factory daemon using the same data directory starts an editor agent. The stored worker files are absent from its deny list, so the same-user editor can read the token and pinned fingerprint even with the default data-directory placement.

findings.title: Privacy probe masks the cross-process credential protection gap
findings.detail: The real-Seatbelt test creates the TLS material and registers both worker files in the same process that starts the gate, retaining all registrations throughout the probe. It consequently passes even if a daemon started separately after pairing has no credential paths in its in-memory deny list.
findings.suggestion: Add a real-Seatbelt probe that persists credentials, releases the pairing registrations, and launches the gate from an independently initialized daemon or process; cover an existing TLS key with the listener disabled as well.
findings.failure_scenario: The current implementation releases the registrations after pairing, yet this test retains them and reports all three files denied.

verification.evidence: test/workers.test.ts:266 creates live registrations with `files.slice(1).map((p) => privateFile(p, "synthetic-private-file"))`, calls `runLocalGates` at :274, and releases registrations only at :295–296. Actual pairing releases them before returning: src/workers/client.ts:55–57: `finally { cert.release(); for (const release of held) release(); }`. Registrations are process-local: src/util/private-reads.ts:4: `const privatePaths = new Map<string, number>();`, and :22 deletes released entries. Sandbox policy consumes that map at src/harness/read-policy.ts:190: `const denyRead = policySpellings([...credentials, ...privateReadPaths()], true, fs);`. runWorker re-registers token and fingerprint only in its own process (src/workers/client.ts:87–88).

Pairing's registrations have been released and cannot populate the daemon's process-local deny list. The privacy probe retains all registrations in the gate-running process, so it passes without testing this lifecycle or cross-process protection gap.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
findings.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the displayed code is supplied by that untrusted connection. An active intermediary can forward the request to the real coordinator, relay its code to the worker, and retain the returned pairing secret. The owner and worker see matching codes, but the intermediary can claim the approved token and the worker pins the intermediary's certificate.
findings.suggestion: Bind the human-compared code to both the coordinator certificate fingerprint and the pairing exchange, so relaying a coordinator response through a different TLS certificate changes the code.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies `/worker/pair` to the coordinator, and relays the real code. After the owner approves it, the attacker claims the worker token.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23-28 sends the initial pairing request with only `{ signal }`; src/workers/tls.ts:100-104 uses `rejectUnauthorized: false`. Subsequent claims trust `{ pin: first.fingerprint }` (client.ts:39). src/db/workers.ts:61 returns `{ code, secret, expiresAt }`, and :83-89 issues the approved token solely from `pairing_secret_hash`, without verifying the worker certificate.
verification.trigger: An active network attacker terminates the initial TLS connection, forwards pairing to the real coordinator, and relays its code. Owner approval succeeds even when codes are compared. The attacker knows the pairing secret and can claim the worker token.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
findings.detail: `protectPrivateFile` maintains an in-memory registry. Pairing releases its registrations before exiting, and `runWorker` registers the files only in the worker process. A separately running daemon on the same machine does not receive those registrations when it constructs Claude or Codex sandbox policies, so its agents can read the persistent worker token and coordinator fingerprint. Mode 0600 does not protect them from agents running as the same user.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every daemon process that launches agents, including when the worker is stopped, and cover separate-process sandbox behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine runs both a worker and a factory daemon under the same user. An agent launched by the daemon reads `<data>/worker/token` and impersonates that worker.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:87-88 protects token and pin through `privateFile(...)`; src/workers/tls.ts:54 calls `protectPrivateFile(path)`. That registry is process-local: src/util/private-reads.ts:4 declares `const privatePaths = new Map<string, number>()`. Daemon editor policy consumes its own registry (src/harness/read-policy.ts:190). Codex editors otherwise allow reads from `/` (src/harness/codex.ts:301-305). The default data directory is `join(homedir(), ".limitless")` (src/config.ts:160), outside the built-in credential directories.
verification.trigger: A paired worker and a separate factory daemon run as the same user with default configuration. A daemon-launched editor can read ~/.limitless/worker/token because the worker process's protection registry does not reach the daemon, allowing worker impersonation.

findings.title: Disabling the listener leaves its existing TLS key unprotected from agents
findings.detail: The TLS key is added to the process-local private-read registry only when the listener is enabled. After an owner removes `workers.listen` and restarts the daemon, the existing key remains on disk but is no longer included in agent sandbox deny paths. An agent running as the same user can read it, compromising the certificate trusted by already paired workers if the listener is later re-enabled.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent TLS key path independently of whether the listener is currently enabled, or securely remove and rotate the material when disabling it.
findings.failure_scenario: A coordinator previously enabled workers, then starts with the listener disabled. A tool-enabled agent reads `<data>/worker-tls/key.pem` before the listener is enabled again.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:15: `if (!listen) return undefined;` skips line 16's `certificate(join(paths.home, "worker-tls"))`, which alone registers the key with `protectPrivateFile(keyPath)` at src/workers/tls.ts:14. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 derives denials from `credentials` and `privateReadPaths()`; its credential list at lines 150-161 does not include the default `.limitless` data directory. src/harness/codex.ts:302 permits `["/", "read"]` unless explicitly denied.
verification.trigger: After previously enabling workers, restart with the listener disabled and launch a tool-enabled editor. Unless a separate configured denial covers the data directory, the retained coordinator TLS private key is readable by the agent.

findings.title: Store untrusted heartbeat fields only after redaction
findings.detail: Heartbeat capabilities are serialized directly into SQLite. Several worker-controlled strings can contain coordinator credentials or private strings, but sanitization occurs only when listing workers. This leaves the unredacted values in persistent storage even though the trust-boundary rules require redaction before storage.
findings.suggestion: Redact and apply private-string policy to worker-supplied capability fields before persisting them, while preserving the fields needed for version matching.
findings.failure_scenario: A paired worker sends a coordinator credential or private string in `osVersion`; the value is written verbatim to the workers table.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:43–46 parses the authenticated request with `Heartbeat.parse(await req.json())` and calls `workers.heartbeat(current, capabilities)`. src/workers/protocol.ts:8 permits `osVersion: z.string().max(128)` without redaction. src/db/workers.ts:143–144 executes `UPDATE workers SET last_heartbeat_at=?,capabilities=? WHERE name=? AND state='approved'` with `.run(this.now(), JSON.stringify(c), w.name)`. Although `list()` applies `this.sanitize(...)` at src/db/workers.ts:124, that happens after the raw capabilities have been persisted.
verification.trigger: With the worker listener enabled, an approved worker posts a valid heartbeat whose osVersion contains a registered coordinator credential or private string of at most 128 characters. The coordinator stores it verbatim in workers.capabilities; later response sanitization does not remove the persisted disclosure.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied in the daemon's agent sandboxes
findings.detail: The request requires the worker token and coordinator fingerprint to be read-denied to gates. The deny registry is process-local, but pairing and the worker loop run as separate CLI processes from the daemon. Their registrations are also released when those commands exit. A daemon on the same machine therefore does not add these files to its agent sandbox deny lists; mode 0600 does not protect them from agents running as the same user.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every daemon process that can launch agents and gates, including when the worker command is not running.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine is both a paired worker and a coordinator. An agent launched by its daemon reads the token under the worker data directory and uses it to impersonate the worker.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:47-48 registers private files, then :55-57 releases those registrations on pairing completion. Running the worker registers them only in its own process (:87-88). src/util/private-reads.ts:4 stores registrations in a module-local Map. src/cli/daemon.ts:29 starts the coordinator listener but does not register existing worker credentials; src/harness/codex.ts:302 grants `/` read access except explicit denies.
verification.trigger: A coordinator machine is also paired as a worker. Its separate daemon does not deny the worker token to editing agents, so an agent can read it and impersonate the worker. This is the same underlying defect as C11.

findings.title: Disabling the listener removes protection for an existing TLS key
findings.detail: The request says the TLS key is read-denied in every agent sandbox. When the listener is disabled, startup returns before registering the previously generated key with the process-local deny registry. The key remains on disk, and editor sandboxes do not otherwise deny the worker TLS directory.
findings.suggestion: Register the existing key path for the daemon lifetime independently of whether the listener is enabled.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner disables workers after having enabled them, then starts a run. An editor agent can read the retained coordinator TLS private key.

verification.evidence: src/cli/daemon.ts:30-31 starts the worker listener before integrations, but src/server/workers.ts:15 returns immediately when it is disabled. Consequently src/workers/tls.ts:14's `protectPrivateFile(keyPath)` never executes. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 stores registrations only in a process-local Map. src/harness/codex.ts:302-305 grants root read access and removes access only for `denyRead` entries.
verification.trigger: An owner enables workers once, disables them, restarts the daemon, and starts a run. With no independent denial covering the key, the editor's sandbox permits reading the retained coordinator TLS private key.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation permanently blocks listener startup
findings.detail: The key file is created before openssl runs, but a failed or interrupted generation leaves it behind. The next start sees incomplete TLS material and throws instead of generating a certificate, so a transient failure prevents the daemon from starting whenever the worker listener is configured.

findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is stopped or openssl fails after the empty key file is created but before the certificate is written; every subsequent daemon start fails with "Incomplete worker TLS material".

candidates.suggestion: Bind the human-compared code to both the coordinator certificate fingerprint and the pairing exchange, so relaying a coordinator response through a different TLS certificate changes the code.
candidates.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies `/worker/pair` to the coordinator, and relays the real code. After the owner approves it, the attacker claims the worker token.

candidates.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
candidates.detail: `protectPrivateFile` maintains an in-memory registry. Pairing releases its registrations before exiting, and `runWorker` registers the files only in the worker process. A separately running daemon on the same machine does not receive those registrations when it constructs Claude or Codex sandbox policies, so its agents can read the persistent worker token and coordinator fingerprint. Mode 0600 does not protect them from agents running as the same user.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every daemon process that launches agents, including when the worker is stopped, and cover separate-process sandbox behavior.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine runs both a worker and a factory daemon under the same user. An agent launched by the daemon reads `<data>/worker/token` and impersonates that worker.

candidates.title: Disabling the listener leaves its existing TLS key unprotected from agents
candidates.detail: The TLS key is added to the process-local private-read registry only when the listener is enabled. After an owner removes `workers.listen` and restarts the daemon, the existing key remains on disk but is no longer included in agent sandbox deny paths. An agent running as the same user can read it, compromising the certificate trusted by already paired workers if the listener is later re-enabled.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persistent TLS key path independently of whether the listener is currently enabled, or securely remove and rotate the material when disabling it.
candidates.failure_scenario: A coordinator previously enabled workers, then starts with the listener disabled. A tool-enabled agent reads `<data>/worker-tls/key.pem` before the listener is enabled again.

candidates.title: Store untrusted heartbeat fields only after redaction
candidates.detail: Heartbeat capabilities are serialized directly into SQLite. Several worker-controlled strings can contain coordinator credentials or private strings, but sanitization occurs only when listing workers. This leaves the unredacted values in persistent storage even though the trust-boundary rules require redaction before storage.
candidates.suggestion: Redact and apply private-string policy to worker-supplied capability fields before persisting them, while preserving the fields needed for version matching.
candidates.failure_scenario: A paired worker sends a coordinator credential or private string in `osVersion`; the value is written verbatim to the workers table.

candidates.title: Worker credentials are not denied in the daemon's agent sandboxes
candidates.detail: The request requires the worker token and coordinator fingerprint to be read-denied to gates. The deny registry is process-local, but pairing and the worker loop run as separate CLI processes from the daemon. Their registrations are also released when those commands exit. A daemon on the same machine therefore does not add these files to its agent sandbox deny lists; mode 0600 does not protect them from agents running as the same user.
candidates.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every daemon process that can launch agents and gates, including when the worker command is not running.
candidates.failure_scenario: A machine is both a paired worker and a coordinator. An agent launched by its daemon reads the token under the worker data directory and uses it to impersonate the worker.

candidates.title: Disabling the listener removes protection for an existing TLS key
candidates.detail: The request says the TLS key is read-denied in every agent sandbox. When the listener is disabled, startup returns before registering the previously generated key with the process-local deny registry. The key remains on disk, and editor sandboxes do not otherwise deny the worker TLS directory.
candidates.suggestion: Register the existing key path for the daemon lifetime independently of whether the listener is enabled.
candidates.failure_scenario: An owner disables workers after having enabled them, then starts a run. An editor agent can read the retained coordinator TLS private key.

candidates.title: Interrupted certificate generation permanently blocks listener startup
candidates.detail: The key file is created before openssl runs, but a failed or interrupted generation leaves it behind. The next start sees incomplete TLS material and throws instead of generating a certificate, so a transient failure prevents the daemon from starting whenever the worker listener is configured.
candidates.suggestion: Generate the certificate and key in temporary files and publish them together, cleaning up incomplete generation safely.
candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon is stopped or openssl fails after the empty key file is created but before the certificate is written; every subsequent daemon start fails with "Incomplete worker TLS material".

candidates.title: A changed pinned certificate is retried indefinitely without an explanation
candidates.detail: The request requires the coordinator fingerprint to be pinned. Although the transport detects a mismatch, the heartbeat loop catches that error along with transient connection failures and retries forever. The operator receives no indication that the certificate changed and that intervention is required.
candidates.suggestion: Surface fingerprint mismatch as a terminal error while retaining retries for transient transport failures.
candidates.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing. The worker remains running but never sends another heartbeat and never reports the pin mismatch.

findings.title: The coordinator TLS key is unprotected when the listener is disabled
