candidates.detail: The startup check accepts any regular file with the owner-read bit set and no group or world permission bits. It does not check the file's owner, and it accepts modes such as 0700 and 0400 despite requiring mode 0600. A file owned by another user can therefore pass the metadata check even when the daemon cannot read it, deferring failure until a configured repository first needs a token.
candidates.suggestion: Check the file owner and enforce the requested mode and readability during configuration loading, with a clear startup error.
candidates.failure_scenario: A key file owned by another user has mode 0600. Its metadata passes this check, but the daemon cannot read it and App-authenticated GitHub calls fail later.

candidates.title: Verify the key is readable by the factory at startup
candidates.detail: The permission check inspects mode bits but does not check the file owner or whether the daemon can actually read the file. A mode-0600 key owned by another user passes configuration loading, then fails only when the first App operation tries to read it. The check also accepts modes such as 0400 and 0700 despite requiring mode 0600.
candidates.suggestion: Verify the file belongs to the running user, is readable, and has the required mode before accepting the configuration.
candidates.failure_scenario: The configured key is a regular mode-0600 file owned by another user. Startup succeeds, but every GitHub operation for an App repository later fails with `cannot read or sign with private key`.

candidates.title: Key validation does not enforce the required mode or ownership
candidates.detail: The mode check accepts owner execute bits, so a key with mode 0700 passes despite the required mode 0600. It also never checks that the file belongs to the process owner, so a mode-0600 file owned by another user can pass startup validation even when the daemon cannot read it. The failure then occurs later during token acquisition instead of at startup.
candidates.suggestion: Validate the required file mode and ownership, and confirm the file is readable during startup.
candidates.failure_scenario: Configure a regular private-key file with mode 0700, or a mode-0600 file owned by another user. Configuration loads instead of refusing with the key-file reason.

candidates.title: Key validation tests omit owner-only executable mode and ownership
candidates.detail: The permission cases cover group and world bits but do not exercise a mode such as 0700 or a file owned by another user. Consequently they pass with the incomplete startup validation and do not catch the underlying key-file defect.
candidates.suggestion: Add a regression case for mode 0700 and a controlled ownership or stat fixture for a key owned by another user, asserting startup refusal.
candidates.failure_scenario: A change that checks only group and world permission bits while ignoring owner execute bits and file ownership passes the current key permission tests.

candidates.title: An App key outside the config directory can be exposed to agents
candidates.detail: The configuration accepts any absolute key path, but the agent read policy automatically denies the config directory, not the configured key file. A key placed in a repository checkout or another agent-readable location can therefore be read by an agent or gate despite the requirement that the key never reach them.
candidates.suggestion: Restrict the key to a protected location or add its canonical path to every agent and gate read-deny policy, including aliases.
candidates.failure_scenario: The operator configures `private_key_path` to a mode-0600 file in a checkout. An agent running as the same user can read that file through its permitted checkout access.

candidates.title: Key validation does not verify the file owner or required mode
candidates.detail: The check accepts any owner-readable file with no group or world permission, including mode 0400 or 0700, and never checks its UID. It therefore does not enforce the requested owner-owned, mode-0600 key file; in particular, a file owned by another account can pass validation where the daemon has elevated access.
candidates.suggestion: Check the file's owner against the daemon's effective UID and enforce the requested permission bits, with a clear startup error.
candidates.failure_scenario: A regular key file owned by a different UID with mode 0600 is readable by an elevated daemon; startup accepts it even though the daemon does not own the file.

candidates.title: Manual landing bypasses the configured App identity
candidates.detail: The request requires “one implementation used by every factory gh invocation for a repository” and says configured repositories use the App without fallback. The manual landing script invokes this checker for its merge, but the checker calls sh directly and never loads or configures the identity provider. Its merge therefore uses the owner's gh login even when the repository is configured for the App; its PR reads and the direct gh calls in land-pr.sh have the same gap.
candidates.suggestion: Load the configured identity in the manual landing path and route its repository-scoped gh calls through the shared provider, including the calls made directly by land-pr.sh.
candidates.failure_scenario: An operator runs scripts/land-pr.sh for an App-configured repository: the PR is merged as the owner, and an App token exchange failure cannot stop that merge.

candidates.title: Startup accepts a key file that the daemon cannot read
candidates.detail: The request says the key must be “a regular file readable only by its owner (mode 0600), or startup refuses.” This check examines permission bits but neither verifies the file's owner nor checks actual readability. A mode-0600 file owned by another user passes configuration validation even though the daemon cannot read it; startup succeeds and GitHub operations fail later. It also accepts owner-executable modes such as 0700 despite the stated mode requirement.
candidates.suggestion: Validate ownership and actual readability at startup, and enforce the requested permission mode.
candidates.failure_scenario: private_key_path points to a regular mode-0600 file owned by another user: loadConfig succeeds, then the first App operation fails while reading the key.

findings.title: Token exchange ignores caller cancellation and timeout
findings.detail: The provider creates its own 30-second timeout and does not accept the caller's abort signal or deadline. A GitHub operation can therefore remain in the shared token exchange after its caller is cancelled, and the initial token request plus the App lookup can each consume 30 seconds before the requested gh command starts.
findings.suggestion: Propagate cancellation and the operation's deadline through identity acquisition, while preserving safe handling of concurrent callers sharing an exchange.
findings.failure_scenario: A run is cancelled while its first installation-token request is stalled. The run continues waiting for the provider's timeout instead of ending promptly.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:2580 passes `ctx.signal` to `findPullRequest`; src/git/repos.ts:1687-1689 calls `githubSh(..., { cwd, signal, timeoutMs: 15_000 })`. However, src/integrations/github-identity.ts:121 first executes `const identity = await githubIdentity(repo)` without passing either option. Its fetch uses only `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(30_000)` (line 26). Caller cancellation is checked later by `sh`: `opts.signal?.throwIfAborted()` (src/util/proc.ts:1178).
verification.trigger: An App-configured repository has no usable cached token, its token exchange stalls, and the run is cancelled during that exchange. The awaiting operation remains blocked until the exchange finishes or its independent 30-second timeout expires; the caller's shorter timeout also does not cover this wait. This requires coincident cancellation and a stalled uncached exchange and causes bounded cancellation delay.

A key at another agent-readable location can therefore be read by an agent or gate running as the same user. The key itself is not registered for output redaction.
candidates.suggestion: Add the resolved key file, including its canonical path and relevant aliases, to the shared read-deny policy used by every agent and gate, or reject paths whose confinement cannot be guaranteed.
candidates.failure_scenario: An operator configures a mode-0600 key at an absolute path inside a checkout. An agent or gate reads that file and can publish the App private key.

candidates.title: Enforce the specified key-file mode and readability at startup
candidates.detail: The mode check accepts owner-executable files such as 0700, and checking the owner-read bit does not establish that the daemon can actually read the file. The request requires a readable mode-0600 file and startup refusal otherwise; an unreadable file currently passes configuration and fails only when an App call is attempted.
candidates.suggestion: Validate the required mode and verify the file can be opened during configuration loading, reporting a clear startup error.
candidates.failure_scenario: A key file has mode 0700, or has mode 0600 but belongs to a different user. Configuration loads even though the required startup validation should refuse it.

candidates.title: Manual landing bypasses the configured App identity
candidates.detail: The request requires “one implementation used by every factory gh invocation for a repository” and says configured repositories use the App. This script invokes gh directly without loading or configuring the identity provider, including for the merge. Consequently manual landing uses the owner's login and can merge even when an App token exchange would fail.
candidates.suggestion: Initialize the configured identity provider in this script and route its repository-scoped gh calls through it.
candidates.failure_scenario: Run scripts/land-pr.sh for an App-configured repository: its private-strings merge step invokes gh with the owner's credentials, so the merge appears owner-authored.

candidates.title: Key validation does not enforce the required mode or readability
candidates.detail: The request says the key must be a regular file with “mode 0600” and that startup refuses otherwise. This check also accepts modes such as 0400 and 0700, and checks the owner-read permission bit without checking whether the process can actually read the file. For example, a 0600 file owned by another user passes startup validation but cannot be read when an App call is attempted.
candidates.suggestion: Enforce the required permission bits and verify that the configured key is readable during startup.
candidates.failure_scenario: Configure a regular private key owned by another user with mode 0600: startup succeeds, but the first App identity request fails to read the key.

candidates.title: Doctor still requires an owner gh login for an App-only configuration
candidates.detail: The request says doctor reports the active identity and whether the App token exchange works. Doctor unconditionally marks gh authentication as failed before checking the App identity, even when every configured repository uses the App and the exchange and installation coverage succeed. This reports a working App-only setup as failed.
candidates.suggestion: Make the gh authentication check reflect whether any configured repository needs the owner's login.
candidates.failure_scenario: With only App-configured repositories and no owner gh login, doctor reports gh authentication failure despite a successful App token exchange and complete repository coverage.

The first configured-repository call reaches `readFileSync(app.privateKeyPath)` at src/integrations/github-identity.ts:64 and reports `cannot read or sign with private key` at line 67.

Verifier: 21 candidates, 21 checked, 4 refuted.

findings.title: Lifecycle transitions can disappear between polls
findings.detail: Comments are derived from the current run status, and an event is persisted only when reconciliation observes that status. A run that enters needs_human and is resumed or resolved before the next poll never records or posts that event. Likewise, a second needs_human episode is suppressed by the first episode's done checkpoint. This does not provide a durable side effect for each transition across restarts or polling intervals.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur, with an identity for each status episode, and reconcile those records independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 calls `await reconcileIssueLifecycle(...)` on each poll. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101–102 adds the event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; line 113 skips it when `!events.has(event) && state(effect) !== "pending"`. No event is recorded before observation. src/db/store.ts:2037–2038 permits a needs_human run to become `resolved`.
verification.trigger: A linked run enters needs_human and is resolved before the next poll (the default interval is 180 seconds). Reconciliation observes resolved and permanently omits the needs-you comment and reason. This confirms the lost-transition defect; owner resolution supplies a concrete path.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates only run for queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Both the reconciler and its timer are conditional on the issue queue's repository and trusted-account configuration. Runs started through CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers in any other configured repository therefore receive no lifecycle labels or comments, even though the requested behavior covers every start path and does not require queue admission to be enabled.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and select linked issues according to the supported repository settings.
findings.failure_scenario: A repository has the GitHub integration configured but is absent from githubQueue.repos; a CLI run with `Closes #42` produces no lifecycle updates.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/index.ts:65–67 starts the queue only when `!!queue?.repos.length && !!queue.trusted.length`. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 is the lifecycle reconciliation call. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10–12 requires trusted queue accounts and membership in `cfg.githubQueue.repos`; line 43 executes `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue`.
verification.trigger: A GitHub-configured repository is absent from githubQueue.repos, or the queue is disabled. A CLI run containing Closes #42 receives no lifecycle labels or comments despite the requirement covering every start path.

findings.title: A partial failure can release an issue before its failure label is applied
findings.detail: The label loop removes in-progress before adding failed. If the add fails, reconciliation logs the failure and queue selection continues in the same poll. The existing latest-run admission check only finds issue-source runs, so it does not protect a failed CLI or MCP run linked through its prompt. The issue can be selected again using its old priority approval before the failed label is retried.
findings.suggestion: Keep admission closed until the failure transition is durably reflected, including for prompt-linked runs; order label writes so a partial transition does not release the issue.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #42` fails; deleting in-progress succeeds but adding failed returns an error. The same poll sees the old priority label and starts a queue run without re-approval.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:13 orders labels as `["limitless:in-progress", "limitless:needs-you", "limitless:failed"]`; lines 68–83 process them in that order, deleting in-progress before adding failed. Lines 93–95 catch a write failure and continue. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191–192 reconciles and then scans candidates. src/db/store.ts:1268 restricts latestIssueRun to `json_extract(runs.source_ref, '$.kind') = 'issue'`, excluding ordinary CLI closures; lines 361–367 exclude failed runs from claim statuses.
verification.trigger: A CLI run linked through Closes #42 fails. Removing in-progress succeeds, adding failed fails, and the issue still has a trusted priority label. The same poll finds neither an active claim nor a latest issue-source run and can enqueue the issue without re-approval.

findings.title: An older run can overwrite a newer run's issue labels
findings.detail: The latest-run map is computed once before any GitHub requests. If another run for the issue is created while a label request is awaiting, the old run remains designated latest and can complete its label transition after the newer run starts. Its completed cursor then prevents correction until the newer run is reconciled on a later poll.
findings.suggestion: Recheck which run owns the issue after awaited operations and before each label mutation and completion checkpoint.
findings.failure_scenario: While reconciliation fetches labels for a failed run, a new run for the same issue starts; the old reconciliation then applies failed and removes in-progress for the active run.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:35–39 builds `latest` once from the initial run snapshot. Line 56 checks that cached map before awaiting the label fetch at line 60. Lines 63–71 re-read only `store.getRun(snapshot.id)` and compare `desiredLabel(run)`, without checking whether a newer linked run now exists. src/db/store.ts:1225 limits claims to active statuses, so a failed old run does not prevent a new run.
verification.trigger: A new linked run is admitted while reconciliation awaits GitHub labels for an older failed run. The cached ownership check remains true, allowing the old run to remove in-progress and apply failed after the new run starts. The interleaving is realistic but requires a narrow concurrent admission window.

findings.title: Persist lifecycle events when they occur, not only when a poll observes them
findings.detail: The needs-human, failure, and cancellation comments are created only when reconciliation observes the corresponding current status. No pending effect exists until the comment loop reaches that event. A status that changes between polls, or while an earlier comment write is failing, is therefore never recorded or retried. The single done cursor also suppresses a second needs-human episode for the same run.
findings.suggestion: Record each lifecycle event and its publication-safe content durably at the state transition, then let polling deliver each recorded event.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next poll; reconciliation sees the resumed status and never posts the required reason. Similarly, a failed started-comment write can delay processing until after needs_human has ended.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:99–103 derives comments from current run fields, including `if (run.status === "needs_human")`. Lines 110–113 process started before needs_human and preserve only already-pending events. Lines 164–166 handle a comment error with `failure(error); break;`, so a failed started comment prevents recording needs_human during that poll. src/db/store.ts:2037–2038 allows needs_human to transition to resolved.
verification.trigger: A linked run leaves needs_human before a poll observes it, or its started-comment write fails while needs_human and the run is resolved before the retry. No durable needs_human event exists, so the required reason is permanently lost. This is the same underlying defect as C1.

findings.title: Reconcile issue-linked runs outside queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle processing is restricted to repositories listed in githubQueue with a nonempty trusted list, and the reconciler is started only when that queue is enabled. The request applies lifecycle updates to issue-linked runs from every start path; it does not condition those updates on queue admission being enabled for the repository.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and determine the target repository from each linked issue.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner starts a run with Closes #12 in a repository not listed in githubQueue, or with the queue disabled. No lifecycle labels or new lifecycle comments are written for that issue.

verification.evidence: src/db/store.ts:356-357 links non-GitHub runs using `closedIssues(run.prompt)`. However, src/integrations/index.ts:66-67 starts reconciliation only when `!!queue?.repos.length && !!queue.trusted.length`; src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:43 additionally skips issues with `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue`, whose definition at lines 10-12 requires membership in `cfg.githubQueue.repos`.
verification.trigger: An owner starts a run containing Closes #12 with the queue disabled or for a repository outside githubQueue.repos. The linked issue receives no lifecycle labels or lifecycle comments.

findings.title: Prevent re-pick while a failed label write is pending
findings.detail: The new re-approval guard depends on the failed label being visible on GitHub. If that write fails, the queue continues selection in the same poll. The existing latestIssueRun lookup only considers issue source references, so it cannot supply a local failure guard for runs linked through a Closes directive.
findings.suggestion: Use the existing admission and claim check to account for the latest linked run and its failure while the GitHub failure-label effect is pending.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with Closes #12 fails, the GitHub failed-label POST fails, and issue #12 still has its previously trusted priority label. latestIssueRun returns no issue-sourced run, so the queue can immediately select the issue again without re-approval.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 reconciles lifecycle effects before selecting issues. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82 posts the failed label, but lines 93-95 catch write errors and continue. src/db/store.ts:1268 restricts latestIssueRun to `json_extract(runs.source_ref, '$.kind') = 'issue'`; lines 361-367 and 1225 restrict claims to active statuses, excluding failed. Consequently, the CLI failure supplies neither guard. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:97 checks re-approval only when GitHub currently has `limitless:failed`; lines 220-225 then admit eligible candidates.
verification.trigger: With the queue enabled and capacity available, a CLI run containing Closes #12 fails. Lifecycle reconciliation removes any in-progress label, but its failed-label POST errors. The issue retains an otherwise eligible trusted priority label, has no earlier issue-sourced run, and is selected again without re-approval during that poll.

findings.title: Authenticate the comment used as a delivery checkpoint
findings.detail: A pending comment is considered delivered when any issue comment contains the predictable marker. The code does not verify the comment author or exact body, although issue comments are untrusted data. A third party can therefore make the reconciler mark a failed write as done without the factory ever posting the required comment.
findings.suggestion: Verify that a matching comment was authored by the configured factory identity and matches the recorded body before marking the effect complete.
findings.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails and leaves its effect pending, another issue participant posts a comment containing the run's lifecycle marker. On the next poll the factory treats that comment as its own and permanently skips the real update.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:159-163 saves `save(effect, "pending")` before the comment POST. On retry, lines 123-129 parse only `{ body: z.string() }` and accept `comments.some((c) => c.body.includes(marker))`, then `save(effect, "done")`, without authenticating the author.
verification.trigger: A comment POST fails before publication, leaving a pending effect. An issue participant posts the predictable lifecycle marker. The next poll permanently completes the checkpoint without publishing the factory's comment. This requires deliberate spoofing combined with a pending write.

findings.title: Lifecycle events can disappear between polls
findings.detail: The reconciler derives needs-human and failure comments only from the current run status. If a run enters one of those states and is resolved or restarted before the next poll, no pending effect was recorded, so that event is never published. The pending-comment tests cover a status change only after a poll has already attempted the comment; they do not cover a transition entirely between polls.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when the transitions occur, and add a test that enters needs_human or failed and leaves it before reconciliation runs.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resolves it before the next queue poll. The issue receives no needs-you comment or label for that event.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:295 schedules subsequent polls using `now() + q.pollSeconds * 1000`. src/db/store.ts:2037-2038 permits needs_human to become `status: "resolved"`. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101-102 creates the needs_human event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; line 113 skips absent events unless their effect is already pending. Labels likewise derive from current status at lines 15-25.
verification.trigger: A managed run enters needs_human and the owner resolves it through the UI before the next poll. No needs_human effect was recorded, so reconciliation never publishes its comment or applies its needs-you label.

findings.title: Restart-between-effects coverage exercises only the start event
findings.detail: The restart test interrupts the initial in-progress label and started comment. The table-driven terminal-state tests restart only after both writes have completed, and the PR and merge tests likewise do not interrupt their transitions. Consequently, regressions in recovery between a needs-you, failed, cancellation, or merge label change and its associated comment are not covered as requested.
findings.suggestion: Exercise interruption during each applicable lifecycle transition, then restart and assert the final label set and exactly one corresponding comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change loses a failed comment after the failed label is written and the daemon restarts; the existing restart test still passes because it covers only the started event.

verification.evidence: test/issue-queue.test.ts:1275 parameterizes interruption only by `["after label", "after comment"]`; lines 1295–1298 assert `"limitless:in-progress"` and `"comment:started"`. The failed-event restart cases at lines 1333–1347 instead reach `comment:${status} === "pending"` before restarting at lines 1349–1350. They do not interrupt between writing the failed label and recording the failed comment.
verification.trigger: A regression affecting recovery after the failed label is written but before the failed comment is checkpointed could escape these tests: that interruption window is exercised only for the started event. This confirms a coverage gap, not a demonstrated production failure.

findings.title: Encoded credentials can reach public issue comments
findings.detail: The comment body is passed directly to literal credential redaction. The private-string check detects encoded private-string entries, but registered credentials are not necessarily entries in that list. A credential encoded in a run error can therefore be published in a form a reader can decode.
findings.suggestion: Decode supported representations before credential redaction, or reject comment text containing encoded registered credentials before publication.
findings.failure_scenario: A failed run's error contains a percent-encoded registered token that is absent from private-strings.txt; the posted failure comment contains the encoded token.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:103 includes `run.error` in the failure comment, and lines 134-137 pass it directly to `redactCredentials` without decoding. src/util/proc.ts:1233-1236 registers only the literal credential, its CRLF-normalized spelling and JSON-escaped variants. The publication check at issue-lifecycle.ts:140-148 checks private-string entries; line 163 posts the resulting body.
verification.trigger: A non-discreet managed run fails with a percent-encoded registered credential in run.error, with encoding that changes its literal spelling and no matching private-string entry. Literal credential redaction misses it and the public failure comment exposes the encoded credential.

findings.title: An unrelated comment can satisfy a pending publication checkpoint
findings.detail: Retry reconciliation trusts a marker found in any issue comment without checking its author or body. Issue comments are untrusted input, so a commenter who knows a run ID can make the factory record an effect as completed even though the factory never posted it.
findings.suggestion: Verify the comment belongs to the expected GitHub identity and matches the saved publication body before marking the effect done.
findings.failure_scenario: A user posts the predictable failed-event marker, and the factory's subsequent comment POST fails before reaching GitHub. On the next poll, the user's marker causes the pending failure comment to be marked done.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:120 constructs `<!-- limitless-lifecycle:${run.id}:${event} -->`. Lines 159-163 persist a pending checkpoint before POST. On the subsequent poll, lines 123-129 inspect only comment bodies and mark the effect done when any body contains the marker.
verification.trigger: A participant posts the predictable failed-event marker before publication. The factory's initial failure-comment POST fails before reaching GitHub. On retry, the participant's unrelated comment satisfies the checkpoint and suppresses the real failure comment. This requires deliberate spoofing and a failed write.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to configured queue repositories
findings.detail: The lifecycle reconciler skips repositories outside githubQueue.repos, and it is not started when the issue queue is disabled. The request requires updates for runs started through CLI, MCP, label, and comment paths as well as the queue; those paths can target repositories that are not configured for automatic issue selection.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and cover all repositories for which linked runs can be created.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #123` targets a configured repository outside githubQueue.repos; it receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

verification.evidence: src/db/store.ts:356-357 links non-GitHub runs through `closedIssues(run.prompt)` using `run.repoSlug`. However, src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10-12 requires `cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`, and :43 executes `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;` before any writes.
verification.trigger: A CLI run includes `Closes #123` in a configured repository outside githubQueue.repos. The reconciler skips its issue, posting neither lifecycle labels nor comments.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to queue-configured repositories
findings.detail: The request covers “any start path: queue, `limitless run` with `Closes #n`, MCP, label or comment trigger.” Reconciliation skips repositories outside `githubQueue.repos`, and the reconciler is not started at all when the queue is disabled. Consequently, runs started through those other paths receive no lifecycle labels or the required comments unless their repository also happens to be configured for the issue queue.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and apply it to linked issues from all supported start paths.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #7` starts in a repository with no issue-queue configuration; no in-progress label or start comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/index.ts:65-67 starts the reconciler's queue only when `!!queue?.repos.length && !!queue.trusted.length`. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:144 also returns immediately without that configuration; :191 is the call to `reconcileIssueLifecycle`. src/config.ts:419 defaults githubQueue to `null`.
verification.trigger: A CLI run includes `Closes #7` with no issue-queue configuration. No lifecycle reconciliation runs, so no in-progress label or start comment is posted.

findings.title: Transient lifecycle events are lost between polls
findings.detail: The request requires each label change and comment to be a recorded side effect with a durable checkpoint. Here needs-human, failed, and cancelled events are discovered only from the current status. If a run enters and leaves one of those states before a poll observes it, no effect is recorded and its comment is permanently lost. The initial in-progress label can likewise be skipped if the run reaches a later state before its first poll.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when the corresponding transitions occur, then reconcile each recorded effect independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll; the reconciler never posts the needs-you reason or applies its label.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101-102 creates the needs-human event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; :113 skips absent events unless their checkpoint is already pending. src/db/store.ts:2037-2038 permits needs_human to become `resolved`. src/integrations/github-notifier.ts:219-221 performs that transition when its PR closes. Polls are separated by `q.pollSeconds * 1000` (src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:295).
verification.trigger: A managed run reaches needs_human and is resolved, for example after its PR closes, before the next lifecycle poll. No pending event exists, so the needs-you label and reason are lost. The demonstrated exit is resolution rather than same-run resumption.

findings.title: A failed label write can allow a failed CLI issue to be picked
findings.detail: A lifecycle write failure is caught and queue selection continues, but `latestIssueRun` only finds runs with an issue source reference. A failed CLI or MCP run linked through `Closes #n` has no such reference. Until the failed label is successfully written, the queue therefore sees neither the failure label nor that latest failed run and can select the issue without re-approval.
findings.suggestion: Include all linked-issue runs in the existing eligibility/admission evidence, including runs linked through their prompt.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run for `Closes #7` fails, the GitHub failed-label write errors, and the issue still has its previously approved priority label; the same poll can create a queue run for it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 awaits lifecycle reconciliation and then continues selection. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82 writes the label; lines 93-95 log failures without stopping selection. src/db/store.ts:1268-1272 makes latestIssueRun consider only issue source references, excluding a plain CLI Closes directive; lines 361-367 and 1225 exclude failed runs from claims. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:97 gates failure re-approval on the GitHub label being present, and lines 253-256 repeat eligibility without checking pending lifecycle effects.
verification.trigger: An otherwise eligible issue #7 has an old trusted priority label and no issue-sourced run. Its CLI Closes #7 run fails; removal of in-progress succeeds, but adding failed errors. With capacity available, the same poll can create a queue run without renewed approval.

findings.title: Re-approval in the same timestamp second is rejected
findings.detail: The requirement specifies the labeled events' order and actor. Comparing parsed timestamps with strict greater-than rejects a trusted priority event that follows the failure event but has the same timestamp precision, even though the timeline preserves their order.
findings.suggestion: Use the ordered timeline events to determine whether a trusted priority application follows the failure event, including ties in timestamps.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub records the failure label and a subsequent trusted priority label with the same second in `createdAt`; the issue remains ineligible.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:64-68 computes `failedAt` using `Math.max(...Date.parse(e.createdAt))`. Lines 97-101 reject a failed issue unless `events.some((e) => trusts(e.actor?.login) && Date.parse(e.createdAt) > failedAt)`. Thus equal timestamps are rejected regardless of timeline order. The poll invokes this policy at lines 220-225 and only adds eligible issues to candidates: `if (result.eligible) candidates.push(...)`.
verification.trigger: With the issue queue enabled, an otherwise eligible failed issue receives a trusted priority label after the failure label, but both GitHub events have the same second-resolution timestamp. The strict timestamp comparison rejects re-approval on every poll until another priority application occurs. This requires unusually fast re-approval, so the timing trigger is uncommon.

candidates.title: Lifecycle transitions can disappear between polls
candidates.detail: Comments are derived from the current run status, and an event is persisted only when reconciliation observes that status. A run that enters needs_human and is resumed or resolved before the next poll never records or posts that event. Likewise, a second needs_human episode is suppressed by the first episode's done checkpoint. This does not provide a durable side effect for each transition across restarts or polling intervals.
candidates.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur, with an identity for each status episode, and reconcile those records independently of the current status.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates only run for queue-enabled repositories
candidates.detail: Both the reconciler and its timer are conditional on the issue queue's repository and trusted-account configuration. Runs started through CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers in any other configured repository therefore receive no lifecycle labels or comments, even though the requested behavior covers every start path and does not require queue admission to be enabled.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and select linked issues according to the supported repository settings.
candidates.failure_scenario: A repository has the GitHub integration configured but is absent from githubQueue.repos; a CLI run with `Closes #42` produces no lifecycle updates.

candidates.title: A partial failure can release an issue before its failure label is applied
candidates.detail: The label loop removes in-progress before adding failed. If the add fails, reconciliation logs the failure and queue selection continues in the same poll. The existing latest-run admission check only finds issue-source runs, so it does not protect a failed CLI or MCP run linked through its prompt. The issue can be selected again using its old priority approval before the failed label is retried.
candidates.suggestion: Keep admission closed until the failure transition is durably reflected, including for prompt-linked runs; order label writes so a partial transition does not release the issue.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #42` fails; deleting in-progress succeeds but adding failed returns an error. The same poll sees the old priority label and starts a queue run without re-approval.

candidates.title: A removed priority label can satisfy failure re-approval
candidates.detail: The re-approval check accepts any trusted priority labeled event after failure, without requiring that event to correspond to a currently applied approved priority label. An old, still-present priority label can therefore supply the queue priority while a different, subsequently removed label supplies the purported re-approval.
candidates.suggestion: Require a currently applied trusted priority label whose latest application occurred after the failure event.
candidates.failure_scenario: priority:1 was applied before failure; after failure a trusted user applies and removes priority:9. The issue remains failed with priority:1, but becomes eligible.

candidates.title: An older run can overwrite a newer run's issue labels
candidates.detail: The latest-run map is computed once before any GitHub requests. If another run for the issue is created while a label request is awaiting, the old run remains designated latest and can complete its label transition after the newer run starts. Its completed cursor then prevents correction until the newer run is reconciled on a later poll.
candidates.suggestion: Recheck which run owns the issue after awaited operations and before each label mutation and completion checkpoint.
candidates.failure_scenario: While reconciliation fetches labels for a failed run, a new run for the same issue starts; the old reconciliation then applies failed and removes in-progress for the active run.

candidates.title: Persist lifecycle events when they occur, not only when a poll observes them
candidates.detail: The needs-human, failure, and cancellation comments are created only when reconciliation observes the corresponding current status. No pending effect exists until the comment loop reaches that event. A status that changes between polls, or while an earlier comment write is failing, is therefore never recorded or retried. The single done cursor also suppresses a second needs-human episode for the same run.
candidates.suggestion: Record each lifecycle event and its publication-safe content durably at the state transition, then let polling deliver each recorded event.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next poll; reconciliation sees the resumed status and never posts the required reason. Similarly, a failed started-comment write can delay processing until after needs_human has ended.

candidates.title: Reconcile issue-linked runs outside queue-enabled repositories
candidates.detail: Lifecycle processing is restricted to repositories listed in githubQueue with a nonempty trusted list, and the reconciler is started only when that queue is enabled. The request applies lifecycle updates to issue-linked runs from every start path; it does not condition those updates on queue admission being enabled for the repository.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and determine the target repository from each linked issue.
candidates.failure_scenario: An owner starts a run with Closes #12 in a repository not listed in githubQueue, or with the queue disabled. No lifecycle labels or new lifecycle comments are written for that issue.

candidates.title: Prevent re-pick while a failed label write is pending
candidates.detail: The new re-approval guard depends on the failed label being visible on GitHub. If that write fails, the queue continues selection in the same poll. The existing latestIssueRun lookup only considers issue source references, so it cannot supply a local failure guard for runs linked through a Closes directive.
candidates.suggestion: Use the existing admission and claim check to account for the latest linked run and its failure while the GitHub failure-label effect is pending.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run with Closes #12 fails, the GitHub failed-label POST fails, and issue #12 still has its previously trusted priority label. latestIssueRun returns no issue-sourced run, so the queue can immediately select the issue again without re-approval.

candidates.title: Authenticate the comment used as a delivery checkpoint
candidates.detail: A pending comment is considered delivered when any issue comment contains the predictable marker. The code does not verify the comment author or exact body, although issue comments are untrusted data. A third party can therefore make the reconciler mark a failed write as done without the factory ever posting the required comment.
candidates.suggestion: Verify that a matching comment was authored by the configured factory identity and matches the recorded body before marking the effect complete.
candidates.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails and leaves its effect pending, another issue participant posts a comment containing the run's lifecycle marker. On the next poll the factory treats that comment as its own and permanently skips the real update.

candidates.title: Lifecycle events can disappear between polls
candidates.detail: The reconciler derives needs-human and failure comments only from the current run status. If a run enters one of those states and is resolved or restarted before the next poll, no pending effect was recorded, so that event is never published. The pending-comment tests cover a status change only after a poll has already attempted the comment; they do not cover a transition entirely between polls.
candidates.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when the transitions occur, and add a test that enters needs_human or failed and leaves it before reconciliation runs.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resolves it before the next queue poll. The issue receives no needs-you comment or label for that event.

candidates.title: A removed priority label can satisfy re-approval
candidates.detail: The post-failure check accepts any trusted priority-label application in the timeline, even when that label is no longer present. An older, still-present priority label can separately satisfy the approved-label check, allowing a repick after the post-failure approval was removed. The new tests only use a post-failure event for a priority label that remains on the issue.
candidates.suggestion: Require the qualifying post-failure application to correspond to a currently applied, trusted priority label, and test removal of that label while an older priority label remains.
candidates.failure_scenario: An issue retains priority:1 from before failure. After failure, a trusted user applies priority:2 and then removes it; the issue is still eligible even though its remaining priority label was not re-applied after failure.

candidates.title: Restart-between-effects coverage exercises only the start event
candidates.detail: The restart test interrupts the initial in-progress label and started comment. The table-driven terminal-state tests restart only after both writes have completed, and the PR and merge tests likewise do not interrupt their transitions. Consequently, regressions in recovery between a needs-you, failed, cancellation, or merge label change and its associated comment are not covered as requested.
candidates.suggestion: Exercise interruption during each applicable lifecycle transition, then restart and assert the final label set and exactly one corresponding comment.
candidates.failure_scenario: A future change loses a failed comment after the failed label is written and the daemon restarts; the existing restart test still passes because it covers only the started event.

candidates.title: Encoded credentials can reach public issue comments
candidates.detail: The comment body is passed directly to literal credential redaction. The private-string check detects encoded private-string entries, but registered credentials are not necessarily entries in that list. A credential encoded in a run error can therefore be published in a form a reader can decode.
candidates.suggestion: Decode supported representations before credential redaction, or reject comment text containing encoded registered credentials before publication.
candidates.failure_scenario: A failed run's error contains a percent-encoded registered token that is absent from private-strings.txt; the posted failure comment contains the encoded token.

candidates.title: An unrelated comment can satisfy a pending publication checkpoint
candidates.detail: Retry reconciliation trusts a marker found in any issue comment without checking its author or body. Issue comments are untrusted input, so a commenter who knows a run ID can make the factory record an effect as completed even though the factory never posted it.
candidates.suggestion: Verify the comment belongs to the expected GitHub identity and matches the saved publication body before marking the effect done.
candidates.failure_scenario: A user posts the predictable failed-event marker, and the factory's subsequent comment POST fails before reaching GitHub. On the next poll, the user's marker causes the pending failure comment to be marked done.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to configured queue repositories
candidates.detail: The lifecycle reconciler skips repositories outside githubQueue.repos, and it is not started when the issue queue is disabled. The request requires updates for runs started through CLI, MCP, label, and comment paths as well as the queue; those paths can target repositories that are not configured for automatic issue selection.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and cover all repositories for which linked runs can be created.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #123` targets a configured repository outside githubQueue.repos; it receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

candidates.title: A removed priority label can satisfy re-approval
candidates.detail: The post-failure check accepts any historical trusted priority application, even when that label is no longer present. The separate approved-label check can be satisfied by a different priority label that predates the failure, so the two checks together do not establish that a current priority label was re-applied after failure.
candidates.suggestion: Require the post-failure event to be the latest trusted application of a currently present approved priority label.
candidates.failure_scenario: An issue retains priority:2 from before failure. A trusted user applies and then removes priority:1 after failure; the historical priority:1 event permits the issue to be picked using the stale priority:2 label.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to queue-configured repositories

Consequently, runs started through those other paths receive no lifecycle labels or the required comments unless their repository also happens to be configured for the issue queue.

findings.title: Status transitions between polls are lost
findings.detail: Comments and labels are derived only from the run's current status. No durable event is recorded when a run enters needs_human or failed, so a transition that ends before the next poll cannot be reconstructed. The single comment key for each status also suppresses later occurrences of the same status.

findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll. The poll sees running and never posts the needs-you comment or applies its label. A second needs_human episode after an observed first episode also receives no new comment.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 calls `await reconcileIssueLifecycle(...)` from the poll; :295 schedules the next poll with `now() + q.pollSeconds * 1000`. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101-102 creates the event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; :112-114 uses `const effect = `comment:${event}`` and skips it when `state(effect) === "done"`. findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run for `Closes #7` fails. Removing in-progress succeeds, adding failed fails, and the issue still has its old trusted priority label. The same poll can pick it again without a new approval.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:13 orders labels as in-progress, needs-you, failed; :68-86 removes unwanted labels before adding failed and catches a failed addition at :93-95. findings.title: An older run can overwrite labels after a newer run starts
findings.detail: The latest-run map is computed once before any GitHub awaits. Re-reading the old run's status does not check whether another run has since claimed the same issue, so an in-flight reconciliation can apply an old terminal label after a newer run has started.
findings.suggestion: Recheck issue ownership after awaited operations and before each label mutation, coordinating it with run admission.
findings.failure_scenario: While reconciliation of an old failed run is awaiting its label read, a new run for the same issue starts. The old reconciliation then removes in-progress or adds failed based on its stale latest-run map.

verification.trigger: A new manual run for the same issue is created while reconciliation of an old failed run awaits GitHub. The old run remains failed, passes the subsequent checks, and can remove in-progress or add failed despite the newer active run.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside queue-enabled repositories

findings.title: Transient lifecycle events disappear before they are checkpointed
findings.detail: Events are inferred only from the current run snapshot. A needs_human or failed state that begins and ends between polls is never recorded. The same loss occurs when an earlier comment fails: the loop breaks before saving later events as pending, so a status change before the next poll erases them.
findings.suggestion: Durably record each lifecycle transition when it occurs, then reconcile its effects independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human while the started comment write is failing, then is resumed before the next poll. No needs-you comment is ever posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 calls `await reconcileIssueLifecycle(...)` during polling. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101–102 adds needs_human only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; :110 processes `"started"` first; :165–167 handles its failure with `failure(error); break;`. The needs_human checkpoint is therefore never reached. At :113, an absent event survives only if `state(effect) === "pending"`. src/db/store.ts:2037–2038 permits needs_human to become resolved.
verification.trigger: In an enabled, non-discreet queue repository, the started comment fails while the run needs human input. The owner resolves the run before the next successful poll. Only started is pending, so the needs-you comment and its reason disappear permanently.

findings.title: A second needs-human episode is treated as already delivered
findings.detail: Comment checkpoints are keyed only by run and event name. Once a needs_human comment is marked done, a resumed run that later reaches needs_human again cannot post its new reason. Label reconciliation can still switch back to needs-you, leaving the issue with a stale explanation.
findings.suggestion: Key lifecycle effects by a durable transition or status episode rather than only by event type.
findings.failure_scenario: A run needs human input, resumes after the owner responds, and later needs human input for a different reason. The second reason is never commented.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:112 uses the fixed key `const effect = `comment:${event}``, and :114 skips it forever when `state(effect) === "done"`; :120 likewise uses a marker containing only run id and event. This cannot distinguish episodes. However, src/app.ts:431–434 implements normal retry through `return this.createRun(...)`, giving the retry separate lifecycle checkpoints; src/app.ts:458–463 merely records question answers. A normal same-run resume from needs_human was not established.
verification.trigger: If the same run enters needs_human again after an earlier delivered episode, its second reason is skipped by the existing done checkpoint. The checkpoint defect is clear, but the candidate's ordinary owner-answer/resume path is not proven.

findings.title: Re-approval can come from a priority label that is no longer applied
findings.detail: The post-failure check accepts any trusted priority labeled event, even if that label was subsequently removed. The separate approved check can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before the failure, so the current approval need not be the one applied after failure.
findings.suggestion: Require a currently applied, trusted priority label whose latest application occurred after the failure label.
findings.failure_scenario: Priority:2 was applied before failure; a trusted user applies and removes priority:1 after failure. The issue remains eligible using the old priority:2 label despite the later approval having been withdrawn.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:74–81 derives `approved` from current labels, but :99 independently accepts `events.some((e) => trusts(e.actor?.login) && Date.parse(e.createdAt) > failedAt)`, without checking that event's label remains applied. The query at :129 requests only `LABELED_EVENT, RENAMED_TITLE_EVENT`, so removal cannot revoke this evidence. The poller calls this policy at :220 and :253 before `factory.createRun(...)` at :287.
verification.trigger: With the queue enabled, an otherwise eligible failed issue retains trusted priority:2 from before failure. A trusted user applies then removes priority:1 after failure and the previous run finished. The historical event passes both re-approval checks, causing another run despite withdrawn approval. Runtime verification was blocked by the missing entities dependency; the code path establishes the behavior.

findings.title: An unrelated comment can impersonate a completed lifecycle write
findings.detail: Recovery treats any issue comment containing the predictable marker as proof that the factory posted its pending comment, without checking its author. An issue participant can supply that marker and cause the actual lifecycle comment to be permanently marked done.
findings.suggestion: Verify the recovered comment was authored by the configured factory identity and matches the pending body before marking the effect done.
findings.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails, another issue participant posts a comment containing the run's marker. On the next poll the factory records the failed comment as delivered and never retries it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:159–163 saves the comment as `"pending"` before POST. On retry, :122–128 parses comments as `z.object({ body: z.string() })` and accepts `comments.some((c) => c.body.includes(marker))`; :129 then executes `save(effect, "done")`. No author or original-body check is performed. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 invokes this reconciliation on polls.
verification.trigger: After a lifecycle POST fails without creating its comment, another participant posts the predictable lifecycle marker before retry. The next poll treats that unrelated comment as successful delivery and permanently suppresses the intended notification.

findings.title: A 404 during label removal is silently recorded as success
findings.detail: The catch treats every HTTP 404 as an already-removed label. GitHub can also return 404 for an inaccessible repository or issue, so a permission or installation failure can be checkpointed as a successful label transition and will not be retried.
findings.suggestion: Confirm the label is absent with a successful fresh read before recording the removal as complete; otherwise log and retry the error.
findings.failure_scenario: The initial label read succeeds, but the App loses repository access before the DELETE. GitHub returns 404 and the reconciliation cursor records the label set as complete even though the label remains.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:58–62 reads current labels, then :80–86 performs DELETE and suppresses any error matching `HTTP 404`: `if (add || !/\bHTTP 404\b/.test(String(error))) throw error;`. It subsequently records `save(effect, "done")` (:88) and `save("labels", target)` (:92). At :56, that completed cursor prevents another reconciliation when the desired status remains unchanged.
verification.trigger: For a removal-only transition, such as cancellation or merge, the initial label GET succeeds but repository access disappears before DELETE. A permission-masking 404 is treated as successful removal, leaving in-progress present with a completed cursor and no retry when access returns.

findings.title: Status transitions between polls never produce their comments
findings.detail: Lifecycle comments are derived from the current run status. A needs_human episode that begins and ends between polls is never recorded as pending, so its required comment is permanently lost. The pending-comment tests cover a transition only after a poll has already observed it.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur and reconcile those records. Add a test that enters and leaves needs_human between polls, then restarts and checks for exactly one comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next issue-queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted.

findings.title: A removed priority label can supply re-approval
findings.detail: The re-approval check accepts any trusted priority-label event after failure, even if that label is no longer present. The separate approved-label check can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before failure. The tests only exercise re-approval using the currently present label and miss this combination.
findings.suggestion: Require a currently applied, trusted priority label whose applicable labeling event is later than the failure event. Add a test with an old current priority and a later trusted priority that has since been removed.
findings.failure_scenario: priority:1 remains from before failure; a trusted user adds and then removes priority:2 after failure. The issue becomes eligible despite having no current priority approval applied after failure.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:74–81 accepts the retained current priority:1 independently of the failure check. findings.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside the issue queue configuration
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation requires the repository to be in githubQueue.repos with trusted accounts configured, and the poller does not start without that configuration. The request requires updates for linked runs from all start paths. The new test explicitly asserts no updates for disabled or unlisted repositories, thereby protecting this omission.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation for linked GitHub issues independently of queue admission configuration, and test a CLI or MCP run when queue polling is disabled.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner starts a run with Closes #7 in a GitHub repository that is not enabled for automatic issue picking; the issue receives neither labels nor comments.

findings.title: Restart coverage does not exercise each lifecycle transition
findings.detail: The interruption matrix only interrupts the initial started event. The needs-human, failure, cancellation, PR, and merge tests restart after their writes have completed, so they do not establish that a restart between each transition's label change and comment preserves the required effect.
findings.suggestion: Exercise interruption after the label update and before the comment for each applicable transition, then reopen the store and verify the final labels and exactly one comment.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression that loses a failed or needs-human comment after its label write can pass the current restart tests.

verification.evidence: test/issue-queue.test.ts:1275 parameterizes only interruption point: `test.each(["after label", "after comment"])`; its assertions specifically check `"limitless:in-progress"` and `"comment:started"` (1295–1298). Other lifecycle cases finish their comments before restarting: `expect(h.comments.get(7)).toHaveLength(2)` (1225), then `h.stop()` (1228). The failed/needs_human interruption cases instead require an already persisted comment checkpoint: `expect(...`comment:${status}`)).toBe("pending")` (1347), before restarting (1349–1350). Thus neither covers stopping those transitions between the label write and comment checkpoint.
verification.trigger: A regression affecting recovery of failed or needs_human transitions interrupted after their label write but before their comment becomes pending could pass these tests: the matching interruption test covers only run start, while terminal-status restart tests begin after comment completion or checkpoint creation.

findings.title: Do not accept an arbitrary issue comment as proof of a factory write
findings.detail: Recovery treats any comment containing the predictable lifecycle marker as proof that the factory posted its comment. Issue comments are untrusted: their author is neither retrieved nor checked. An attacker who can comment can therefore suppress a pending lifecycle notification.
findings.suggestion: Authenticate the author of a matching comment against the GitHub identity used for the write, and require an exact, validated marker before recording the effect as done.
findings.failure_scenario: A comment POST fails or the daemon restarts after marking it pending. Another issue participant posts a comment containing `<!-- limitless-lifecycle:<run-id>:failed -->`. On the next poll, reconciliation marks the failed notification done without posting it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:159-163 saves `comment:<event>` as `pending` before awaiting the POST. On retry, lines 122-128 parse comments using only `z.object({ body: z.string() })` and accept `comments.some((c) => c.body.includes(marker))`; lines 129-130 then `save(effect, "done"); continue;`. No author or identity check protects this reconciliation.
verification.trigger: A comment POST fails before acceptance, leaving its checkpoint pending. An issue participant posts the predictable lifecycle marker before a later poll. Reconciliation accepts that participant's comment as the factory notification and permanently skips the intended comment.

findings.title: Tie re-approval to a priority label that is still applied
findings.detail: The post-failure check accepts any historical trusted priority-label event, even if that label has since been removed. The separately computed `approved` set can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before the failure, so a withdrawn re-approval still permits the issue to run.
findings.suggestion: Require the latest trusted application of a currently applied priority label to be later than the failure event.
findings.failure_scenario: An issue retains `priority:2` from before failure. A trusted account applies `priority:1` after failure and subsequently removes it to withdraw approval. The old `priority:2` satisfies `approved`, while the historical `priority:1` event satisfies this check, so the failed issue is picked again.

findings.detail: The request covers “any start path,” but reconciliation skips every repository outside `githubQueue.repos`, and the reconciler is not started at all when the queue is disabled.
